## Dīgha Nikāya
## Commentary on the Mahāvagga
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta
## Discourse Related to Past Lives

The Mahāpadāna Sutta, beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard), was preached at the Kareri Monastery. In this sutta, the following is the explanation of the terms not yet clarified. Regarding "Karerikuṭikāyaṃ": Kareri is the name of the Varuṇa tree. Because a Kareri pavilion stood at the door of that monastery, it is called the "Kareri Monastery." This is similar to how a monastery is called the "Kosamba Monastery" because it stands at the door of a Kosamba tree.

It is said that within the Jetavana Monastery complex, there are four great dwellings: the Kareri Monastery, the Kosamba Monastery, the Gandhakuṭi, and the Salaḷāgāra Monastery. Each was built at a cost of one hundred thousand pieces of currency. Among these, King Pasenadi of Kosala built the Salaḷāgāra Monastery, while the others were built by the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. Thus, the Blessed One resided in the Kareri Monastery, which was built by the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika upon pillars, resembling a celestial mansion.

"Pacchābhattaṃ" (after the meal) means: for monks who eat only one meal a day, even if it is within the noon period after eating in the morning, it is still considered after the meal. However, in this context, it refers to the time after the meal in the ordinary sense. "Piṇḍapātapaṭikkantānaṃ" means those who have returned from the alms-round, having finished the business of eating and having risen from their seats.

"Karerimaṇḍalamāḷe" refers to a sitting hall (sālā) constructed not far from that Kareri pavilion. That Kareri pavilion is situated between the Gandhakuṭi and the hall...
2:
It is situated between the two (the Gandhakuṭī and the Karerikuṭi); therefore, the Gandhakuṭī, the Karerikuṭi, and the hall are collectively called the "Karerimaṇḍalamāḷa." "Pubbenivāsapaṭisaṃyutta" refers to a discourse arising in connection with past lives (pubbenivāsa), which is defined as the continuity of aggregates (khandha) that lived in the past, distinguished as "one birth, two births," and so on. "Dhammī" means a talk associated with the Dhamma.

"Arose" means that the reflection arose: "How wonderful indeed! How marvelous is the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) of the Blessed One, the Dasabala! Who can remember past lives? Who cannot remember them?" Tirthikas (titthiyas) can remember them; disciples (sāvakas), Paccekabuddhas, and the Blessed Buddhas can also remember them. Which Tirthikas can remember? Those Tirthikas who are kammavādīs (believers in action) who have reached the peak of their practice can remember; even they can only remember forty aeons (kappas), and cannot remember beyond that. Disciples can remember one hundred thousand aeons. The two Chief Disciples can remember one incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) and one hundred thousand aeons. Paccekabuddhas can remember two incalculables and one hundred thousand aeons. For the Blessed Buddhas, however, there is no such limit; they can remember as far back as they desire.

Tirthikas can only remember following the succession of aggregates; they cannot remember by skipping the succession. Even when remembering in succession, when they reach the realm of non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), they cannot see the arising and passing away of aggregates; they become like a red ant fallen into a net, or like a person with weak legs fallen into a pit. They stop at that realm of non-percipient beings and hold the wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) that "there is only this much, there is nothing beyond this." Thus, the Tirthikas' recollection of past lives is like a blind man walking by relying on the tip of a staff. Just as blind people can only walk if there is someone holding the tip of the staff, and must sit in that very place if there is no one, so too the Tirthikas can only remember following the succession of aggregates and cannot remember if they leave the succession.

Disciples also can only remember following the succession of aggregates; when they reach the realm of non-percipient beings, they cannot see the arising and passing away of aggregates. Nevertheless, for those disciples, there is no period when there are no aggregates of beings wandering in saṃsāra. In the realm of non-percipient beings, they exist for five hundred aeons; having bypassed that much time and relying on the method granted by the Buddhas, they can continue to remember other births beyond that, like the Elder Sobhita. The two Chief Disciples and the Paccekabuddhas can remember by reflecting on death (cuti) and rebirth (paṭisandhi). For the Blessed Buddhas, however, there is no need to look at death and rebirth; whatever place they wish to see, they see that very place.
3:
When the Tirthikas (titthiyas) recollect past lives, they can only remember what they themselves have seen, done, or heard. The disciples and Paccekabuddhas are the same. The Buddhas, however, can remember everything that has been seen, done, or heard, whether by themselves or by others.

The knowledge of past lives of the Tirthikas is like the light of a firefly. The knowledge of the disciples is like the light of a lamp. The knowledge of the Chief Disciples is like the light of the morning star (Sodhitārā). The knowledge of the Paccekabuddhas is like the light of the moon. The knowledge of the Blessed Buddhas is like the light of the autumn sun. For the Blessed Buddha, there is no limit such as this many hundreds of births, thousands of births, or hundreds of thousands of births; or this many hundreds of aeons, thousands of aeons, or hundreds of thousands of aeons. When he recollects anything, there is no error and no obstruction. It is connected only with reflection, and with the arising of the mind that attends to it as desired. It goes without snagging, like an arrow shot with force through a bundle of weak leaves, or like the thunderbolt (vajira) weapon of Sakka, the King of Devas, released from the top of Mount Meru. Thus, the talk arose, came to be, and spread concerning the Buddha: "How wonderful and great is the knowledge of past lives of the Blessed One!" To show all of this in brief, the Pali text says only this much: "In this way past lives, in that way past lives." In this context, "iti pi" means "in this way also."

2-3. The talk mentioned here in "Assosi kho... pe... atha Bhagavā anuppatto" is exactly as stated in the commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta. There is only this difference: there, he heard with omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa); here, he heard with the divine ear (dibba-sota). There, he heard before the talk concerning praise and dispraise was finished; here, it is the talk concerning past lives. Therefore, the Blessed One thought, "These monks are praising the virtues of my knowledge of past lives, but they do not know the root cause of the completion of my knowledge of past lives; I shall tell them the completion of that knowledge," and so he arrived. He sat on the noble Buddha-seat, which is always prepared for the preaching of the Dhamma by the Buddhas and was dusted off by the monks at that moment, and asked, "Monks, for what talk are you gathered here now?" At the end of the reply beginning with "Venerable Sir, in this place...", wishing to preach the Dhamma discourse related to past lives to them, he said, "Do you desire..." and so on. In that context, "iccheyyātha no" means "do you desire?" Then the monks, being joyful, requested him, saying, "It is the right time for the Blessed One to preach this Dhamma discourse," and so on. In that context, "etassa" means "of the preaching of this Dhamma discourse."
4:
Then the Blessed One, accepting their request and wishing to preach, urged those monks to listen and attend well, saying, "Monks, if that is so, listen." Wishing to show the recollection that is not shared with others and which cuts off the path of the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra), he said, "Monks, from this aeon..." and so on. In that context, "yaṃ Vipassī" means "in which aeon the Buddha Vipassī." This word "yaṃ" is found in the sense of the nominative case (paṭhamā-vibhatti) in passages such as "Venerable Sir, I shall report to the Blessed One the words heard and received from those Tāvatiṃsa devas." It is found in the sense of the accusative case (dutiyā-vibhatti) in passages such as "That matter which we have asked, you have answered for us; we shall ask another matter, please speak on that also." It is found in the sense of the instrumental case (tatiyā-vibhatti) in passages such as "Monks, that cause in a single world-system... is an impossible cause." In this context, however, it should be understood as being in the sense of the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti). Therefore, it is said, "in which aeon." "Udapādi" means he was enlightened, making the ten thousand world-systems tremble.

"Bhaddakappe" means the "Auspicious Aeon," so called because it is adorned by the appearance of five Buddhas; the Blessed One praised this aeon and spoke thus. From the time our Blessed One received the prophecy (byādika), there has never been another single aeon in which five Buddhas appeared. Before our Blessed One received the prophecy, in the past, four Buddhas named Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara appeared in a single aeon. After those Buddhas, for one incalculable (asaṅkhyeyya) period, it was void of the appearance of a Buddha.

At the end of that incalculable aeon, a single Buddha named Koṇḍañña appeared in one aeon. After that also, for one incalculable period, it was void of Buddhas. At the end of that incalculable aeon, four Buddhas named Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita appeared in a single aeon. After that also, for one incalculable period, it was void of Buddhas. At the end of that incalculable aeon, more than one hundred thousand aeons plus one incalculable before this aeon, three Buddhas named Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada appeared in a single aeon. After that also, for one incalculable period, it was void of Buddhas. At the end of that incalculable aeon, one hundred thousand aeons before this aeon, a single Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in one aeon. After that Buddha, thirty thousand aeons before this aeon, two Buddhas named Sumedha and Sujāta appeared in a single aeon. After that, eighteen thousand aeons before this aeon, three Buddhas named Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī...
5:
The Buddhas appear in an aeon. Apart from that, ninety-four aeons ago from this present aeon, a single Buddha named Siddhattha appeared in one aeon. Ninety-two aeons ago from this aeon, two Buddhas, the Blessed Tissa and the Blessed Phussa, appeared in one aeon. Ninety-one aeons ago from this aeon, the Blessed Vipassī appeared. Thirty-one aeons ago from this aeon, two Buddhas, the Blessed Sikhī and the Blessed Vessabhū, appeared. In this Bhadda-kappa, four Buddhas have already appeared: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Buddha, Gotama; the Blessed Metteyya will appear in the future. Thus, because this aeon is adorned by the appearance of five Buddhas, the Blessed One praised this aeon, calling it "Sundara-kappa" (Beautiful Aeon) and "Sāra-kappa" (Essential Aeon), and spoke thus:

Is this matter of "so many Buddhas have appeared or will appear in this aeon" known only to the Buddhas, or is it known to others as well? It is known to others as well. To whom? To the Suddhāvāsa Brahmas. When the world is established, the world-dwelling becomes like a single incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and a single courtyard, and as it stands, rain begins to fall for the world to remain stable. At first, it is like a continuous fall of frost. Furthermore, there arise streams of water the size of sesame seeds, broken rice, rice grains, mung beans, kidney beans, jujube fruits, terminalia fruits, cucumbers, pumpkins, and gourds, which gradually become streams of water measuring one usabha, two usabhas, half a gāvuta, one gāvuta, two gāvutas, half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and so on, up to a hundred yojanas, a thousand yojanas, and a hundred thousand yojanas, filling the interior of the hundred billion world systems up to the Brahma realms that have not yet perished. Then, that water gradually recedes. As the water recedes, the celestial realms are established in their natural places; the order of the establishment of those celestial realms has already been described in the Pubbenivāsakathā of the Visuddhimagga.

When the water reaches the place where the human world is established, the water remains stable due to the force of the wind, as if the mouth of a water filter were closed. The surface of the earth appears on the water like a lotus leaf. The site of the Mahābodhi-pallaṅka (Great Throne of Enlightenment) is the last to perish when the world is destroyed and the first to be established when the world is re-established. In that place, a lotus plant grows as a preliminary sign. If a Buddha is to appear in that aeon, a lotus flower blooms. If no Buddha is to appear, no lotus flower blooms. When it blooms, if one Buddha is to appear, one lotus flower blooms. If two, three, four, or five Buddhas are to appear, five lotus flowers bloom. Those lotus flowers bloom on a single stalk with their pollens touching each other. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas...
6:
"Come, friends, let us look at the preliminary sign," they say, and go to the place where the Mahābodhi-pallaṅka is established. In an aeon where no Buddhas appear, there is no blooming of flowers. When those Brahmas see a plant without flowers, they become distressed, saying, "Friends, the world will be in utter darkness; beings will die and perish, filling the four woeful states (apāya); the six celestial realms and the nine Brahma realms will become empty."

However, when the flowers bloom, they see them and joyfully utter exclamations, saying, "We shall see the miracles such as the shaking of the ten thousand world systems during the Sabbaññū-bodhisattas' descent into the mother's womb, their renunciation, their attainment of Buddhahood, their preaching of the Dhammacakka, their performance of the Yamaka-pāṭihāriya (Twin Miracle), their descent from the celestial realm, their relinquishing of the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), and their entry into Parinibbāna," and "The four woeful states will diminish; the six celestial realms and the nine Brahma realms will be filled," and then they return to their own Brahma realms. In this Bhadda-kappa, five lotus flowers bloomed. By the power of those signs, four Buddhas have appeared, and the fifth Buddha will also appear. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas, having seen those lotus flowers, knew this matter. Therefore, it was said, "It is also known to others."

## Āyuparicchedavaṇṇanā

5-7. Thus, the Blessed One, having shown the Pubbenivāsa (Past Lives) by defining the aeons in the manner of "Monks, from this aeon..." and so forth, now speaks the words beginning with "Monks, the Blessed Vipassī..." in order to show the definition of the lineage and so on of those Buddhas. In that Āyupariccheda (Definition of Lifespan), both 'paritta' (small) and 'lahuka' (light/short) are synonyms for being few. That which is few is both paritta and lahuka.

"Whether it be little or more" means slightly more than a hundred years, or living for only twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty years without reaching a hundred years. A person who lives this long is very rare; it is a situation where one must go to various places to see, saying, "That person lives for this long." Among them, the laywoman Visākhā lived for one hundred and twenty years. Likewise, the Brahmin Pokkharasāti, the Brahmin Brahmāyu, the Brahmin Sela, the Brahmin Bāvariya, the Elder Ānanda, and the Elder Mahākassapa also lived for one hundred and twenty years. The Elder Anuruddha lived for one hundred and fifty years, and the Elder Bākula lived for one hundred and sixty years. This Elder Bākula was the longest-lived. Even that Elder did not live up to two hundred years.
7: All Bodhisattas, such as the Blessed Vipassī, also take conception in their mother's womb with a somanassa-sahagata ñāṇa-sampayutta asaṅkhārika (joyful, associated with knowledge, unprompted) consciousness preceded by loving-kindness (mettā). Due to the conception taken with that consciousness, the lifespan is incalculable (asaṅkheyya). Thus, all Blessed Buddhas have an incalculable lifespan. Why do those Buddhas not remain for an incalculable period? It is because of the adversity of climate and food (utu-bhojana-vipatti). Indeed, by the power of climate and food, the lifespan both decreases and increases. In that regard, when kings become unrighteous (adhammika), then the crown prince, the generals, the wealthy, the whole city, and the whole country become unrighteous. Then the devas who protect them, the bhummadevas who are friends of those devas, the ākāsadevas who are friends of those devas, the uṇhavalāhaka devas who are friends of those devas, the abbhavalāhaka devas who are friends of those devas, the sītavalāhaka devas who are friends of those devas, the vassavalāhaka devas who are friends of those devas, the Cātumahārājika devas who are friends of those devas, the Tāvatiṃsa devas who are friends of those devas, and the Yāma devas who are friends of those devas, and so on, become unrighteous. Thus, up to the highest point of existence (bhavagga), all the assemblies of devas and Brahmas, excluding the noble disciples (ariyasāvaka), become unrighteous. Because those devas and Brahmas are unrighteous, the moon and the sun revolve irregularly; the wind does not blow according to its proper path; the wind blowing improperly shakes the mansions of the ākāsadevas; when the mansions are shaken, the minds of the devas do not incline towards enjoyment; when the minds of the devas do not incline towards enjoyment, the climate, characterized by cold and heat, becomes irregular in terms of time; when the climate is irregular, the rain god does not rain well; sometimes it rains, sometimes it does not; it rains in some places, it does not rain in others; even when it rains, it does not benefit the crops at times such as sowing, sprouting, growing, flowering, or the formation of the milky grain; it rains and stops in such various ways. For that reason, the crops ripen irregularly; their fragrance, color, and taste diminish. Even in rice placed in a single pot, the rice in one part is raw, in another part it is overcooked, and in another part it is perfectly ripened. When that rice is eaten, it is digested in three different ways within the stomach. For that reason, beings have many diseases and short lifespans. Thus, first, by the power of climate and food (utu-bhojana), the lifespan decreases.
8: When kings are righteous (dhammika), then the sub-kings also become righteous; in the same manner as previously mentioned, all beings up to the Brahma world become righteous. Because of their righteousness, the moon and the sun revolve in harmony, and the wind blows according to its proper course. The wind blowing in its proper course does not disturb the mansions of the deities of the sky (ākāsasoṭṭhaka-deva). Because those mansions are not disturbed, the minds of the deities are inclined toward enjoyment and play. Thus, the seasons are harmonious in their timing, and the rain-god pours down rain well. From the time of sowing, the rain falls at the right time and ceases at the right time, benefiting the crops. For that reason, the crops ripen evenly and are endowed with good fragrance, good color, good taste, and nutritious essence. When food prepared from those crops is eaten, it is well digested. For that reason, beings are free from disease and long-lived. Thus, by the power of seasonal food, the lifespan increases. In that regard, the Blessed One Vipassī was enlightened during the period of an 80,000-year lifespan; the Blessed One Sikhī was enlightened during the period of a 70,000-year lifespan. It should be understood that although it is presented as if it decreases sequentially, it does not actually decrease continuously in this way; it should be known that it decreases only after increasing and increasing again. How so? In this eon, the first Buddha Kakusandha was enlightened during the period of a 40,000-year lifespan. Dividing the lifespan into five parts, he attained Parinibbāna while four parts had passed and the fifth part was still remaining. When that lifespan decreased and reached the ten-year period, and then increased again to become an Asankheyya (incalculable), and then decreased from there, it stood at a 30,000-year lifespan. At that time, the Blessed One Koṇāgamana was enlightened. In the case of that Buddha as well, after he attained Parinibbāna in the same manner, the lifespan reached the ten-year period, increased again to become an Asankheyya, and then decreased to stand at a 20,000-year lifespan. At that time, the Blessed One Kassapa was enlightened. In the case of that Buddha as well, after he attained Parinibbāna in the same manner, the lifespan reached the ten-year period, increased again to become an Asankheyya, and then decreased to reach the 100-year lifespan. At that time, our Blessed One was enlightened. Thus, it should be understood that it decreases only after decreasing and decreasing, and increasing and increasing. In that regard, whatever the lifespan of the people among whom the Buddhas are enlightened, that same lifespan applies to those Buddhas as well. ## The explanation of the lifespan limit is finished.

## Description of the Definition of the Bodhi Tree

In the definition of the Bodhi tree, the phrase "pāṭaliyā mūle" means at the foot of the Pāṭalī tree (the Trumpet flower tree). On that day, the trunk of that Pāṭalī tree was fifty cubits high, rising upwards; its branches were fifty cubits long, making it a total of one hundred cubits in height. On that day, that Pāṭalī tree was covered from its base throughout with flowers, as if they were tied at the very top; a celestial fragrance wafted strongly. At that time, not only did this single tree bloom, but all the Pāṭalī trees in the entire ten thousand world systems also bloomed. Not only did the Pāṭalī trees bloom, but on the trunks of all trees in the ten thousand world systems, trunk-lotuses bloomed; on the branches, branch-lotuses; on the vines, vine-lotuses; and in the sky, sky-lotuses bloomed. Great lotuses also emerged, piercing through the surface of the earth. The great ocean was also covered with lotuses of five colors, as well as blue and red lotuses.

The entire ten thousand world systems were entangled with banners and flower-vines, and were spread and scattered with flower-garlands and clusters tied here and there, shining brightly with flowers of various colors, resembling the Nandavana, Cittalatāvana, Missakavana, and Phārusakavana gardens. Banners planted at the edge of the eastern world system struck the edge of the western world system. Banners planted at the edges of the western, southern, and northern world systems also struck the edge of the southern world system. Thus, the world systems were mutually endowed with glory and prosperity. "Abhisambuddho" means having penetrated and realized the glory and prosperity of all Buddha-qualities and having realized the Four Noble Truths.

In the words beginning with "Monks, the Blessed One Sikhī realized the Four Noble Truths at the foot of the Puṇḍarīka tree," the explanation of the terms should be understood in this same manner. Here, Puṇḍarīka refers to the White Mango tree. The dimensions of that tree were also the same. On that day, that tree was also well-covered with flowers having a celestial fragrance. Not only was it covered with flowers, but it was also covered with fruits. On one side of that tree hung young fruits, on another side medium-sized fruits, on another side semi-ripe fruits, and on another side very ripe fruits that were extremely delicious, as if celestial essence (ojā) had been infused into them. Like that tree, the flowering trees in the entire ten thousand world systems were adorned with flowers, and the fruit-bearing trees were adorned with fruits.

"Sālo" refers to the Sal tree. The dimensions of that tree were also the same; likewise, the glory and prosperity of the flowers should be understood. For the Sirīsa tree (Kukko), it is the same manner. For the Udumbara tree (cluster fig)...
10:
...there are no flowers, but the abundance of fruits is in the same manner as already described for the mango tree. Likewise, it is the same for the Nigrodha tree, and likewise for the Assattha tree. Thus, although the throne (pallaṅka) is the same for all Buddhas, the Bodhi trees are different kinds of trees. Among those Bodhi trees, whatever tree at whose foot the Buddhas penetrate and realize the Enlightenment (Bodhi) which is the knowledge of the four paths, that particular tree is called the Bodhi tree. This is known as the Definition of the Bodhi Tree.

## Description of the Definition of the Pairs of Disciples

In the definition of the pairs of disciples, "Khaṇḍatissā" refers to Khaṇḍa and Tissa. Between those two, Khaṇḍa was the younger brother of the [Buddha's] father, and Tissa was the son of the court chaplain (purohita). Khaṇḍa reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī); Tissa reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration (samādhi-pāramī). Excluding the Blessed One Vipassī, they were said to be the most excellent because they possessed qualities not shared with others. Because they were noble, they were called the "Noble Pair" (bhadda-yuga). "Abhibhūsambhavā" refers to Abhibhū and Sambhava. Between those two, Abhibhū reached the pinnacle of the perfection of wisdom. Together with the Blessed One Sikhī, he went from the city of Aruṇavatī to the Brahma realm and preached the Dhamma while showing various miracles to the assembly of Brahmas. Then, having enveloped the ten thousand world systems in darkness, he caused light to overwhelm those who were struck with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), wondering "What is this?" He made a resolution, "Let all beings see my physical form (rūpa-kāya) and hear my voice," and while reciting two verses beginning with "Ārambhatha," he made his voice heard. Sambhava was one who reached the pinnacle of the perfection of concentration.

"Soṇuttarā" refers to Soṇa and Uttara. Among them also, Soṇa reached the perfection of wisdom, and Uttara reached the perfection of concentration. "Vidhurasañjīvā" refers to Vidhura and Sañjīva. Among them, Vidhura reached the perfection of wisdom, and Sañjīva reached the perfection of concentration. That Sañjīva, who frequently entered meditative attainments, would reflect through the power of attainment while staying at night or during the day in dwellings, caves, pavilions, and so on. One day, he entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) inside a forest. At that time, hunters and others, thinking "He is dead," cremated him. That Sañjīva, rising from the attainment at the determined time, shook his robes and entered the village for alms. Starting from that incident, they knew him as "Sañjīva" (The Revived). "Bhiyyosuttarā" refers to Bhiyyosa and Uttara. Among them, Bhiyyosa was superior in wisdom, and Uttara was the most excellent in concentration. "Tissabhāradvājā" refers to Tissa and Bhāradvāja. Among them, Tissa reached the perfection of wisdom, and Bhāradvāja reached the perfection of concentration.
11:
...it was so. "Sāriputtamoggallānā" refers to Sāriputta and Moggallāna. Among them, Sāriputta was the most excellent in the field of wisdom, and Moggallāna was the most excellent in the field of concentration. This is known as the Definition of the Pairs of Disciples.

## Description of the Definition of the Assemblies of Disciples

In the definition of the assemblies of disciples, the first assembly of disciples of the Blessed One Vipassī was endowed with four factors: all the monks were "Ehi-bhikkhu" (Come-monks); all the monks possessed bowls and robes created by psychic power; all the monks arrived without being invited; and those monks assembled on the fifteenth-day Uposatha. At that time, the Blessed One, holding a fan and being seated, recited the Pātimokkha. In the second and third assemblies also, it was in this same manner. Likewise, it should be understood for all the assemblies of the remaining Buddhas. For our Blessed One, although there were assemblies from the time he first became a Buddha, because he preached this Sutta at a later period, he did not conclude by saying, "Monks, now my assembly of disciples is only one," but said, "There has been."

In that statement, the "one thousand two hundred and fifty monks" refers to the one thousand who were formerly matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas) and the two hundred and fifty monks who were the retinue of the two chief disciples; when combined, they become one thousand two hundred and fifty monks. In that regard, the story should be told starting from the time the two chief disciples made their aspiration, showing the manner of their ordination. Among those who had been ordained, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reached the fruit of Arhatship on the seventh day. The General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta), on the fifteenth day, while the Blessed One was preaching the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta to his nephew, the wandering ascetic Dīghanakha, in the Sūkarakhata cave on the slopes of Vulture Peak (Gijjhakūṭa), sent forth his knowledge according to the sequence of the teaching and reached the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa). The Blessed One, knowing that the Elder had reached the fruit of Arhatship, flew into the sky and descended at the Veḷuvana monastery itself. The Elder also, reflecting "Where has the Blessed One gone?", knew that he was staying at Veḷuvana, and he himself flew into the sky and descended at Veḷuvana. At that time, the Blessed One recited the Pātimokkha. Referring to that assembly, the Blessed One said, "one thousand two hundred and fifty monks." This is known as the Definition of the Assemblies of Disciples.
12:
## Introduction to the Definition of the Attendant

In defining the attendant, the name "Ānanda" is mentioned with the intention of referring to the permanent attendant. In the early period after the Buddha's enlightenment, there were attendants who were not permanent. At times, Nāgasamāla would take the alms-bowl and robes and follow the Buddha; at other times, it was Nāgita, Upavāna, Sunakkhatta, Cunda Sāmaṇera, Sāgata, or Meghiya.

Among them, once, while the Buddha was traveling on a long journey with the Venerable Nāgasamāla, they reached a fork in the road. The Elder, departing from the path, said, "Venerable Sir, I will go by this way." Then the Buddha said, "Monk, come, let us go by this way." That monk replied, "Here, Venerable Sir, please take Your alms-bowl and robes; I will go by this way," and he attempted to place the alms-bowl and robes on the ground. Then the Buddha said, "Monk, take them," and having taken the alms-bowl and robes, He proceeded. As for the monk who went by the other path, robbers plundered his alms-bowl and robes and also split his head. That monk, thinking, "Now the Buddha alone is my refuge, there is no other," went to the Buddha while blood was flowing. When the Buddha asked, "Monk, what is this?", he reported the matter. Then the Buddha, saying, "Monk, do not worry; it was because I foresaw this matter that I forbade you," comforted the monk.

Once, the Buddha went to Jantu village in the Pācīnavaṃsa Migadāya forest together with the Venerable Meghiya. Then Meghiya, after wandering for alms in Jantu village, saw a delightful mango grove by the riverbank and said, "Venerable Sir, please take Your alms-bowl and robes; I will strive in the recluse's Dhamma in that mango grove." Although the Buddha forbade him three times, he went there and was oppressed by unwholesome thoughts. Upon his return, he reported the matter. Regarding that matter also, the Buddha said, "It was because I foresaw this matter that I forbade you," and He proceeded in due course to the city of Sāvatthī.

While residing on the noble Buddha-seat prepared at the front of the Gandhakuti in that city of Sāvatthī, surrounded by the community of monks, He addressed the monks: "Monks, I am now old. Some monks, saying 'I will go by this way,' go by another path; some leave my alms-bowl and robes behind. Choose a monk who will be my permanent attendant." Spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in the monks. Then the Venerable Sāriputta rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and said...
13:
"Venerable Sir, longing for You alone, I have fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for over an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons. Is it not fitting for a great wise attendant like me? I shall serve You." Then the Buddha rejected him, saying, "Enough, Sāriputta. Wherever you reside, that place is not empty for Me. Your instruction is like the instruction of the Buddhas; I have no need for you as an attendant." In this manner, the eighty great disciples, starting with Mahāmoggallāna, rose up. The Buddha rejected all of them as well.

The Venerable Ānanda, however, remained silent. Then the monks said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Friend Ānanda, the Bhikkhu Saṅgha requests the position of attendant; you should also make a request." The Venerable Ānanda said, "Friends, what kind of position is an attendancy obtained by requesting? Does the Teacher (the Buddha) not see me? If He is pleased, He will say, 'Let Ānanda serve Me.'" Then the Buddha said, "Monks, there is no need for others to urge Ānanda; he will know of his own accord and serve Me." Then the monks said, "Friend Ānanda, rise! Friend Ānanda, rise! Request the position of attendant from the Dasabala (the Buddha)." The Elder rose and requested eight boons: four refusals and four requests.

The four refusals were: "Venerable Sir, if the Buddha does not give me the fine robes He receives, does not give me the alms-food, does not allow me to stay in the same Gandhakuti, and does not go with me when accepting an invitation; only then will I serve the Buddha." When the Buddha asked, "Ānanda, what fault do you see in making such a request?", he replied, "Venerable Sir, if I receive these things, there will be those who disparage me, saying, 'Ānanda enjoys the fine robes received by the Dasabala, enjoys the alms-food, stays in the same Gandhakuti, and goes together to invitations; he serves the Tathāgata because he receives these gains. What burden would there be for one who serves like this?'" Thus he requested these four refusals.

The four requests were: "Venerable Sir, if the Buddha goes to an invitation accepted by me; if I may have the opportunity to see the Buddha at the very moment when an audience comes from other countries and regions to see the Buddha; if I may have the opportunity to approach the Buddha at the very moment when doubt or uncertainty arises in me; and if the Buddha, upon returning, would preach to me the Dhamma He preached in my absence; if it be so, I..."

## Introduction to the Section on the Many
It is the tradition, it is the custom, that all Bodhisattas renounce the world and become monks when a son worthy of their lineage is born. Why? For all Omniscient Bodhisattas, from the time they descend into their mother's womb, many various miracles as previously described occur. At that time, if the birthplace, father, mother, wife, and son of these Bodhisattas were not well-known, people would think, "This person has no birthplace, and his father, wife, and son are not known. He might be a deity, or Sakka, or Māra, or Brahmā. It is not surprising for deities to have such miracles." Thus, the multitude would not consider the Dhamma as something to be heard or believed. If that were so, there would be no realization of the Dhamma (abhisamaya). Without realization, the arising of a Buddha would be in vain, and the Dispensation (Sāsana) would not be the means for deliverance from saṃsāra. Therefore, for all Bodhisattas, it is the tradition and custom that "they renounce the world and become monks when a son worthy of their lineage is born." Thus, the section on the many (Sambahulavāra) is presented through the power of sons and so forth.

## Introduction to the Definition of the Many
Among those (names of the sons):
Samavattakkhandha, Atula, Suppabuddha, Uttara, Satthavāha, Vijitasena, and Rāhula was the seventh.
In this way, the seven sons of the seven Bodhisattas should be known in order.

Among those sons, when the noble Rāhula was born, the birth record was taken and placed in the hand of the Great Being (Mahāpurisa). At that moment, love for the son established itself, causing his whole body to tremble. The Bodhisatta said, "Just by the birth of one son, such love for a son has arisen. If I were to have over a thousand sons, and if this bond of love were to increase in each of them like this, it would be difficult to sever. A Rāhu (obstruction) has arisen; a bond has arisen." On that very day, he renounced the royal glory and went forth into the forest. This is the way of the birth of sons for all Bodhisattas. This is the definition of the sons.
16:
Sutanā, Sabbakāmā, Sucittā, Rocinī, Rucaggatī, Sunandā, and the seventh was Bimbā.

These were the mothers of those seven Bodhisattas. As for Bimbādevī, when she gave birth to Prince Rāhula, she became known as the Mother of Rāhula (Rāhulamātā). This is the definition of the wives (Bhariyapariccheda).

The two Bodhisattas, Vipassī Buddha and Kakusandha Buddha, departed for the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana) riding a well-yoked noble chariot. The two, Sikhī Buddha and Koṇāgamana Buddha, departed for the Great Renunciation mounted on the back of a noble elephant. Vessabhū Buddha departed for the Great Renunciation while staying in a golden palanquin. Kassapa Buddha, while staying in the great upper chamber of his palace, developed the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), and arising from that jhāna, using it as a basis, he made the resolution: "May the palace fly into the sky and descend at the Bodhimaṇḍa." The palace traveled through the sky and descended at the Bodhimaṇḍa. The Great Being (Mahāpurisa) also descended from there, stood on the ground, and thought: "May the palace remain in its original place." That palace then remained in its original place. The Great Being also strove in meditation for seven days and, sitting on the Bodhi-throne, penetrated and realized Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Our Bodhisatta, however, departed for the Great Renunciation riding the noble horse Kanthaka. This is the definition of the vehicles (Yānapariccheda).

The monastery (vihāra) of Vipassī Buddha was situated in a place measuring one yojana. The monastery of Sikhī Buddha was three gāvutas; the monastery of Vessabhū Buddha was half a yojana; the monastery of Kakusandha Buddha was one gāvuta; the monastery of Koṇāgamana Buddha was half a gāvuta; the monastery of Kassapa Buddha was situated in a place measuring twenty usabhas. Our Buddha's monastery was situated in a place measuring sixteen karīsas by standard measure, and eight karīsas by royal measure. This is the definition of the monasteries (Vihārapariccheda).

For Vipassī Buddha, they had gold bricks made, one cubit long, one span wide, and eight inches thick, and purchased the monastery site by laying them edge to edge. For Sikhī Buddha, they purchased it by laying gold spikes (or gold ploughshares). For Vessabhū Buddha, they had gold elephant footprints made and purchased it by laying them edge to edge. For Kakusandha Buddha, they purchased it by laying gold bricks in the manner already mentioned. For Koṇāgamana Buddha, they purchased it by laying gold tortoises in the manner already mentioned.
18:
Difference in lineage (kulavematta) means that some are born into the warrior caste (khattiya), while others are born into the brahmin caste. Difference in exertion (padhanavematta) means that for some Buddhas, the period of exertion is short, as it was for the Blessed One Kassapa. For other Buddhas, it is a long period, as it was for our Blessed One.

Difference in radiance (rassimavematta) means that the bodily aura of the Blessed One Maṅgala extended to ten thousand world systems. The bodily aura of our Blessed One extended only to a distance of one fathom (byāma) around him. This difference in radiance is related to their aspiration (ajjhāsaya); the aura spreads as far as one desires. The Blessed One Maṅgala had the aspiration that his aura should always spread to ten thousand world systems. However, regarding the qualities of realized knowledge (paṭivedhaguṇa), there is no difference whatsoever among any of the Buddhas.

Furthermore, the classification of our Blessed One's co-natals (sahajāta) and the classification of the constellations (nakkhatta) are shown. Along with the Omniscient Bodhisatta, these seven were born at the same time: the mother of Rāhula, the Elder Ānanda, the minister Channa, the horse Kanthaka, the four great treasure pots, the Mahābodhi tree, and the minister Kāḷudāyī. The Great Being (Mahāpurisa) descended into his mother's womb under the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha; he also renounced the world, turned the Wheel of Dhamma, and performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya) under the same constellation. He was born, attained Buddhahood, and entered Parinibbāna under the constellation of Visākhā on the full moon day of Kason (Vesākha). The assembly of disciples took place and he relinquished the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra) under the constellation of Māgha on the full moon day of Tabodwe (Māgha). He descended from the celestial realm under the constellation of Assayuja on the full moon day of Thadingyut (Assayuja). These points are presented as the general classification (sambahulapariccheda).

Now, regarding the words beginning with 'At that time, to those monks,' those monks were filled with great wonder, saying, 'Friends, the continuity of past aggregates (pubbenivāsa) has this destination: from death to rebirth. This task of sending the mind backward from rebirth to death is extremely difficult. The Blessed One teaches it as if showing footprints in the sky.' Having said, 'Friends, it is wonderful indeed,' and wishing to present another reason, they said, 'The one called the Tathāgata is wonderful indeed,' and so on. In that passage, 'yatra hi nāma' is a particle used in the sense of wonder, meaning 'that such a Tathāgata.' In the word 'chinnapapañca,' 'papañca' refers to these three defilements: craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and wrong view (diṭṭhi). In the word 'chinnavaṭuma,' 'vaṭuma' refers to the round of kamma (kammavaṭṭa) consisting of wholesome and unwholesome deeds. 'Pariyādinnavaṭṭa' is a synonym for that 'vaṭuma,' meaning one for whom the entire round of kamma is exhausted. 'Sabbadukkhavītivatta' means one who has transcended all suffering known as the round of results (vipākavaṭṭa)...
19:
...in the past. Although the word 'anussarissati' is a future tense form due to the power of the particle 'yatra,' in this context, the meaning should be understood in the sense of the past tense. The Blessed One has already remembered those Buddhas; it is not that he will only remember them now. 'Evaṃsīlā' means they possessed such virtue through the virtue of the path (magga-sīla), the virtue of the fruition (phala-sīla), and both mundane and supramundane virtue. In the phrase 'evaṃdhammā,' the qualities belonging to the side of concentration (samādhi) are intended here. It means 'they possessed such concentration' through the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruition, and both mundane and supramundane concentration. 'Evaṃpaññā' means they possessed such wisdom through the power of the wisdom of the path and so on. In the phrase 'evaṃvihārī,' if it is asked why 'dwelling' (vihāra) is mentioned again when the qualities belonging to concentration have already been taken, the answer is that it is not a mere repetition; it is said because it intends to show their dwelling in the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as 'those Blessed Ones were accustomed to dwelling in such attainment of cessation.'

In the phrase 'evaṃvimuttā,' there are five kinds of liberation (vimutti): liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti), liberation by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-vimutti), liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimutti), liberation by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi-vimutti), and liberation by escape (nissaraṇa-vimutti). Among these, the eight attainments are called 'liberation by suppression' because they are free from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so on, which they have pushed aside. The seven contemplations such as the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) are called 'liberation by substitution of opposites' because they are free from the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) and so on, which are abandoned by their respective opposite parts. The four noble paths are called 'liberation by eradication' because they are free from the defilements which they have absolutely cut off. The four fruits of recluseship are called 'liberation by tranquilization' because they arise when the defilements have been stilled by the power of the path. Nibbāna is called 'liberation by escape' because it is the escape from, the departure from, and the standing far away from all defilements. Thus, the meaning should be understood here as 'they were thus liberated' by the power of these five kinds of liberation.

'Paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito' means 'having arisen from staying alone in seclusion.'

What is the connection (anusandhi) of the words 'Monks, from this...'? This sutta is connected with both the phrase 'Monks, only the Tathāgata has well penetrated this Dhamma-element (dhammadhātu)' and the phrase 'The deities also reported this matter to the Tathāgata.' Among these, I shall analyze the phrase regarding the deities' report at the end of the sutta, showing the commotion of going to the celestial realm. However, by the power of the connection with the phrase 'Dhamma-element' (dhammadhātu), this...
20:
...discourse is begun. In that passage, the eleven terms such as 'being of the warrior caste by lineage' should be understood exactly as explained in the Nidānakanda.

## Commentary on the Nature of the Bodhisatta (Bodhisatta-dhammatā-vaṇṇanā)

In the words 'Monks, at that time the Bodhisatta Vipassī,' and so on, 'Vipassī' is the name of that Bodhisatta. That name was acquired because of his skill in seeing various meanings and purposes. 'Bodhisatta' means a wise being or a being who understands easily. Alternatively, he is called 'Bodhisatta' because his mind is entered into, attached to, and inclined toward the four paths called 'Bodhi.' In the phrase 'sato sampajāno,' 'sato' is mindfulness itself. 'Sampajāno' is wisdom. The meaning is that he entered his mother's womb making mindfulness clearly present and discerning with wisdom. By the word 'okkamī' (descended), the manner of the Bodhisatta's entry is shown in the Pali text, but not the sequence of the entry. That sequence of entry appears in the Commentary and should be understood as follows:

All Bodhisattas fulfill the thirty perfections (pāramī), renounce the five great sacrifices (mahāpariccāga), reach the summit of the three modes of conduct (cariyā)—namely, conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariyā), conduct for the benefit of the world (lokattha-cariyā), and conduct for the sake of Buddhahood (buddhattha-cariyā)—and while standing in the third existence similar to King Vessantara, they give the seven great donations, cause the earth to quake seven times, and then, in the second thought-moment before death, they are reborn in the Tusita heaven. The Bodhisatta Vipassī also acted in the same way and was reborn in the Tusita heaven, where he remained for 57 crores and 6 million years. In other cases, Bodhisattas born in celestial realms with long lifespans do not stay until the end of their lifespan. Why? Because it is difficult to fulfill the perfections in those celestial realms. Those Bodhisattas perform 'adhimuttikālakiriya' (voluntary passing) and are reborn only in the human world. However, the Bodhisatta Vipassī, who had fulfilled the perfections, had everything completed to attain omniscience in this single existence, and thus he remained in that celestial realm until the end of his lifespan.

For the deities, the five omens (pubbanimitta) appeared, indicating that 'by human calculation, he will pass away within seven days from now.' These are: the fading of flowers, the soiling of clothes, sweat coming from the armpits, the loss of bodily radiance, and the deity's restlessness in his celestial seat. Among these, the flowers refer to those [worn] on the day of conception...
21:
The flowers worn [by the devas] remained unwithered for a period of over five hundred million, seven hundred and sixty thousand years, yet at that time, they withered. The same occurred with their garments and ornaments. For such a long duration, these devas had never experienced cold or heat; however, as the time of their death approached, drops of sweat began to pour from the pores of their bodies. Throughout this vast period, no signs of physical decay, such as broken teeth or graying hair, had ever appeared in their bodies. The goddesses appeared as if they were sixteen years of age, and the gods appeared as if they were twenty; but as the time of death neared, their physical forms (attabhāva) took on a withered and faded appearance. For all this time, there had never been such a thing as weariness in the celestial realms; but as the time of death approached, they began to sigh and feel lethargy, no longer finding delight in their own abodes.

Just as omens such as falling meteors, earthquakes, and lunar eclipses become apparent only to great kings, princes, and high ministers in the world, so too these premonitory signs (pubbanimitta) appear only to devas of great power, and not to all devas. Just as among humans only those skilled in astrology recognize omens, so too not all devas recognize these signs; only the wise devas know them. Among those devas, those who were reborn there through meager wholesome kamma become fearful when these signs appear, thinking, "Who can know where we shall go and be reborn now?" However, devas of great merit do not fear, thinking, "Based on the charity (dāna) we have given, the virtue (sīla) we have observed, and the meditation (bhāvanā) we have cultivated, we shall enjoy splendor in the higher celestial realms."

The Bodhisatta Vipassī also saw these premonitory signs and did not fear, thinking, "Now, immediately following this existence, I shall become a Buddha." Then, when those signs became manifest, devas and Brahmas from the ten thousand world systems gathered and entreated him, saying, "Lord, when you fulfilled the ten perfections (pāramīs), you did not do so aspiring for the splendor of Sakka, Māra, Brahma, or a Universal Monarch; you fulfilled them solely aspiring for Buddhahood to save the world. Lord, now is the right time for you to become a Buddha; Lord, now is the opportune moment for you to become a Buddha."

Then the Great Being (Mahāsatta), the Bodhisatta, did not yet give his consent to those devas, but instead performed the Five Great Observations (pañcamahāvilokana) regarding the time, the continent, the region, the family, and the lifespan of the mother. Among those five, he first observed the time, asking, "Is it the right time to become a Buddha, or is it not yet time?" During that observation, a period where the lifespan is greater than one hundred thousand years is not the right time. Why? Because at that time, the processes of conception, aging, and death for beings are...
22:
(The Three Marks of Existence) are not apparent. The Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas is never devoid of the Three Marks of Existence. When they are taught "Impermanence (anicca), Suffering (dukkha), and Non-self (anatta)," they do not wish to listen nor do they wish to believe, asking, "What is this that is being taught?" Because of this, the realization of the Four Noble Truths (abhisamaya) cannot occur. Without that realization, the Dispensation (sāsana) does not lead to liberation from the round of suffering (aniyyānika). Therefore, that period is not the right time (for a Buddha to appear). A period where the lifespan is less than one hundred years is also not the right time. Why? Because at that time, beings are thick with defilements (kilesa). Advice given to those with thick defilements does not remain in the place of advice; it disappears quickly like a mark drawn on water with a stick. Therefore, that period is also certainly not the right time. Only the period when the lifespan is below one hundred thousand years and above one hundred years is called the right time. At that time, humans had a lifespan of eighty thousand years. Then the Mahāsatta Bodhisatta observed the time, concluding, "It is the time to take conception."

Next, when observing the continent, he looked at the four great continents along with their surrounding islands and observed, "Buddhas are not born in the other three great continents; they are born only in the continent of Jambudīpa."

Then, thinking, "Jambudīpa is very large, measuring ten thousand yojanas; in which region do Buddhas appear?" he observed the regions and saw the Majjhimadesa (Middle Country). The Majjhimadesa is exactly as described in the Vinaya Pali, starting with "To the east is the market town named Gajaṅgala," and so on. This Majjhimadesa is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in width, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference. In this region alone, Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, the eighty Great Disciples, Universal Monarchs, and other powerful royal families, brahmin families, and wealthy merchant families arise. "In this region, there is a city named Bandhumatī; there I shall take conception," he decided.

Next, when observing the family, he observed, "Buddhas are born only in a family esteemed by the world. At present, the royal family (Khattiya) is the family esteemed by the world; I shall take conception in that family. The King named Bandhuma shall be my father."

Next, when observing the mother, he observed, "The mother of a Buddha must not be frivolous or addicted to intoxicants. She must be one who has fulfilled perfections for a hundred thousand aeons and has kept the five precepts unbroken since birth. This Queen named Bandhumatī is endowed with such qualities; she shall be my mother."
23:
When he considered how long her lifespan remained, he saw that it was ten months and seven days. Having thus performed these Five Great Observations, he gave his consent to the devas, showing them favor by saying, "Friends, the time has come for me to attain Buddhahood." He then dismissed those devas, saying, "You may go," and surrounded by the Tusita devas, he entered the Nandavana Grove in the Tusita heaven. In all deva worlds, there is a Nandavana Grove. In that grove, the devas wander about, reminding him of the opportunities of his past wholesome kamma, saying, "Pass away from here and go to a happy destination (sugati)." While the Bodhisatta was wandering in that grove, surrounded by devas who were thus reminding him of his merit, he passed away. At the moment of passing away, he knew, "I am about to pass away," but he did not know the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) itself. After taking conception, he also knew it, but he did not know the rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhi-citta). However, he did know, "I have taken conception in this place."

Some elders, however, say, "The sequence of reflection is attained; he will know only in the second or third thought-moment (cittavāra)." The Elder Tipitaka Mahāsīva stated, "The conception of Great Beings is not like that of others; their mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) reach the pinnacle. Nevertheless, because one cannot know a consciousness with that same consciousness, he does not know the death-consciousness. At the very moment of passing away, he knows, 'I am about to pass away.' He does not know the rebirth-consciousness. He knows, 'I have taken conception in such a place.' At that moment, the ten thousand world systems of the universe tremble." Thus, with mindfulness and clear comprehension, he descended into his mother's womb. Among the nineteen types of rebirth-consciousness, he took conception with the Great Resultant consciousness (mahāvipāka-citta) that is unprompted, associated with knowledge, accompanied by joy, and preceded by the preliminary stage of loving-kindness. Elder Mahāsīva, however, says it was with a consciousness accompanied by equanimity. Just like our Buddha, that Bodhisatta took conception on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, in conjunction with the Uttarāsāḷha nakshatra. At that time, a festival free from intoxicants and made beautiful and bustling with flowers and perfumes was celebrated in the city starting seven days before the full moon. On the seventh day, the Bodhisatta's mother rose early in the morning, bathed with scented water, adorned herself with all ornaments, ate noble food, observed the Uposatha precepts, entered the Sirigabbha chamber, and while lying on the royal couch (sirisayana), she fell asleep and saw this dream: "The four..."
24:
...four Great Kings, together with the couch, lifted the mother and carried her to Lake Anotatta, where they bathed her. They dressed her in celestial garments, anointed her with celestial perfumes, and adorned her with celestial flowers. Not far from there was a silver mountain, and inside that silver mountain was a golden mansion. There, they laid her down with her head toward the east. Then the Bodhisatta, having become a noble white elephant, wandered on a golden mountain not far from there, descended from it, climbed the silver mountain, entered the golden mansion, and after circling his mother three times clockwise, he seemed to pierce her right side and enter her womb. Then the Queen awoke and reported the dream to the King. At dawn, the King summoned sixty-four learned Brahmins. He had costly seats prepared on ground that had been smeared with fresh cow dung and honored with auspicious offerings such as parched rice. To the Brahmins seated there, he donated noble thick milk-rice prepared with butter, honey, and molasses, served in full gold and silver bowls covered with gold and silver lids. He also satisfied them with other gifts such as new clothes and red cows. After satisfying them with whatever they desired, he told them the dream and asked, "What will happen?"

The Brahmins replied, "Great King, do not worry. A pregnancy has been established in the Queen's womb. That pregnancy is not a female but a male. A jewel of a son will be born to you. If that son remains in the household life, he will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti). If he leaves the household life and ordains, he will surely become a Buddha who can open the veil of defilements in the world." This is the sequential explanation of the statement "He descended into his mother's womb." In this context, "dhammatā" (natural order) refers to the natural order of this descent into the mother's womb; it means this is the nature, this is the law (niyāma). There are five types of Niyāma: Kamma-niyāma, Utu-niyāma, Bīja-niyāma, Citta-niyāma, and Dhamma-niyāma. Among these five, the fact that wholesome kamma gives good results and unwholesome kamma gives bad results is Kamma-niyāma. To illustrate this Kamma-niyāma, stories are told in verses such as "Na antalikkhe," and so on. Furthermore, if a woman quarrels with her husband and hangs herself by the neck...
25:
A woman wishing to die placed her neck in a noose. A man who was sharpening a billhook saw her action and, wishing to cut the rope, ran towards her, encouraging her by saying, "Do not be afraid, do not be afraid!" At that moment, the rope turned into a cobra. The man fled in terror. The woman, however, died right there. Such stories should be presented in this context.

The simultaneous flowering and fruiting of trees in various regions at various times, the blowing or non-blowing of the wind, the intensity or mildness of the sun's heat, the falling or non-falling of rain, and the blooming of lotuses by day and their withering by night—all such phenomena are called *Utuniyāma* (The Law of Seasons/Physical Order).

The production of only rice from rice seeds, the production of only sweet flavors from sweet seeds, and the production of only bitter flavors from bitter seeds—this process of fruition is called *Bījaniyāma* (The Law of Seeds/Biological Order).

The occurrence of receiving consciousness (*sampaṭicchana*) and so forth immediately after eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) and so forth, due to the preceding mental states assisting the succeeding mental states through the condition of decisive support (*upanissaya-paccaya*), is called *Cittaniyāma* (The Law of Mind/Psychic Order).

The shaking of the ten thousand world-systems during events such as the Bodhisatta’s descent into his mother’s womb is called *Dhammaniyāma* (The Law of Phenomena/Natural Order). Among these laws, *Dhammaniyāma* is intended in this context. Therefore, wishing to show this very meaning, the Buddha said, "Monks, this is the nature (*dhammatā*)," and so forth.

In that Pāḷi text, "descends into the womb" (*kucchiṃ okkamati*) means "has already descended into the womb." This is because such shaking occurs only after the Bodhisatta has descended, not while he is in the process of descending. "Immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) means having a great extent or being vast. "Magnificent" (*uḷāra*) is a synonym for that immeasurable quality. In passages such as "they eat magnificent foods," the word *uḷāra* refers to something delicious. In passages such as "the Venerable Vacchāyana praises the Ascetic Gotama with magnificent praise," it refers to something noble. In this context, however, the meaning of "vast" is intended. In the phrase "divine majesty of the gods" (*devānaṃ devānubhāvaṃ*), it means that the radiance of the garments worn by these gods spreads for twelve yojanas; likewise, the radiance of their bodies, ornaments, and mansions also spreads. The light that appears surpasses even this majesty of the gods.
26:
"Lokantarika" refers to the Lokantarika hells located in the spaces between every three world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*). It is like the empty space in the middle of three cartwheels or three alms-bowls placed touching each other. This Lokantarika hell is eight thousand yojanas in extent. "Agha" means being perpetually open. "Asaṃvuta" means having no foundation at the bottom. "Andhakāra" means being a mass of great darkness. "Andhakāra-timisā" means being filled with a blinding darkness that makes one like a blind person because it prevents the arising of eye-consciousness. It is said that eye-consciousness does not arise there.

"Of such great power" means that the moon and the sun appear simultaneously over three continents; such is their great power. They dispel darkness and provide light over an area of nine hundred thousand yojanas on each side; such is their great majesty. "Could not experience with their radiance" means they cannot reach that hell with their own light. Those moons and suns travel around the center of the Cakkavāḷa mountains, whereas the Lokantarika hells are situated beyond the Cakkavāḷa mountains. Therefore, those moons and suns cannot illuminate that place with their radiance.

"The beings who are there as well" refers to the beings born in that great Lokantarika hell. What kind of kamma did they perform to be born there? They are born there because of committing grave and cruel offenses against their parents or against rightfully practicing recluses and brahmins, or because of performing other cruel deeds such as habitual killing every day. They are like the thieves Abhaya and Nāga of Sri Lanka. The bodies of these beings are three *gāvutas* in size, and they have long claws like bats. They cling to the Cakkavāḷa mountains with their claws like bats on a tree. While crawling, when they reach within reach of one another, they think, "We have found food!" and as they struggle there, they flip over and fall into the water that supports the world. When the wind blows, they fall off like *madhuka* fruits and drop into the water. As soon as they fall, they dissolve like a lump of raw dough in extremely salty water.

"Friends, it seems there are other beings as well!" means that on that day, they see each other and think, "Friends, just as we are suffering great misery, it seems other beings have also come to this place to suffer this misery." This light does not last even as long as it takes to drink a cup of gruel. It appears only for a moment, like a flash of lightning, and while they are still saying, "What is this?", it disappears. "Trembles" (*saṅkampati*) means shaking all around. The other two terms are merely synonyms of the first. Furthermore, the phrase "immeasurable as well" and so forth is stated for the purpose of conclusion.
27: "The four deities approach from the four directions for protection"—in this statement, "four" refers to the four Great Kings (Cātumahārājā). In the ten thousand world systems, however, there are forty thousand, with four in each. Among those Great Kings, the Great Kings of this world system, holding swords in their hands, approach to protect the Bodhisatta and enter the Sirigabbha chamber. The remaining Great Kings (from the ten thousand world systems), starting from the chamber door, clear away the assembly of demons such as the Paṃsupisāca who might cause obstruction, and take up protection as far as the edge of the world system. For what purpose is this protection taken? From the moment of conception, when the embryonic stage (kalala) begins, if a hundred thousand Maras were to come, lifting a hundred thousand Mount Merus to harm the Bodhisatta or the Bodhisatta's mother, would not all those Maras vanish in the midst? Regarding this matter, the Blessed One said in the story of causing fresh blood to flow: "Monks, there is no cause, there is no opportunity, for the Tathāgata to be deprived of life by the effort of another. Monks, the Tathāgatas attain Parinibbāna without the effort of another (only of their own accord). Monks, go to your respective dwellings; monks, the Tathāgatas are those who do not need protection by others." Likewise, although there can be no danger to their lives through the effort of others, there are demons, wild beasts, and birds with ugly, unsightly, and terrifying appearances. By seeing their forms or hearing their sounds, fear or terror could arise in the Bodhisatta's mother. Protection is taken to prevent those beings. Furthermore, these deities do this because of the respect arising from the power of the Bodhisatta's merit and because they are urged by their own respect. Do the four Great Kings who enter and stay within the chamber show themselves to the Bodhisatta's mother or not? They do not show themselves during times of bodily activities such as bathing, adorning, or eating. However, they do show themselves when she enters the Sirigabbha chamber and reclines on the noble couch. In that regard, although seeing non-humans (amanussa) such as demons and deities is terrifying to humans, the Bodhisatta's mother does not feel fear even when seeing those deities, due to her own meritorious power and the meritorious power of her son. Toward those deities, a thought arises just as it would toward the ordinary palace guards. "Pakatiyā sīlavatī" means being naturally endowed with virtue. During the time when the Buddha has not yet appeared, people take precepts while bowing and crouching in the presence of hermits and wanderers. The Bodhisatta's mother also, in the presence of the hermit Kāladevila...
28: She undertakes the precepts in the presence of others. However, while the Bodhisatta is in the womb, she is unable to sit at the feet of another; even sitting on an equal seat to undertake the precepts is merely a matter of reflection. Therefore, it means she undertakes the precepts by herself. Regarding the phrase "among men," no sensual desire arises in any man, starting from the Bodhisatta's father to any other man, toward the Bodhisatta's mother. As for the physical appearance of the Bodhisatta's mother, even skilled sculptors are unable to carve or paint it in statues or paintings. It cannot be said that a man would not feel passion upon seeing the mother, but if there were a man who wished to approach her with lustful intent, his legs would be unable to move, as if they were shackled with divine fetters. Therefore, it is said, "unsurpassable," and so on. Regarding "with the five cords of sensual pleasure," the previous phrase "associated with the cords of sensual pleasure" showed the rejection of objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) through the power of men's desire, and here it shows the attainment of the objects. At that time, hearing that such a noble son was conceived in the Queen's womb, kings from all directions sent gifts that are objects of the five sense doors, such as precious ornaments and musical instruments. Because the past kamma of the Bodhisatta and his mother was so extraordinary, there was no limit or measure to the gains and offerings. Regarding "having an unwearied body," unlike other women who become weary due to the burden of the fetus, or experience swelling of the hands and feet, the mother did not experience any such weariness. "Residing within the belly" means the son who is inside the womb. "Sees" means seeing only after the stages such as the kalala-drop have passed, when the limbs and organs are complete and the faculties are not deficient. For what benefit does she see? It is only for the benefit of living in comfort. Just as a mother, whether lying down or sitting with her son, watches over him for his comfort, thinking, "If my son's hand or foot is hanging down, I will lift it up," similarly, the Bodhisatta's mother watches over him for his comfort during her rising, walking, moving, or sitting, and when swallowing food that is hot, cold, salty, bitter, or spicy, which might cause suffering to the fetus, thinking, "Does my son have such suffering?" While watching, she sees the Bodhisatta sitting cross-legged without wavering. Other beings in the womb sit crouching, pressing against the stomach (old food receptacle), with the womb membrane behind them, leaning against the backbone, with their chin on their two fists...
29: The Bodhisatta does not reside like monkeys huddling in a tree hollow when it rains. Instead, the Bodhisatta sits cross-legged, keeping his backbone to the back, like a Dhamma teacher on a preaching seat, looking forward toward the East. His past kamma purifies his physical basis; when the basis is pure, the Sukhumacchavi-lakkhaṇa (the characteristic of delicate skin) arises. At that time, the skin of the abdomen is unable to conceal the Bodhisatta; he is clearly visible to the observer as if he were outside. The Blessed One, wishing to clarify this meaning with a simile, spoke the words beginning with "Seyyathāpi." The Bodhisatta, however, does not see his mother while in the womb, because eye-consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa) cannot arise within the womb. "Kālaṅkaroti" (passes away) occurs not because of the cause of childbirth, but only because of the exhaustion of the lifespan. Because the place where the Bodhisatta resided is like a shrine-room (cetiya-ghara), it is not fit for others to use; nor is it possible to remove the Bodhisatta's mother and place another in the position of Chief Queen. Therefore, the Bodhisatta's mother has only that much lifespan; thus, death occurs at that time. At what age does she pass away? It is in the Majjhimavaya (middle age). In the Pathamavaya (first stage of life), beings have strong desire and passion for their own bodies; therefore, a woman pregnant at that age cannot protect the fetus, and the fetus is prone to many diseases. After passing two parts of the Majjhimavaya, in the third part, the physical basis is clear; children born from a clear physical basis are free from disease. Therefore, it is the natural law (dhammatā) in this Dispensation that the Bodhisatta's mother enjoys pleasures in the Pathamavaya and passes away after giving birth in the third part of the Majjhimavaya. In the phrase "nine months or ten months," the word "or" (vā) also includes seven, eight, eleven, or twelve months. Among these, one born at seven months survives but cannot withstand cold or heat. One born at eight months does not survive. Those born in the remaining months survive. "The gods receive him first" refers to the reception by the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās who have ended their defilements. How do they receive him? Some say, "They receive him by taking the form of midwives." Rejecting that view, it is said: At that time, the Bodhisatta's mother stood wearing a cloth adorned with gold, covered down to her toes with a Dukūla robe like a fish's eye. Then, the birth occurred as easily as water flowing from a filter. Then, those Brahmās approached in their natural Brahma forms and first...
30: ...received him with a golden net. From the hands of those Brahmās, the Four Great Kings received him with a rug of antelope skin. From the hands of those kings, humans received him with a coil made of Dukūla cloth. Therefore, it is said, "The gods receive him first, and then humans receive him." "Cattāro naṃ devaputtā" refers to the Four Great Kings. "Paṭiggahetvā" means having received him with an antelope skin rug. "Mahesakkho" means having great power, a great retinue, and being endowed with the marks. "He comes out purely" means that unlike other beings who come out clinging to the birth canal with damaged limbs, he comes out without clinging. "Udena" means by water. "Kenaci asucinā" means that while other beings, due to the kamma-produced winds, are turned head-down and feet-up, descending into the birth canal as if falling into a seventy-fathom hell-pit, or like an elephant being pulled out of a palm tree sprout, experiencing intense suffering and coming out smeared with various impurities, the Bodhisatta is not so. The kamma-produced winds cannot turn the Bodhisatta head-down and feet-up. Like a Dhamma teacher descending from a preaching seat, or a man descending a ladder, he comes out purely, standing upright with both hands and feet extended, without being smeared by any impurity from within the mother's womb. "Udakassa dhārā" refers to streams of water. Among those waters, the cold water falls into a golden bowl, and the hot water falls into a silver bowl. This was said to show their drinking and usable water, which is not mixed with the impurities of the earth, and their water for play and enjoyment, which is not shared with others. There is no measure to the water drawn in other gold and silver pots or the water in ponds such as Haṃsavattaka. "Sampatijāto" means at the moment just after birth. In the Pali text, it is shown as if he had just come out of the mother's womb; it should not be understood that way. Just after coming out, the Brahmās first received the Bodhisatta with a golden net; from the Brahmās' hands, the Four Great Kings with an antelope skin rug; from the kings' hands, humans with a Dukūla cloth coil. When released from the hands of humans, he stood upon the earth. "Setamhi chatte anudhāriyamāne" means while the divine white umbrella was being held over him. In this context, the retinue of the umbrella...
31: The five royal regalia, such as the sword, also certainly appear. In the Pāḷi text, however, only the umbrella is mentioned, like the umbrella used when a king travels. Among those royal regalia, only the umbrella is visible; the person holding the umbrella is not visible. Likewise, only the sword, the palmyra fan, the peacock-tail fan, the yak-tail fan, and the diadem are visible; the persons holding those regalia are not visible. It is said that deities who do not show their forms hold all those regalia. It is also said thus: "Deities hold in the sky an umbrella with many branches and a thousand circumferences. Yak-tail fans with golden handles are seen waving, but those holding the yak-tail fans and the umbrella are not seen." The phrase "and all directions" refers to looking at all directions as if one were standing above, having ascended seven footsteps; it should not be understood otherwise. The Great Being (Mahāsatta), having been released from the hands of humans and standing on the ground, looked toward the East. Many thousands of world systems became a single plain. At that time, deities and humans, making offerings with fragrant flowers and such, said, "Great Being, there is no one equal to you in this world; where could there be anyone superior to you?" Thus, having looked at the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, below, and above—the ten directions—and seeing no one equal to himself, he turned toward the North, saying "This is the North," and took seven footsteps. This is how the meaning should be understood here. "Āsabhī" means noble. "Aggo" means foremost of all through virtues. The remaining two terms are merely synonyms of this meaning. With the two phrases "This is the last birth; now there is no further new existence," he proclaimed the attainment of Arahantship to be achieved in this very existence. In this context, standing on the ground with level feet is the omen for attaining the four bases of power (iddhipāda). Facing the North is the omen for going forth overcoming the multitude of people. Taking seven footsteps is the omen for attaining the seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga). The deities carrying the white umbrella is the omen for attaining the noble umbrella of liberation (vimutti). Receiving the five royal regalia is the omen for liberation through the five kinds of deliverance (vimutti). Looking at all directions is the omen for attaining unobstructed knowledge (anāvaraṇañāṇa). Uttering the noble words is the omen for preaching the irreversible Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Making the lion's roar (sīhanāda), "This is the last birth," is the omen for attaining Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa nibbāna-dhātu).
32:
It should be understood. These occurrences are mentioned in the Pāḷi; however, many others are not mentioned there but are presented by drawing from other treatises.

On the day the Great Man was born, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. The deities of the ten-thousandfold world system gathered in a single universe (Cakkavāḷa). First, the deities received him, and afterwards, humans received him. Lutes strung with strings and drums covered with hide sounded of their own accord without anyone playing them. The shackles and bonds on the feet of humans and such were broken into pieces. All diseases were calmed; they disappeared like copper rust washed away by an acidic cleanser. Those born blind saw forms. Those born deaf heard sounds. The lame became endowed with speed. Mindfulness was established even in those born mute and deaf. Ships traveling to other regions reached good ports. Jewels situated in the sky and on the earth shone with their own radiance. Enemies attained a mind of loving-kindness.
