The fire in the Avīci hell was extinguished. Light appeared in the Lokantarika hells. Water in the rivers did not flow. The water in the great ocean acquired a sweet taste. The wind did not blow. Birds in the sky, on mountains, and in trees descended to the ground. The moon was exceedingly beautiful. The sun was neither hot nor cold, being free from impurities and endowed with the proper season. Deities, standing at the doors of their celestial mansions, engaged in great festivities by clapping their hands, shouting, and throwing their garments. A great rain fell throughout all four great islands. The multitude of people was not oppressed by hunger or thirst. Door-leaves opened of their own accord. Trees that flower and bear fruit bore flowers and fruits. The ten-thousandfold world system became like a single expanse of banners and garlands.

Among those occurrences, the trembling of the ten-thousandfold world system is the precursor for the attainment of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). The gathering of deities in a single universe is the precursor for their simultaneous gathering to receive the Dhamma when the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is preached. The deities receiving him first is the precursor for the attainment of the four fine-material sphere jhānas (rūpāvacara-jhāna). Humans receiving him afterwards is the precursor for the attainment of the four immaterial sphere jhānas (arūpāvacara-jhāna). The lutes strung with strings sounding of their own accord is the precursor for the attainment of the successive meditative attainments (anupubbavihāra-samāpatti). The sounding of the drums covered with hide is the precursor for the proclamation of the great Drum of Dhamma. The breaking of the shackles and bonds is the precursor for the total cutting off of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna). The freedom from disease of the multitude of people is the precursor for the realization of the Four Noble Truths. The blind seeing forms is the precursor for the attainment of the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu)...
33:
...precursors. The deaf hearing sounds is the precursor for the attainment of the divine ear element (dibba-sotadhātu). The lame being able to walk swiftly is the precursor for the attainment of the four bases of power (iddhipāda). The establishment of mindfulness in the mute and deaf is the precursor for the attainment of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna). Ships traveling to foreign lands reaching good ports is the precursor for the attainment of the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The jewels shining by their own power is the precursor for the manifestation of the light of Dhamma in the world.

Enemies obtaining a mind of loving-kindness is the precursor for the attainment of the four sublime abodes (brahmavihāra). The extinguishing of fire in the Avīci hell is the precursor for the extinguishing of the eleven fires (burning in the world). The appearance of light in the Lokantarika hell is the precursor for the dispelling of the mass of darkness known as ignorance (avijjā) and the seeing of the light of wisdom. The sweetness of the water in the great ocean is the precursor for having the single taste of the flavor of Nibbāna. The stillness without wind blowing is the precursor for the destruction of the sixty-two types of wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). Birds descending to the ground is the precursor for the multitude of people listening to the exhortation and establishing themselves in the refuges (saraṇagamana) for as long as life lasts. The moon being exceedingly bright is the precursor for gaining the affection and love of the many. The sun being free from heat and cold and having a pleasant season is the precursor for reaching the happiness of both body and mind. The deities standing at the doors of their mansions and enjoying themselves by clapping hands and so on is the precursor for reaching Buddhahood and uttering inspired verses (udāna). The falling of great rain throughout all four great islands is the precursor for the raining of the great Rain of Dhamma. The absence of hunger and thirst is the precursor for obtaining the Deathless (amata) known as mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati). The absence of thirst is the precursor for being happy with the bliss of liberation (vimuttisukha). The door-leaves opening of their own accord is the precursor for the opening of the door of the Eightfold Noble Path. Trees bearing flowers and fruits is the precursor for blossoming with the flowers of liberation and being endowed with the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala). The entire ten-thousandfold universe becoming as if decorated with banners and streamers is the precursor for being decorated with the banner of the Noble Ones (Ariyas). Thus it should be understood. This is called the 'Section on Many Occurrences' (Sambahuḷavāra).

Regarding this, a question is asked: "When the Great Man stood on the ground, faced the north, took seven steps, and spoke bold words, did he travel on the ground or through the sky? Did he travel while being clearly visible or while being invisible? Did he travel without clothes or while being adorned? Did he travel as a child...
34:
...or as an adult? Did he remain that way afterwards, or did he become a small child again?" This question was already answered by the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷābhaya at the lower floor of the Lohapāsāda palace. The Elder, after preaching extensively regarding Niyati-vāda (determinism), Pubbekata-kamma-vāda (past-action determinism), Issaranimmāna-vāda (creationism), and so forth, finally answered thus: "Although the Great Man traveled on the ground, it appeared to the multitude of people as if he traveled through the sky. Although he traveled while being clearly visible, it appeared to the multitude of people as if he traveled without being seen. Although he traveled without clothes, it appeared to the multitude of people as if he traveled while being adorned. Although he traveled only as a child, it appeared to the multitude of people as if he were a youth of sixteen years. Afterwards, however, he was just a small child; he was not like that (youth)." The assembly was delighted, saying, "The Elder answered the question just like the Buddha himself." The Lokantarika-vāra is in the same manner as already stated.

It should be understood that these natural laws (sabba-dhammatā) preached from the beginning are constant occurrences for all Bodhisattas.

## Commentary on the 32 Marks of a Great Man
"Addasa kho" means he saw (the child) who was being carried carefully wrapped in a blanket. "Mahāpurisassa" means of the man who is great by way of birth, clan, family, region, and so forth. "Dve gatiyo" means two kinds of destinies, two kinds of fulfillments. Here, the word "gati" refers to the destination where beings go, distinguished as hell and so forth, in the passage: "Sāriputta, there are these five destinies" (M. Ni. 1, 153). In the passage: "I do not know the coming or going (gati) of these monks who are virtuous and of good character" (M. Ni. 1, 508), it refers to inclination (ajjhāsaya). In the passage: "Nibbāna is the destiny (refuge) of the Arahant" (Pari. 339), it refers to the refuge. In the passage: "Brahmā, I know your destiny, and I know your power and majesty" (M. Ni. 1, 503), it refers to fulfillment or outcome (nipphatti). Here also, it should be understood that it is used in the sense of fulfillment (nipphatti). "Anaññā" means there is no other destiny or fulfillment.

"Dhammiko" means endowed with the ten wholesome courses of action, and free from following the four wrong paths (agati). "Dhammarājā" is a synonym (vevaccana) of the preceding term. Alternatively, he is called Dhammarājā because he attained kingship through righteousness.
35: "Caturanto" means the ruler of the earth bounded on four sides by the four oceans, such as the Eastern Ocean. "Vijitāvī" means one who has won his battles. "Janapadatthāvariyappatto" means one who has achieved stability and firmness in this country. When a harsh king oppresses the world with taxes and punishments, people abandon the central districts (janapada) and live in the border regions, relying on mountains and seashores. Under an excessively soft king, people oppressed by the violent looting of thieves abandon the border regions and live in the center of the janapada. Under such kings, the janapada cannot achieve stability. To show that when this prince rules, his janapada will be as firm as if placed on a stone slab and surrounded by iron plates, it is said "Janapadatthāvariyappatto." In the term "Sattaratanasamannāgato," it is called "Ratana" (treasure/gem) because it produces delight. Alternatively: "Because of being revered and esteemed, being of great value, Being incomparable, being rare to see, And being the requisite of noble beings, For these reasons, it is called a Treasure (Ratana)." From the time the Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana) appears, there is no other place for other deities; all deities offer flowers, scents, etc., and pay homage to that Wheel Treasure. Because of this sense of being revered and esteemed, it is called a Treasure. Because the Wheel Treasure is of such value that it cannot be measured in wealth, it is called a Treasure due to being of great value. Because the Wheel Treasure is unlike any other treasure in the world, it is called a Treasure due to being incomparable. Only in an aeon (kappa) where Buddhas appear do Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti) appear. Buddhas appear only rarely. Therefore, it is called a Treasure due to being rare to see. That treasure appears only to a noble being endowed with birth, appearance, family, and power; it does not appear to others. Therefore, it is called a Treasure due to being the requisite of noble beings. Like the Wheel Treasure, the remaining treasures are the same. Because he is endowed with these seven treasures as a retinue and as all forms of enjoyment and requisites, he is called "Sattaratanasamannāgato." Now, to show those treasures in their individual nature, the words beginning with "Tassimāni" are said. In those terms such as "Cakkaratanaṃ," the brief meaning is: the Wheel Treasure appears, capable of bringing and giving the glory and wealth of the four great islands surrounded by two thousand small islands. Likewise, the Elephant Treasure appears, capable of traveling through the sky and traversing the earth bounded by the ocean in a single morning; the Horse Treasure is of a similar nature; endowed with four factors...
36: ...the Gem Treasure appears, capable of dispelling a mass of darkness for a distance of one league (yojana) and making light visible. The Queen Treasure appears, free from the six defects and pleasing to the heart. The Householder Treasure appears, capable of seeing gold jars located within the earth for a distance of one league. The Counselor Treasure appears, the eldest son born from the womb of the chief queen, capable of governing and instructing the entire country. 'Parosahassaṃ' means a number exceeding one thousand. 'Surā' means those who are brave and fearless. 'Vīraṅgarūpā': the limb of a hero is called vīraṅga, which is a name for energy (vīriya); those who have such energetic bodies are called vīraṅgarūpā—those of an energetic nature, energetic character, accomplished through energy, and free from laziness. It means they do not get tired even if they fight all day. 'Sāgarapariyantaṃ' refers to the earth bounded by the ocean, which is delimited by the Cakkavāḷa mountains. 'Adaṇḍena': those who rule by punishing beings who commit offenses with a hundred or a thousand-fold punishment rule by the punishment of fines. Those who discipline by cutting or beating rule by the punishment of weapons. This Universal Monarch, however, discards both types of punishment and rules without punishing. 'Asatthena': those who oppress others with weapons such as single-edged swords are said to rule by the sword. This king, however, does not cause even a small fly to bleed with a weapon, but rules righteously, having a manner of movement such that rival kings welcome him saying, "Come, Great King," and thus conquers and rules the aforementioned earth, living as its sovereign lord. Having thus spoken of one fulfillment, the words beginning with 'Sace kho pana' are spoken to state the second fulfillment. Therein, the veil (āvaraṇa) of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, defilements, and craving has been opened and destroyed; because of such opening, he is called 'Vivaṭacchado' (one who has removed the veil). There is also a variant reading 'Vivaṭṭacchadā,' but the meaning is the same. Having thus spoken of the second fulfillment, the words beginning with 'Ayañhi deva kumāro' are spoken to show the marks that are the signs of that fulfillment. Therein, 'Suppatiṭṭhitapādo' means that when others place their feet on the ground, the toes, the heel, or the side of the foot usually touches first, or the middle remains hollow. When lifting the foot, only a part like the toes usually lifts first. This boy is not like that. This boy's sole touches the ground all at once, like the surface of a golden sandal; it lifts from the ground all at once. Therefore, this boy is called 'Suppatiṭṭhitapādo'.
37:
'Cakkāni' refers to the presence of two wheels on the soles of the feet. The spokes, rims, and hubs of these wheels are exactly as described in the Pāli Canon. The distinction is understood through the phrase 'sabbākārapari-pūrāni' (complete in all aspects): at the center of the soles, the hub is visible; the circular line demarcating the hub is visible; the rim surrounding the hub's mouth is visible; the opening of the axle-hole is visible; the spokes are visible; the circular lines on the spokes are visible; and the rubies near the rim are visible. This is what appears in the Pāli Canon. However, many pairs not mentioned in the Pāli Canon should be noted as follows: a spear, the Sīrivaccha mark, the Nandi mark, the Sovatthika mark, a crest-garland, the Vaḍḍhamānaka mark, a pair of fish, a victory throne, a goad, a palace, a gatepost, a white umbrella, a sword, a palm-leaf fan, a peacock fan, a yak-tail whisk, a diadem, a ruby, an alms bowl, a flower wreath, a blue lotus, a red lotus, a white lotus, a Puṇḍarīka lotus, a full pot, a full bowl, the ocean, the Cakkavāḷa mountains, the Himavā mountains, Mount Meru, the moon, the sun, the constellations, the four great islands, the two thousand small islands—all these, up to the entire retinue of a Cakkavatti king, are merely the attendants of the wheel-mark.

'Āyatapaṇhi' means having long heels or full heels. For others, the forefoot is long and the calf rests above the heel, making the heel appear as if it were cut off; but it is not so for the Bodhisatta. If the Bodhisatta's foot is divided into four parts, two parts form the forefoot, the calf rests on the third part, and on the fourth part stands the heel, which is like a ball of red wool, as if turned on a lathe to be perfectly round.

'Dīghangulī' means that while some fingers of others are long and some are short, it is not so for the Bodhisatta. The fingers and toes of the Bodhisatta are long like those of a monkey; they are thick at the base and gradually taper toward the tips, resembling sticks of haritāla (orpiment) kneaded with resin oil and rolled smooth. Therefore, he is called 'Dīghangulī'.

'Mudutalunahattapādo' means that his hands and feet are as tender as a tuft of cotton that has been beaten a hundred times and soaked in clarified butter. Just as they are tender at birth, they will remain tender even when he grows up. Because he has tender palms and soles, he is called 'Mudutalunahattapādo'.

'Jālahattapādo' does not mean having the spaces between the fingers connected by skin. Such a hand would be like a frog's hand, which is a human defect and would disqualify one from monkhood. For the Bodhisatta...
39:
Dust and dirt (rajojalla) refers to dust or grime. The phrase 'does not adhere (to the body of the Great Man)' means that just as water droplets do not stick to a lotus leaf but roll off, so too does dirt not stick. As for washing the hands and feet, the Buddhas perform this for the sake of physical comfort, for the merit of the donors, and also as a minor duty (vatta). This is because it is taught that a monk entering a monastery must wash his feet before entering.

Because the body hairs turn upwards at the tips as if looking at the beauty of the face, he is called 'Uddhaggaloma' (one with upward-pointing hair).

'Brahmujugatta' (one with a straight body like Brahma) means having a body as straight as Brahma's, being one whose tall body emerges straight. Generally, beings tend to bend at three places: the waist, the knees, and so on. When they bend at the waist, they lean backward, and at the other two places, they lean forward. Some tall people lean to the side; some walk with their faces tilted up as if counting the stars; some are thin and resemble a spit; some lean forward and walk tremblingly. This mark is to show that this Great Man will emerge straight, be tall in stature, and be like a golden gatepost in the celestial realm. It should be understood that the marks of the Great Man which are not yet complete at birth are taught with reference to how they will become in the future.

'Sattussada' (one with seven protuberances) means one who is fleshy and full at seven places: the backs of the two hands, the backs of the two feet, the two shoulders, and the neck (the upper back). In others, veins often stand out on the backs of the hands and feet, and joints and bones appear on the shoulders and neck. Though such people might look like petas (hungry ghosts), the Great Man is not like that. Because the Great Man is fleshy and full at these seven places, the veins are hidden, and the backs of the hands etc. appear like well-cast blocks of gold, or like a stone-carved statue or a painted image.

'Sīhapubbaddhakāya' (one with a body like the front of a lion) means that while only the front part of a lion is full and the hind part is not, the Great Man's body is full throughout like the front of a lion. That body, like a lion's, in various places by way of being low or high...
40:
...there is no lack of beauty or lack of proportion. Where it should be long, it is long; where it should be short, thick, slender, broad, or round, it is exactly so. Thus the Blessed One taught:

"Monks, when the fruit of pleasant kamma manifests, those limbs that are beautiful when long are long. Those limbs that are beautiful when short are short. Those limbs that are beautiful when thick are thick. Those limbs that are beautiful when slender are slender. Those limbs that are beautiful when broad are broad. Those limbs that are beautiful when round are round."

In this way, no painter or any powerful being in the world can replicate the physical form of the Great Man, which is fashioned by various types of wholesome consciousness and adorned with the ten perfections (pāramīs).

'Citantaramsa' (one with the space between the shoulders filled) means that 'antaramsa' refers to the space between the two shoulders. One who is fleshy and full in that space is called 'Citantaramsa'. In others, that area tends to be hollow, and the two sides of the spine appear separately. In the Great Man, however, a layer of flesh rises from the waist up to the shoulders and stays covering the back like a golden plate that has been set up.

'Nigrodhaparimaṇḍala' (proportioned like a banyan tree) means being as symmetrical as a banyan tree. Just as a banyan tree of fifty or a hundred cubits is equal in its trunk and main branches so that its height and width are the same, so too the Great Man's height is equal to the span of his outstretched arms (byāma). In others, if the height is long, the arms may be short, resulting in disproportion, but it is said that it is not so for the Great Man. That is why it was taught: "Yāvatakwassa kāyo" etc. There, "yāvatako assa" is joined (by sandhi) as "yāvatakwassa".

'Samavaṭṭakkhandha' (one with a well-rounded neck) means having a neck that is perfectly round. Some people have necks that are long, crooked, or flat like those of cranes, herons, or pigs...
41:
When (others) speak, their network of veins becomes visible, and a thin voice comes out; it is not so for the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta's body is like a well-cast block of gold; when he speaks, the network of veins does not appear, and he has a great voice like the sound of thunder.

In the term 'Rasaggasaggī', they are called 'rasaggasā' because they swallow and carry flavors. This is a name for the taste-nerves (rasaharaṇī). Those nerves are particularly excellent for that Great Man; therefore, he is called 'Rasaggasaggī'. For the Bodhisatta, seven thousand taste-nerves, all facing upwards, converge in the neck. Even when a piece of food the size of a sesame seed is placed on the tip of the tongue, it spreads throughout the whole body. Because of this, while practicing the Great Striving (mahāpadhāna), he was able to sustain his body with a single grain of rice or a handful of mung bean soup. For others, because they do not have such nerves, the essence (ojā) cannot spread throughout the whole body. Therefore, those people have many diseases.

Because he has a jaw like a lion's, he is called 'Sīhahanu'. In a lion's jaw, only the lower jaw is full, while the upper jaw is not. For the Bodhisatta, however, both jaws are as full as the moon on the twelfth day, like a lion's lower jaw. At that time, the fortune-telling Brahmins, looking at the end of the jaw, noted: "In these jaws, forty teeth—twenty below and twenty above—will stand evenly and without gaps," and they reported: "Great King, this child will have forty teeth," and so on. This is the meaning: other people who have a full set of teeth have only 32. This Great Man will have 40. Some teeth of others are high and some are low, being uneven; for this Great Man, they will be as even as a conch-shell slice cut with a metal plate. The teeth of others are wide-gapped like crocodiles'; when they eat fish or meat, the gaps become filled. For this Great Man, the teeth will be without gaps, like a row of diamonds set on a gold plate or like a line drawn with a brush. Others have decayed teeth. Therefore, some of their fangs are black or discolored. This Great Man has extremely white fangs; he will have fangs endowed with a brilliance that surpasses even the morning star (Venus).

'Pahūtajivha' means one with a large tongue. The tongues of others are thick, thin, short, rough, or uneven. The Bodhisatta's tongue, however, is soft, long, broad, and beautiful in color. To dispel the doubts of those who came to test this mark, the Great Man, because it is soft, rolls that tongue like a ball of thread and touches both nostrils; because it is long, (he touches) both ear-holes...
42: ...contemplates; because it is extensive, it covers the entire forehead up to the hairline. Thus, by showing the softness, length, and extensiveness of that tongue, he dispels their doubts. Referring to the tongue endowed with these three qualities, it is called Pahūtajivha. Brahmassara means others have broken voices, cracked voices, or voices like a crow. This Great Man, however, will be endowed with a voice like that of Mahābrahmā; because Mahābrahmā is not disturbed by bile or phlegm, his voice is clear. The kamma performed by the Bodhisatta also purifies the base (vatthu) of that voice. Because the base of the voice is pure, the voice that emerges from the navel is clear and endowed with the eight factors. Because he sounds like a karavīka bird, he is called Karavīkabhāṇī, meaning one who has a voice as sweet as the sound of an intoxicated karavīka bird. Abhinīlanetta does not mean the entire eye is blue; rather, in the places where it should be blue, they are endowed with a blue color like a very pure ummā flower. In places where it should be yellow, it is yellow like the kaṇikāra flower; in places where it should be red, it is red like the bandhujīvaka flower; in places where it should be white, it is white like the star Venus; in places where it should be black, it is black like a gallnut. They appear like ruby lattice windows opened in a golden mansion. In the term Gopakhuma, pakhuma refers to the entire eye socket; that eye socket is thick for a black calf and clear for a red calf; it means one who has eye sockets like those of a young red calf born at that moment. Others' eye sockets are not perfect, being either protruding or sunken like those of elephants or mice. The eyes of the Bodhisatta, however, are surrounded by eyelashes that are soft, smooth, dark blue, and delicate, like polished rubies. Uṇṇā is the uṇṇāloma hair. 'Between the eyebrows' means it grows right in the middle of the two eyebrows at the bridge of the nose; it rises upwards and stays in the middle of the forehead. 'Pure white' means it is clean and bright, having a color like the star Venus. 'Soft' means it is like a layer of cotton wool that has been dipped in clarified butter and beaten a hundred times. 'Like cotton wool' means it is like silk-cotton or vine-cotton; this is an analogy for the whiteness of that uṇṇāloma. If that uṇṇāloma is pulled from the tip, it is half the length of an arm.
43:
(The hairs) are distributed evenly, curling to the right, with the tips pointing upwards. They are endowed with a most pleasing splendor, like a silver bubble placed in the middle of a golden plate, or like a stream of milk flowing from a golden pot, or like the planet Venus in the sky at dawn.

'Uṇhīsasīsa' (turban-headed) is spoken of based on two meanings: having a full forehead and having a well-formed head. Starting from the right ear-edge of the Great Man (Mahāpurisa), a layer of flesh arises, covering and filling the entire forehead, and ending at the left ear-edge; this layer of flesh is beautiful like a royal turban (diadem) worn by kings. Seeing this mark of the Great Man, kings are said to have fashioned their turbans. This is one meaning. Others have imperfect heads; some have heads like monkeys, some like fruits, some like bones, some like elephants, some like gourds, and some have sloping heads. The head of the Great Man, however, is perfectly full like a water bubble, as if rounded like a starfruit. Between these two, in the first method, he is called 'Uṇhīsasīsa' because his head appears as if wrapped with a turban. In the second method, he is called 'Uṇhīsasīsa' because his head is rounded in all parts like a turban.

## Commentary on the Naming of Vipassī

The words 'with all desirable things' (sabbakāmehi) are spoken as if they were done after the marks were read; however, it should not be understood this way. It should be understood that the prognosticators were first satisfied, and only then was the reading of the marks performed. The details of this matter have been explained in the section on 'Descent into the Womb' (Gabbhokkanti). 'They suckled' (pāyenti) means they fed him milk. Sixty nurses, free from defects and endowed with sweet milk, were provided to serve the prince; likewise, there were sixty nurses each skilled in various other tasks. Sixty men were employed to command these nurses, and sixty ministers were employed to record what should and should not be done by those people. Thus, there were six groups of attendants: four groups of sixty women and two groups of sixty men. 'White umbrella' (setacchatta) refers to the white umbrella of the devas. The ancestral white umbrella of the lineage remained only in the treasury chamber. In the phrases 'let not cold or...' (mā naṃ sītaṃ vā), the meaning should be understood as 'let it not overcome' (mā abhibhavi). 'Svāssudaṃ' is 'so assudaṃ'. 'From lap to lap' (aṅkeneva aṅkaṃ) means from one person's arms to another person's arms, from one...
44: ...shoulder to another's shoulder (touching). 'Parihariyati' means is carried or is brought. 'Mañjussara' means one who has a voice that is not harsh. 'Vaggussara' means one who has a voice that is skilled and proficient. 'Madhurassara' means one who has a sweet voice. 'Pemaniyassara' means one who has a voice that inspires love. Among these (four types of voice), regarding the sweetness of the voice of the karavīka birds, it should be known thus: when karavīka birds peck at a ripe mango that has a sweet taste with their beaks, drink the juice that flows out, flap their wings and sing, four-footed animals dance as if intoxicated. Four-footed animals searching for food also drop the grass in their mouths and listen to that sound. Wild beasts, while chasing young prey, stop without putting down their raised feet. The young prey being chased also forget the fear of death and stop. Birds flying in the sky also spread their wings and stop while listening to that sound. Fish in the water also spread their fins and stop while listening to that sound. Thus, karavīka birds have sweet voices. Queen Asandhimittā, the queen of King Dhammāsoka, asked the Saṅgha, 'Venerable sirs, is there anyone who has a voice like the voice of the Buddha?' (The Saṅgha replied), 'The karavīka bird has.' (When she asked), 'Venerable sirs, where are those birds?' (they replied), 'They are in the Himālayas.' That queen said to the king, 'Great King, I wish to see a karavīka bird.' The king sent a golden cage, saying, 'Let the karavīka bird come and perch in this cage.' The cage went and stood before a karavīka bird. That bird thought, 'This is a cage come by royal command; I cannot help but go,' and perched in that cage. The cage returned and stood before the king. (However), they could not make the karavīka bird sing. Then the king asked, 'Friends, why does this bird not sing?' (They replied), 'Great King, it is because it does not see its relatives.' Then the king had the bird surrounded by mirrors. That bird, seeing its own reflection, thought, 'My relatives have come,' flapped its wings, and sang with a sweet voice like someone blowing a ruby flute. The people of the whole city danced as if intoxicated. Asandhimittā thought, 'Even the voice of this animal is this sweet; how much more (sweet) would be the voice of the Buddha who has attained the glory of Omniscience?' She developed joy (pīti), and without letting go of that joy, she, along with seven hundred palace women, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). Thus it is sweet.
45: It should be known that the voice of Prince Vipassī was a hundred times, a thousand times sweeter than the voice of the karavīka bird. 'Kammavipākaja' means it is not produced by meditation; rather, by the power of the fruit of kamma, a physical eye (māṃsacakkhu) similar to the eye of the devas arises. With that eye, from among sesame seeds placed in a sesame cart, he could identify and pick out a single sesame seed, saying, 'This sesame seed is that sesame seed.' In the word 'Vipassī', this is the etymological definition: he sees clearly, free from the darkness caused by closing the eyes at all times; because he sees with open eyes, he is called 'Vipassī'. In the second sense: because he sees by investigating and investigating, he is called 'Vipassī'. It means he sees by selecting and investigating. It means he sees and understands cause and effect, or he carries out (the task). One day, while the king was sitting in the place of judgment and deciding cases, they brought the adorned Great Man (Prince Vipassī) and placed him in his hands. While the king was fondling the prince on his lap, the ministers (unfairly) made property that had an owner into property without an owner. The Bodhisatta made a sound of displeasure. The king said, 'What is this? Investigate!' When they investigated, seeing no other reason, they thought, 'This must be because the case was judged unfairly,' and they again made the property that had an owner as having an owner. Wishing to test, 'Does the prince do this knowingly?' they again made property with an owner as having no owner. Again, the Bodhisatta made the sound in the same way. Then the king realized, 'The Great Man knows,' and from then on, he was mindful and not negligent. Referring to this incident, it is said, 'The prince sees and understands cause and effect by investigating and investigating.' In the words 'Vassika' etc., a comfortable place for living during the rainy season is called 'Vassika'. In the remaining ones (Hemantika, Gimmhika), it is the same way. Here, the etymological definition is: living during the rainy season is 'Vassa'; because it is suitable for the rainy season, it is called 'Vassika'. In the remaining words, it is the same way. Among those (three palaces), the Vassika palace should be neither too high nor too low. The doors and windows should also be neither too many nor too few. The floors, coverings, and food here are suitable only when they are a mixture (of hot and cold). In the Hemantika palace, the pillars and walls are low. The doors and windows are few and have small openings. To let heat in, the edges of the walls are extended. As for the floors, coverings, and clothes, here...
46:
Blankets and such with warming properties are suitable (during the winter season). The food is prepared with the finest oils and butter, relies on spicy flavors, and is dry without water. In the summer season, the pillars and walls are high. In this summer palace, the doors and air-windows (latticed windows) are very wide. Floor coverings and such made of fine dukūla cloth are suitable. The food is abundant and relies on sweet flavors. Near the air-windows, new pots are placed, filled with water, and covered with blue lotuses and such. In various places, water-drop machines (fountains) are constructed, from which streams of water flow like rain falling from the devas.

'Nippurisehi' means devoid of men (only women are present). In this context, it is not only that men are absent from the dancing and musical performances; men are absent from all places. Even the doorkeepers are only women, and those who perform services such as bathing are also only women. The King thought, "If one who enjoys such sovereign bliss and luxury sees a man, the perception of 'manhood' may arise; let not that perception arise in my son," and thus he placed only women in all affairs.

## The Explanation of the First Recitation Section (Paṭhamabhāṇavāra) is Finished.

## Explanation of the Old Man (Jiṇṇapurisa)

43-4. In the second recitation section, 'gopānasivaṅkaṃ' means curved like the rafters of a house. 'Bhaggaṃ' means bent in three places: the shoulders, the waist, and the knees. 'Daṇḍaparāyanaṃ' means walking with a staff, having a staff as one's support. 'Āturaṃ' means oppressed by old age. 'Gatayobbanaṃ' means having passed youth, standing in the final stage of life. 'Disvā' means seeing that man shown by the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās through their psychic power in front of the chariot, at a time when the chariot went ahead and the troops followed behind, even though he was well-guarded and surrounded by an army about half a league (yojana) in size. The Suddhāvāsa Brahmās thought, "The Great Being (Mahāpurisa) is stuck in the five cords of sensual pleasure like an elephant sunk in the mud; we shall cause him to gain mindfulness," and thus they showed that old man. Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw the man thus shown. The Brahmās showed that man so that the Bodhisatta would not be heedless and would be able to converse with the charioteer. "Who is this man?" he asked, "What does 'old man' mean? I have never seen such a person before."
47:
'Tena hi' means: if I too must have such hair and such a body, then, friend charioteer, if that is so (let us return). 'Alaṃ dānajja uyyānabhūmiyā' means: although he set out thinking "I will go to the garden today," he spoke in accordance with spiritual urgency (saṃvega), having a mind that was agitated and trembling, thinking that there was no more use for that garden. Upon returning to the palace, he dismissed the assembly of women and sat alone in his chamber. 'Yatra hi nāma' means: where there is birth, aging is manifest; that birth is indeed loathsome and blameworthy. He sat like one pierced in the heart by the first arrow, as if digging up and cutting the root of birth.

The King had been listening attentively since the time the prognosticators spoke. Hearing that "the Prince returned from the road while going to the garden," he summoned the charioteer. Regarding the words "Mā heva kho" etc., he thought, "Let him only exercise kingship, let him not become a monk; let the words of the Brahmins not be true."

## Explanation of the Sick Man (Byādhipurisa)

Just as before, he saw the man shown by the Suddhāvāsa Brahmās. 'Ābādhikaṃ' means one who is pained by an uneven sensation that destroys the postures. 'Dukkhitaṃ' means one who is suffering from the pain of disease. 'Bāḷhagilānaṃ' means one who is severely ill. 'Palipannaṃ' means one who is wallowing (in his own excrement and urine). Here too, he sat like one pierced by a second arrow, as if digging up the root of birth, thinking: where there is birth, these two (aging and sickness) are manifest; that birth is blameworthy, only non-arising is secure.

## Explanation of the Dead Man (Kālaṅkatapurisa)

'Vilātaṃ' means a litter (palanquin). 'Petaṃ' means one who has gone from this life. 'Kālaṅkataṃ' means one who is dead; it means one who has died having exhausted that period of time for which he was to live. This man was also shown by the Brahmās just as before. Here too, he sat like one pierced by a third arrow, as if digging up the root of birth, thinking: where there is birth, these three (aging, sickness, and death) are manifest; that birth is blameworthy, only non-arising is secure.
49:
Regarding those who went forth following him (anupabbajita): Why is it not said here, "having departed from the royal city of Bandhumatī," as is said later regarding the renunciation of Khaṇḍa and Tissa? It is because they heard the news only after they had already departed from the city. All those people were the attendants of Prince Vipassī. They had come early in the morning to serve him, but not finding the Prince, they went to eat their morning meal. When they returned after eating and asked, "Where is the Prince?", they heard, "He has gone to the garden." Thinking, "We will pay respects to the Prince right there," they were departing from the city when they met the returning charioteer. When they heard the words, "The Prince has become a monk," they took off all their jeweled ornaments right where they heard the news, accepted saffron-dyed cloths from the market stalls, shaved their hair and beards, and went forth as monks. Thus, because they heard the news only after leaving the city and reaching the outskirts, it is not said here, "having departed from the royal city of Bandhumatī."

"He set out on a wandering (desacārī)" means that in every place he reached, a large pavilion was built and alms were prepared. He wandered for four months, accepting only the alms-food offered by the crowds of people who came and invited him for the next day.

"Crowded by many people" means he was surrounded by this assembly of monks. When did such a thought arise in the Great Being? It arose on the fourteenth day, knowing that "tomorrow will be the full moon day of Visākhā." At that time, the Great Being thought, "These people surrounded me before when I was a layman, and now they surround me in the same way; what is the use of this company?" Being weary of living in company, he thought, "I will go this very day," but then reconsidered, "Today is no longer the proper time; if I go now, all these people will know. I will go only tomorrow."

On that day, in a village similar to Uruvelā, the villagers invited him for the next day. Those villagers prepared only thick milk rice (ghanāmuddhapāyāsa) for the Great Being and the eighty-four thousand monks. Then, on the next day, the Great Being performed the meal duties in that village together with those monks and returned only to his usual dwelling place. There, those monks performed the major and minor duties for the Great Being and then entered their respective places for the night and day rest. The Great Being also entered the leaf-hut and sat down.

When the time of midday arrived, the birds rested quietly.
The great forest seemed to roar; the sound of that forest appeared to me as something fearsome.
50:
In such a time of fear for all beings, a time of heat, for those who delight in such solitude, he thought, "This is the time (for striving)," and having come out (from the dwelling) and closed the door of the leaf-hut, he proceeded towards the Bodhimaṇḍa. On other occasions, although he had seen the Bodhimaṇḍa while wandering in that area, the desire to sit there had never once arisen. But on that day, the Great Being's knowledge had reached maturity; therefore, upon seeing the adorned Bodhimaṇḍa, the desire to ascend it arose. That Great Being approached from the southern direction, circumambulated it to the right, and having prepared a fourteen-cubit throne (pallaṅka) on the eastern side, he resolved upon the fourfold effort (caturaṅgaviriya) and sat down, vowing, "I shall not rise from this seat until I become a Buddha." It is with reference to this that it was said, "He dwelt alone, secluded from the group."

In another way: those five monks came to serve the Great Being in the evening and sat surrounding the leaf-hut. Saying, "The time is long past, let us investigate," they opened and looked into the leaf-hut. Not seeing the Great Being, they did not follow and search for him, thinking, "Where has he gone?" They said, "The Great Being seems to be weary of living in company and wishes to dwell alone; we shall see him only after he becomes a Buddha," and they set out wandering towards the middle region of Jambudīpa.

## Explanation of the Bodhisatta's Insight (Abhibhesa)

'Vāsūpagatassa' means of one who has come to stay for a night at the Bodhimaṇḍa. 'Rahogatassa' means of one who has gone to a secluded place. 'Paṭisallīnassa' means of one who is dwelling in solitude. 'Kicchaṃ' means suffering. The two terms 'cavati ca upapajjati ca' (passing away and being reborn) are said with reference to repeated death and rebirth. In the term 'jarāmaraṇassa', since the Great Being had seen only aging, sickness, and death when he renounced the world, only aging and death became manifest to him. Therefore, he said, "jarāmaraṇassa." To one who thus firmly enters with aging and death as the basis—like one descending from the peak of existence—[the Buddha said]: Monks, then to the Bodhisatta Vipassī, this thought occurred.

'Yoniso manasikārā' means attention by way of means (upāya-manasikāra) and initial attention (pathama-manasikāra). For one who attends to impermanence and so on as impermanence and so on, it is called wise attention (yoniso manasikāra). This wise attention also arises by the power of contemplation (anupassanā) which observes arising and passing away, thinking, "When what exists do birth and so on come to be? When what does not exist do they not come to be?"...
51:
Alternatively—therefore, through this wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) and through this skillful attention (upāya manasikāra), the penetration (abhisamaya) of the Bodhisatta's wisdom arose. The Bodhisatta's wisdom, which asks 'When what exists does aging-and-death (jarāmaraṇa) occur?', has met with the cause of that aging-and-death. What is that cause? It is indeed birth (jāti). Therefore, he said, 'When there is birth, aging-and-death occurs.' The meaning here is that the meeting of the Bodhisatta with the wisdom that comprehends the cause of aging-and-death has occurred. In this manner, all terms should be understood.

In this place, 'When there is mentality-materiality (nāmarūpa), there is consciousness (viññāṇa),' although it should be said 'When there are volitional formations (saṅkhāra), there is consciousness' and 'When there is ignorance (avijjā), there are volitional formations,' both were not taken. Why? Because ignorance and volitional formations belong to the past life, and this insight (vipassanā) cannot be associated with those past lives. This is because the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) enters into and contemplates only by the power of the present. If it is asked, 'Can one become a Buddha without seeing ignorance and volitional formations?'—Indeed, it is not possible. However, in this context, those ignorance and volitional formations are seen only by the power of existence (bhava), clinging (upādāna), and craving (taṇhā). Here, the discourse on Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) is explained in detail. That discourse has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga.

'Paccudāvattati' means it turns back. Here, which consciousness turns back? Both the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) and the insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) turn back. Among them, the rebirth-linking consciousness turns back because of the cause (paccaya); the insight-knowledge turns back because of the object (ārammaṇa). Both cannot transcend mentality-materiality; they cannot go beyond mentality-materiality. By this much, in 'jāyetha vā' etc., when consciousness is the cause of mentality-materiality, and mentality-materiality is also the cause of consciousness, and both are being mutual causes for each other, by this much cause 'there is birth... pe... upapajjetha vā (there is rebirth-linking)'; apart from this, what else would be birth... pe... rebirth-linking? Are these not the only things that are birth... pe... rebirth-linking? Having thus shown the five terms along with the repeated death and rebirth-linking, and again assigning the meaning stated as 'ettāvatā'—having said, 'Because of this mentality-materiality as cause, consciousness occurs; because of consciousness as cause, mentality-materiality occurs'—thereafter, in the manner of the forward causal condition (anuloma-paccaya), based on mentality-materiality because of consciousness, in order to show birth, aging, and death later on, he said, 'Because of mentality-materiality as cause, the six sense-bases (saḷāyatana) occur,' and so on. Therein, 'kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo hoti' means the arising of the entire mass of suffering characterized by birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. Thus, the Great Being saw the arising of the entire mass of suffering in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha).
52:
Samudaya, samudaya means arising, arising. 'In things unheard of before' means in things not heard before, not previously heard. In the terms beginning with 'the eye (cakkhu) arose,' there are only the various types of wisdom that see arising and passing away. Because of the sense of seeing, it is called 'eye' (cakkhu); because of the sense of making known, it is called 'knowledge' (ñāṇa); because of the sense of knowing in various ways, it is called 'wisdom' (paññā); because of the sense of arising through piercing and penetrating, it is called 'true knowledge' (vijjā); and because of the sense of making bright, it is called 'light' (āloka). Thus—'Because of the sense of seeing, the eye arose. Because of the sense of knowing, knowledge arose. Because of the sense of knowing in various ways, wisdom arose. Because of the sense of penetrating knowledge, true knowledge arose. Because of the sense of making bright, light arose. The eye-dhamma, which has the sense of seeing, is the meaning (the result). The knowledge-dhamma, which has the sense of knowing, is the meaning. The wisdom-dhamma, which has the sense of knowing in various ways, is the meaning. The true knowledge-dhamma, which has the sense of penetrating knowledge, is the meaning. The light-dhamma, which has the sense of making bright, is the meaning.' What is taught by these many terms? It only teaches the mere knowing of the causal law that 'when this cause exists, this result occurs.' Or, it teaches the tender insight (taruna-vipassanā) that enters the cognitive process (vīthi).

'I have attained this path' means I have reached this path. 'Path' (magga) refers to the path of insight (vipassanā-magga). 'For the sake of enlightenment' (bodhi) means for the sake of knowing the Four Noble Truths, or for the sake of knowing Nibbāna. Alternatively, it is called 'Bodhi' because it knows; it is a name for the Noble Path (Ariya-magga), and it is also said to be for the sake of that Noble Path. This is because the path of insight is the fundamental basis of the Noble Path. Now, wishing to bring forth and show that path, he said 'because of the cessation of mentality-materiality,' and so on. In this context, by the terms such as 'the cessation of consciousness,' only Nibbāna is taught. Thus, the Great Being saw the cessation, which is the non-arising of all suffering in the round of rebirth.

Cessation, cessation (nirodha) means non-arising, non-arising. The terms such as 'eye' (cakkhu) are just as the meanings previously stated. Here, however, by all these terms, he only teaches the mere knowing of cessation as 'when this cause does not exist, this result does not occur,' or he teaches the powerful insight (balava-vipassanā) that leads to the attainment of the Path.

'At another time' means at a time other than that, after knowing the causal law and the cessation of the causal law. 'In the aggregates of clinging' (upādānakkhandhā) means in the aggregates that are the cause of clinging. 'Being one who habitually contemplates arising and passing away' means while habitually contemplating that arising and passing away which was first seen. 'He dwelt' means he dwelt carrying the insight that leads to the Path which has reached its peak. Why is this said? All Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections (pāramī), in their final birth...
53:
...on the very day of their birth, they go forth into the homeless life, become monks, strive in the practice of meditation, ascend the Seat of Enlightenment (Bodhipallaṅka), and after subduing the army of Māra, in the first watch of the night, they recollect the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsanussati-ñāṇa); in the second watch, they purify the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa); in the third watch, they contemplate Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), and arising from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), they enter into the five-constituent aggregates (pañcavokāra-khandha), seeing the fifty characteristics by way of arising and passing away, and having developed insight up to the knowledge of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū-ñāṇa), they penetrate and know all the qualities of a Buddha through the Noble Path (Ariya-magga). This Great Being also was one who had fulfilled the perfections. That Great Being, having done everything according to the stated order, in the final watch, arose from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, entered into the five-constituent aggregates, and strove in the insight of arising and passing away in the manner described. To show that matter, he spoke these words.

In those words, 'This is matter (rūpa)' means this is matter, this much is matter, there is no matter beyond this; it refers to the nature of being subject to change, and beginning with the distinction between the great elements (mahābhūta) and derived matter (upādā-rūpa), it means the absolute comprehension of matter by way of characteristic (lakkhaṇa), function (rasa), manifestation (paccupaṭṭhāna), and proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna). By this term 'This is the arising of matter,' it means seeing the arising of matter thus comprehended. Therein, 'thus' means the arising occurs in this way. Its detail is: 'One who sees the characteristic of arising as "because of the arising of ignorance, matter arises; because of the arising of craving, matter arises; because of the arising of kamma, matter arises; because of the arising of nutriment (āhāra), matter arises," is said to see the arising of the aggregate of matter'—thus it should be known. Regarding cessation also: 'Because of the cessation of ignorance, matter ceases... pe... one who sees the characteristic of change is also said to see the cessation of the aggregate of matter'—this is its detail.

In the terms 'This is feeling (vedanā)' etc., it also means this is feeling, this much is feeling, there is no feeling beyond this. This is perception (saññā), these are formations (saṅkhāra), this is consciousness (viññāṇa), this much is consciousness, there is no consciousness beyond this. It refers to the nature of experiencing, perceiving, forming, and knowing, and beginning with the distinctions of feeling such as pleasure (sukha), perception such as perception of forms, formations such as contact (phassa), and consciousness such as eye-consciousness, it means the absolute comprehension of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness by way of characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause. By the terms 'This is the arising of feeling' etc., it means seeing the arising of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness thus comprehended. Therein also, 'thus' means the arising occurs in this way. Their details should be known in the same way as stated for matter: 'Because of the arising of ignorance, feeling arises.' The distinction here is: in the three mental aggregates, it is not said 'because of the arising of nutriment,' but 'because of the arising of contact (phassa).' In the aggregate of consciousness...
56:
These are the names of ignorance (avijjā) and other factors that have formations (saṅkhāra) as their causes. All terms such as "the stilling of all formations" (sabbasaṅkhārasamatha) refer only to Nibbāna. This is because, upon reaching Nibbāna, the agitations of all formations are stilled and cooled; therefore, it is called "the stilling of all formations." Upon reaching Nibbāna, all acquisitions (upadhi) are relinquished, all cravings (taṇhā) are exhausted, all defilements and lust (rāga) fade away, and all sufferings cease; therefore, it is called "the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, and cessation" (sabbūpadhipaṭinissaggo taṇhākkhayo virāgo nirodho). That craving weaves together one existence with another, and kamma with its result; therefore, it is called "vāna" (weaving). Because of the exit from that weaving, it is called "Nibbāna."

"That teaching would be wearying to me" means that teaching the Dhamma to those who do not understand would be exhausting and oppressive to me. It means there would only be physical weariness and physical suffering; for the Buddhas, neither of these exists in the mental aspect.

"Apissu" is a particle (nipāta) meaning "moreover" (anubrūhana). This word indicates that "not only did such a thought occur, but these verses also became manifest." In the words such as "Vipassī," it means the Blessed One Vipassī, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. "Anacchariyā" means consistent with what is wonderful. "Paṭibhaṃsu" means they became the objects of analytical insight (paṭibhāna-ñāṇa), reaching the state of being contemplated.

"Kicchena" means with difficulty and hardship, not through painful practice (dukkhapaṭipadā). This is because, for the Buddhas, all four paths (magga) are only pleasant practice (sukhapaṭipadā). However, during the period of fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), while still being one with lust, hatred, and delusion, this was said in reference to the practice of attainment (āgamanīyapaṭipadā), such as when he reached the state of being cut and mutilated in lives like Khantivādī, or when he gave away his decorated head, drew blood from his throat, plucked out his well-adorned eyes, and gave away his lineage-sustaining son and beloved wife to all who came to ask.

In the word "Halaṃ," the letter "ha" is merely a particle; it means "alaṃ" (enough/no need). "Pakāsituṃ" means for the purpose of teaching. It means there is no need to teach this Dhamma that was attained with such difficulty; what benefit would there be in teaching it? "Rāgadousaparetehi" means by those who are oppressed by lust and hatred, or by those who follow after lust and hatred.

"Paṭisotagāmi" (going against the stream) refers to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, which is the opposite of permanence and so forth—namely, impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness. "Rāgarattā" means those who are infatuated with the lust for sensual pleasures (kāmarāga), the lust for existence (bhavarāga), and the lust for views (diṭṭhirāga). "Na dakkhandi" means they cannot see according to this nature of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness...
57:
(Beings) will see; who would be able to make such beings who cannot see accept (the Dhamma) in this way? "Enveloped in a mass of darkness" means overwhelmed by the mass of ignorance (avijjā). "Because of the state of having little effort" means by the state of having no effort, by the state of not wishing to teach (the Dhamma).

Why did the mind of the Blessed One incline in this manner? Did that Blessed One not fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) and reach omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) by making the aspiration: "Having been liberated (from saṃsāra), I shall liberate (others); having crossed over, I shall help (others) cross over," and "What benefit is there in realizing the Dhamma in an obscure form in this world? Having attained omniscience, I shall save the multitude of beings including devas"? It is true that he made such an aspiration; nevertheless, his mind inclined this way due to the power of reflection. After attaining omniscience, when the Blessed One reflected on the thickness of the defilements of beings and the profundity of the Dhamma, the thickness of beings' defilements and the profundity of the Dhamma became manifest in every aspect. At that time, he thought: "These beings are full of defilements and are extremely defiled, like a jar of vinegar, like a jar filled with curd, like an old cloth smeared with the cream of oil, or like a hand smeared with eye-ointment. They are reddened with lust, corrupted with hatred, and bewildered by delusion. How will these beings be able to penetrate and know?" Thus, it should be understood that his mind inclined this way due to the power of reflecting on the thickness of defilements.

"This Dhamma is also as deep as the mass of water supporting the earth, as difficult to see as a mustard seed covered by a mountain, and as difficult to know as touching the tips of a horsehair split a hundred times. While I was striving to penetrate this Dhamma, there was no gift I had not given, no virtue (sīla) I had not observed, and no perfection (pāramī) I had not fulfilled. Although there was no lack of effort for me like this, the earth did not tremble when I was subduing Mara's army, nor did it tremble when I was recollecting the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsānussatiñāṇa) in the first watch, nor did it tremble when I was purifying the divine eye (dibbacakkhuñāṇa) in the middle watch. However, in the last watch, when I penetrated the Dhamma of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), my ten-thousandfold world system trembled. How will the ordinary worldly people be able to penetrate this Dhamma, which even one with sharp wisdom like me penetrated with such hardship and weariness?" Thus, it should be understood that his mind inclined this way due to the power of reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma.
58: Furthermore, the Blessed One's mind inclined in this way because he desired to teach upon being entreated by the Great Brahma. Indeed, the Blessed One knew: 'If my mind inclines toward the state of having little effort, the Great Brahma will entreat me to teach the Dhamma. These beings also hold the Brahma in high regard. Those beings will think—The Blessed One, who is the Teacher, did not wish to teach the Dhamma; then the Great Brahma entreated him and made him teach; O friends... the Dhamma is indeed wonderful, the Dhamma is indeed noble—and they will desire to listen.' Based on this reason also, the Blessed One's mind inclined toward the state of having little effort; it should be understood that it did not incline because he truly did not wish to teach. In the word 'aññatarassa,' although it says 'a certain one,' it should be understood as the Great Brahma who is the chief in this universe. 'O friends... the world is perishing!'—that Brahma uttered this sound so that the Brahmas in the ten-thousandfold world system would hear it and all would assemble. 'Yatra hi nāma' means in which world. 'Appeared in front' means appearing together with those ten thousand Brahmas. 'Apparajakkhajātika' refers to those who have little dust of lust, hatred, and delusion in their eye of wisdom. 'Assavanatā' means because of not hearing. 'Will come to be' means that those who have performed merit under previous Buddhas and are like matured lotuses, longing only for the Dhamma upon meeting the sunlight (of teaching), will be those who understand the Dhamma and are worthy of reaching the state of an Ariya at the end of a single verse; they will be not just one or two, but hundreds of thousands. 'Ajjhesana' means this entreaty made three times. 'Buddhacakkhu' (Buddha-eye) refers to the knowledge of the higher and lower faculties of beings (indriyaparopariyattañāṇa) and the knowledge of their tendencies and underlying dispositions (āsayānusayañāṇa). These two knowledges are called 'Buddhacakkhu.' Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa) is called 'Samantacakkhu' (the all-seeing eye). The three path knowledges (maggañāṇa) are called 'Dhammacakkhu' (the Dhamma-eye). As mentioned in 'apparajakkha' and so forth, those with little dust such as lust in their eye of wisdom are called 'apparajakkha.' Those with much dust are called 'mahārajakkha.' Those with sharp faculties such as faith are called 'tikkhindriya.' Those with dull faculties are called 'mudindriya.' Those with good qualities such as faith are called 'svākāra.' Those who can remember the taught subject matter and can be easily made to understand are called 'suviññāpaya.' Those who are accustomed to seeing danger in the next life and in faults are called 'paralokavajjabhayadassāvī.'
59:
In this context, the Pali text states: "A person with faith has little dust of defilements; a person without faith has much dust of defilements. ... One who exerts effort ... one who is lazy ... one who is mindful ... one who is negligent ... one who is concentrated ... one who is unconcentrated ... one who is wise ... one who is unwise has much dust of defilements. Likewise, a person with faith has sharp faculties ... a wise person frequently contemplates the danger in the world beyond; an unwise person does not frequently contemplate the danger in the world beyond. The 'world' (loka) refers to the world of aggregates (khandha), the world of elements (dhātu), the world of sense bases (āyatana), the world of the existence of success (sampatti-bhava), the world of the existence of failure (vipatti-bhava), the world of the origin of success (sampatti-sambhava), and the world of the origin of failure (vipatti-sambhava). In terms of one world: all beings subsist on nutriment. In terms of two worlds: mind and matter (nāma and rūpa). In terms of three worlds: the three feelings (vedanā). In terms of four worlds: the four nutriments (āhāra). In terms of five worlds: the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha). In terms of six worlds: the six internal sense bases (ajjhattika āyatana). In terms of seven worlds: the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). In terms of eight worlds: the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma). In terms of nine worlds: the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). In terms of ten worlds: the ten sense bases. In terms of twelve worlds: the twelve sense bases. In terms of eighteen worlds: the eighteen elements (dhātu). 'Fault' (vajja) means all defilements are faults, all misconducts are faults, all volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) are faults, and all kamma leading to rebirth are faults. Thus, perceiving a keen sense of danger in this world as well as in this fault appears clearly like a murderer (vadhaka) standing with a raised sword. Through these fifty aspects, one knows, sees, recognizes, and penetrates these five faculties; this is the Buddha's Knowledge of the Higher and Lower Faculties of Beings (Indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa)," as stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

"Uppaliniyaṃ" means in a lotus pond. The same method applies to the remaining words. "Antonimuggaposīni" means other lotuses also grow while remaining submerged within the water. "Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni" means those that stand having emerged above the water. Among those standing above the water, those waiting for the touch of the sun's rays are the lotuses that will bloom today. Those standing level with the water are the lotuses that will bloom tomorrow. Those still growing within the water without having emerged yet are the lotuses that will bloom on the third day. There are also other red and blue lotuses born in the water that have not yet emerged; they will never bloom and will only become food for fish and turtles. These lotuses are not included in the Pali text. However, they are mentioned because they are presented as an analogy. Just like these four types of lotuses, there are four types of individuals: Ugghaṭitaññū, Vipañcitaññū, Neyya, and Padaparama. Among these four:
60:
An individual who attains the realization of Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) at the very moment a teaching is delivered in brief is called an "Ugghaṭitaññū." An individual who attains the realization of Dhamma only when the meaning of a teaching delivered in brief is explained in detail is called a "Vipañcitaññū." An individual who attains the realization of Dhamma gradually through instruction, questioning, wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra), and by associating with, attending to, and serving virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta) is called a "Neyya." An individual who, despite much hearing, much speaking, much learning, much memorizing, and much reciting, does not attain the realization of Dhamma in that lifetime is called a "Padaparama."

At that time, when the Blessed One surveyed the ten thousand world systems, which were like a lotus pond, He saw: "Individuals like the Ugghaṭitaññū who are like the lotuses that will bloom today; individuals like the Vipañcitaññū who are like the lotuses that will bloom tomorrow; individuals like the Neyya who are like the lotuses that will bloom on the third day; and individuals like the Padaparama who are like the lotuses that will become food for fish and turtles." Even as He saw them, He saw them in every aspect, thinking: "This many people have little dust of defilements; this many people have much dust of defilements. Among them, this many people are Ugghaṭitaññū."

Among these individuals, the Buddha's Dhamma teaching brings fulfillment of benefit in this very life for the first three types; for the Padaparama individuals, however, it serves for the benefit of becoming a latent tendency (vāsanā) in the future.

Then, the Blessed One, knowing the Dhamma teaching that could benefit these four types of individuals and having formed the desire to teach, once again divided all beings in the three planes of existence into two groups: the capable (bhabba) and the incapable (abhabba). Referring to this division, it is taught in the Vibhaṅga and Paṭisambhidāmagga: "Those beings who are possessed of the obstruction of kamma (kammāvaraṇa), possessed of the obstruction of result (vipākāvaraṇa), possessed of the obstruction of defilement (kilesāvaraṇa), who lack faith, lack desire, and are unwise, are incapable of entering the right path of assurance (sammatta-niyāma) regarding wholesome states; these beings are called 'abhabba.' What kind of beings are called 'bhabba'? Those beings who are not possessed of the obstruction of kamma ... (as before) ... these beings are called 'bhabba.'"

In making this distinction, He set aside all incapable individuals and took hold of only the capable individuals with His knowledge, dividing them into six groups: "This many people have a lustful temperament (rāga-carita); this many people have temperaments of hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), speculative thought (vitakka), faith (saddhā), and wisdom (buddhi)." Having done this, thinking "I shall teach the Dhamma"...
61:
Brahma, knowing that intention and being filled with joy, addressed the Blessed One with verses. With reference to this meaning, it was said: "Monks, then the Great Brahma..." and so forth.

In that context, "ajjhabhāsi" means addressing specifically, or addressing by initiating an important matter.

"Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhito" means just like standing on the summit of a solid mountain made entirely of rock. Indeed, for one standing on such a mountain summit, there is no need for actions such as raising or stretching the neck to see. "Tathūpamaṃ" means having an analogy similar to that rocky mountain. The summary meaning here is: Just as a man with sight standing on a mountain summit looks upon the people all around, so too, O Blessed One, who are wise, endowed with Omniscience, and the All-Seeing One (Samantacakkhu), being free from sorrow Yourself, ascend the palace made of the wisdom of Dhamma and look upon the multitude of beings who are immersed in sorrow and oppressed by birth and old age; please contemplate them.

The meaning here is: At the foot of a mountain, a large field is made all around, and in those plots, huts are built and lamps are lit at night. At that time, a fourfold darkness occurs. Then, a man with sight standing on the mountain summit, looking down at the ground, does not see the field, the plots, the huts, or the people sleeping there, but sees only the flames of the lamps inside the huts. In the same way, for the Blessed One who has ascended the palace of Dhamma and looks upon the multitude of beings, those beings who have never performed meritorious deeds do not enter the range of the Buddha's vision even if they are sitting right by His right thigh in the same monastery; they are like arrows shot at night. However, the individuals to be guided (veneyya) who have performed meritorious deeds enter the range of His vision even if they are far away; they appear clearly like a flame or like Mount Himavanta. With reference to this matter, it was said:

"The virtuous are visible even from afar like Mount Himavanta; the non-virtuous are not visible in this world, like arrows shot at night."

"Uṭṭhehi" is a request and entreaty to the Blessed One to set out on a journey to teach the Dhamma. In terms such as "Vīra," the Blessed One is called "Vīra" (Hero) because He possesses effort and energy. The Mara of the devas (Devaputta-māra), the Mara of death (Maccu-māra), and the Mara of defilements (Kilesa-māra)...
62:
Because he has conquered, he is called "Vijitasaṅgāma" (Victor in Battle). Because he is capable of leading sentient beings to save them from dangers such as rebirth, he is called "Satthavāha" (Caravan Leader). Because he is free from the debt of sensual desire, he should be known as "Aṇana" (Debtless).

"Apārutā" means they have been opened. "Amatassa dvārā" refers to the Noble Path. That Noble Path is the door to entering Nibbāna, which is called the Deathless (Amata). The Buddha shows, "I have opened that door." "Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ" means let all people release or place their faith. The meaning of the last two phrases is: "Out of concern for physical and mental weariness, I remained without preaching this sublime and supreme Dhamma which I have studied and well-developed; but now, let all people bring the vessel of faith, and I shall fulfill their desires."

## Explanation of the Pair of Chief Disciples

"Bodhirukkhamūle" means he disappeared from the foot of the Ajapāla Banyan tree, which is not far from the Bodhi tree. "Kheme Migadāye" refers to the Isipatana Deer Park; at that time, that place was a park named "Khema," and because it was a place where safety was granted to deer, it was called "Migadāya." Referring to that place, he said "Kheme Migadāye." Like the Buddha Vipassī, other Buddhas also, when they first set out to preach the Dhamma, travel through the air and descend at that very spot. Our Blessed One, however, seeing the underlying support (upanissaya) of Upaka the Ājīvaka, thought: "Upaka is traveling this road; when he sees me, he will speak and then go; later, when he becomes weary and returns, he will realize the Fruit of Arahantship." Knowing this, he traveled the 18-yojana journey on foot. "Dāyapālaṃ āmantesi" means that upon seeing him, he looked repeatedly and called the one who approached, saying, "Venerable Sir, our Master has arrived."

75-6. "Anupubbiṃ kathaṃ" means he preached the gradual discourse: the talk on giving (dāna), followed by the talk on virtue (sīla) after giving, followed by the talk on heaven (sagga) after virtue, and followed by the talk on the path (magga) after heaven. Therein, "Dānakathā" means: this giving is the root of happiness, the foundation of wealth, the abode of riches; it is the refuge, shelter, hiding place, and support for those in distress. In this world and the next, there is no support, abode, object, refuge, shelter, hiding place, or reliance equal to giving. This giving is like a lion-throne (sīhāsana) made of jewels because it is worthy of reliance; it is like the great earth (mahāpathavī) because it is a foundation.
63:
In the sense of being an object of focus, it is like a rope to be held. This giving (dāna) is like a boat in the sense of crossing over from suffering; it is like a brave man on the battlefield in the sense of providing relief; it is like a well-fortified city in the sense of protecting from danger; it is like a lotus in the sense of not being smeared by the stains of stinginess and so on; it is like fire in the sense of burning away those defilements; it is like a cobra in the sense of being difficult to approach; it is like a lion in the sense of being fearless; it is like a noble elephant in the sense of being endowed with strength; it is like a white bull in the sense of being designated as highly auspicious; it is like the flying horse king Valāhaka in the sense of leading to the land of safety. Giving bestows the bliss of Sakka, the bliss of Māra, the bliss of Brahmā, the bliss of a Cakkavatti, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramī-ñāṇa), the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa), and the supreme enlightenment (abhisambodhi-ñāṇa) in the world. Thus, he spoke words connected with the virtues of giving.

Because one who gives is capable of undertaking virtue, he preached the discourse on virtue (sīlakathā) immediately after the discourse on giving. The discourse on virtue means: virtue is the reliance, the foundation, the object, the protection from danger, the hiding place, the destination, and the support. For the riches of this world and the next, there is no reliance, foundation, object, protection, hiding place, destination, or support equal to virtue. There is no ornament like virtue, no flower like the flower of virtue, no scent like the scent of virtue. The world with its gods cannot tire of looking at one who is adorned with the ornament of virtue, wears the flower of virtue, and is anointed with the scent of virtue. Thus, he spoke words connected with the virtues of morality.

To show that by depending on this virtue, one can attain this heaven (sagga), he preached the discourse on heaven (saggakathā) immediately after virtue. The discourse on heaven means: this heaven is desirable, pleasant, and gladdens the heart; in this heaven, one enjoys oneself constantly and obtains riches constantly; the Cātumahārājikā gods enjoy celestial happiness and celestial riches for nine million years; the Tāvatiṃsa gods enjoy them for thirty-six million years. Thus, he spoke words connected with the virtues of heaven. The mouths of the Buddhas are not sufficient to describe the bliss of heaven. It is also said: "Monks, I could preach the talk connected with heaven in many different ways."

Having attracted them with the discourse on heaven in this way, just as one might decorate an elephant and then cut off its trunk, he showed: "This heaven is also not permanent, not stable; one should not form desire and lust (chandarāga) for this heaven." He preached the faults of sensual pleasures in this way: "Sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair; the danger in these sensual pleasures is very great."
64:
## The Buddha preached on Danger (Ādīnava), Degradation (Okāra), and Defilement (Saṅkilesa).

Among those words, "Ādīnava" means fault (dosa). "Okāra" means lowliness, a base state (lāmakabhāva). "Saṅkilesa" means the defilement of beings in saṃsāra because of those faults. It is as he preached: "Friends... how defiled are these beings!" Thus, having caused alarm through the danger of sensual pleasures, he showed the benefit of renunciation (nekkhamma), meaning he showed the advantages of monkhood. The remaining words should be understood according to the method stated in the Ambaṭṭhasutta-vaṇṇanā and according to their clear meaning. "They obtained" (alatthuṃ) means how did they obtain? They obtained it by becoming "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, monks). When the Blessed One looked at their support (upanissaya) of bowls and robes created by their merit, seeing their past offerings of robes in many lives, he said, "Come, monks," and so on. In an instant, they were seen with shaven heads, wearing saffron-dyed robes, and with the eight requisites attached to their bodies, sitting and paying homage to the Blessed One like elders of a hundred years' standing. In the words "He showed" (sandassesi) and so on, he showed the benefit of this life (idhalokattha) and the benefit of the next life (paralokattha). When showing the benefit of this life, he showed it as impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta); he showed the aggregates (khandha), the elements (dhātu), the sense bases (āyatana), and dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). When showing the arising (udaya) of the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha), he showed the five characteristics; likewise for the feeling aggregate (vedanākkhandha) and so on. Likewise, when showing the passing away (vaya), he showed the fifty characteristics by way of arising and passing away (udayabbaya). When showing the benefit of the next life, he showed hell, the animal realm, the peta realm, and the asura realm, as well as the results of the three kinds of merit, and the fulfillment (sampatti) of the six celestial realms and the nine Brahma realms. "He exhorted" (samādapesi) means he made them take up the good Dhamma (kalyāṇadhamma) such as the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla), the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and the ten subjects of discourse (kathāvatthu). "He inspired" (samuttejesi) means he well-sharpened or encouraged them. He preached by making them alarmed by the benefits of this life and the next life as if they had already experienced them. Indeed, when the Blessed One preached alarming them with the benefits of this life, which is a variety of thirty-two kinds of punishment (kammakāraṇa) and twenty-five great dangers, the listener feels terror and trembling like one who is bound with hands behind the back, beaten at the crossroads, and led out through the south gate; or like one whose head is placed on the execution block; or like one impaled on a stake; or like one being trampled by an intoxicated elephant.
