65: When preaching the benefits of the future life, it is like one who is born in hell and so forth, or like one enjoying the fulfillment of the celestial realm. 'He gladdened' (sampahamsesi) means He encouraged them with the virtues they had attained; it means He preached by making the benefits great. Regarding 'the faults of formations' (saṅkhāra): previously, He preached the faults of sensual pleasures for the sake of attaining the first path. Here, however, for the sake of attaining the higher paths, He showed the faults of formations, their lowliness, and the weariness caused by those formations, saying, 'Monks, formations are impermanent, formations are unstable, formations provide no relief. Monks, it is fitting to be weary of all formations, it is fitting to be detached from them, it is fitting to be liberated from them,' and so on. Just as He showed the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma) previously, here too He showed the benefits of Nibbāna, saying, 'Monks, Nibbāna is peaceful, it is sublime, it is a refuge, it is a shelter,' and so on. ## Description of the Renunciation of the Great Multitude (Mahājanakāyapabbajjāvaṇṇanā) 'Great Multitude' (Mahājanakāya) refers to the group of people who were the attendants of those two princes. Because the Sangha was not yet complete, they approached the Buddha and the Dhamma as their refuge, taking only the two-word (dvevācika) refuge. 'They received' (alatthuṃ) means they received the state of 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, Monk) according to the method previously mentioned. In the subsequent turns of ordination after this, it was the same way. ## Description of the Permission for Wandering (Cārikāanujānanavaṇṇanā) 'A reflection arose' (parivitakko udapādi): when did this arise? It arose when seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed since He attained Buddhahood. The Buddha was dwelling while performing the service to His father (pitu-saṅgaha). The Great King also reflected: 'My eldest son has renounced and become a Buddha. My second son has renounced and become a Chief Disciple. The son of the chaplain has become the second Chief Disciple. All these remaining monks also used to follow and surround my son when they were laypeople. All these people...'
66: 'Even now, it is only my responsibility. I alone will serve these venerable ones with the four requisites; I will not give the opportunity to others.' Thinking thus, from the entrance of the monastery gate to the gate of the city of Rājagaha, the King had acacia fences built on both sides of the road, covered with mats, and screened with cloth. He had various flower-garland canopies, as large as palm tree trunks and adorned with golden stars, hung from above. On the ground below, he had exquisite carpets spread. Inside, on both sides, he had small flower plants and full jars placed. To make the entire path fragrant, he had flowers placed between perfumes and perfumes placed between flowers, and then he had the Buddha informed that it was time. The Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks, entered the city of Rājagaha only within the curtained enclosure, and after finishing His meal, returned to the monastery. Not a single other person had the chance even to behold Him; how then could they get the chance to offer alms, to pay homage, or to hear the Dhamma? The citizens thought thus: 'Today, it has been over seven years and seven months since the Buddha appeared in the world. We have not even had the chance to behold Him, let alone to offer alms, pay homage, or hear the Dhamma. The King, being attached, thinking "The Buddha is for me alone, the Dhamma is for me alone, the Sangha is for me alone," serves them by himself. When a Buddha appears, He appears for the benefit and welfare of the world including the devas. Hell is not hot only for the King and cool like a blue lotus pond for others. Therefore, let us speak to the King. If he gives us the chance to behold the Buddha, it is well. If he does not, we will even fight the King to invite the Sangha and perform meritorious deeds such as giving alms.' Thinking that it was not possible for ordinary citizens alone to do this, they decided to take a nobleman as a companion. They approached the General and told him the matter, asking, 'Sir, will you be on our side or on the King's side?' The General said, 'I am on your side. However, you must give me the first day to make an offering.' They accepted. The General approached the King and said, 'Great King, the citizens are angry with you.' When asked 'Why, friend?', he replied, 'They say that only Your Majesty is serving the Buddha and they do not get the chance to behold Him. If they get the chance to behold Him now, they will not be angry. If they do not, they wish to fight with Your Majesty, Great King.' The King said, 'Friend, I will fight. I cannot give up the community of monks.' 'Great King, your own servants say they will fight you. Whom will you call upon to fight? Are you not the General?' When he asked this, without the citizens...
67: 'Great King, I am unable,' the General replied. Then the King, realizing 'The citizens are powerful, and the General is also on their side,' said, 'Give me the permission to offer alms to the community of bhikkhus for seven years and seven months.' The citizens did not accept. The King reduced it to 'six years, five years, four years, three years, two years, one year.' Even with these reductions, they did not accept. He then pleaded for another seven days. The citizens granted it, thinking, 'Now it is no longer appropriate to act too harshly with the King.' The King, within those seven days, bestowed the alms-service he had prepared for seven years and seven months. For six days, he gave alms in a way that some people could not see. On the seventh day, he summoned the citizens and asked, 'Friends, will you be able to give such an alms-offering?' They replied, 'Is it not only because of us that this alms-offering arose for Your Majesty?' and said, 'We are able.' The King, wiping his tears with the back of his hand, paid homage to the Buddha and said, 'Venerable Sir, I intended to serve the community of six million eight hundred thousand monks with the four requisites for the rest of my life without giving a turn to others. Now the citizens do not permit me; they are angry, saying "We do not get the chance to give alms." May the Blessed One favor them starting from tomorrow.' Then, on the second day, the General prepared a great alms-offering (mahādāna) and stationed people around, saying, 'Today, guard so that no other person can offer even a single spoonful of rice.' On that day, a wealthy merchant's wife, weeping, said to her daughter, 'Dear daughter, if your father were alive, today I would be the first to offer alms to the Buddha.' The daughter said to her mother, 'Mother, do not worry. I will act so that the community of monks headed by the Buddha will partake of our alms first.' Then, she filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand with milk-rice prepared without water, mixed with ghee, honey, sugar, and so on. She covered it with another bowl, surrounded it with clusters of jasmine flowers to make it look like a bouquet, and when the Buddha was entering the village, she came out of the city herself, surrounded by her maidservants. On the way, the General's attendants stopped her, saying, 'Mother, do not go this way.' One named Mahāpuññā is one who has pleasant speech; although they spoke repeatedly, they were unable to reject her words. She asked, 'Elder brothers, uncles, why do you not let me pass?' The General's men replied, 'Mother, we have been placed here to not allow anyone else to give food.' She said, 'Do you see food in my hands? It is only a bouquet of flowers.'
68:
“Let us see,” they said. When asked, “Does your General not even allow the offering of a handful of flowers?” they replied, “Mother, he does.” “Then move aside, move aside,” she said, and approaching the Buddha, she requested, “Venerable Sir, please accept this handful of flowers.” The Buddha, looking at one of the General's attendants, accepted the handful of flowers. That woman prostrated to the Buddha and made a wish: “Venerable Sir, wherever I am reborn in successive lives, may I never have a livelihood filled with worry and anxiety. Like these Sumana flowers, may I be beloved and cherished wherever I am reborn. May my name also be Sumana.” The Buddha said, “May you be happy.” The woman prostrated, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.

The Buddha went to the General's house and sat on the prepared seat. When the General approached with gruel, the Buddha closed his bowl. “Venerable Sir, the community of monks has sat down,” he said. “We have a meal obtained in the interim,” the Buddha replied. The General removed the flowers and saw the alms-food. The young attendant said, “Master, the woman deceived me, saying they were flowers.” The milk-rice was sufficient for all the monks, with the Buddha at the head. The General also offered his own gifts. After the meal, the Buddha preached the blessing and departed. When the General asked, “Who offered that meal?” they replied, “It was the merchant's daughter, Master.” “That woman is wise; by living in the house of such a woman, it is not difficult for a man to attain the bliss of heaven,” he said, and taking her, he placed her in the position of chief wife.

The next day, the townspeople gave alms; the day after, the King gave alms. Thus, they strove to give alms on alternate days. The King employed spies and gave more than the townspeople; the townspeople did the same, giving more than the King. The palace dancers said to the young monks, “Friends, take this; this offering was not made by hands that clean the bodies and clothes of laypeople or wash the saliva and mucus of children, but was prepared purely and cleanly.” The next day, the townspeople, while giving alms, said, “Friends, take this; this offering was not made with rice, milk, curd, or butter collected from towns and villages, nor with things brought by breaking the legs, heads, or backs of others, but was made only with genuine butter and milk.” Thus, when seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed, this thought occurred to the Buddha. Therefore, it is said, “When seven years, seven months, and seven days had passed since he became Buddha, (this thought) arose.”
69:
“A certain Great Brahmā” refers to the Brahmā who requested the preaching of the Dhamma.

“Eighty-four thousand monastery precincts” refers to eighty-four thousand vihāras. All these monasteries were large ones, like the Mahāvihāra, Abhayagiri-cetiya-pabbata, and Cittalapabbata Mahāvihāra, which could accommodate twelve thousand monks.

“Patience is the highest austerity (tapo)” means that what is called endurance-patience (adhivāsana-khanti) is the highest practice. “Titikkhā” is a synonym for patience. It means that endurance-patience, called titikkhā, is a noble practice. “Nibbāna is supreme,” the Buddhas declare that Nibbāna is supreme in every way. “One who harms others is not a renunciant (pabbajita)” means that one who harms, tires, or oppresses others because of a lack of endurance-patience is not a renunciant. The fourth line is a synonym for that meaning. The phrase “is not a renunciant (pabbajita)” is the same as “is not an ascetic (samaṇa).” “One who harms others” means one who makes others weary. Alternatively, “parūpaghātī” means one who destroys virtue (sīlūpaghātī). Virtue is called “para” (other/supreme) because of its noble meaning. If a monk makes any other being weary and harms others, or destroys his own virtue, he is not a renunciant. Alternatively, if a person harms others because of a lack of patience, even knowingly taking the lives of gadflies or mosquitoes, he is not a monk. Why? Because he has not yet removed the dust of defilements (mala). “One removes one's own dust of defilements; therefore, one is called a renunciant (pabbajita)” is the characteristic of a renunciant. Even if a person does not kill others but harms them with sticks and so on, he is a harmer of others and is not an ascetic (samaṇa). Why? Because he has not calmed his harmfulness. “Because one calms evils, one is called an ascetic (samaṇa)” is the characteristic of an ascetic.

In the second verse, “sabbapāpassa” means of all evil. “Akaraṇaṃ” means not committing. “Kusalassa” means of the wholesome belonging to the four planes. “Upasampadā” means attainment. “Sacittapariyodapanaṃ” means purifying one's own mind; such purification occurs through the Path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga). Thus, by abandoning all evil through the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), fulfilling the wholesome through tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), and purifying the mind through the Fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), this is the teaching, the instruction, the exhortation of the Buddhas.
70:
In the third verse, ‘anūpavādo’ means not reviling or disparaging anyone with words. ‘Anūpaghāto’ means not harming or killing with the body. ‘Pātimokkhe’ refers to that Pātimokkha, the Atipamokkha, the noble virtue; it is called ‘Pātimokkha’ because it protects from the wrong paths (agati) and liberates from the dangers of woeful states (duggati), or because it liberates the person who guards that virtue. Restraint in that Pātimokkha is called ‘pātimokkha-saṃvara’. ‘Mattaññutā’ means knowing the measure in receiving and using requisites. ‘Pantañca sayanāsanaṃ’ refers to a lodging that is secluded from noise. It should be understood that through these two factors (moderation and secluded lodging), contentment with the four requisites is also indicated. ‘Etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ’ means that not reviling others, not harming others, possessing the virtue of Pātimokkha restraint, knowing the measure in receiving and using requisites, and living in a secluded monastery to master the eight attainments (samāpatti) are the instruction and exhortation of the Buddhas. These verses should be known as the Pātimokkhuddesa verses of all the Buddhas.

## Description of the Devas' Announcement

By explaining the life story (apadāna) of Vipassī Buddha in detail, the well-penetrated nature of the Dhamma-element (dhamma-dhātu), which was said as “Monks, this Dhamma-element has been well-penetrated and realized by the Tathāgata,” has been shown. Now, to show the announcement of the devas, which was said as “The devas also reported this matter to the Tathāgata,” the words beginning with ‘ekamidāhaṃ’ are spoken.

In those words, ‘subhagavane’ means in the forest of that name. ‘Sālarājamūle’ means at the foot of a sal tree, which is the chief of trees. ‘Kāmacchandaṃ virājetvā’ means having dispelled sensual desire by uprooting it with the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmi-magga). Just as in the dispensation of Vipassī Buddha, devas who have practiced the holy life (brahmacariya) in the dispensations of the other Buddhas also come and report. In the Pali text, however, it appears only by the power of Vipassī Buddha and our Buddha.

Among those devas, they are called ‘Avihā’ because they do not fall away from or abandon their own prosperity. They are called ‘Atappa’ because they do not cause distress to any being. They are called ‘Sudassa’ because they are beautiful to look at, handsome, and inspiring. They are called ‘Sudassī’ because they see well or because their sight is good. They are supreme in all qualities and in the prosperity of life; they are called ‘Akaniṭṭha’ because there are no juniors in that realm.
71:
Standing at this point, the recitation sections (bhāṇavāras) should be combined. In this Sutta, three bhāṇavāras are preached by way of the life story (apadāna) of the Blessed One Vipassī. Just as with the Blessed One Vipassī, it is also preached by way of the life stories of Sikhī and the others. In the Pāḷi text, however, it is abbreviated. Thus, by way of the seven Buddhas, our Blessed One preached twenty-one (21) bhāṇavāras. Likewise, (including the bhāṇavāras preached) by way of the Aviha devas, Atappa devas, Sudassa devas, Sudassī devas, and Akaniṭṭha devas, the total is one hundred and twenty-six (126) bhāṇavāras. In the Tipitaka Word of the Buddha, there is no other Sutta equal in extent to one hundred and twenty-six bhāṇavāras; this Sutta should be known as the 'King of Suttas' (Suttantarāja). Following this, connecting both sequences of events, the words 'Thus, O bhikkhus' (iti kho bhikkhave) and so forth are spoken. The meaning of those words is entirely clear.

## Thus ends the Commentary on the Mahāpadāna Sutta in the Commentary on the Dīgha Nikāya named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī.
72:
## 2. Commentary on the Mahānidāna Sutta

## Commentary on the Introduction

The sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and ending with "Kurusū" is the Mahānidāna Sutta. In this sutta, the explanation of obscure terms is as follows: "Kurusū viharati" means that a district which is the dwelling place of the princes of the district named Kuru is also called "Kuru" by popular usage (ruḷhī). In that Kuru district (the Blessed One was residing).

However, the teachers of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) say this: During the time of King Mandhātu, the people of the three great continents heard that "Jambudīpa is a noble island, very delightful and pleasant, being the place where noble ones such as Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, Great Disciples, and Cakkavatti Kings appear." Thus, when King Mandhātu, the Cakkavatti, traveled to the four great continents preceded by the Wheel-treasure (Cakkaratana), they followed the king. At that time, the king asked the Minister-treasure (Pariṇāyaka-ratana), "Is there any place more pleasant and delightful than the human world?" The minister replied, "Great King, why do you speak thus? Do you not see the power of the moon and the sun? Is not the dwelling place of those (devas) more pleasant and delightful than this (human world)?" The king, preceded by the Wheel-treasure, went to that (deva world). When the four Great Kings of the Cātumahārājika realm heard that "King Mandhātu has arrived," they reflected, "This king is of great power and majesty; we are unable to stop him by fighting," and they handed over their own royal sovereignty. After enjoying that sovereignty, the king asked again, "Is there any place more pleasant and delightful than this?"

Then, they told the king about the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. "Great King, the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is much more pleasant and delightful than this. In that realm, these four Great Kings of the Cātumahārājika serve as doorkeepers near Sakka, the King of Devas. Sakka is of great power and majesty. The appurtenances and places of that Sakka are: the Vejayanta Palace, which is a thousand yojanas high; the Sudhammā celestial assembly hall, five hundred yojanas high; the Vejayanta chariot and the elephant king Erāvaṇa, each one hundred and fifty yojanas; the Nandavana Garden, Cittalatāvana Garden, Phārusakavana Garden, and Missakavana Garden, adorned with a thousand celestial trees; and the Pāricchattaka tree (Kovivāra), which is a hundred yojanas high. Beneath that tree is the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone seat, sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas high, having the color of a Jayakusuma flower. Due to the softness of that stone seat, when Sakka sits down, half of his body sinks into it," they said.
73: Upon hearing those words, the king, wishing to go to that place, sent forth the Wheel-treasure. That Wheel-treasure stood in the sky together with the fourfold army. Then, from the center of the two deva realms, the Wheel-treasure descended and stood on the ground together with the fourfold army headed by the Minister-treasure. The king alone proceeded to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. As soon as Sakka, the King of Devas, heard that "King Mandhātu has come," he went to welcome the king and said, "Great King... your coming is a good coming; Great King... this deva realm is indeed your property; Great King... please rule over it," and divided the royal sovereignty into two portions, giving one portion along with the celestial dancers. By merely being established in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the king's human state disappeared and the state of a deva became manifest. When that king sat upon the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone seat together with Sakka, the difference could be known only by the blinking of the eyes. The devas, not noticing that difference, were confused about the distinction between Sakka and King Mandhātu. That king, enjoying celestial bliss in that deva realm, ruled until thirty-six successive Sakkas had arisen and passed away. Then, unable to be satiated with sensual pleasures, he passed away from that deva realm and, while remaining in his own garden, his body being touched by hot winds and the hot sun, he died. When the Wheel-treasure returned and stood on the ground, the Minister-treasure had King Mandhātu's footprint engraved on a gold plate and administered the kingship, saying, "This is the royal sovereignty of King Mandhātu." Those people who had followed from the three great continents, being unable to return to their own places, approached the Minister-treasure and pleaded, "Lord... we came by the power of the king; now we are unable to return; please grant us a place to live." That Minister-treasure gave each of them a district. Among those districts, the place where the people from the Pubbavideha island lived was named "Videha country" based on their former perception; the place where the people from the Aparagoyāna island lived was named "Aparanta district"; and the place where the people from the Uttarakuru island lived was named "Kuru country." They were called by plural names based on the many villages, market towns, etc. Therefore, it is said, "He was residing in the Kuru countries." In the phrase "the market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma," some teachers explain the meaning of the word Kammāsadhamma by replacing the letter 'dha' with 'da'. Because a person named Kammāsa was tamed (damita) in this place, it is called "Kammāsadamma." Kammāsa refers to Kammāsapāda the man-eater (Porisāda). When a scab formed where a thorn had pierced his foot, it grew looking like variegated wood. Therefore, he became known as "Kammāsapāda." Because he was tamed in that place...
74:
...he was restrained from being a man-eater. Who restrained him? The Mahāsatta (Bodhisatta) restrained him. If asked in which Jātaka? Some teachers say in the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka. These elders, however, say it was in the Jayaddisa Jātaka. At that time, the Mahāsatta tamed Kammāsapāda. Thus it was said:

"When I was the son born of the breast of King Jayaddisa, the ruler of Pañcāla,
Being the son born of the breast of the ruler of Pañcāla,
I sacrificed my life and released my father from danger,
And I also caused Kammāsapāda to have faith."

Some others, however, explain the meaning with the letter 'dha' itself. It is said that the people of the Kuru country had the Kuru-vatta (Kuru practice). In that practice, there was a kammāsa (spot or flaw). Therefore, that place was called Kammāsadhamma, meaning "in this place, the kammāsa-dhamma (flawed practice) occurred." The name of the market town situated there is also this very name. Why is it not expressed with the locative case (sattamī vibhatti)? It is because of the opportunity of dwelling. For the Blessed One, there was no specific dwelling place called a vihāra in that market town. Away from the market town, there was a large forest on a pleasant stretch of ground well-supplied with water. Making that market town his alms-resort village, the Blessed One resided in that forest. Therefore, the meaning should be understood here as: "In the Kuru countries, there is a market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma; making that market town his alms-resort village, he resided (nearby)."

'Āyasmā' is a term of endearment; it is a term of respect. 'Ānando' is the name of that Elder. 'Ekamantaṃ' is a bhāva-napuṃsaka-niddesa (neuter gender used adverbially), as in "the moon and the sun revolve unevenly," etc. Therefore, the meaning should be noted here as: sitting in such a way that one is sitting to one side. Or, this accusative case (upayoga-vibhatti) is used in the sense of the locative. 'Nisīdi' means he approached and sat down. Wise people, when approaching those worthy of respect, are skilled in the matter of seating and sit to one side. This Venerable Ānanda, being one of those wise people, sat to one side.

How does one sit so that it is sitting to one side? It is by avoiding the six faults of sitting. They are: being too far, being too near, being upwind, being on a high place, being directly in front, and being directly behind. One who sits too far away must speak with a loud voice if they wish to speak. One who sits too near causes physical contact. One who sits upwind disturbs with their body odor. On a high place...
75:
One who sits in a high place commits an act of disrespect. One who sits directly in front must meet eye-to-eye if they wish to look. One who sits too far behind must turn their neck if they wish to look. Therefore, this venerable one also circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right, paid respects with reverence, and avoiding these six faults regarding sitting, sat directly in front of the right knee. He entered within the six-colored Buddha rays, like descending into a clear lake of lac-dye, or like being covered with a golden plate, or like entering the middle of a ceiling made of red lotus garlands. Thus sat the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma (Dhamma-bhaṇḍāgārika). Therefore, it is said, "He sat on one side."

At what time and for what reason did this venerable one approach the Blessed One? It was in the evening, for the purpose of asking a question regarding Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda). On that day, the venerable one had wandered for alms in the village of Kammāsadhamma, as if placing bags of a thousand coins at every house to favor the families. After eating his meal and returning, he performed the major and minor duties for his teacher, the Blessed One. When the Blessed One entered the Gandhakuṭi, he paid respects and went to his own place for the day's rest. After his disciples performed their duties and departed, he swept the place of rest, spread out the leather mat, took water from the pitcher, cooled his hands and feet with water, and sat cross-legged, entering the attainment of the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphalasamāpatti). Then, emerging from the attainment at the designated time, he applied his knowledge to Dependent Origination. He contemplated the twelve factors of Dependent Origination three times, from the beginning "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations" (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā) to the end of the factors, from the end to the beginning, from both ends to the middle, and from the middle to both ends. As he contemplated thus, Dependent Origination became clear to him, appearing as distinctly as an upturned bowl.

Then he thought: "This Dhamma of Dependent Origination has been taught by all Blessed Buddhas as 'deep and deep in appearance.' Yet to me, though I am a disciple established in only a portion of knowledge, it appears exceedingly clear and obvious. Does it appear thus clear only to me, or is it the same for others?" Then this thought occurred to him: "I will take this question and ask the Blessed One. Based on this matter, the Blessed One will teach me a discourse, like lifting Mount Meru with a stalk of grain. When the Blessed Buddhas reach these four topics—Vinaya regulations, Bhummantara, Dependent Origination, and Samayantara—their roar is great, their knowledge penetrates, and the Buddha-knowledge..."
76:
...the greatness of His knowledge is manifest, the teaching is deep, adorned with the three characteristics, and associated with emptiness (suññatā). Although the Venerable Ānanda normally approached the Blessed One a hundred or a thousand times a day, he never approached without cause or benefit. On that day, however, taking this question, he thought: "I will approach this great elephant of a Buddha and listen to the heron-like call of His knowledge; I will approach this lion-king of a Buddha and listen to the lion's roar of His knowledge; I will approach this Sindh horse of a Buddha and observe the swift stride of His knowledge." Thinking thus, he rose from his day's rest, shook out and took his leather mat, and approached the Blessed One in the evening. Therefore, it is said, "Approaching in the evening for the purpose of asking a question regarding Dependent Origination."

In the phrase "Yāva gambhīro," the word "yāva" signifies exceeding a limit; because it is deep beyond measure, it means "exceedingly deep." "Gambhīrāvabhāso" means it appears deep, it is seen as deep. Indeed, one kind of water appears deep even though it is shallow, like old water blackened by rotting leaves and such. Even if that water is only knee-deep, it appears as if it were a hundred fathoms deep. Another kind of water appears shallow even though it is deep, like the very clear water in the Maṇigaṅgā River. Even if that water is a hundred fathoms deep, it appears as if it were only knee-deep. Another kind of water is shallow and appears shallow, like water in a pot or similar vessel. Another kind of water is deep and appears deep, like the water of the great ocean at the foot of Mount Meru. Thus, water alone receives four names. In the case of Dependent Origination, however, it is not so. This Dependent Origination receives only one name: it is deep and it appears deep. "Though it is of such a nature, to me it appears exceedingly shallow. It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!" Thus, expressing his wonder, he asked the question and sat down in silence.

The Blessed One, hearing the words of the Venerable Ānanda, thought: "Ānanda says that this question, which is the range of a Buddha (Buddha-visaya), is shallow to him—as if he were reaching out his hand to grasp the highest heaven (bhavagga), or striving to split Mount Meru to extract its essence, or wishing to cross the great ocean without a boat, or striving to turn over the earth to take the essence of the soil. I shall tell him of the depth of this Dhamma." Thinking thus, He spoke the words beginning with "Mā hevaṃ."

In that statement, in the place of "Mā hevaṃ," the syllable "ha" is merely a particle. It means "Do not say so." The Blessed One spoke these words "Mā hevaṃ" to the Venerable Ānanda as an exaltation, not as a reproach.
77:
## Explanation of Exaltation (Ussādanā)

In that statement, regarding the exaltation: "Ānanda, you are one of great wisdom, possessed of clear intellect. Therefore, to you, the deep Dependent Origination appears shallow. To others, however, this Dhamma should not be regarded as shallow; it is deep and appears deep." In this regard, they provide four similes. A great wrestler, supported by the taste of good food for six months, having practiced, and having trained with the wrestlers' stone during festivals, was going to the battlefield. On the way, people showed him the wrestlers' stone. The wrestler asked, "What is this?" They said, "It is the wrestlers' stone." When he said, "Bring it," they replied, "We cannot lift it." So he went himself and asked, "Where is the heavy part of this stone?" and lifting two stones with both hands, he threw them like toy balls and went on his way. In that case, although the stone was light to the wrestler, it cannot be said to be light to others. Like the wrestler supported by good food for six months, the Venerable Ānanda is one who has fulfilled the perfections for a hundred thousand aeons. Just as the stone is light to the wrestler because of his great strength, so Dependent Origination is shallow to the Elder because of his great wisdom. That Dhamma cannot be said to be shallow to others.

In the great ocean, the fish named Timi is two hundred leagues (yojanas) long; the Timiṅgala fish is three hundred leagues; the Timipiṅgala fish is four hundred leagues; the Timirapiṅgala fish is five hundred leagues. The four types of fish—Ānanda, Nanda, Ajjhāroha, and Mahātimi—are one thousand leagues long. In this regard, they illustrate with the Timirapiṅgala fish alone. When that fish moves its right ear, the waters move in an area of five hundred leagues. It is the same with the left ear, the tail, and the head. When it exerts itself in play, moving both ears, striking the water with its tail, and moving its head from side to side, the waters boil like water in a pot placed on a stove in an area of seven hundred or eight hundred leagues. In an area of about three hundred leagues, the water is unable to cover its back. That fish might say, "They say this great ocean is very deep, very deep. Where is it deep? We do not even get enough water to cover our backs." In that case, although the great ocean is shallow to the large-bodied Timirapiṅgala fish, it cannot be said to be shallow to other small fish. Similarly, although Dependent Origination is shallow to the Elder who is endowed with wisdom, it cannot be said to be shallow to others.
78: The King of Garuḍas is one hundred and fifty yojanas in size. His right wing is fifty yojanas; likewise, his left wing is fifty yojanas. The mass of feathers is sixty yojanas, the neck is thirty yojanas, the face is nine yojanas, and the feet are twelve yojanas in size. When that King of Garuḍas strives to show the wind from flapping his wings, even a place of seven or eight hundred yojanas is not enough. That King of Garuḍas would say: 'They say this sky is endless, endless; how can it be endless? We do not even get enough space to spread the wind from flapping our wings.' In that case, although it is said that the sky is very narrow for the large-bodied King of Garuḍas, it cannot be said to be narrow for other small birds. Similarly, although it is said that the Dhamma of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) is very shallow for the Elder Ānanda who is endowed with wisdom, it cannot be said to be shallow for others. The King of Asuras, Rāhu, is four thousand eight hundred yojanas from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair. The distance between his two hands is one thousand two hundred yojanas. In thickness, he is six hundred yojanas. The palms and soles are three hundred yojanas each; the face is likewise three hundred yojanas. Each finger joint is fifty yojanas; the distance between the two eyebrows is likewise fifty yojanas. The forehead is three hundred yojanas. The head is nine hundred yojanas. When that King of Asuras, Rāhu, descends into the great ocean, the very deep water is only as deep as his knees. He would say: 'They say this great ocean is deep, deep; where is the depth? We do not even get enough water to cover our knees.' In that case, although it is said that the great ocean is shallow for the large-bodied King of Asuras, Rāhu, it cannot be said to be shallow for others. Similarly, although it is said that the Dhamma of Dependent Origination is very shallow for the Elder, it cannot be said to be shallow for others. Aiming at this meaning, the Blessed One said, 'Do not say so, Ānanda; do not say so, Ānanda.' To the Elder, even the very deep Dhamma of Dependent Origination became apparent as very shallow because of four reasons. What are the four reasons? They are: the fulfillment of past support (merit) accumulated in the past, living in the presence of the Buddha, being a Stream-enterer (sotāpanna), and having great learning (bāhusacca).## Account of the Achievement of Past SupportCounting back from this aeon, one hundred thousand aeons ago, the Blessed One named Padumuttara appeared in the world. For that Blessed One, there was a city named Haṃsāvatī and a king named Ānanda.
79:
The father's name is not mentioned, but the mother was a queen named Sumedhā, and the Bodhisatta was a prince named Uttara Kumāra. On the day his son was born, that prince renounced the world to become a monk. Striving in the practice of meditation, he gradually attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). After uttering the solemn utterance beginning with "Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ" and staying for seven days on the Bodhi-throne, he thought, "I shall set my foot upon the ground," and stretched out his foot. At that time, a great lotus flower burst through the earth and appeared. The outer petals of that lotus were ninety cubits, the filaments were thirty cubits, the pericarp of the great lotus was twelve cubits, and the pollen was about the measure of nine jars. The Blessed One himself was fifty-eight cubits in height. The span between the two hands of that Blessed One was eighteen cubits, the forehead was five cubits, and the palms and soles were eleven cubits. As soon as the Blessed One stepped on the twelve-cubit pericarp of the great lotus with his eleven-cubit foot, the pollen, measuring nine jars, rose up and spread to a height of fifty-eight cubits, then fell back like scattered red arsenic powder. Because of this reason, the Blessed One became famous as "Padumuttara."

That Blessed One had two Chief Disciples named Devila and Sujāta. He had two Chief Female Disciples named Amitā and Asamā. There was an attendant named Sumana. The Blessed One Padumuttara, honoring his father, resided in the capital of Haṃsāvatī surrounded by one hundred thousand monks. The younger brother of that Blessed One was named Sumana Kumāra. To that younger brother, the Great King, his father, granted a revenue village at a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas from Haṃsāvatī. That younger brother used to come occasionally to visit his father and the Blessed One. Then one day, a rebellion broke out in the border region. Prince Sumana sent word to the King, saying, "A rebellion has broken out in the border region." The King sent back word, "Why have I placed you in that region?" The prince went out, suppressed the rebels, and sent word to the King, "Great King, the province is peaceful." The King was delighted and said, "Let my son come quickly." That prince had one thousand ministers. While on the way with those ministers, the prince consulted them, "My father is delighted; if he grants me a boon, what boon should I take?" Then some ministers suggested, "Take elephants, take horses, take chariots, take a province, or take the seven kinds of jewels." Other ministers, however, said, "Sirs, you are the sons of the Lord of the Earth; wealth is not scarce for you. All this wealth that is obtained must eventually be abandoned. Only merit can be taken along. Therefore, when the King grants a boon, take the boon to serve the Blessed One Padumuttara for three months." The prince said, "You are my good friends; I did not have such a thought, but you have made it arise. I shall do exactly so," and went to his father...
80:
The prince bowed, and the father embraced him, kissed his head, and said, "Dear son, I grant you a boon." When he said this, the prince replied, "Great King, very well. I wish to make my life meaningful by serving the Blessed One with the four requisites for three months. Please grant me only this boon." When the King said, "Dear son, it is not possible; ask for another boon," the prince replied, "Great King, those known as Khattiyas do not speak double words. Please grant me only this boon; other boons are of no use to me." The King said, "Dear son, the minds of the Buddhas are difficult to know. If the Blessed One does not wish it, what is the use even if I give it?" The prince then said, "Great King, very well. I will act so as to know the mind of the Blessed One," and went to the monastery.

At that time, the Blessed One had finished his meal and had entered the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). The prince went to the monks who were sitting in the pavilion. When the monks asked, "Prince, why have you come?" he said, "I have come to pay homage to the Blessed One; please give me the opportunity to pay homage to the Blessed One." They said, "Prince, we ourselves do not get the opportunity to pay homage to the Blessed One at any moment we desire." He asked, "Venerable sirs, who gets the opportunity to pay homage?" and they answered, "Prince, the Venerable named Sumana Thera gets it." He asked, "Venerable sirs, where is that Elder?" and after inquiring about the place where the Elder resided, he went there, bowed, and said, "Venerable sir, I wish to pay homage to the Blessed One; please grant me the opportunity to pay homage." The Elder said, "Prince, come," and taking the prince, he left him at the courtyard of the Fragrant Chamber and went up into the Fragrant Chamber. Then the Blessed One asked, "Sumana, why have you come?" He replied, "Venerable sir, the prince has come to pay homage to the Blessed One." "In that case, dear monk, prepare a seat," He said. The Elder prepared a seat, and the Blessed One sat on the prepared seat. The prince bowed to the Blessed One and spoke pleasant words of greeting. When asked, "Prince, when did you arrive?" he replied, "Venerable sir, I arrived even as you were entering the Fragrant Chamber. The monks, however, said, 'We do not get the opportunity to pay homage to the Blessed One at any moment we desire,' and sent me to the Elder. The Elder, however, granted me the opportunity with just a single word. Venerable sir, I think the Elder must be one who is very much loved and cherished in your Sāsana." "Yes, prince, it is so. This monk is one who is loved and cherished in my Sāsana," He said. When asked, "Venerable sir, by doing what in the Buddha's Sāsana does one become loved and cherished?" He replied, "Prince, it is because of giving gifts, undertaking virtue, and observing the Uposatha." "Blessed One, I too wish to be one who is loved and cherished in the Buddha's Sāsana like the Elder. Please accept my invitation for the three-month Rains Retreat." The Blessed One, seeing that there would be benefit in going, said, "Prince, the Tathāgatas [delight] in a secluded dwelling..."
81:
"They enjoy themselves," he said. The prince replied, "The Blessed One knows, the Sugata himself knows." He then said, "Venerable Sir, I will go ahead and build a monastery. When I send word, please come together with a hundred thousand monks." Having received this promise, he went to his father and said, "Great King, the Blessed One has given me his word. When I send word, please invite the Blessed One to come." After paying respects to his father, he departed. He had a monastery built at every league (yojana) along the hundred-and-twenty-league journey. Upon reaching his city, he searched for a site to build a monastery and saw the garden of a wealthy man named Sobhana. He purchased it for a hundred thousand and spent another hundred thousand to have the monastery built. In that monastery, he had a Gandhakuṭi chamber built for the Blessed One, and for the other monks, he had dwellings for night and day, caves, and pavilions constructed. After completing the surrounding walls and the gateways, he sent word to his father, saying, "My task is complete; please invite the Blessed One."

The Great King, after offering a meal to the Blessed One, said, "Venerable Sir, Sumana's task is complete. He is waiting for your arrival." The Blessed One, surrounded by a hundred thousand monks, set out, staying at the monasteries built at every league. When the prince heard that the Blessed One had arrived, he went out to meet him for a distance of one league, making offerings of flowers and perfumes. He then invited the Blessed One to the monastery and said:

"May the Great Sage Buddha accept this garden named Sobhana, which I purchased for a hundred thousand and built for another hundred thousand," and thus he donated the monastery. On the day of the commencement of the rains (Vassa), the prince gave offerings and called his wife, children, and ministers, saying, "This Blessed One has come to us from afar. Those who are Buddhas value only the Dhamma; they do not value material offerings (āmisa). Therefore, for three months, I will wear only two garments, observe the ten precepts, and remain right here. You all should continue to give offerings to the hundred thousand monks who have ended their defilements in this same manner for the three months."

The prince stayed in a place similar to where the Elder Sumana resided. Seeing all the major and minor duties the Elder performed for the Blessed One, he thought, "This Elder is very much loved and cherished in this position. I, too, should make an aspiration for this rank." After the rains retreat, near the time of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he entered the village and gave a great gift (mahādāna) for seven days. On the seventh day, he placed sets of triple robes (ticīvara) at the feet of the hundred thousand monks and...
82:
...paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, the merit I have performed, starting from the construction of monasteries at every league along the way, was not done out of a desire for the prosperity of Sakka, the prosperity of Māra, or the prosperity of Brahma. It was performed only with the desire to become an attendant of a Blessed One. Therefore, may I also become an attendant of a Blessed One in the future, just like the Elder Sumana." Having said this, he prostrated himself with the fivefold touching.

The Blessed One, reflecting on whether this clansman's aspiration was great and could be fulfilled, saw that: "In the future, a hundred thousand aeons from this present aeon, a Blessed One named Gotama will arise. He will become the attendant of that Buddha." Knowing this, he said:

"May all that you wish for and aspire to be fulfilled,
May all your intentions be perfected,
Like the full moon on the fifteenth day."

Upon hearing these words, the prince reflected, "The words of the Buddhas are never twofold (they are certainly true)." From the very next day, he acted as if he were one who followed closely behind, carrying the Blessed One's bowl and robes. He gave offerings for a hundred thousand years during the time of that Buddha and was reborn in the celestial realm. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he offered an upper robe to an Elder who was on his alms round so that he could receive the bowl. Being reborn again in the celestial realm, he passed away from there and became the King of Vārāṇasī. He built wooden monasteries for eight Paccekabuddhas, provided them with jeweled footstools, and served them with the four requisites for ten thousand years. These are the well-known accounts.

Having given offerings for a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven along with our Bodhisatta. Passing away from there, he took conception in the house of Amitodana the Sakyan. When the Buddha eventually renounced the world and attained Supreme Enlightenment, and visited Kapilavatthu for the first time, the princes made a pact to follow the Blessed One. He renounced the world along with Prince Bhaddiya and others and was ordained by the Blessed One. Not long after, he heard a Dhamma discourse from the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta and was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Thus, because this venerable one was endowed with past supporting conditions (upanissaya), by the power of those past conditions, even the extremely profound Dhamma of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) became clear and manifest to him.
83:
## Titthavāsādivaṇṇanā
Titthavāsa refers to the repeated learning, listening, questioning, and retaining of teachings in the presence of teachers. This Titthavāsa was extremely pure for the Venerable Ānanda; therefore, even this extremely profound Dhamma of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda) appeared to him as if it were very shallow.

For those who are Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), the Dhamma of Dependent Origination usually appears as shallow. This Venerable Ānanda was also a Stream-enterer. Just as for those with great learning, when a lamp is lit inside a small room of four cubits, the couches and stools are clearly visible, so too is the discernment of mind and matter (nāmarūpa) very clear. This Venerable Ānanda was the foremost among those of great learning. Due to the power of his great learning, the profound Dhamma of Dependent Origination appeared very shallow to him.

## Paṭiccasamuppādagambhīratā
Dependent Origination is called profound due to four aspects: depth of meaning (atthagambhīratā), depth of phenomena (dhammagambhīratā), depth of teaching (desanāgambhīratā), and depth of penetration (paṭivedhagambhīratā).

Among these four, the meaning that arises due to the cause of birth (jāti) for aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) is profound. ...pe... The meaning that arises due to the cause of ignorance (avijjā) for volitional formations (saṅkhāra) is profound. This nature is called depth of meaning (atthagambhīratā).

The nature of ignorance being a cause for volitional formations is profound. ...pe... The nature of birth being a cause for aging and death is profound. This nature is called depth of phenomena (dhammagambhīratā).

In some discourses, the Blessed One taught Dependent Origination in forward order (anuloma); in some, in reverse order (paṭiloma); in some, in both forward and reverse order. In some, he taught starting from the middle in forward order, reverse order, or both. In some, he taught with three connections (sandhi) and four groups (saṅkhepa); in some, with two connections and three groups; in some, with one connection and two groups. Such teaching is called depth of teaching (desanāgambhīratā).

The meaning of ignorance as not knowing, not seeing, and not penetrating the Truths is profound. The meaning of volitional formations as constructing, striving, being with lust, and being without lust is profound. The meaning of consciousness (viññāṇa) as being empty (suññata), without activity (abyāpāra), without transmigration, and manifesting in rebirth is profound. The meaning of mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) as arising together, being inseparable, being separable, inclining, and changing is profound. The meaning of the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) as being predominant, being the doors of the world, being like a field, and having objects is profound.
84:
The meaning of contact (phassa) as touching, impacting, meeting, and assembling is profound. The meaning of feeling (vedanā) as experiencing the taste of an object, being pleasant, being painful, being neutral, and experiencing without a soul or self is profound. The meaning of craving (taṇhā) as great delight, being immersed in attachment, flowing like a river, entangling like a creeper, and being difficult to fill like the river of craving or the ocean of craving is profound. The meaning of clinging (upādāna) as taking, grasping, adhering, misinterpreting, and being difficult to overcome is profound. The meaning of existence (bhava) as striving, constructing, and casting into the place of rebirth, the destination (gati), the station, and the abode is profound. The meaning of birth (jāti) as being born, repeated birth, descending, arising, and manifesting is profound. The meaning of aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) as ending, breaking, destruction, and change is profound. Thus, what is the nature of ignorance and so on? By what penetration should ignorance and so on be penetrated according to their own characteristics? That nature is profound. This is to be known as the depth of penetration (paṭivedhagambhīratā).

All these depths appeared very shallow to the Venerable Ānanda. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to sharpen the Venerable Ānanda's knowledge, said "Mā hevaṃ" and so on. The meaning here is: "Ānanda, you are one of great wisdom and clear intellect; therefore, the profound Dependent Origination appears shallow to you. For that reason, do not say, 'Does this Dhamma appear shallow only to me, or does it appear so to others as well?'"

## Apasādanāvaṇṇanā
In the words said to be "reprovingly," this is the meaning: "Ānanda, do not say, 'Yet, it appears very shallow to me.' If this Dhamma appears very shallow to you, why did you not become a Stream-enterer by your own nature? You only penetrated the Path of Stream-entry by standing in the method given by me. Ānanda, only this Nibbāna is profound, while Dependent Origination is shallow to you; even so, why can you not realize the fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala) by eradicating these four defilements: the coarse fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of ill-will, and the coarse underlying tendencies of sensual lust and ill-will? Why can you not realize the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) by eradicating those same defilements along with their subtle underlying tendencies? Why can you not realize the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) by eradicating these eight defilements: the five fetters starting with lust for form, and the underlying tendencies of lust for existence, conceit, and ignorance?"
85:
Why do you not penetrate and know the disciple’s perfection-knowledge (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) like the Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Moggallāna, who fulfilled the perfections for one incalculable (asaṅkheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons? Why do you not penetrate and know the knowledge of a private Buddha (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa) like the Paccekabuddhas, who fulfilled the perfections for two incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons? If this (Dependent Origination) were evident to you in all its aspects, why do you not realize the omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) like the Buddhas, who fulfilled the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons? Do you not desire these noble attainments? Look at how great your error is! While being a disciple and standing in limited, partial knowledge (padesañāṇa), you say of the extremely profound Dependent Origination, 'It is evident to me.' This statement of yours is contrary to the words of the Buddhas. It is most appropriate to say that a monk like you should not speak in opposition to the words of the Buddhas.

Ānanda, while I, the Buddha, was striving to penetrate this Dependent Origination, did not four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons pass away? For the sake of penetrating this Dependent Origination, there is no gift I have not given, no perfection I have not fulfilled. When I conquered the army of Māra, intending to penetrate Dependent Origination, this great earth did not tremble even by two inches. Likewise, it did not tremble when I attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) in the first watch, nor when I attained the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa) in the middle watch. However, at the time of dawn, when new strength is gained in the final watch, as soon as I saw that 'Ignorance conditions volitional formations by way of nine modes,' the ten-thousandfold world system trembled like the sound of a bronze gong struck with a metal rod, releasing thousands of sounds, and shaking like a drop of water on a lotus leaf blown by the wind. Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is thus profound and has a profound appearance. Ānanda, because of not knowing this Dhamma in due order... (pe) ... they cannot transcend (the round of rebirth).

'Etassa dhammassa' means this causal state (paccaya-dhamma). 'Ananubodhā' means not knowing in due order by the power of the full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā). 'Appaṭivedhā' means not penetrating by the power of the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇapariññā) and the full understanding by abandonment (pahānapariññā). 'Tantākulakajāta' means being tangled like a weaver’s thread. For example, when a weaver’s thread is kept disorderly and bitten by mice, it becomes tangled here and there, making it difficult to match end with end or beginning with beginning. Similarly, beings are straying and confused within this Dependent Origination. They are unable to straighten this Dependent Origination. While one might be able to straighten that weaver's thread by one's own effort, however...
86:
However, setting aside the two types of Bodhisattas (the aspirants for Perfect Buddhahood and Private Buddhahood), there are no other beings who are capable of straightening the sequence of causes (Dependent Origination) by their own nature. For example, just as when tangled weaver's thread is put into sour gruel and struck with a comb, knots and tangles form in various places; similarly, these beings, becoming strayed in the sequence of causes and unable to straighten them, reach a state of confusion and entanglement through the power of the sixty-two types of wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi). Whoever follows these wrong views, all of them are simply unable to straighten the sequence of causes.

'Kulāgaṇṭhikajāta': The thread of weavers soaked in sour gruel is called 'kulāgaṇṭhika'. 'Kulā' refers to a small bird; some teachers say its nest is called 'kulāvaka'. Since both are so tangled that it is difficult to join end with end or beginning with beginning, the comparison should be applied as in the previous method.

'Muñjapabbajabhūta' means becoming like muñja grass and like pabbajja grass. When a rope made by pounding these grasses becomes old and lies in some place, it is difficult to pick it up and join end with end or beginning with beginning, saying 'this is the end' or 'this is the beginning'. One might be able to straighten that grass rope by one's own effort and diligence, however, setting aside the two types of Bodhisattas, no other beings are capable of straightening the sequence of causes by their own nature. Thus, this mass of beings, unable to straighten the sequence of causes and becoming knotted by the power of wrong views, cannot transcend the state of deprivation (apāya), the bad destination (duggati), perdition (vinipāta), and the round of rebirth (saṃsāra).

In that passage, 'apāya' refers to hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, and the host of asuras. All these are called 'apāya' because they lack 'aya', which means growth or progress. Similarly, it is called 'duggati' because it is the destination of suffering. It is called 'vinipāta' because one falls away from the mass of happiness. The remaining term 'saṃsāra' is defined as:

'The continuous and uninterrupted flow of the aggregates (khandha), and the flow of the elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana) is called saṃsāra.'

They cannot transcend or cross over all of these. Indeed, they take up repeated deaths and births, from death to rebirth and from rebirth to death, within the three realms, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, like a boat tossed by the wind in the great ocean, or like an ox yoked to a mill...
87:
(Venerable Ānanda) is merely revolving. It should be understood that the Blessed One spoke all these words while rebuking Venerable Ānanda.

## Description of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādavaṇṇanā)

Now, because this sutta is connected only by the two phrases, 'Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is profound' and 'It is like a tangled skein,' the Buddha, wishing to begin the discourse to show the profound nature of Dependent Origination with this sequence (anusandhi): 'Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is profound,' said: 'Is there a cause for aging and death?' and so forth. The meaning therein is: the cause of this aging and death is called 'idappaccaya' (this conditionality); therefore, because of this cause, aging and death exist. When asked, 'Is there a cause for aging and death? By what cause does aging and death come to be?', Ānanda, a wise person should remain silent because the question should be set aside, as when asked, 'Is that soul the same as that body?', or one should say, 'This matter has not been declared (avyākata) by the Blessed One.' Instead of doing so, just as when asked, 'Is the eye permanent or impermanent?', one should answer categorically (ekaṃsa), 'Impermanent'; so too, one should answer categorically, 'It exists.' Again, when asked, 'By what cause does aging and death come to be? What is the name of that cause from which aging and death arise?', it should be said, 'With birth as condition, aging and death come to be.' This is the intended meaning. This method applies to all terms.

In the statement, 'With name-and-form as condition, contact,' when it is said 'with the sixfold base as condition,' only the six types of resultant contact (vipāka-phassa) such as eye-contact are taken. Here, however, it should be understood that this is said because the Buddha wished to show the specific effect of contact, whether included or not included by the term 'with the sixfold base as condition,' and to show other specific causes beyond the sixfold base. What did the Blessed One teach through this section? He taught the root (nidāna) of the causes. This sutta is called 'Mahānidāna' (The Great Discourse on Causes) because it teaches the causes clearly without any confusion.

Now, to show that those various causes are the true, non-deviating, and not-otherwise causes, he said: 'It is said: With birth as condition, aging and death come to be,' and so forth. Therein, 'pariyāyena' means by way of cause. 'Sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ' are two indeclinables. The meaning of that phrase is: 'In every way, entirely...'
89:
In the statement, "With clinging as condition, existence comes to be," clinging to sense-pleasures (kāmupādāna) is the cause of the three types of kamma-existence (kammabhava) and the three types of rebirth-existence (upapattibhava). Likewise, the remaining types of clinging should be understood as the causes of the twenty-four types of existence. In this context, twelve types of kamma-existence are directly obtained. To these existences, the types of clinging are conditions by way of conascence (sahajāta) and strong dependence (upanissaya).

"Craving for forms" (rūpataṇhā) refers to craving that arises for the object of form. The same method applies to craving for sounds (saddataṇhā) and so forth. That craving is a condition for clinging by way of conascence and strong dependence.

In the statement, "This is the feeling (vedanā) which is the condition for craving," resultant feeling (vipākavedanā) is a condition for craving by way of strong dependence; other types of feeling are conditions by other methods.

Having thus shown the initial craving which is the root of the round of rebirths (saṃsāravaṭṭa), the Blessed One now wishes to show the active craving (samudācarataṇhā) that arises through nine factors—just as one might clear from the path a person who is shouting while being struck on the back or dragged by the hair—and thus said: "Ānanda, thus conditioned by feeling, craving arises," and so forth. In that context, craving is of two kinds: craving that seeks (esanataṇhā) and craving for what is sought (esitataṇhā). The craving by which one travels through difficult paths, spiked paths, etc., to seek wealth is called craving that seeks (esanataṇhā). The craving that arises when that sought-after wealth is obtained is called craving for what is sought (esitataṇhā). Both of these are merely names for active craving (samudācarataṇhā). Therefore, craving conditioned by feeling is of two kinds. "Search" (pariyesanā) means seeking objects such as forms; that search occurs only when there is craving. "Gain" (lābha) means obtaining objects such as forms; that gain occurs only when there is a search. "Decision" (vinicchaya), however, is of four kinds by way of wisdom, craving, views, and thought (vitakka). In this regard: "One should know the decision for happiness; knowing the decision for happiness, one should pursue internal happiness" (Majjhima Nikāya)—this statement refers to decision by wisdom (ñāṇavinicchaya). "Decision is of two kinds: decision by craving and decision by views" (Mahāniddesa). The 108 instances of craving mentioned in this way are decision by craving (taṇhāvinicchaya). The 62 types of views are decision by views (diṭṭhivinicchaya). In the sutta: "Great King, desire (chanda) has thought (vitakka) as its cause" (Dīgha Nikāya), the intended meaning here is only the thought (vitakka) which is called "decision" (vinicchaya). Indeed, after obtaining gain, one decides through thought upon what is desired, what is undesired, what is good, and what is bad...
90:
"He decides" (vinicchinnāti) means deciding: "This much will be for the sake of my visual objects, this much for the sake of sounds, etc.; this much will be for me, this much for others; this much I will consume, this much I will store." Therefore, it is said, "Conditioned by gain, decision (vinicchaya) arises."

"Desire and lust" (chandarāgo) refers to the arising of weak lust and strong lust for the object thought about with unwholesome thoughts. This state, in this context, is craving itself. "Desire" (chando) is the name for weak lust. "Attachment" (ajjhosāna) is the strong decision (clinging) as "I" and "mine." "Possession" (pariggaha) is the act of taking possession by the power of craving and views. "Stinginess" (macchariya) is the inability to tolerate sharing with others. For this reason, the former teachers gave the etymological definition (vacanattha) that it is called macchariya because it arises as: "May this wonderful thing (wealth) be for me alone, let it not be a wonder for others." "Protection" (ārakkha) is guarding well by way of closing doors, securing with boxes, and so forth. It is called "adhikaraṇa" because of the meaning "he does it" (adhikaroti); it is a name for a cause. "By reason of protection" (ārakkhādhikaraṇa) is a neuter abstract noun meaning "because of the cause of protection" (ārakkhahetu). In the phrase "taking up the rod, etc." (daṇḍādānādīsu), taking up a rod for the sake of restraining others is called "taking up the rod" (daṇḍādāna). Taking up a single-edged weapon, etc., is called "taking up weapons" (satthādāna). "Quarrel" (kalaha) is verbal or physical dispute. The initial opposition is called "strife" (viggaha). The subsequent opposition is called "dispute" (vivāda). "Tuvaṃ tuvaṃ" (You! You!) is disrespectful speech.

Now, to show that active craving (samudācarataṇhā) by the reverse method (paṭiloma), the teaching is turned back starting with "by reason of protection." In that context, "craving for sense-pleasures" (kāmataṇhā) is the attachment to forms, etc., arising by the power of lust for the five cords of sense-pleasure. "Craving for existence" (bhavataṇhā) is lust accompanied by the eternalist view (sassatadiṭṭhi). "Craving for non-existence" (vibhavataṇhā) is lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (ucchedadiṭṭhi). "These two things" (ime dve dhammā) refers to these two states: craving as the root of the round and active craving. "By the duality" (dvayena) means that although they reach a single state by the characteristic of craving, they have a single meeting point in feeling through the two portions of the root of the round and the active craving; it means they have a single cause because they are conditioned by feeling. Convergence (samosaraṇa) is of three kinds: convergence by arrival (osaraṇasamosaraṇa), convergence by conascence (sahajātasamosaraṇa), and convergence by condition (paccayasamosaraṇa). In this regard: "All those things converge in desire (kāma)"—this statement is called convergence by arrival. "Friends, all these things have desire as their root, contact as their origin, and they converge in feeling"—this statement is called convergence by conascence. "They have a single meeting point in feeling by way of two aspects"—this statement should be understood as convergence by condition.
91:
"Eye-contact" (cakkhusamphassa) and so forth are all only resultant contacts (vipākaphassa). Among those contacts, excluding the four supramundane resultant contacts, there are thirty-two remaining contacts. In the statement "namely, contact" (yadidaṃ phasso), contact reaches the state of being a condition for feeling in many ways.

In the words "by whatever qualities, Ānanda" (yehi ānanda ākārehi) and so forth, the distinct natures of feeling, etc., are called "qualities" (ākāra). Those same qualities, when well-presented, are called "signs" (liṅga) because they make known the various hidden meanings. They are called "marks" (nimitta) because they are the cause of knowing various things. They are called "designations" (uddesa) because they are thus pointed out. Therefore, the meaning here is: "Ānanda, by whatever qualities... by whatever designations there is a description of the mental body (nāmakāya), the collection of mental states; if there were the quality of experiencing, the sign of experiencing, the mark of experiencing, and the designation 'feeling' in feeling; if there were the quality of perceiving, the sign of perceiving, the mark of perceiving, and the designation 'perception' in perception; if there were the quality of volitional activity, the sign of volitional activity, the mark of volitional activity, and the designation 'volition' in the mental formations; if there were the quality of cognizing, the sign of cognizing, the mark of cognizing, and the designation 'consciousness' in consciousness—then there is the description of the mental body as 'this is the mental body.' If those feelings, etc., and qualities, etc., which are the causes for the description of the mental body did not exist, would designation-contact (adhivacanasamphassa), which has name-description as its object, be manifest in the physical body (rūpakāya), the collection of form? Mind-contact (manosamphassa), named designation-contact, arises in the mind-door based on the four mental aggregates; would that mind-contact be manifest in the physical body, or would it arise based on the five sensitive forms (pasādarūpa)?" He asked this. Then, the Venerable Ānanda, just as one would not accept the arising of a mango from a rose-apple tree if no mango tree existed, did not accept the arising of that contact from the physical body and replied, "No, Bhante, it would not be so."

In the second question (dutiyapañhe), the meaning of qualities (ākāra) and so forth should be understood by way of the quality of being deformed, the sign of being deformed, the mark of being deformed, and by way of the designation "form" (rūpa). "Impingement-contact" (paṭighasamphassa) is the contact that arises based on the aggregate of form which is accompanied by impingement (paṭigha). Here too, the Elder, just as one would not accept the arising of a rose-apple from a mango tree if no rose-apple tree existed, did not accept the arising of that contact from the mental body and replied, "No, Bhante, it would not be so."
92:
The third problem is taught by way of both (name and form). In that problem, the Elder Ānanda, unable to accept the arising of both types of contact without name-and-form—like the appearance of mangoes or rose-apples in the sky—replied, "Venerable Sir, it is not so."

Having thus shown the causes of the two types of contact separately, the Buddha now begins the fourth problem with the words, "Ānanda, in whatever way," to show without distinction (comprehensively) that both types of contact have name-and-form as their cause. The phrase "yadidaṃ nāmarūpaṃ" means that this very name-and-form, which occurs in the six sense bases, is the root and the support. In the eye-door and others, the faculties such as the eye and the objects such as visible forms are called 'form' (rūpa); the associated aggregates are called 'name' (nāma). Thus, those five types of contact are indeed contacts that have name-and-form as their cause. In the mind-door as well, the heart-base (hadayavatthu) and physical objects are called 'form'; the associated states and mental objects are called 'name'. Thus, it should be understood that mind-contact (manosamphassa) also has name-and-form as its cause. Name-and-form is the cause for that contact in many ways.

"If it were not to descend" means if it were not to arise by way of rebirth, as if entering (the mother's womb). "Would there be a consolidation?" means if there were no rebirth-consciousness, would the remaining name-and-form alone be able to consolidate and mix within the mother's womb in the form of the embryonic drop (kalala) and so on? (It would not). "Having descended, if it were to depart" means having descended by way of rebirth, if it were to depart or cease by way of death (cuti). The cessation of that name-and-form does not occur merely by the cessation of that (rebirth) consciousness, nor by the cessation of the second or third consciousness thereafter. The thirty types of kamma-born matter (kammajarūpa) arise together with the rebirth-consciousness. While those forms exist, sixteen moments of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) arise and cease. During this period, no danger can befall the gestating child or the child's mother. This is called the period without opportunity (anokāsa) [for danger]. If the forms that arose with the rebirth-consciousness can support the seventeenth bhavaṅga consciousness, the process continues and the continuity is linked. If they cannot, the process does not occur and the continuity is broken; this is called departure (vokkamanā). It is with reference to this that it was said, "Having descended, if it were to depart."

"For such a state of existence" means for the state of being a being of the five-aggregate realm (pañcavokāra) in such a complete way. "While still a child" means while still a tender infant. "If it were to be cut off" means...
93:
Would growth, increase, and expansion cease? This means when consciousness is cut off, only name-and-form alone arises; would it then not reach growth in the first stage of life, increase in the middle stage, and expansion in the final stage? Alternatively, it means would it still be able to reach growth, increase, and expansion by reaching ten years, twenty years, a hundred years, or a thousand years? Ānanda, therefore, whether in taking rebirth in the mother's womb, or while staying in the womb, or while coming out of the womb, or when having been born during the period of ten years and so on, consciousness alone is the cause of that name-and-form. Therefore, this consciousness alone is the root of name-and-form; this is the cause.

For example, when a king wishes to suppress his retinue, he might say, 'Who made you the Crown Prince? Who made you the General? Did I not do it? If I had not done it, would you, by your own nature, be the Crown Prince or the General? We shall see your power yet!' Similarly, consciousness is the cause of name-and-form. In meaning, it is as if it says to name-and-form: 'Who made you "name"? Who made you "form"? Who made you "name-and-form"? Did I not do it? If I had not taken the lead and taken rebirth in the mother's womb, would you be name, or form, or name-and-form? We shall see your power yet!' That consciousness is the cause of name-and-form in various ways.

"The arising of the root of suffering" means the arising of the mass of suffering. "This name-and-form" means this very name-and-form is the root, the cause. For example, when the king's servants wish to suppress the king, they might say, 'Who made you the king? Did we not do it? If I did not stand in the position of Crown Prince, and I in the position of General, could you be the sole king? We shall see your kingship yet!' Similarly, name-and-form, in meaning, is as if it says to consciousness: 'Who made you the rebirth-consciousness? Did we not do it? Without depending on the three mental aggregates and the heart-base (hadayavatthu), could that which is called rebirth-consciousness exist? We shall see your state as rebirth-consciousness yet!' That name-and-form is also the cause of consciousness in various ways. "To this extent" means when consciousness is the cause of name-and-form, and name-and-form is the cause of consciousness, and both exist by depending on each other reciprocally...
94: By this much, birth, aging, death, passing away, and rebirth are manifest; or rather, repeated passing away and rebirth occur. 'Adhivacanapatha' (path of designation) is the path of terminology that arises by emphasizing the mere word without looking at the meaning, such as 'Sirivaḍḍhaka' (increaser of glory) or 'Dhanavaḍḍhaka' (increaser of wealth). 'Niruttipatha' (path of language) is the path of terminology that arises by expressing the root cause, such as 'sato' (one who has mindfulness) because of being able to remember, or 'sampajāno' (one who has clear comprehension) because of knowing well. 'Paññattipatha' (path of concept) is the path of terminology that arises by making known in various ways, such as 'wise one, skilled one, intelligent one, profound one, one who can refute the views of others.' Thus, by these three terms, he teaches only the aggregates (khandhas) which are the basis for designation and so on. 'Paññāvacara' means that which is to be understood by entering into it with wisdom. 'The wheel of the round turns' means the turning of the round of saṃsāra. 'Itthatta' means being in this state; this is a name for the five aggregates. 'For the sake of designating' means for the purpose of designating names. It means that by this much, all five aggregates are to be known by wisdom for the purpose of designating names such as 'feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā),' and so on. 'This name-and-form together with consciousness' means that this name-and-form arises by mutually conditioning with consciousness; it means 'by this much.' This is the concluding statement here.## Description of the Designation of SelfThe Blessed One, having shown the sequence (anusandhi) of the phrase 'Ānanda, this Dependent Origination is deep and has a deep appearance,' now wishing to show the sequence of the phrase 'it is like a tangled ball of thread,' began the teaching with 'Ānanda, by how much' and so on. Therein, in the words 'Ānanda, either a material self that is limited' and so on, whoever takes a kasiṇa-sign that has not been developed as the self, he designates a material, limited self. Whoever is one who has obtained various kasiṇas, he designates that self sometimes as blue, sometimes as yellow. Whoever takes a kasiṇa-sign that has been developed as the self, he designates a material, unlimited self. Or, whoever removes the kasiṇa-sign that has not been developed and takes either the space in contact with the sign, or the four aggregates arising therein, or only the consciousness among those aggregates as the self, he designates an immaterial, limited self. Whoever removes the developed sign and takes either the space in contact with the sign, or the four aggregates arising therein, or only the consciousness among those aggregates as the self, he designates an immaterial, unlimited self.
95:
In that context, 'Ānanda' refers to one among those four types of adherents of views. 'Even now' means at this very moment, not after this. This statement is preached by way of annihilationism (uccheda). 'That which will be in the future' refers to that which will occur in such a future world. This statement is preached by way of eternalism (sassata). 'Being even that which is not' means although it is of a nature that is not. 'For the sake of being true' means for the sake of becoming a true nature. 'I shall prepare' means I shall fulfill. By this statement, he shows the dispute. The annihilationist thinks, 'Although the eternalist's self is of a nature that is not, and of a nature that does not cease, I shall prepare it to become the annihilationist nature which is the true nature; I shall make him know eternalism and make him adopt only annihilationism.'
