The eternalist also thinks, 'Although the annihilationist's self is of a nature that is not, and of a nature that is not permanent, I shall prepare it to become the eternalist nature which is the true nature; I shall make him know annihilationism and make him adopt only eternalism.' 'When this is so' means for one who designates a self that has form and is limited. 'Having form' (rūpī) refers to one who has attained a fine-material kasina. The latent tendency of the wrong view 'the self is limited' means this view of a limited self lies latent; that view does not lie latent by clinging like a large creeper or a small creeper. It should be understood as lying latent in the sense of not being abandoned. 'It is fit to say thus' means it is appropriate to say that such a kind of view lies latent in that person. This method is the same in all places. 'Formless' (arūpī) here means one who has attained an immaterial kasina, or it should be understood as one who takes the immaterial aggregates as an object. By this much, the sixteen types of adherents of views who hold to a self—by way of the four who attain kasina, their four disciples, the four thinkers (takki-ka), and their four disciples—have been shown.

## Commentary on the Non-designation of Self

Having shown those who designate a self, now to show those who do not designate a self, he said: 'Ānanda, in how many ways' and so forth. Who are those who do not designate? First, all Noble Ones (ariyas) do not designate. Any person who is learned, a bearer of the Tipitaka, a bearer of two Pitakas, or a bearer of one Pitaka, or at the very least, a Dhamma preacher who has well-decided and learned even one Nikāya, or a person practicing insight (vipassanā)—they also do not designate. For them, in the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-kasina), knowledge arises only as the counterpart sign. In the immaterial aggregates, knowledge arises only as immaterial aggregates.
96:
## Explanation of the Contemplation of Self

After showing those who do not designate a self, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with "Ānanda, to what extent," and so forth, to show those who do designate a self, who designate it by repeatedly contemplating through the power of views. Their repeated contemplation occurs because the identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) with twenty bases has not yet been abandoned. Therefore, to show that identity view with twenty bases, He spoke those words.

Among those passages, by the words "or feeling," He taught the identity view that takes the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) as its object. By the words "My self is not subject to feeling," He taught the identity view that takes the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) as its object. By the words "My self is subject to feeling, my self has the nature of feeling," He taught the identity view that takes the aggregates of perception (saññā), volitional formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa) as its object. These three aggregates are subject to feeling because they are associated with feeling. For these three aggregates, the nature of feeling is inseparable.

Now, to show the fault in that doctrine, He spoke the words beginning with "Ānanda, in that case." In that passage, "in that case" means among those three types of persons who hold such views. The words beginning with "Ānanda, whenever" were spoken to show the fault—such as sometimes arising and sometimes not arising—to the self of whichever person repeatedly contemplates whichever feeling as self.

Among the terms such as "impermanent" (anicca), they are impermanent because they do not exist after having come to be. They are called "conditioned" (saṅkhata) because they are prepared and combined by various causes. They are called "dependently arisen" (paṭiccasamuppanna) because they arise only due to a proper cause in dependence on various conditions. All the words beginning with "exhaustion" are synonyms for dissolution (bhaṅga). Whatever dharma dissolves, that dharma also is exhausted, wanes, fades away, and ceases. Therefore, it is said, "dharma having the nature of exhaustion," and so forth.

In the phrase "My self has vanished," the word "vyagā" is "vi-agā" (vanished). It means my self has vanished, has ceased. Does the thought "This is my self" occur to a single person in all three periods of time? Why would it not? For a person with views, there is no such thing as stability or stillness, like a stake driven into a heap of chaff; like a forest monkey, they grab one thing and let go of another. "It is mixed with impermanence, happiness, and suffering" means that specifically, one who repeatedly contemplates various feelings as self also repeatedly contemplates impermanence, happiness, and suffering as self. One who contemplates feeling as self without specification [contemplates] the mixed...
97:
...contemplates oneself as a self that has the nature of arising and passing away. Feelings are of three kinds and they also have the nature of arising and passing away; this person regards that very feeling as the self. For one who contemplates thus, the self would be impermanent, and there would be the arising of many feelings in a single moment. That person admits to an impermanent self, yet there is no arising of many feelings in a single moment. With this meaning in mind, it was said: 'Ānanda, therefore, for this reason also, it is not proper to regard "feeling is my self".'

'Friend, where' refers to that place where there is no feeling or experience in any way within the mere aggregate of form. 'Api nu kho tattha' means: would such an I-making (ahaṅkāra) as 'I am' arise in that palm-leaf fan or in that window which is devoid of feeling? 'Ānanda, therefore' means: because the mere aggregate of form cannot rise up and say 'I am', therefore, for this reason also, it is not proper to regard it thus. 'Api nu kho tattha ayam-aham-asmīti siyā' means: among those feelings, or among the remaining three aggregates, could even a single dharma be spoken of as 'This is I'? Or, when those three aggregates have ceased along with feeling due to the cessation of feeling, would the thought 'This is I' or 'I am' arise? Then, the Venerable Ānanda, not accepting that point—just as the sharpness of a rabbit's horn [is non-existent]—replied, 'No, Bhante.'

By this much, what is being taught? It is the teaching on the round of rebirth (vaṭṭakathā). When the Blessed One teaches the vaṭṭakathā, in some places He teaches it by making ignorance (avijjā) the starting point; in some places, craving (taṇhā); and in some places, views (diṭṭhi). Among those ways of teaching, He taught with ignorance as the starting point thus: 'Monks, the first beginning of ignorance is not apparent, such that one could know: "Before this, ignorance did not exist; it has arisen only since then." Monks, it is also said thus. However, it can be known that ignorance arises due to this cause.' He taught with craving as the starting point thus: 'Monks, the first beginning of craving for existence (bhavataṇhā) is not apparent...' and so forth. He taught with views as the starting point thus: 'Monks, the first beginning of the view of existence (bhavadiṭṭhi) is not apparent...' and so forth. In this sutta, He taught only with views as the starting point.
98:
A person with wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) takes feelings such as pleasure as the self, and through the power of I-making (ahaṅkāra), my-making (mamaṅkāra), and misapprehension (parāmāsa), they pass away from one state and arise in another throughout all types of existence (bhava), modes of birth (yoni), destinations (gati), stations of consciousness (viññāṇatthiti), and abodes of beings (sattāvāsa). Like a boat tossed by the wind in the ocean, they constantly wander and are no longer able to even lift their head from the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha).

Having thus taught the round of rebirth to the person with wrong view who is confused about dependent origination, the Blessed One, now wishing to teach the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa/Nibbāna), said: 'Ānanda, when a monk...' and so forth.

Because the Blessed One is skilled in teaching, He began that discourse on the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭakathā) by way of a person who habitually dwells in the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), saying: 'He no longer regards feeling as self,' and so forth. Such a monk distinguishes and contemplates all form—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—as 'impermanent'; this is one [mode of] comprehension (sammasana). He contemplates it as 'suffering'; this is one comprehension. He contemplates it as 'non-self'; this is one comprehension. By the power of the knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa) described in this way, because it occurs in all things, he does not regard feeling as self, nor does he regard any other dharma [as self]. Such a person who does not so regard does not cling to anything in the world. Among the things such as form in the world diversified by the world of aggregates, etc., he no longer clings to even a single dharma as 'self' or as 'belonging to self'.

'Being unattached, he is not agitated' means that one who does not cling is no longer tormented by the fever of craving, views, and conceit. 'He is personally cooled' means he is cooled by the personal extinguishing of defilements. To show how the knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) arises in one who is thus cooled, He said: 'Birth is exhausted,' and so forth.

'Thus is that view' means the view of an Arahant who is thus liberated from defilements is of such a kind. There is also a variant reading 'itissa diṭṭhi'. It means an Arahant liberated from defilements has such a view. 'That view is improper' means that [the view that an Arahant knows nothing] is improper. Why? If such [an improper view] existed, it would amount to saying 'the Arahant knows nothing at all.' It is improper to say of an Arahant who has known thus and become liberated that 'he knows nothing.'
100:
Therefore, it is said, "They have diverse bodies." Their rebirth perception (paṭisandhisaññā) is either three-rooted (tihetu), two-rooted (dvihetu), or rootless (ahetu); thus, it is said, "They have diverse perceptions." "Some devas" refers to the six heavens of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara). Among those devas, some have dark-colored bodies, some have yellow-colored bodies, and so on. Their perception is either two-rooted or three-rooted, but never rootless. "Some fallen asuras (vinipātika asuras)" refers to those like the ogresses Uttaramātā, Piyaṅkaramātā, Phussamittā, Dhammaguttā, and other mansion-dwelling ghosts (vemānika petas) who are free from the four lower realms. Their bodies are diverse in color—yellow, white, black, or variegated—and diverse in form—thin, stout, short, or tall. Their perception is also diverse, being two-rooted, three-rooted, or rootless, just like humans. They do not possess great power and majesty like the devas; rather, they have little power like poor humans, and they suffer from the difficulty of obtaining food and clothing, being oppressed by misery. Some suffer during the waning moon and enjoy happiness during the waxing moon. Because they have fallen from a happy state, they are called "fallen" (vinipātika). Among them, those who are three-rooted individuals can achieve the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya). The ogress Piyaṅkaramātā, having heard the Venerable Anuruddha reciting the Dhamma at dawn, spoke to her son Piyaṅkara to make him listen:

"Dear Piyaṅkara, do not make a sound. The monk is reciting verses of the Dhammapada. If we understand and practice the Dhammapada, it will lead to our welfare and happiness. Let us refrain from killing living beings, let us not knowingly speak lies, and let us learn to observe our virtue (sīla); perhaps we may be released from this state of being a demon (yakkha)."

After saying this, she attained the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) on that very day. The ogress Uttaramātā also became a Stream-enterer just by hearing the Buddha's teaching.

"Brahmakāyika" refers to the Brahma’s Retinue (brahmapārisajja), the Brahma’s Ministers (brahmapurohita), and the Great Brahmas (mahābrahmā). "Those who have arisen first" means all those Brahmas have arisen through the first jhāna. Among them, the Brahmapārisajja Brahmas arise through a limited (paritta) jhāna; their lifespan is one-third of an aeon (kappa). The Brahmapurohita Brahmas arise through a medium (majjhima) jhāna; their lifespan is half an aeon, and their bodies are larger and more extensive. The Mahābrahmā Brahmas arise through a superior (paṇīta) jhāna; their lifespan is one aeon, and their bodies are very large and extensive. Thus, although these Brahmas have diverse bodies, they have a single perception through the power of the first jhāna; therefore, they should be understood as "having diverse bodies but a single perception."
101:
Just like those Brahmas, the beings in the four lower realms are similar. In the hells, some beings have bodies the size of a gāvuta, some half a yojana, and some one yojana. Devadatta's body, however, is a hundred yojanas. Among animals, some are small and some are large. In the realm of ghosts (peta loka), some are sixty cubits, some seventy, and some eighty cubits tall. Some are beautiful, and some are ugly. Similarly, it is the same for the Kālakañjika asuras. Furthermore, in this realm, there are ghosts called Dīghapiṭṭhika who are as large as sixty yojanas. As for perception, all of them have only rootless unwholesome resultant perceptions (akusalavipāka ahetuka saññā). Thus, the beings of the lower realms also fall under the category of "having diverse bodies but a single perception."

"Ābhassara" means that the radiance from the bodies of these Brahmas spreads out as if flames were falling intermittently from a torch. Among them, those who arise by developing the second and third jhānas (according to the fivefold method) to a limited (paritta) degree are called Parittābha; their lifespan is two aeons. Those who develop them to a medium (majjhima) degree are called Appamāṇābha; their lifespan is four aeons. Those who develop them to a superior (paṇīta) degree are called Ābhassara; their lifespan is eight aeons. Here, all are included under the superior category. All these Brahmas have a single extensive body, but their perception is diverse, either having only sustained thought (vicāra) without initial thought (vitakka), or having neither initial nor sustained thought.

"Subhakiṇhā" means they are suffused and spread with beautiful radiance; it means they are a solid mass of beautiful aura. Their radiance does not flicker or break like that of the Ābhassara Brahmas. Through the power of the fourth jhāna (in the fivefold method) which is limited, medium, or superior, they arise as Parittasubha, Appamāṇasubha, and Subhakiṇhā, with lifespans of 16, 32, and 64 aeons respectively. Thus, all these Brahmas should be understood as having a single body and a single perception through the fourth jhāna perception. The Vehapphala Brahmas also attain the fourth station of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). Non-percipient beings (asaññasatta) are not included in these stations of consciousness because they lack consciousness, but they are included in the abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).

The Suddhāvāsa Brahmas stand on the side of liberation (vivaṭṭapakkha); they do not appear at all times. They do not appear in a world void of Buddhas for a hundred thousand aeons or an incalculable period (asaṅkheyya). They only appear when Buddhas arise within sixteen thousand aeons; they are like the site of the Buddha's encampment (khandhāvāra) when He turns the Wheel of Dhamma. Therefore, these Brahmas are not included in the stations of consciousness or the abodes of beings. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "Sāriputta, that is not the abode of beings..."
102:
"In this long period of time, there is hardly any abode where I have not lived before, except for the Suddhāvāsa devas" (M. Ni. 1, 160). According to this sutta, it is taught that the inhabitants of the Suddhāvāsa realms are indeed included in the fourth station of consciousness and the fourth abode of beings. Since there is no reason to reject this sutta, it should be accepted and confirmed.

The meaning of the terms beginning with "Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ" has been explained in the Visuddhimagga. In the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), just as perception is subtle, consciousness is also extremely subtle; thus, it is neither said that consciousness exists nor that it does not exist. Therefore, it is not included among the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti) but is taught only among the spheres (āyatana).

"Tatra" means "in those stations of consciousness." "Tဉ္စ pajānāti" means "he understands that station of consciousness." "Tassa ca samudayaṃ" means he understands the cause of that station of consciousness through the method "With the arising of ignorance, matter arises," etc. (Paṭi. Ma. 1, 49). "Tassa ca atthaṅgamaṃ" means he understands the cessation of that station of consciousness through the method "With the cessation of ignorance, matter ceases," etc. "Assādaṃ" means he understands the gratification of that station of consciousness, such as the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on matter... dependent on consciousness. "Ādīnavaṃ" means he understands the danger of that station of consciousness, such as "Matter is... consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change." "Nissaraṇaṃ" means he understands the escape from that station of consciousness, which is the removal and abandonment of desire and lust for matter... for consciousness (Saṃ. Ni. 2, 26). "Kallaṃ nu tena" means "Is it fit for that monk to delight in that station of consciousness as 'I' or 'mine' through the power of craving, conceit, and views?" In this way, it should be understood in all places. In the formless (arūpa) realms, the origin (samudaya) should be applied through the power of the four mental aggregates, and in the non-percipient (asaññasatta) realm, through the power of the single aggregate of matter. The phrase "With the arising of nutriment, with the cessation of nutriment" should also be applied here.

"Yato kho Ānanda bhikkhu" means "Ananda, when a monk..." "Anupādā vimutto" means one who is liberated without clinging through the four types of grasping. "Paññāvimutto" means one who is liberated by wisdom. It means one who, without realizing the eight liberations (vimokkha), brings about the non-arising of the mental and material aggregates through wisdom alone and is thus liberated. Such a person may be a dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) or one who, established in any of the jhānas such as the first jhāna, attains Arahantship...
103:
There are five types of persons who have reached (the fruit of Arahantship). It is also preached thus: "What is the person liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta)? Here, a certain person does not dwell having touched the eight liberations (vimokkha) with his body, but having seen with wisdom, his taints (āsavas) are exhausted; this person is called a person liberated by wisdom" (Puggalapaññatti, 15).

## Commentary on the Eight Liberations

Thus, having shown the conclusion and the name of one monk, to show the name of the remaining monk, he said: "These eight, indeed" and so forth. In that context, for what reason is it called 'liberation' (vimokkha)? It is because of the sense of resolution (adhimuccana). What is meant by the sense of resolution? It is the sense of being well-freed from opposing states, and the sense of well-entering into the object by way of delighting in it. It refers to the occurrence of the mind in the object without doubt, in a state of being unrestrained, like a child who falls asleep throwing his limbs into his father's lap. This meaning does not exist in the last liberation, but it exists in all the preceding liberations. In the phrase "possessing form, one sees forms" (rūpī rūpāni passati), the fine-material jhāna produced by way of the blue kasina and so forth, whether in objects within one's own continuity such as hair and so forth, or in the blue kasina and so forth, is called 'form' (rūpa); because of having that fine-material jhāna, one is called 'possessing form' (rūpī). "He sees forms externally" means looking at external forms such as the blue kasina and so forth with the eye of jhāna. By this statement, he shows the four fine-material sphere jhānas of a person who has jhānas produced in kasinas occurring in one's own continuity and in external objects. "Internally not perceiving form" (ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī) means the absence of the perception of form in one's own continuity; it means one who does not produce fine-material sphere jhāna in one's own hair and so forth. By this statement, he shows the fine-material sphere jhānas of a person who, having performed the preliminary work (parikamma) externally, has jhānas produced only externally. "He is resolved only on the beautiful" (subhanteva adhimutto hoti)—by this statement, he shows the jhānas occurring in the extremely pure blue-colored kasinas and so forth. In that jhāna, although there is no reflection of 'it is beautiful' within the absorption (appanā), because one who dwells taking a pure and beautiful kasina as an object reaches a state that can be said to be 'resolved on the beautiful', this was preached. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga, however: "How is it that one is resolved only on the beautiful and thus it is a liberation? Here, a monk dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness (mettā)... etc... because loving-kindness is developed, beings are not repulsive. He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā)... etc... because equanimity is developed, beings are..."
104:
“...not repulsive. Thus, dwelling with an extreme inclination only towards the beautiful (subha) is called liberation (vimokkha) (in the Paṭisambhidāmagga).”

All that is to be said regarding the terms beginning with “Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ” has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. This eighth liberation is called the eighth noble liberation because the four mental aggregates are pure in every respect and because they are liberated.

“Anuloma” (forward order) means occurring from the beginning to the end. “Paṭiloma” (reverse order) means occurring from the end to the beginning. “Anulomapaṭiloma” (forward and reverse) is said by way of moving back and forth without stopping because the attainments (samāpatti) have been thoroughly mastered. “Yatthicchaka” (wherever desired) indicates the location (okāsa), meaning it occurs in whatever place one desires. “Yadicchaka” (whichever desired) indicates the attainment, meaning whichever attainment one desires. “Yāvatiicchaka” (for however long desired) indicates the duration (addhāna), meaning for as long a time as one desires. “Samāpajjati” means he enters into those various attainments. “Vuṭṭhāti” means he emerges and stands from that attainment.

“Ubhatobhāgavimutta” means one who is liberated in two ways. It means one is liberated from the material body (rūpakāya) by the formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti), and liberated from the mental body (nāmakāya) by the Path (magga). It is also stated thus:
“Just as a flame blown by the force of the wind, (O Upasīva—said the Blessed One)
Goes to its end and cannot be reckoned;
Even so the Sage (Muni), liberated from the mental body,
Goes to his end and cannot be reckoned.”

That Ubhatobhāgavimutta person is of five types, such as one who reaches the fruit of Arahatship after emerging from any of the attainments like the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), or one who, being a non-returner (anāgāmī), reaches the fruit of Arahatship after emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Some teachers, however, say: “The fourth fine-material jhāna also has two factors and is associated with equanimity; the formless jhānas are the same. Therefore, a person who reaches the fruit of Arahatship after emerging from the fourth fine-material jhāna is also an Ubhatobhāgavimutta.”

This problem of the Ubhatobhāgavimutta arose at the Lower Lohapāsāda and reached a decision only after a long time, based on the explanation of the Elder Tipitaka Cūḷasumana.
105:
A disciple of the Elder residing at Girivihāra heard that problem from a monk who had come for alms and said: “Friend, when our teacher was preaching the Dhamma at the Lower Lohapāsāda, no one had ever heard such a statement.” “Venerable sir, what did the Elder say?” “The fourth fine-material jhāna has two factors and is associated with equanimity, yet it can only remove the defilements; it arises only in the vicinity of the place where defilements are born. These defilements in the five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava) arise depending on some object such as blue (nīla), and the fine-material jhāna cannot transcend that object. Therefore, only the person who reaches the fruit of Arahatship after removing the defilements by the power of formless jhāna, having excluded all material objects, is called an Ubhatobhāgavimutta,” so the Elder said, friend. Having said this, he cited this Sutta: “What kind of person is liberated in both ways (ubhatobhāgavimutta)? In this Dispensation, a certain person dwells having personally experienced the eight liberations with the body, and by wisdom, that person's taints are exhausted. This person is called an Ubhatobhāgavimutta person.”

“Ānanda, by this liberation in both ways” means, Ānanda, because of this aforementioned liberation in both ways. All the remaining words are clear in every instance.

## The Explanation of the Mahānidāna Sutta is finished.
106:
## 3. Explanation of the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta

“Evaṃ me sutaṃ” and so forth is the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. In that Sutta, the explanation of terms in order is as follows: “Gijjhakūṭe” means vultures (gijjha) dwell on those mountain peaks, or the peak (kūṭa) of that mountain resembles a vulture; therefore, it is called Gijjhakūṭa (Vulture Peak); on that Gijjhakūṭa mountain. “Abhiyātukāmo” means one who desires to go for the purpose of subduing. “Vajjī” means the Vajjī kings. “Evamahiddhike” means endowed with such great royal power; by this word, the unity of those kings is stated. “Evamahānubhāve” means endowed with such great majesty; by this word, their state of being trained in elephantry and so forth is stated. With reference to that reason, it is said: “These Licchavī princes are indeed trained in arts, well-trained indeed, for they can shoot arrows one after another through a small drum-hole without missing.” “Ucchecchāmi” means I shall slaughter them to the root. “Vināsessāmi” means I shall cause them to perish, I shall make them invisible. In the term “Anayavyasana,” that which is not “aya” (prosperity) is “anaya,” which is a name for non-prosperity. Because it destroys welfare and happiness, it is called “vyasana,” which is a name for the ruin of relatives and so forth. “Āpādessāmi” means I shall cause them to reach.

Thus, that king spoke only this talk of war at times such as standing or sitting; he gave orders to the troops, “Prepare to go.” Why? Depending on a port village near the Ganges river, King Ajātasattu's authority extended for about half a league (yojana), and the Licchavī kings' authority also extended for about half a league. It means this was a place where their authorities overlapped. In that place, valuable goods also used to come down from the foot of the mountains. Hearing that news, while King Ajātasattu was planning, “I will go today, I will go tomorrow,” the Licchavī kings, being united and joyful, went first and took everything. When King Ajātasattu arrived later and learned of that matter, he had to return in anger. Those kings did the same in subsequent years as well. Then King Ajātasattu, bearing a deep grudge, acted in this way.

At that time, the king thought: “Fighting against a group is a heavy task; there is no such thing as a harmless blow (it involves much injury). If it is done after consulting with a wise person, it will be faultless. As for a wise person, there is no one equal to the Buddha, and the Buddha is dwelling in the nearby Dhura-vihāra. I will send...”
107:
“I will ask. If there is any benefit in my going, the Blessed One will remain silent. If there is no benefit, he will say, ‘Great King, what is the use of your going there?’” (Thus King Ajātasattu reflected). That king then sent the Brahmin Vassakāra. The Brahmin went and reported this matter to the Blessed One. This account is stated in the words beginning with ‘Atha kho rājā... pe... āpādessāmī’.

## Commentary on the Conditions for Non-decline of Kings

‘Fanning the Blessed One’ means that the Elder Ānanda was standing in the place of performing his duties and fanning the Blessed One. Although the Blessed One feels neither cold nor heat, (this was done as a service). When the Blessed One heard the Brahmin's words, he did not speak to the Brahmin but, wishing to speak with the Elder, said, “Ānanda, what have you heard?” and so forth.

‘Assemble frequently’ means assembling three times a day, or assembling during the intervals; these are indeed frequent assemblies.

‘Assembling in large numbers’ refers to those who assemble without becoming weary, thinking, ‘We assembled yesterday, and the day before; why must we assemble again today?’

‘As long as’.

“Ānanda, for the Vajjis, only growth is to be expected, not decline” means: those who do not assemble frequently do not hear the news coming from various directions. Because they do not hear it, they cannot know, ‘The boundaries of such-and-such a village or town are in disorder; thieves are rising up in such-and-such a place.’ Thieves, knowing that ‘The kings are negligent,’ attack and destroy villages, towns, and so forth, causing the ruin of the countryside. In this way, the decline of kings occurs. However, those who assemble frequently hear various reports. Therefore, they can send troops to suppress the enemies. Thieves also think, ‘The kings are not negligent; we are not able to move about in groups,’ and thus they disperse and flee. In this way, the growth of kings occurs. Therefore, it was said, “Ānanda, for the Vajjis, only growth is to be expected, not decline.”

In that passage, ‘pāṭikaṅkhā’ means that which is desired, or the meaning that it will certainly happen.

In the words beginning with ‘in harmony’—when the drum signal for assembly sounds, those who do not come, making excuses such as ‘I have work today’ or ‘I have an auspicious ceremony,’ are not those who assemble in harmony. Those who, as soon as they hear the drum, come to the assembly even if they are in the middle of eating, dressing, or adorning themselves—coming while still half-eaten, half-adorned, or half-dressed—are called those who assemble in harmony. After assembling, they consult together, do what should be done, and together...
108:
If they do not rise in harmony, it is not called rising in harmony. In rising thus, those who go first might have the thought: “We have only heard external talk; now there will be the words of decision.” Only those who rise simultaneously are called those who rise in harmony. Alternatively—hearing that “In such-and-such places, the village boundaries or town boundaries are in disorder, and thieves are rising and rampant,” when it is asked, “Who will go and suppress these enemies?” those who go saying, “I first, I first,” are also called those who rise in harmony. When the affairs of one person are declining or ruined, the remaining kings send their sons and brothers to support that person’s affairs; or when a guest king arrives, they do not say, “Go to that person’s house, go to this person’s house,” but all together they honor him; or at the time of one person’s auspicious ceremony, or when illness occurs, or when other such happiness or suffering arises, if all go to that place as companions, they are called Vajjis who perform their duties in harmony.

In the words beginning with “apaññattaṃ,” if they cause taxes, offerings, or punishments that were not previously practiced to be collected, they are said to enact what was not enacted. If they do not cause the collection of taxes and so forth that have come down by ancient tradition, they are said to abolish what was enacted. When someone is arrested and presented as a “thief,” if they pass judgment of execution or destruction without investigation, they are said to not undertake and practice the ancient Vajji law. People who are oppressed by the new taxes and so forth of those who enact what was not enacted say, “We are greatly oppressed; who can live in the kingdom of these kings?” and entering the borders, they become thieves or companions of thieves and attack the countryside. For those who abolish what was enacted and do not take the traditional taxes and so forth, the treasury declines. Then, when the elephants, horses, soldiers, harem, and so forth do not receive their regularly designated provisions, their strength and power decline. They are neither able to fight in war nor able to serve. In the kingdom of those who do not undertake and practice the ancient Vajji law, people become angry, saying, “Our sons, fathers, and brothers, though not thieves, have been made out to be thieves and have been executed or killed,” and entering the borders, they become thieves or companions of thieves and attack the countryside; thus the decline of kings occurs. However, among those who enact only what is enacted, the people are joyful, saying, “The kings act only according to tradition,” and they complete their affairs such as farming and trading. For those who do not abolish what was enacted and take the traditional taxes and so forth...
109:
For the kings who collect taxes and duties, the treasury increases. Because of this increase, the elephant corps, cavalry, infantry, and palace staff receive their regular provisions and clothing, and being endowed with strength and power, they are able to engage in battle and perform their service.

“Ancient Vajji Law” (Porāṇa-vajjidhamma) refers to this: In the Vajji country in ancient times, when a person was arrested and brought forward as a “thief,” the kings would not (immediately) command, “Arrest this thief,” but would hand him over to the judicial ministers (Vinicchaya-mahāmatta). Those ministers would investigate, and if he was not a thief, they would release him. If he was a thief, they would say nothing themselves but hand him over to the legal experts (Vohārika). They too, if he was not a thief, would release him. If he was a thief, they would hand him over to the masters of the law (Suttadhara). They too would investigate, and if he was not a thief, would release him. If he was a thief, they would hand him over to the eightfold clan tribunal (Aṭṭhakulika). They too would act in the same manner and hand him over to the commander-in-chief (Senāpati); the commander-in-chief to the viceroy (Uparāja); and the viceroy to the king. The king would investigate, and if he was not a thief, would release him. If he was a thief, however, he would have the “Book of Ancient Precedents” (Paveṇipottaka) read. In that book, it is written: “For one who commits such-and-such an offense, such-and-such a punishment is to be inflicted.” The king, comparing that person’s action with that record, would inflict the appropriate punishment. In this way, the people who live undertaking and practicing this ancient Vajji law do not criticize (the king). Reflecting, “The kings act only according to ancient tradition; there is no fault in these kings, the fault is only in us,” they perform their own affairs without negligence. In this way, the growth of kings occurs. With this intended, it was said, “Ānanda, for the Vajjis, there is only growth, not decline.”

“They pay respect” means: when they make any offering to those elder kings, they do it well. “They honor” means: they act with a mind directed toward respect. “They revere” means: they love and cherish them with the mind. “They worship” means: they show signs of reverence. “They think they should be listened to” means: they go to serve them two or three times a day, thinking that the words of those elder kings are worthy of listening to and worthy of trust. In that Vajji country, those who do not perform such offerings and so forth to the elders, and do not go to serve them to receive advice, are abandoned by those kings and, having no one to admonish them, become intoxicated only with pleasure and play, and thus decline from kingship. However, those who practice (respectfully) in that way are told by the elder kings, “This should be done; this should not be done,” according to ancient tradition. When they reach the battlefield, they are shown the arts of war, such as “Thus one should enter; thus one should withdraw.” Receiving the advice of those elder kings and practicing according to that advice, they are able to maintain the royal tradition. With this intended, it was said, “Ānanda, for the Vajjis, there is only growth, not decline.”
110:
"Women" refers to the noble housewives. "Girls" refers to their unmarried daughters. In the phrase "taking by force" (okkassa pasayha), both "okkassa" and "pasayha" are names for acting with violence or force. It is also read as "ukkassā". Among these terms, "okkassa" means dragging away. "Pasayha" means seizing by overwhelming and oppressing. The people living in the kingdom of kings who act in this way become angry, saying, "These kings are forcibly seizing the mothers of our sons in our homes, and the young daughters whom we have personally cared for and raised, cleaning away their mucus and such, and making them live in their own houses." They then go to the borders, become bandits or associates of bandits, and attack the countryside. However, in the kingdoms of kings who do not act in this way, people perform their duties without anxiety or worry, thereby increasing the king's treasury. Thus, in this matter, one should understand the causes of prosperity and decline.

"The Vajjian shrines of the Vajjis" refers to the dwelling places of yakkhas (spirits) which are called shrines (cetiyas) because they are places held in high esteem in the Vajjian country of the Vajjis. "Those that are internal" refers to the shrines located inside the city. "Those that are external" refers to the shrines located outside the city. "Formerly given" refers to the charitable gifts given in the past. "Formerly performed" refers to the deeds performed in the past. "Will not let them decline" means they will not let them diminish but will perform them exactly as they were always done. Deities do not provide good protection to those who diminish the offerings (bali) given in accordance with righteousness; although they cannot cause suffering that has not yet arisen, they increase existing ailments such as coughs and headaches, and they do not provide help when encountering war. To those who do not let them decline, however, they provide good protection; although they cannot cause happiness that has not yet arisen, they cure existing ailments such as coughs and headaches, and they provide help on the battlefield. Thus, in this matter, one should understand the causes of prosperity and decline.

In the phrase "righteous protection, defense, and guard," "protection" (rakkhā) is called "āvaraṇa" because it prevents one from going to undesirable places. It is called "gutti" because it guards (gopāyana) desirable things from being destroyed. In that context, surrounding and guarding with soldiers is not what is meant by righteous protection for monks. Only such actions as not cutting trees in the monastery gardens, not killing in cattle stalls, and not fishing in ponds are called righteous protection. By the words "How then (might monks) who have not yet arrived (come)," the Buddha is inquiring into the state of mind that has arisen in those kings.
111:
In that matter, those who do not desire the arrival of future Arahants are those who lack faith and devotion. When the Saṅgha of monks arrives, they do not go out to welcome them, they do not go to pay respects, they do not offer hospitality, they do not ask questions, they do not listen to the Dhamma, they do not give alms, they do not listen to the talk of appreciation (anumodanā), and they do not arrange places for them to stay. Then, a bad reputation defaming them spreads: "This king lacks faith, is not devoted, and even when the Saṅgha of monks arrives, he does not welcome them... or arrange places to stay." Upon hearing such news, the Saṅgha of monks no longer travels through that city gate; even if they do travel, they no longer enter the city. In this way, future Arahants simply do not arrive. The Arahants who have already arrived do not live in comfort, and those who arrived without knowing the situation say, "We came with the intention of staying, but who can stay with such behavior from these kings?" and they depart. Thus, as future ones do not come and those who have arrived live in misery, that place becomes a place where the Saṅgha of monks does not reside. Then, there is no longer protection from the deities, and because there is no deity protection, yakkhas and ghosts find an opportunity. When yakkhas and ghosts increase, they cause diseases and pains that have never occurred before. The merits obtained by paying respects to the virtuous and asking questions are also no longer obtained. Conversely, the way the "white side" (wholesome) arises, which is the opposite of the aforementioned "black side" (unwholesome), should also be understood in this same manner regarding prosperity and decline.

The Buddha spoke the words "Ekamidāhaṃ" to make it clear that he had previously taught these seven principles of non-decline (aparihāniya dhamma) to the Vajjis. In that context, "Sārandade cetiye" refers to the monastery of this name. Before the Buddha appeared, that place was a shrine (cetiya) where a yakkha named Sārandada resided. Later, when a monastery was built and offered to the Buddha at that site, it was called the Sārandada Cetiya Monastery because it was built at the Sārandada Cetiya.

"Akaraṇīyā" means not to be done, or not to be seized. "Yadidaṃ" is merely a particle (nipāta). "Yuddhassa" uses the genitive case in the sense of the instrumental, meaning they cannot be seized by direct battle. "Aññatra upalāpanāya" means except through persuasion. Persuasion (upalāpanā) means supporting and treating them with kindness by sending elephants, horses, chariots, gold, and silver, saying, "There is no use in quarreling; let us be united now." It means they can only be seized through trust by such kind treatment. "Aññatra mithubhedāya" means except through sowing internal discord. By making them divided among themselves, they can also be seized.
112:
(The Buddha) showed the possibility of capturing (the Vajjis). The Brahmin, having obtained the method from the Buddha's teaching, spoke this. 

Did the Buddha not know that the Brahmin would obtain a method from these words? He knew. If he knew, why did he speak? It was out of compassion (anukampā). The Buddha had this thought: "Even if I do not speak, (this Brahmin) will go and capture all (the Vajjis) within a few days. But if I speak, he will have to break their unity and will only be able to capture them after three years. Living for this much longer is indeed noble. Those who live for this duration will perform wholesome merits which are their refuge."

'Abhinanditvā' means being pleased and joyful in mind. 'Anumoditvā' means expressing joy verbally, saying, "These words spoken by the Venerable Gotama are indeed very excellent." 'Pakkāmi' means going to the King. Then the King asked, "Teacher, what did the Buddha say?" The Brahmin replied, "Great King, according to the words of the Venerable Gotama, no one can capture the Vajjis (by military force). However, they can be captured either by persuasion or by sowing discord among them." Then the King said, "If it is by persuasion, our elephants, horses, and so on will be lost. I will capture them only by sowing discord. How should it be done?"

"Great King, if that is the case, you should start a conversation about the Vajjis in the midst of the assembly. Then I will say, 'Great King, what is the use of those Vajjis? Let those kings live by their own farming and trade,' and then I will leave. At that time, you should say, 'Why does this Brahmin forbid speaking about the Vajjis?' In the afternoon, I will send a gift to them. You should seize that gift, blame me, and without binding or beating me, shave my head and banish me from the city," he suggested. "Then I will say, 'I built the walls and moats in that city. I know the weak spots, the shallow spots, and the deep spots. Soon I will make it possible to (capture) that city directly.' When you hear these words, you should say, 'Go then'," he advised. The King did everything accordingly.

When the Licchavīs heard that the Brahmin was coming out, they said, "The Brahmin is a crafty and deceitful person; do not let him cross the Ganges River." Then some Licchavīs said, "He was treated this way because he spoke on our behalf," and so they said, "In that case, friends, let him come." When the Brahmin went and met the Licchavī kings, he was asked, "Why have you come?" and he told the whole story. The Licchavī kings also thought, "It is not right to impose such a heavy punishment for such a small fault..."
113:
Saying, "It is appropriate," they asked, "What is your rank and office in that city (Vesālī)?" He replied, "I am a judicial minister." They said, "Let that very office be yours." He administered justice very well, and the princes learned various arts and sciences from him.

Being established in virtue, one day he took a Licchavī prince aside to a secluded place and asked, "Young man, do people plow the fields?" The prince replied, "Yes, they do." He asked again, "Do they use a pair of oxen?" and the prince replied, "Yes, they use a pair of oxen." Having said only this much, he returned. Then, another person asked, "Teacher, what did he say?" Not believing what the prince said, he thought, "This man is not telling me the truth," and thus a rift was created with him. On another day, the Brahmin took another Licchavī prince to a secluded place and asked, "With what curry do you eat?" and returned. When another person asked him, he also did not believe the answer, and a rift was created in the same way. On another day, the Brahmin took yet another Licchavī prince to a secluded place and asked, "I heard that you are very poor." When asked, "Who said this?" he replied, "That Licchavī prince said so." He took another to a secluded place and asked, "I heard that you are a coward." When asked, "Who said this?" he replied, "That Licchavī prince said so." In this way, by telling one what the other had not said, he caused dissension among those kings for three years, making them unable to even walk the same path together, and then he caused the assembly drum to be beaten. The Licchavī princes said, "Let the lords assemble, let the heroes assemble," but they did not assemble.

The Brahmin sent a message to the King (Ajātasattu), saying, "Now is the time; come quickly." As soon as the King heard this, he had the war drums beaten and set out. When the people of Vesālī heard this, they had the drums beaten, saying, "Do not let the King cross the Ganges." Even upon hearing the drum, they said, "Let the heroic kings go," and so on, but did not assemble. They had the drums beaten, saying, "Do not allow entry into the city; let us stay with the gates closed." Not a single person assembled. King Ajātasattu entered through the open gates, brought all the Licchavī princes to ruin, and returned.

## Commentary on the Conditions for Non-decline of Monks

Then, in the passage beginning with "Not long after (Vassakāra the Brahmin) had departed," the phrase "having caused them to assemble" means causing them to assemble by sending monks with psychic powers to distant monasteries and by going in person to nearby monasteries, saying, "Venerable sirs, please assemble; the Blessed One desires your assembly."
114:
## The Conditions for Non-decline
Aparihāniya means that which is not a cause for decline, but a cause for growth. The phrase "I shall teach the Dhamma" means that he would speak making it clear, just as the thousands of moons and suns illuminate, or as thousands of lamps are lit inside a square house.

Among those teachings, "frequent assemblies" is just as taught in the seven principles for the Vajjī kings. In this Dispensation (Sāsana) as well, if they do not assemble frequently, they will not hear the news of the Dispensation arriving from various directions. Because they do not hear such news, they will not know that "the consecrated boundary (sīmā) of a monastery in the upper region is in disorder; the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies have ceased; in the upper region, monks are practicing medicine, acting as messengers, and so on; and many are making a living by seeking donations and offering flowers, etc." Evil monks, knowing that "the community of monks is negligent," will gather together and cause the Dispensation to decline.

However, monks who assemble frequently hear of various news and events. Because they hear such things, they send a group of monks to rectify the boundary, and they cause the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies to be performed. In places where wrong livelihoods are prevalent, they send those who practice the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma (the lineage of the noble ones) to preach it. They cause evil monks to be subdued by the masters of the Vinaya. The evil monks, saying, "The community of monks is not negligent; we are not able to wander about in groups," will disperse and flee. Thus, in this matter, decline and growth should be understood.

Regarding the words "in harmony" and so on, if the drum or bell is struck with the desire to repair a stupa, to roof a Bodhi-tree house or an Uposatha hall, to make a covenant, or to give an exhortation, saying, "Let the Saṅgha assemble," those who remain distracted, giving excuses such as "I have robe-work to do," "I have a bowl to fire," or "I have repair work to do," are not said to assemble in harmony. Only those who leave all such work behind and assemble simultaneously, thinking, "I will arrive first, I will arrive first," are said to assemble in harmony.

Even after assembling, if they do not rise together after performing the task that should be done through deliberation, they are not said to rise in harmony. In rising thus, for those who leave first, the thought may occur to others: "We have only heard the preliminary talk; now there will be the decision." Only those who rise simultaneously are said to rise in harmony.

Alternatively, when hearing that "the monastery boundary in the upper region is in disorder, the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā have ceased, and evil monks who practice medicine and so on are numerous in the upper region," if it is asked, "Who..."
115:
...will go and subdue those people?" and if they go, saying, "I first, I first," they are said to rise up in harmony.

When seeing a visiting monk, if they all perform the major and minor duties without saying, "Go to this monastery, go to that monastery, who is this person?"; or when seeing one with worn-out bowl and robes, if they seek a bowl and robes through that monk's alms-round duties; or if they seek medicine for a sick monk; or if they attend to and care for even a helpless sick monk in their own respective monasteries without saying, "Go to another monastery, go to another monastery"; or if there is a single lazy person who has studies to do, and they support a wise monk to have him teach those scriptures—then they are said to perform the duties of the Saṅgha in harmony.

## On the passage beginning with Apannatta
In the words beginning with "Apannatta" (not authorized), if they authorize a new, unrighteous covenant or a training rule, it is called authorizing what has not been authorized, as did the monks in Sāvatthī in an old case. If they present a teaching that is not in accordance with the Dhamma or the Vinaya, it is called abolishing what has been authorized, as did the Vajjiputtaka monks in Vesālī one hundred years after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna. If they knowingly transgress the minor and lesser offenses (khuddānukhuddaka), it is called not training in the training rules as they were authorized, as did the monks Assaji and Punabbhasu. Without authorizing any new covenant or training rule, and while presenting the teaching in accordance with the Dhamma and Vinaya, if they do not abolish the minor and lesser training rules, they are said to not authorize what has not been authorized, not abolish what has been authorized, and train in the training rules as they were authorized, like the Venerable Upasena or the Venerable Yasa Kākaṇḍakaputta.

"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. Our training rules have reached the laypeople. The laypeople also know, 'This act is allowable for the monks who are sons of the Sakyan, this act is not allowable for you.' If we were to abolish the minor and lesser training rules, there would be those who would speak in blame, saying, 'The ascetic Gotama authorized training rules for his disciples that lasted only as long as a puff of smoke; they practiced these training rules only as long as their teacher was present. Since their teacher attained Parinibbāna, they no longer practice these training rules.' If it is timely and appropriate (pattakalla) for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha..."
117:
One hears a sound; because of that sound, one attains forest-born joy (pīti). By contemplating that very joy, one is established in the supreme fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). In this way, the Blessed One praised even a monk sleeping in the forest more than a monk dwelling in a village monastery who is absorbed in jhāna. Therefore, regarding that special benefit, He said, "They will have longing for forest dwellings."

"They will establish mindfulness within themselves" means they will personally establish mindfulness in their own internal continuum. "Pesalā" refers to those who possess dear virtue. In this Dispensation, monks dwelling in monasteries who do not desire the arrival of fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī) lack faith and devotion. They do not perform duties for the arriving monks, such as welcoming them, receiving their bowls and robes, arranging seats, or holding fans. At that time, the sound of criticism spreads: "The monks dwelling in such-and-such monastery lack faith and devotion; they do not perform minor and major duties for those who enter the monastery." Hearing these words, monks do not enter the monastery even when passing by its gate. Thus, those who have not yet come simply do not come. As for those who have arrived, they do not live happily; even those who arrived unknowingly, thinking they would stay, depart, saying, "Who could stay with such behavior from these resident monks?" In this way, that monastery becomes an uninhabitable place for other monks. Then, the resident monks, having no opportunity to see virtuous ones, do not gain the dispelling of doubts, nor a teacher of training, nor the hearing of the pleasant Dhamma. For those monks, there is no learning of the Dhamma not yet learned, nor recitation of the Dhamma already learned. Thus, there is only decline for those monks, not growth.

However, regarding "Ye pana sabrahmacārīnaṃ" etc., those monks who desire the arrival of fellow practitioners possess faith and devotion. They perform duties such as welcoming the arriving fellow practitioners and arranging seats for them. They take those monks along for alms-round, dispel their doubts, and gain the hearing of the pleasant Dhamma. At that time, their fame spreads: "The monks in such-and-such monastery have such faith and devotion; they are perfect in their duties and are supportive." Hearing these words, monks come even from afar. The resident monks perform duties for them; they approach, pay homage to visiting monks who are senior to them, and sit down. They take a seat and sit near monks who are junior to them. Having sat down, they ask, "Will you stay in this monastery or will you go?" If they say, "We will go," the resident monks say, "The lodgings are suitable, alms-food is easy to obtain," etc., and do not allow them to leave. If the visitor is an expert in the Vinaya (vinayadhara), they recite the Vinaya in his presence. If he is a bearer of the Suttas (suttantika), they recite those respective teachings in his presence. Abiding in the advice of the visiting elders, they reach the fruition of Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). The visitors—
118:
—become those who say, "Though we arrived saying we would stay for only a day or two, because living with these people is pleasant, we shall stay for ten or twelve years." Thus, one should understand decline and growth in this Dispensation. In the second set of seven: Those who delight in work are called "kammārāma". Those who find pleasure in work are "kammarata". Those who repeatedly strive in delighting in work are "kammārāmatamanuyutta". Here, "work" refers to duties to be performed. These include: managing robes, sewing robes, repairing, making needle cases, bowl bags, unbound accessories, waistbands, water filters, stands, foot-washing jars, brooms, and so on. Some people, while performing these tasks, spend the whole day doing only these. It is with reference to such practice that this prohibition was spoken. However, one who performs these tasks only at the appropriate time, and at the time for learning, engages in learning; at the time for recitation, engages in recitation; at the time for duties at the cetiya courtyard, performs duties at the cetiya courtyard; at the time for reflection, engages in reflection—such a person is not called "kammārāma" (one who delights in work).

Regarding "not delighting in talk" (na bhassārāmā): One who spends day and night in mutual conversation about women, men, etc., and does not set a limit to such talk, is called "one who delights in talk" (bhassārāma). One who preaches the Dhamma or answers questions all day and night is a person of few words and one who sets a limit to speech. Why? Because it was said: "Monks, when you gather, there are two duties: Dhamma talk or noble silence."

Regarding "not delighting in sleep" (na niddārāmā): One who is overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha) while walking, sitting, or lying down, and is just sleeping, is called "one who delights in sleep" (niddārāma). One whose mind sinks into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) due to physical illness is not called one who delights in sleep. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Aggivessana, I know that in the last month of summer, after returning from the meal, I fold the outer robe (dukuṭa) in four, lie on my right side, and fall asleep mindful and clearly comprehending."

Regarding "not delighting in company" (na saṅgaṇikārāmā): One who lives in a mixed state as a second to one person, a third to two people, or a fourth to three people, and finds no delight in being alone, is called "one who delights in company" (saṅgaṇikārāma). One who finds delight in being alone in all four postures should be known as one who does not delight in company.
120:
Those with exerted effort (āraddhavīriya) are those who have exerted physical and mental energy. Among them, those who abandon physical socializing and dwell alone through the power of the eight bases of exertion in the four postures are said to have "exerted physical effort" (kāyika-vīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ). Those who abandon mental socializing and dwell alone through the power of the eight attainments (samāpatti), who prevent defilements arising while walking from reaching the state of standing, who prevent defilements arising while standing from reaching the state of sitting, and who prevent defilements arising while sitting from reaching the state of lying down—suppressing defilements right where they arise—are said to have "exerted mental effort" (cetasika-vīriyaṃ āraddhaṃ).

One with established mindfulness (upaṭṭhitasatī) is one who can remember and repeatedly recall things done long ago, etc. This is like Mahāgatimbaya Abhaya Thera, Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya Thera, and Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya Thera. Mahāgatimbaya Abhaya Thera, on the fifth day after his birth, saw a crow pecking at the auspicious milk-rice with its beak and made the sound "hum hum". Later, when he became a great elder, monks asked, "Venerable sir, from what time do you remember?" He replied, "Friends, I remember from the time I made that sound on the fifth day after my birth."

On the ninth day after the birth of Dīghabhāṇaka Abhaya Thera, his mother bent down to kiss him, and her hair bun came loose. Then, about a pyi-measure of jasmine flowers fell onto the infant's chest, causing pain. When that elder became a great elder and was asked, "Venerable sir, from what time do you remember?", he replied, "I remember from the ninth day after my birth."

Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya Thera said, "Friends, it is possible to have three gates of Anurādhapura closed, let people exit through only one gate, ask each 'What is your name?', and then in the evening, tell them their names again without asking a second time." It is with reference to such monks that "one with established mindfulness (upaṭṭhitasatī)" was said.

Wise ones (paññavanto) are those endowed with wisdom that perceives the arising and passing away of the five aggregates. Alternatively, by these two terms, the Blessed One taught right mindfulness and vipassanā wisdom, which are the supports for vipassanā for monks practicing insight meditation.

In the fourth set of seven: Because mindfulness itself is a factor of enlightenment, it is called the "mindfulness factor of enlightenment" (sati-sambojjhaṅga). In this way, it should be understood in all places. Among them, sati-sambojjhaṅga has the characteristic of being firmly established on the object; dhammavicaya-sambojjhaṅga has the characteristic of investigating phenomena; vīriya-sambojjhaṅga has the characteristic of exertion (striving).
121: The Factor of Enlightenment of Joy (pītisambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of spreading; the Factor of Enlightenment of Tranquility (passaddhisambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of calming; the Factor of Enlightenment of Concentration (samādhisambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of non-distraction; the Factor of Enlightenment of Equanimity (upekkhāsambojjhaṅga) has the characteristic of reflection. 'They will develop' means they will increase the Factor of Enlightenment of Mindfulness (satisambojjhaṅga) by bringing it about through four causes, the Factor of Enlightenment of Investigation of States (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga) through six causes, the Factor of Enlightenment of Energy (vīriyasambojjhaṅga) through nine causes, the Factor of Enlightenment of Joy through ten causes, the Factor of Enlightenment of Tranquility through seven causes, the Factor of Enlightenment of Concentration through ten causes, and the Factor of Enlightenment of Equanimity through five causes. By these words, the Factors of Enlightenment associated with Insight (vipassanā), the Path (magga), and the Fruit (phala), which are a mixture of mundane and supramundane, are taught. In the fifth group of seven, 'Perception of Impermanence' (aniccasaññā) refers to the perception that arises together with the Contemplation of Impermanence (aniccānupassanā). The same method applies to the Perception of Non-self (anattasaññā) and so forth. These seven are mundane insight. By the power of the teaching that states, 'This Nibbāna is peaceful, this Nibbāna is sublime; this is the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all attachments, the cessation,' it should be understood that in this context, two are also supramundane. In the group of six, 'Bodily action accompanied by loving-kindness' (mettā-kāyakamma) refers to bodily action performed with a mind of loving-kindness. The same method applies to verbal and mental actions. Although these qualities are mentioned in terms of monks, they can also be found among laypeople. For monks, fulfilling the Abhisamācārika duties with a mind of loving-kindness is called bodily action accompanied by loving-kindness. For laypeople, going to worship pagodas, going to worship the Bodhi tree, going to invite the Saṅgha, seeing a monk entering the village for alms and going out to welcome him, reaching out to receive the bowl, preparing a seat, accompanying him, and such actions are called bodily action accompanied by loving-kindness. For monks, explaining the training rules of conduct (ācārapaññatti), teaching meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), preaching the Dhamma, and teaching the Buddha's words of the Three Piṭakas with a mind of loving-kindness is called verbal action accompanied by loving-kindness. For laypeople, saying, 'Let us go to worship the pagodas, let us go to worship the Bodhi tree, let us listen to the Dhamma, let us make offerings with lamps, flowers, and scents, let us undertake and practice the three types of good conduct, let us donate ticket-food (salāka-bhatta) and so forth, let us donate rainy-season robes (vassāvāsika), let us donate the four requisites to the Saṅgha today, invite the Saṅgha and prepare food and so forth, prepare seats, set out drinking water, go out to welcome and escort the Saṅgha,' and so on...
122: ...when speaking such as 'Please sit in the prepared seats,' 'May you have the desire,' 'May you make effort,' 'Please perform the service,' it is called verbal action of loving-kindness (mettā-vacīkamma). When monks wake up early in the morning, attend to their physical needs, perform duties such as cleaning the pagoda courtyard, and then sit in a secluded place thinking, 'May the monks in this monastery be happy, be free from danger, be free from suffering,' this is called mental action of loving-kindness (mettā-manokamma). When laypeople think, 'May the venerable ones be happy, be free from danger, be free from suffering,' this is called mental action of loving-kindness. 'In presence and in absence' refers to being face-to-face and behind one's back. Therein, helping new monks with tasks like making robes is called bodily action of loving-kindness in presence. Performing all major and minor duties for senior elders, such as washing their feet, paying homage, and fanning them, is called bodily action of loving-kindness in presence. If both of them see wooden utensils or other items left untidily and, instead of being indifferent, put them away as if they were their own property, this is called bodily action of loving-kindness in absence. Speaking words of praise such as 'Venerable Deva, Venerable Tissa' is called verbal action of loving-kindness in presence. Speaking affectionately to someone inquiring about an absent person, saying, 'Where is our Venerable Deva? Where is our Venerable Tissa? When will he return?' is called verbal action of loving-kindness in absence. Opening eyes moist with the essence of loving-kindness and looking with a clear face is called mental action of loving-kindness in presence. Reflecting, 'May Venerable Deva and Venerable Tissa be free from illness and be healthy,' is called mental action of loving-kindness in absence. 'Gains' (lābha) refers to requisites such as robes that are obtained. 'Righteously' (dhammika) means requisites obtained through the righteous practice of alms-gathering, avoiding wrong livelihoods such as deception. 'Even as little as the alms-food received in the bowl' means, at the minimum, enough alms-food for one or two people that has entered the bowl. Regarding 'one who consumes without discriminating,' there are two types of discrimination here: discrimination of material things (āmisa) and discrimination of persons. Therein, mentally discriminating, 'I will give this much, I will not give that much,' is called discrimination of material things. Mentally discriminating, 'I will give to this person, I will not give to that person,' is called discrimination of persons. One who does neither and consumes without discriminating is called 'one who consumes without discriminating' (appaṭivibhattabhogī).
123: Regarding 'consuming together with virtuous fellow practitioners' (sādhāraṇabhogī), the characteristic of one who consumes together is as follows: whatever excellent material things are obtained, they are not given to laypeople with the intention of seeking further gains, nor are they used alone; rather, when receiving them, one should accept them with the thought, 'May this be property belonging to the Saṅgha,' and view them as Saṅgha property to be used after ringing the bell. Who fulfills this Sāraṇīyadhamma (Qualities of Courtesy) and who does not? First of all, an unvirtuous person cannot fulfill it. This is because virtuous people do not accept donations from him. Only one with pure virtue (sīlavanta) can fulfill it without breaking the practice. The manner of that practice is as follows: if someone gives with reference to their mother, father, teacher, etc., such giving is merely giving what ought to be given and is not yet called Sāraṇīyadhamma; it is merely attending to a concern (palibodha). Sāraṇīyadhamma is suitable only for one who is free from such concerns. One who gives with such reference should give to the sick, the attendants of the sick, visitors, traveling monks, and to new monks who do not yet know how to handle the outer robe and the bowl. After giving to them, whatever remains should be given starting from the seat of the senior elders, without leaving even a little, giving as much as each person takes. If nothing remains, one should go for alms again and, after giving whatever excellent alms-food is obtained starting from the seat of the senior elders, consume what remains for oneself. Since it is said 'with the virtuous,' it is appropriate even if one does not give to an unvirtuous person. This Sāraṇīyadhamma is easy to perfect in a well-practiced assembly, but not easy in an unpracticed assembly. In a well-practiced assembly, one who has obtained from elsewhere does not take (a share). One who has not obtained from elsewhere takes only according to measure and does not take more. This Sāraṇīyadhamma is perfected only after 12 years for one who gives whatever is obtained by repeatedly going for alms; it is not less than that. If, in the twelfth year, the practitioner of Sāraṇīyadhamma leaves a bowl full of alms-food at a rest house and goes to bathe, and the senior elder of the Saṅgha asks, 'Whose bowl is this?' and is told, 'It is the bowl of the practitioner of Sāraṇīyadhamma,' and says, 'Bring it,' and after distributing and consuming all the food, leaves the empty bowl—if at that time the monk sees the empty bowl and feels displeasure (domanassa), thinking, 'They have consumed it without leaving even a little for me,' then the Sāraṇīyadhamma is destroyed. He must practice it again for another 12 years. This is like the probation (parivāsa) of the followers of other sects; if it is broken even once, it must be practiced all over again.
124:
“I have gained well; my fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī) enjoy the food in my bowl without even asking.” Thus, he inspires joy within himself; for such a person, the virtues of friendliness (sāraṇīyadhamma) are said to be fulfilled.

For one who fulfills these sāraṇīyadhamma, there is no envy (issā) and no stinginess (macchariya). Such a person is beloved by people and can easily obtain the four requisites. Even while giving away the food in his bowl, it never runs out. Among the requisites to be distributed, he receives the most excellent ones. In times of danger or famine, the devas take care and provide assistance.

In this regard, there are these stories—Tissa Thera, who resided on Senagiri Mountain, lived depending on Mahāgiri village. Fifty great elders, while traveling to Nagadīpa to pay homage to the pagodas, wandered for alms in Giri village but left without receiving anything. Tissa Thera, upon entering the village, saw those elders and asked, “Venerable sirs, did you receive alms?” They replied, “Friend... we have wandered (but received nothing).” Knowing that the venerable ones did not receive alms, Tissa Thera said, “Venerable sirs... please wait here for a moment until I return.” They said, “Friend... the fifty of us did not receive even enough to moisten our bowls.” He replied, “Venerable sirs... those who reside here permanently are capable; even if they do not receive alms, they know the conditions of the alms-round route.” The elders waited.

Tissa Thera entered the village. At the very first house, a great female lay devotee had prepared milk-rice and was standing, looking out for the Thera. As soon as the Thera reached the door, she offered alms until his bowl was full. The Thera took that food, went to the elders, and said to the senior monk of the Saṅgha, “Venerable sirs... please accept this offering.” The senior monk thought, “So many of us received nothing, yet this monk obtained it so quickly and returned; how is this?” and looked at the faces of the other elders. Tissa Thera, understanding by their look, said, “Venerable sirs... this is alms food obtained righteously; please accept it without doubt.” He then offered as much as they desired to all the elders, starting from the most senior, and he himself also partook as much as he wished.

Then, after the meal, the elders asked, “Friend... when did you penetrate the supramundane Dhamma (lokuttara dhamma)?” He replied, “Venerable sirs... I do not possess supramundane Dhamma.” They asked again, “Friend... are you one who has attained jhāna?” He replied, “Venerable sirs... I do not possess this jhāna either.” They asked again, “Friend... is this not a miracle of psychic power (pāṭihāriya)?” He replied, “Venerable sirs... I have fulfilled the sāraṇīyadhamma. From the time I fulfilled that Dhamma, even if there were a hundred thousand monks, the food in my bowl does not run out.” Hearing this, the elders said, “Sādhu, Sādhu, virtuous one, this is appropriate for you.” This is the story regarding the point that “the food in the bowl does not run out.”

That same Thera went to the Giribhaṇḍa Mahāpūjā festival at Cetiyapabbata Mountain and asked, “What is the most excellent item here?” They replied, “Venerable sir... it is two bark-cloth robes.” That...
125:
“It will come to me,” he said. Hearing this, the minister told the King, “Great King, a young monk said this.” The King said, “The young monk has such a mind; however, fine and soft clothes are suitable for the great elders,” and he kept them, saying, “I will offer them to the great elders.” While the King was offering them to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha as they stood in order, those clothes, which were placed at the very top, did not reach the hands of the great elders. Only other clothes reached them. However, when they were offered to the young monk, they reached his hands. The King placed the clothes into the young monk's hands, looked at the minister's face, invited the young monk to sit, gave the offering, and after dismissing the Saṅgha, sat near the young monk and asked, “Venerable sir, when did you penetrate this Dhamma?” That young monk, not wishing to speak what was not true even by way of a figure of speech, said, “Great King, I do not possess supramundane Dhamma.” When asked, “Venerable sir, did you not say before that it would come?” he replied, “It is true, Great King. I am one who fulfills the sāraṇီya Dhamma. From the time I fulfilled that Dhamma, the most excellent of the items to be distributed always comes to me.” The King said, “Venerable sir, it is very good; this is very appropriate for you,” and after paying respects, he departed. This is the story regarding the point that “the most excellent of the items to be distributed arrives.”

During the Brāhmaṇatissa famine, the villagers of Bhātaragāma fled without informing Nāgā Therī. At dawn, the Therī said to the young nuns, “The village is very quiet; go and investigate the situation.” Those nuns went and, knowing the fact that everyone had fled, returned and informed the Therī. Hearing this, the Therī said, “Do not think about their departure; strive only in your own study, inquiry, and wise reflection (yoniso manasikāra).” At the time for alms-round, she donned her robes and, together with twelve nuns including herself, stood at the foot of a banyan tree at the village gate. The deity residing in the tree offered alms to all twelve nuns and requested, “Venerable ladies, do not go elsewhere; please always come only to this place.” The Therī had a brother, an elder named Nāga Thera. That elder, thinking, “The danger is great; it is not possible to subsist here, I will go to the other shore,” set out from his residence with twelve monks including himself. He reached Bhātaragāma village, intending to see the Therī before leaving. The Therī heard that “the elders have arrived,” went to them, and asked, “Venerable sirs, what is the matter?” The elder explained the situation. The Therī said, “Please stay at the monastery for just this one day and depart only tomorrow.” The elders went to the monastery.
126:
On the next day, after collecting alms at the foot of the tree, the Therī approached the Thera and said, “Please partake of this alms food.” The Thera said, “Therī, it will be appropriate,” and remained silent. “Dear brother, this alms food is righteously obtained; please partake of it without hesitation,” the Therī urged. The Thera repeated, “Therī, it will be appropriate.” The Therī took the bowl and threw it into the air. The bowl remained suspended in the sky. The Thera said, “Even if it stays at a height of seven palm trees, it is still only the alms food of bhikkhunīs.” He continued, “Danger cannot exist at all times; when the danger has subsided and the Ariyavaṃsa Dhamma is being preached, if I were to be mentally reproached with ‘O alms-collector, did you not waste time partaking of the alms food of bhikkhunīs?’, I would not be able to endure it. Therīs, strive without negligence,” and he continued his journey.

The tree deity thought, “If the Thera partakes of the alms food from the Therī’s hand, I will not stop him. If he does not partake, I will stop him.” Standing there with this thought, and seeing the Thera departing, the deity descended from the tree, said, “Venerable sir, please give me the bowl,” took the bowl, and brought the Thera back to the foot of the tree. After arranging a seat and offering alms, the deity made a promise to provide until the meal was finished, and thus supported the twelve nuns and twelve monks for seven full years. This is the story regarding the point that “the devas exert effort.” In that story, the Therī was one who fulfilled the sāraṇīya Dhamma.

In the passages beginning with “akhaṇḍāni,” if a person’s training rules are broken at the beginning or at the end among the seven groups of offences, that person’s virtue (sīla) is called “khaṇḍa” (broken), like a cloth torn at the edges. If it is broken in the middle, it is called “chidda” (spotted), like a cloth with a hole in the middle. If two or three are broken in succession, that person’s virtue is called “sabala” (mottled), like a cow of a different color, such as black, appearing on the back or belly.
