If it is broken here and there with different spots, it is called “kammāsa” (unblemished), like a cow variegated with different spots. If they are not broken in any way, those virtues are called akhaṇḍa, acchidda, asabala, and akammāsa. Because those virtues liberate one from the slavery of craving and make one a free person, they are called “bhujissa” (freeing). Because they are praised by wise ones such as the Buddha, they are called “viññuppasattha” (praised by the wise). Because they are not tarnished by craving and wrong view, and because no one can point a finger and say, “You have committed this offence before,” they are called “aparāmaṭṭha” (untarnished). Because they cause the arising of access concentration (upacāra samādhi) or absorption concentration (appanā samādhi), they are called “samādhisamvattanikāni” (conducive to concentration).
128:
## Section Explaining the Disadvantages of Lacking Virtue

In Pāṭaligāma, the term 'āvasathāgāra' refers to a rest house (zayat) for guests. It is said that the friends of the two kings used to visit Pāṭaligāma frequently, driving families out of their homes and staying for a month or half a month. Because these people were constantly harassed, they thought, "When these people come, there will be a place for them to stay," and they built a large rest house in the center of the town. In one part of that rest house, they made a place to store utensils, and in another part, a place to stay. When they heard that "The Buddha has arrived," they approached with the intention: "Although we should go and invite him, the Buddha has arrived at our dwelling place of his own accord; today let us request the Buddha to preach the auspicious Dhamma (Maṅgala) at the rest house."

Therefore, they made this request. Regarding the phrase "to where the āvasathāgāra (rest house) was," those people did not know the Buddha's mind—whether he would wish to stay inside the village, as Buddhas usually delight in the forest and enjoy only the forest—so they came without having prepared the rest house yet. Now, having learned the Buddha's mind, they approached the rest house thinking, "Let us go and prepare it first."

"Fully spread out" means arranging everything so that the preparation is complete. 'Dussīla' refers to one who lacks virtue or is devoid of virtue. 'Sīlavipanna' refers to one whose virtue is ruined, whose restraint (saṃvara) is ruined. 'Pamādādhikaraṇa' means occurring because of the cause of negligence (pamāda).

Although this sutta is presented in terms of laypeople, it is also applicable to monks. A layperson earns a living through various crafts; if they are negligent—whether in farming, trade, or by killing living beings and so on—they cannot complete those tasks in time, and even their initial capital is ruined. If they commit acts such as killing or stealing during prohibited times, they face great destruction of wealth due to royal punishment. Similarly, an immoral monk, due to negligence, suffers the loss of virtue, the word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana), meditative absorption (jhāna), and the seven noble treasures (ariya-dhana).

For a layperson, an evil reputation spreads in the midst of the four assemblies: "This person, though born in such a family, lacks virtue, follows base teachings, has abandoned this life and the next, and does not even donate a single meal-ticket (salāka-bhatta)." For a monk as well: "This person cannot guard his virtue, cannot learn the Buddhavacana..."
129:
"...earns a living by practicing medicine and so on, and is endowed with the six types of disrespect." In this way, an evil reputation spreads. 'Avisārada' (lack of confidence) means that a layperson first approaches an assembly of many people with fear, thinking, "Someone will know of my deeds, and then they will rebuke me" or "They will hand me over to the king's palace." He sits with an unhappy face, drooping shoulders, downcast eyes, and scratching the ground with his index finger; he is unable to speak boldly. A monk also approaches with fear, thinking, "Many monks are assembled; someone will surely know of my deeds. Then they will prohibit my Uposatha or Pavāraṇā, cause me to fall from monkhood, and expel me." He is unable to speak boldly. Although some immoral people wander about like those full of pride, in their hearts they are indeed unhappy.

'Dying confused' means that while that person is lying on his deathbed, the place where he practiced his immoral deeds appears in his mind. When he opens his eyes, he sees this world; when he closes his eyes, he sees the next life. The four lower realms (apāya) appear in his vision. It is as if his head is being struck by a hundred spears. He dies crying out, "Stop it, stop it!" Therefore, it is said, "He dies confused."

The meaning of the fifth point is very clear. The benefits (of virtue) should be understood as the opposite of the aforementioned disadvantages. 'For much of the night with a Dhamma talk' means that he showed, inspired, and dismissed them for much of the night, using other Dhamma talks not included in the Pāḷi text, or a talk of appreciation (anumodanā) for the rest house—like making the celestial Ganges descend, or like squeezing a huge honeycomb a league (yojana) in size to feed them honey. 'Abhikkantā' refers to the night that has passed, ended, or reached its conclusion.

'Suññāgāra' (empty place) means that although there was no separate secluded house, they enclosed a side with a curtain right there and prepared a couch, thinking, "The Teacher will rest here." The Buddha, thinking, "Their use of these four postures will be of great benefit to them," slept there like a lion king. With reference to that, it is said, "He went to an empty place."
130:
## Commentary on the Founding of the City of Pāṭaliputta

'Sunidha-Vassakārā' refers to the two Brahmins named Sunidha and Vassakāra. 'Magadha-mahamattā' refers to the chief ministers of the King of Magadha, or chief ministers endowed with great authority in the Magadha country. 'Pāṭaligāme nagaraṃ' refers to the building of a city at Pāṭaligāma. 'Vajjīnaṃ paṭibāhāya' means to block the revenue routes of the Vajji princes. 'Sahasseva' means in groups, a thousand in each group. 'Vatthūni' refers to plots of land for housing. 'Cittāni namanti nivesanāni māpetuṃ' means inclining the minds of the master builders to construct houses for the king and his chief ministers.

Those experts, by the power of their craft, could see about 30 cubits underground: "In this place there is a nāga, in this place there is a yakkha, in this place there is a ghost, or a stone, or a tree stump." At that time, they would recite their lore and build the city as if consulting with the devas. Alternatively, devas would enter their bodies and incline their minds to build houses in those specific places. Those devas would mark the plots by driving stakes into the four corners and then depart. For families with faith, devas with faith would do this; for families without faith, devas without faith would do it.

Why is this so? Because the devas with faith think: "In this place, after people have built their houses, they will first invite the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and listen to the auspicious Dhamma. Then we shall have the opportunity to see those with virtue, hear the Dhamma, have our questions answered, and listen to the talk of appreciation (anumodanā). People will make offerings of alms-food and share the merit with us."

'Tāvatiṃsehi'—for example, just as a reputation arises that "The people of that clan are wise" because of one wise person in a clan, or "The monks of that monastery are learned" because of one learned monk in a monastery, so too a reputation arises that "The Tāvatiṃsa devas are wise" because of Sakka, the king of devas, and Vissakamma, the celestial architect. Therefore, it is said "Tāvatiṃsehi." It means it is as if the city was built in consultation with the Tāvatiṃsa devas.

'Yāvatā ariyaṃ āyatanaṃ' means as far as there are abodes of the Noble Ones. 'Yāvatā vaṇippatho' means as far as the merchants'...
131:
...wherever goods brought are piled and traded, or where merchants reside. 'Idaṃ agganagaraṃ' means that among the dwellings of the Noble Ones and the trading places of merchants, this city will be the foremost and most noble. 'Puṭabhedanaṃ' means the place where bundles of goods are opened, or the place where packages of merchandise are unloaded. It implies that even goods not available on the entire island (Jambudīpa) will be available here, and goods that cannot be sold out elsewhere will arrive at this location. Therefore, it means that bundles will be opened only at this place. It is stated that taxes amounting to five hundred thousand per day will arise, with four portions at the four gates and one at the rest house.

In the words 'aggito vā' and so on, the meaning of the particle 'ca' (and) is 'vā' (or). It means it will be destroyed by fire, or by water, or by internal dissension. One part will be destroyed by fire, which they will be unable to extinguish. One part will be eroded by the river Ganges. As for the other part, it means it will be destroyed only by the internal dissension of people who are divided by slanderous speech, saying, 'This person does not speak of that person's affairs, and that person does not speak of this person's affairs.' Having spoken thus, the Blessed One went to the banks of the Ganges at dawn, washed His face, and stayed there awaiting the time for alms-round.

Sunidha and Vassakāra also thought: 'Our king is an attendant of the ascetic Gotama. That king will ask us, "I heard that the Blessed One has arrived at Pāṭali village; did you approach that Venerable One?" If we answer that we did, he will further ask, "Did you invite Him?" If we answer that we did not, he will blame and rebuke us. Furthermore, we are building a city at the place where we are now; wherever the ascetic Gotama arrives, inauspicious beings depart. Let us have that Venerable One speak words of blessing for this city.' Having thought thus, they approached the Blessed One and invited Him. Therefore, the words 'Atha kho sunidhavassakārā' and so on were spoken.

'Pubbaṇhasamayaṃ' means in the morning time. 'Nivāsetvā' means having dressed in the inner robe and fastened the waistband in the manner of entering a village. 'Pattacīvaramādāya' means having taken the bowl and robes and keeping them close to the body.

'Sīlavantettha' means those who possess virtue in this place. 'Saññate' means those who are restrained in body, speech, and mind.
132:
'Tāsaṃ dakkhiṇamādiyye' means one should share the merit of the four requisites offered to the Saṅgha with those guardian deities of the house; one should dedicate the merit. 'Pūjitā pūjayanti' means they (the deities) provide good protection, saying, 'Although these people are not our relatives, they share merit with us in this way.' 'Mānitā mānayanti' means the deities who are honored by occasional offerings of respect and hospitality cherish those people, saying, 'Although these people are not our relatives, they honor us every four or six months.' Those deities who thus cherish them ward off arising dangers.

'Tato naṃ' refers to that wise person. 'Orasaṃ' means nourished by being held to the breast; it means they strive for that person only to ward off arising dangers, just as a mother compassionately protects the son born of her own breast; thus they compassionately protect. 'Bhadrāni passati' means he sees auspicious results.

'Uḷumpaṃ' is a raft made by striking wooden logs together for the purpose of crossing to the other shore. 'Kullaṃ' is a raft made by binding vines and such together.

In the verse 'Ye taranti aṇṇavaṃ', 'aṇṇavaṃ' is the name of a body of water that is at least one league (yojana) deep and wide. Here, 'sara' refers to the river. The meaning is: those who cross the deep and wide river of craving (taṇhā), they cross by making the bridge of the Noble Path (ariyamagga). 'Visajja pallalāni' means they cross by abandoning the low-lying areas (swamps) filled with water without touching or being affected by them. However, while this multitude of people wishes to cross even a small amount of water, they must bind a raft. The meaning is that the Blessed One and the wise disciples of the Buddha have already crossed without the need for a raft.

## The Commentary on the First Recitation Section is finished.

## Commentary on the Talk on the Noble Truths

Koṭigāma is a village established at the pinnacle of King Mahāpanāda's palace. 'Ariyasaccānaṃ' means of the truths that make one a Noble One. 'Ananubodhā' means because of not knowing repeatedly. 'Appaṭivedhā' means because of not knowing through penetration. 'Sandhāvitaṃ' means one has run by going from one birth to another. 'Saṃsaritaṃ' means one has wandered by going back and forth repeatedly.
134:
If one is reborn (in the deva realm) and realizes Arahantship, that is well. If unable, one will certainly come to the human realm and realize it. Even if one reaches the fruit of Once-Returner in the deva realm, if one is reborn in the human realm and realizes Arahantship, that is well. If unable, one will certainly go to the deva realm and realize it.

In the word 'avinipātadhammo', falling downwards is called 'vinipāta'; because there is no nature of falling downwards, one is called 'avinipātadhamma'. It means one who has the nature of not falling into the four lower realms. 'Niyato' means one who is fixed by the law of Dhamma (dhamma-niyāma). 'Sambodhiparāyaṇo' means one for whom the Enlightenment of the three higher paths is the destination, the goal, and the foundation ahead; one who will certainly reach it.

## Commentary on the Mirror of Dhamma Discourse

'Vihesā' indicates that for the Blessed One who observes the destination of the wisdom, the arising of the wisdom, and the future lives of various individuals, there is only physical weariness; Ānanda, mental weariness does not exist in the Buddhas. 'Dhammādāsaṃ' refers to the mirror that is the Dhamma. 'Yena' means the person who is endowed with that mirror of Dhamma. 'Khīṇāpāyaduggativinipāto' is a teaching using synonyms for hell and so on. Hell and such are called 'apāya' because they are devoid of the merit that is growth. They are called 'duggati' because they are the destination and foundation of suffering. They are called 'vinipāta' because those who do evil must fall into them against their own will.

'Aveccappasādena' means with unshakable and indestructible confidence because of knowing the qualities of the Buddha as they truly are. The same method applies to the two preceding terms (Dhamma and Saṅgha). The details of the words 'Itipi so bhagavā' and so on have been taught in the Visuddhimagga.

'Ariyakantehi' means (with virtues) that are loved and cherished by the Noble Ones. The five precepts are cherished by the Noble Disciples because they are not abandoned even in another life. He taught this with reference to those virtues. In this context, all types of restraint virtue (saṃvara-sīla) can also be obtained.

'Sotāpanno'hamasmi' (I am a stream-enterer)—this is merely the peak of the teaching. Those such as Once-Returners also receive a declaration in the manner of 'I am a Once-Returner' and so on. It is permitted to receive a declaration in a suitable place without conflicting with any of the training rules.
135:
## Commentary on the Story of Ambapālī the Courtesan

In the words 'Vesāliyaṃ viharati', the prosperity of the city of Vesālī should be understood according to the method taught in the Khandhaka, such as 'At that time, the city of Vesālī was prosperous and wealthy.' 'Ambapālīvane' means in the mango grove which was the garden of the courtesan Ambapālī. 'Sato bhikkhave'—when the Blessed One saw Ambapālī, He specifically introduced the teaching on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhāna) so that mindfulness could be maintained. In that context, one is called 'sato' because of being mindful. One is called 'sampajāno' because of knowing clearly. It means one should dwell being endowed with both mindfulness and clear comprehension. The points mentioned in the words 'kāye kāyānupassī' and so on will be taught in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta.

'Nīlā' is a general description. 'Nīlavaṇṇā' and so on are the detailed classifications of that word 'nīlā'. In that regard, the natural complexion of those Licchavī princes was not blue/dark; this was taught because they were smeared with blue/dark-colored perfumes. 'Nīlavatthā' means the loincloths, velvets, silks, etc., of those kings were also only blue/dark in color. 'Nīlālaṅkārā' means they were adorned with blue gems and blue flowers. The chariots of those kings were also decorated with blue gems, surrounded by blue cloths, had blue banners, and were equipped with blue horse-trappings, blue ornaments, and blue horses; even the goads were blue. The meaning should be understood in this manner for all terms. 'Parivaṭṭesi' means collided. In the words 'Kiṃ je ambapālī', 'je' is a form of address; it means 'Lady Ambapālī, why is this?' There is also a reading 'kiñcā', but the meaning is the same. 'Sāhāraṃ' means together with the countryside. 'Aṅguliṃ phoṭesuṃ' means they moved their fingers (snapped their fingers). 'Ambakāyā' means because of a young woman.

'Yesaṃ' is the use of the genitive case in the sense of the instrumental; it means 'those who have not seen.' 'Oloketha' means look. 'Avaloketha' means look repeatedly. 'Upasaṃharatha' means bring close. It means, 'Bring this assembly of Licchavīs close to the Tāvatiṃsa gods in your mind; place them close. Just as the Tāvatiṃsa gods are beautiful, inspiring, and have various colors such as blue, etc., so too are these Licchavī kings; look at them by making them equal to the Tāvatiṃsa gods.'

Why does the Blessed One, while forbidding the taking of signs (nimitta) in the objects of sight, etc., in hundreds of suttas, encourage the taking of signs with great effort in this place? It is because He desires their welfare. In that place, some monks were slack in their energy...
136:
When he was being enticed by the wealth and luxury of those kings, he spoke to arouse the intention to strive in the Dhamma of a recluse, saying: "For those who strive in the Dhamma of a recluse with unremitting mindfulness, such a mass of sovereign wealth is easily obtained." He also spoke thus to make manifest the characteristic of impermanence. This was because, before long, all these kings would fall into the hands of King Ajātasattu and meet their destruction. At that time, the monks who stood watching the success of those kings' royal splendor would develop the meditation on the characteristic of impermanence, thinking, "The destruction of such wealth and luxury is indeed evident," and they would reach the fruit of Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Thus, he spoke to make manifest the characteristic of impermanence.

As for the question of why they invited the Buddha even though they knew Ambapālī had already invited him—it was because of their lack of faith and also out of social duty. It occurred to those kings that Ambapālī was a frivolous woman and might claim she had invited him even if she had not. Furthermore, it is the social duty of people to invite someone after listening to a discourse before they depart.

## Explanation of the Entry into the Rains Retreat at Beluva Village (Veḷuvagāmavassūpagamanavaṇṇanā)

Veḷuvagāmaka refers to Beluva village near the city of Vesālī. In the words beginning with "yathāmittaṃ," "mitta" refers to friends. "Sandiṭṭha" refers to acquaintances who have merely met in various places but are not very close. "Sambhutta" refers to well-loved, intimate, and firm friends. The meaning is that those monks should enter the rains retreat in whatever places they have such friends. Why did he speak thus? It was so that those monks could live comfortably. For those monks, there were insufficient monasteries and a scarcity of alms-food in Beluva village. However, around the city of Vesālī, there were many monasteries and alms-food was easily obtained; therefore, he spoke in this way. If so, why did he not release them saying, "Go wherever you wish"? It was because he had compassion and care for those monks. The Blessed One had this thought: "I will attain Parinibbāna in about ten months. If these monks go far away, they will not be able to see me at the time of my Parinibbāna. At that time, those monks will feel distressed, thinking, 'The Blessed One did not even give us a word of warning when he was about to attain Parinibbāna; had we known, we would not have stayed so far away.' If they stay around Vesālī, they can come to hear the Dhamma about eight times a month and receive the instructions of the Blessed One." Thinking thus, he did not release them to go far.

"Khara" means harsh. "Ābādha" means an unbalanced disease. "Bāḷhā" means severe. "Māraṇantikā" means ending in death, or capable of bringing one near to death. "Mindful and clearly comprehending, he endured them" means that he endured by maintaining mindfulness well and discerning with wisdom. "Without being distressed" means by not following the desire of the sensation...
138:
Whether in terms of the Dhamma or in terms of persons, without making a distinction between the two, it means "without an inner and without an outer." If one thinks, "I will not preach this much of the Dhamma to others," it is called making the Dhamma internal. If one thinks, "I will preach this much to others," it is called making the Dhamma external. If one thinks, "I will preach to this person," it is called making the person internal. If one thinks, "I will not preach to this person," it is called making the person external. The meaning is that the Dhamma is taught without making such distinctions. The "teacher's fist" (ācariya-muṭṭhi) is like what exists among teachers outside the Dispensation. Those teachers do not tell anyone anything during their youth, and only when they are lying on their deathbed (maraṇamañca) do they tell their beloved disciples. It is shown that for the Blessed One, there is no Dhamma at all that is kept as a "teacher's fist," thinking, "I will preach this Dhamma in my old age at the final hour."

It refers to one who thinks, "I alone shall lead the Bhikkhu-saṅgha," or "Let there be a reference for my own benefit," or "Let the Bhikkhu-saṅgha be one that refers to me and relies on me; let it not be so after I have passed away; let something happen." The Blessed One does not have such thoughts, as he had already abandoned envy and stinginess (issā-macchariya) at the seat of enlightenment (Bodhi-pallaṅka). "Sa kinti" means "Who is that person?" "Āsītiko" refers to a person who is eighty years old. This is intended to show the state of having reached the final stage of life. "Veṭhamissakena" means by means of bindings such as bandages or hoops used for repair. It should be understood like an old cart that is kept going by being bound together with thongs. It shows that the four postures of the Blessed One are maintained by the binding of the fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala).

Now, to make that meaning clear, he said, "Ānanda, yasmiṃ samaye," and so on. There, "sabbanimittānaṃ" refers to the signs of forms (rūpa-nimitta) and so on. "Ekaccānaṃ vedanānaṃ" refers to mundane feelings. "Ānanda, therefore" is said because, since one lives happily through this dwelling in the fruit of attainment (phalasamāpatti-vihāra), you all should also live in this way for that benefit. "Be islands unto yourselves" means you should live making yourselves your own island and refuge, like an island in the great ocean. "Having yourselves as a refuge" means you should be your own destination; do not make another your destination. The same method applies to the terms "Dhamma-dīpa" (Dhamma as an island) and "Dhamma-saraṇa" (Dhamma as a refuge). "Tamatagge" is "tam agge." The letter "ta" in the middle is a euphonic conjunction (padasandhi). It means "these people are the highest." Thus, cutting off all association with the darkness of ignorance, reaching the state of being the most supreme...
139:
Ānanda, these monks will be my monks. Among all those who have the desire to practice, they will be the highest. All those monks who have the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) as their resort will also be the highest. Thus, he concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of the fruit of Arahatship.

## The Explanation of the Second Recitation Section (Dutiya-bhāṇavāra) is finished.

## Explanation of the Talk on the Intimation of the Sign (Nimittobhāsakathāvaṇṇanā)

He entered the city of Vesālī for alms. At what time did he enter? It was when he departed from the city of Ukkacela and arrived at Vesālī. After the Blessed One had completed the rains retreat at Beluva village, he departed and turned back along the same path he had come, intending to go to Sāvatthī. In due course, he reached Sāvatthī and entered the Jetavana monastery. The General of the Dhamma (Venerable Sāriputta), after performing the major and minor duties for the Blessed One, went to the place for his day's rest. In that place, after showing the duties to his disciples and when the disciples had left, he swept the place for the day's rest, spread out his leather mat, washed his feet, and sat down cross-legged, entering into the fruit of attainment (phalasamāpatti).

When he emerged from the attainment at the designated time, this thought arose: "Do the Buddhas pass away into Parinibbāna first, or do the chief disciples (aggasāvaka) pass away into Parinibbāna first?" Then, knowing that "the chief disciples pass away into Parinibbāna first," he looked at his own life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra). The Venerable realized, "My life-force will last only seven more days," and he considered, "In what place should I attain Parinibbāna?" Then, he thought again, "Venerable Rāhula has attained Parinibbāna in Tāvatiṃsa; Venerable Aññāsikoṇḍañña has attained Parinibbāna at Lake Chaddanta; where should I attain Parinibbāna?" Then, mindfulness arose in him regarding his mother.

"My mother, though she is the mother of seven Arahats, does not yet have faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Does she have the supporting condition (upanissaya)?" Upon reflection, he saw the supporting condition for the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). He looked to see, "By whose preaching of the Dhamma will she realize the Dhamma?" and he saw, "It will be only by my preaching, not by anyone else's. If I remain indifferent, there will be those who criticize me, saying, 'Venerable Sāriputta is the refuge of all others. On the day he preached the Samacitta Sutta, one hundred billion devas and Brahmās reached Arahatship...'"
140:
The number of devas who penetrated the three paths is countless. In other instances as well, many realizations of the Dhamma (abhisamaya) were seen. There were eighty thousand clans who, having gained clarity of mind in the Elder alone, were reborn in the deva realms. (The Elder thought,) "I am not yet able to dispel even the mere wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi) of my own mother. Therefore, I shall attain parinibbāna in the very birth chamber where I was born, after releasing my mother from her wrong view." Having made this resolution, he called the Elder Cunda, saying, "Today, I shall take leave of the Blessed One and depart." He said, "Friend Cunda, give the signal to our company of five hundred monks, saying, 'Friends, take your bowls and robes; the Dhamma-senāpati wishes to go to Nālaka village.'" The Elder Cunda did as he was told. The monks packed their lodgings, took their bowls and robes, and came to the Elder. The Elder packed his own lodging, swept the day-quarters, and standing at the doorway of the day-quarters, looked back at it, thinking, "This is my last look; there will be no more coming back." Surrounded by five hundred monks, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and addressed him with these words:

"O Lord of the World, Great Sage, I shall now be severed from existence,
There is no more going or coming; this is my final salutation.
My life is very brief; when seven days have passed from now,
I shall cast off this body, like laying down a heavy burden.
O Blessed One, may the Exalted One grant me permission; may the Sugata grant me permission,
The time for my parinibbāna has arrived; the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra) has been relinquished."

If the Buddhas were to say, "Attain parinibbāna," it would be praising the quality of death; if they were to say, "Do not attain parinibbāna," it would be speaking in praise of the cycle of rebirth (saṃsāra-vaṭṭa), and thus those of wrong view would find fault. Therefore, they say neither. Thus, the Blessed One said to the Elder, "Sāriputta, in what place will you attain parinibbāna?" When he replied, "Venerable Sir, there is the birth chamber in Nālaka village in the Magadha country; I shall attain parinibbāna there," the Buddha said, "Sāriputta, you know the time for your departure. Now, for your elder and younger brothers, it will be difficult to see a monk like you; therefore, preach the Dhamma to them."

The Elder, knowing that "The Blessed One desires from me a Dhamma discourse preceded by a display of psychic power," paid homage to the Blessed One, flew up into the sky to the height of a palm tree, descended again, and paid homage to the Blessed One.
141:
Standing in the sky at the height of seven palm trees, he displayed psychic powers and preached the Dhamma. The entire city gathered. The Elder descended, paid homage to the Blessed One, and said, "Venerable Sir, it is time for me to go." The Blessed One, saying "I shall see the Dhamma-senāpati off," rose from the Dhamma-seat, proceeded toward the Gandhakuṭi, and stood upon the jeweled stone slab. The Elder circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right and paid homage at four points, saying, "Venerable Sir, one incalculable period (asaṅkhyeyya) and a hundred thousand aeons ago, I prostrated at the feet of the Blessed Anomadassī and prayed that I might see you. That prayer of mine is now fulfilled; I have seen you. That first sight was the beginning; this sight is the last. There will be no more seeing you again." Then, joining his ten fingernails and raising his brilliant palms in salutation, he withdrew while facing the Buddha as long as he remained in sight, saying, "From now on, there is no more going or coming to any place by the power of death and rebirth," and having paid homage, he departed. A great earthquake shook as far as the edge of the waters. The Blessed One said to the monks standing around, "Monks, follow after your elder brother." The monks followed as far as the main gate. The Elder turned them back, saying, "Friends, stop here; be mindful and heedful," and proceeded only with his own company. People followed him weeping and wailing, saying, "In the past, the Venerable One went on journeys from which he returned; but this journey is not for the sake of returning again." He turned them back also, saying, "Friends, do not be heedful; conditioned things (saṅkhāra) are of such a nature."

Then, the Venerable Sāriputta, showing favor to the people along the way for seven days, arrived at Nālaka village in the evening and stood at the foot of a banyan tree near the village gate. At that time, his nephew named Uparevata, while going out of the village, saw the Elder, approached, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder asked him, "Is your grandmother at home?" "She is, Venerable Sir," he replied. "Go and tell her that we have arrived here. If she asks why we have come, say, 'He will stay in the village for just one day today; please prepare the birth chamber and arrange lodgings for five hundred monks.'" He went and said, "Grandmother, my uncle has arrived." "Where is he now?" she asked. "At the village gate," he replied. "Is he alone, or is there someone else?" she asked. "Five hundred monks are with him," he replied. When she asked for what reason he had come, he told her the reason. The Brahmin lady thought, "How can there be lodging for so many people?"
142:
She had the preparations made. Thinking, "He entered the Dispensation when he was young, and now that he is old, he likely wishes to return to lay life," she had the birth chamber renovated, lodgings built for the five hundred monks, lamps lit, and then sent word to the Elder.

The Elder ascended the mansion with the monks. Having ascended, he entered the birth chamber and stayed there. While staying there, he dismissed the monks, saying, "Go to your own places of stay." As soon as those monks had left, a severe affliction arose in the Elder. Violent dysentery with blood occurred, such that blood was entering one vessel and leaving another. The Brahmin lady, thinking "I do not like my son's condition," stood leaning against the door of her own room.

The Four Great Kings looked out, wondering, "Where is the Dhamma-senāpati staying?" Seeing him lying on the couch where he would attain parinibbāna in the birth chamber at Nālaka village, they said, "Let us go to pay our final respects," and they arrived, paid homage, and stood there. The Elder asked, "Who are you?" "Venerable Sir, we are the Great Kings," they replied. When asked why they had come, they replied, "We have come to attend to the sick." "Let it be; there are those to attend to me. You may go," he dismissed them. After they had left, Sakka, the King of Devas, and after him, the Deva Suyāma and others, along with Mahābrahmā, arrived in the same manner. The Elder dismissed them in the same way as well.

The Brahmin lady, seeing the coming and going of the deities, thought, "Who are these people who pay homage to my son and then leave?" She went to the door of the Elder's room and asked, "Dear Cunda, how is the condition?" Cunda explained the situation and said, "Venerable Sir, the Great Upāsikā has come." The Elder asked, "Why have you come at such an improper time?" She said, "Dear son, I have come to see you," and then asked, "Dear son, who were those who came first?" "Upāsikā, they were the Four Great Kings," he said. "Dear son, are you superior to the Four Great Kings?" she asked. "Upāsikā, they are like temple guards. From the time our Master (the Buddha) took conception, they have been those who provided protection, holding swords in their hands," he said. "Dear son, who came after they left?" she asked. "It was Sakka, the King of Devas," he said. "Dear son, are you superior even to Sakka, the King of Devas?" she asked. "Upāsikā, he is like a novice (sāmaṇera) who carries utensils. When our Master descended from Tāvatiṃsa, he was the one who descended carrying the bowl and robes," he said. "Dear son, who was that who came after him, shining so brilliantly?" she asked. "Upāsikā, this is Mahābrahmā, whom you worship as the teacher of your God (Brahma)," he said. "Dear son, are you superior even to my object of worship, Mahābrahmā?" she asked. "Yes, Upāsikā, these are our..."
143:
On the day the Blessed One was born, the four Mahābrahmās received the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) with a golden net. At that moment, the Great Female Brahmin (Rūpasārī) thought: "If even my son's majesty is this great, how much greater must be the majesty of the Blessed One, my son's teacher?" In that very instant, the five kinds of rapture (pīti) pervaded her entire body. The Venerable Sāriputta thought: "Rapture and joy have arisen in my mother; now is the time to preach the Dhamma." He then asked, "Great Lay-devotee, what are you thinking about?" The female Brahmin replied, "Dear son, I was thinking that if your own virtues are this great, what must the virtues of your teacher, the Blessed One, be like?"

"Great Lay-devotee, at the time my teacher, the Blessed One, was born, when he went forth into the homeless life, when he attained Enlightenment, and when he turned the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. In virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, there is no one equal to the Blessed One." Thus, he preached the Dhamma in detail concerning the virtues of the Buddha, beginning with "Itipi so Bhagavā..." At the end of her beloved son's discourse, the female Brahmin was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Then she said to her son, "Dear son Upatissa, why did you do this? Why did you not give me such Deathless Dhamma for so long?"

The Elder thought: "Now I have repaid the debt of my mother Rūpasārī's milk for nursing and caring for me; this is enough." He then dismissed her, saying, "Great Lay-devotee, you may go." Then he asked, "Cunda, what time is it?" Cunda replied, "Venerable Sir, it is the time of dawn." "If so, assemble the community of monks," the Elder commanded. When Cunda reported that the Saṅgha had assembled, the Elder said, "Cunda, help me up and let me sit," and he sat up. The Elder addressed the monks: "Friends, for forty-four years you have wandered with me. If there has been any physical or verbal action of mine that displeased you, may you, friends, forgive me." The monks replied, "Venerable Sir, we have followed you like a shadow and there has been nothing displeasing. May you, Venerable Sir, forgive us instead."

Then, at the break of dawn, making the great earth roar, the Elder attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu). Devas and humans alike performed acts of worship and honor at the Elder's passing.
144:
Venerable Cunda took the Elder's bowl, robes, relics, and water-filter and went to Jetavana Monastery. Accompanied by Venerable Ānanda, he approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One, having received the relics and the water-filter, proclaimed the virtues of the Elder with five hundred verses. After causing a reliquary (cetiya) for the relics to be built, he signaled to Venerable Ānanda to prepare for the journey to Rājagaha. Venerable Ānanda informed the monks. Surrounded by the community of monks, the Blessed One traveled to Rājagaha. Upon reaching Rājagaha, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna attained Parinibbāna. The Blessed One took his relics, had a cetiya built, and then left Rājagaha, traveling gradually toward the Ganges River until he reached the town of Ukkacela.

Sitting on the bank of the Ganges in that town, surrounded by the community of monks, he preached the Sutta concerning the Parinibbāna of Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Then, departing from Ukkacela, he traveled to Vesālī. After arriving, the Blessed One dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robes, and entered Vesālī for alms. This is the sequence of events here. "Nisīdana" in this context refers to a leather mat (sitting rug). "Udena Cetiya" refers to the monastery built at the site of the yakkha Udena's shrine. The same applies to Gotamaka Cetiya and others. "Bhāvitā" means developed. "Bahulīkatā" means practiced frequently. "Yānīkatā" means made into a vehicle (well-harnessed). "Vatthukatā" means made into a foundation (in the sense of a basis). "Anuṭṭhitā" means established. "Paricitā" means accumulated from all sides, well-developed. "Susamāraddhā" means well-undertaken.

Having preached thus without limitation, he then spoke the words beginning with "Tathāgatassa kho..." wishing to show a specific limit. Here, "kappa" refers to the life-span (āyu-kappa). Whatever the human life-span is in a particular era, if the Buddha wished to remain for that full duration, he could. "Kappāvasesaṃ vā" means "either a little more or slightly more," referring to a period exceeding a hundred years. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "There is no such thing as a Buddha roaring (making a claim) in an impossible place. Just as he suppressed the feelings ending in death (maraṇantika-vedanā) that arose at Veḷuva village for ten months, he could enter that meditative attainment (samāpatti) repeatedly, suppressing it for ten months at a time, and remain for the entire Bhadda-kappa. Why does he not remain? Because the clung-to material body (upādinnaka-rūpa-khandha) is oppressed by things like the breaking of teeth. Buddhas attain Parinibbāna while they are still beloved by the people, at the four-fifths mark of their life-span, before reaching states like the breaking of teeth. When the Buddha and his great disciples attain Parinibbāna, like a single tree stump..."
145:
...one would have to remain like that, or else remain surrounded by young novices. If that were the case, it would lead to the reproach: "Oh, look at the assembly of the Buddhas!" Therefore, they do not remain (some say). Although this is said, that statement is not to be favored; only the term "āyu-kappa" (life-span) is confirmed and determined in the Commentary.

In the phrase "because Māra had possessed his mind," the word "taṃ" is merely a particle. Just as any other worldling (puthujjana) whose mind is possessed or oppressed by Māra would be unable to penetrate (the Buddha's hint), so too (Venerable Ānanda) was unable to penetrate it. Why? Māra can possess the mind of one who has not yet entirely abandoned the twelve perversions (vippallāsa). Because the Elder (Ānanda) had not yet abandoned four perversions, Māra was able to possess his mind. When Māra possesses a mind, how does he do it? He either shows a terrifying form or causes a terrifying sound to be heard. Then, beings, seeing or hearing that object, lose their mindfulness and stand with their mouths agape. He then thrusts his hand through their mouths and stirs their hearts. At that time, they remain in a state of unconsciousness and forgetfulness. But for the Elder, how could Māra be able to thrust his hand through his mouth? He only showed a terrifying object. Seeing that object, the Elder failed to penetrate the hint and sign (of the Buddha). Even though the Blessed One knew this, why did he call him three times? It was for the purpose of lessening (Ānanda's) grief in the future by blaming him, saying, "This matter is your fault alone, it is your mistake alone," when he would later entreat, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One remain."

## Explanation of the Talk on Māra's Request

In the phrase "Māro pāpimā," "Māro" is so called because he kills beings by binding them to what is harmful. "Pāpimā" is a synonymous name for that Māra. He is called "pāpimā" because he is endowed with evil (yut-nyant) qualities. Kaṇha, Antaka, Namuci, and Pamattabandhu are also names of that Māra. "Bhāsitā kho panesā" refers to the fact that this Māra came to the Bodhi tree in the eighth week after the Blessed One attained Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) and said: "Venerable Sir, the purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections (pāramī) has been achieved; you have penetrated and realized Omniscience. What benefit is there for you to continue wandering in the world?" and entreated him then, just as he did today, saying, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One now attain Parinibbāna." The Blessed One then said to that Māra:
146:
He refused, saying, “I shall not attain final Nibbāna yet,” and so forth. Referring to that matter, [Māra] said, “Venerable Sir, you have spoken these words before,” and so forth.

In that context, 'viyatta' refers to those who are skilled and wise through the power of the Path. Likewise, those who have been disciplined are called 'vinīta'; those who are bold are called 'visārada'. 'Bahussuta' refers to those who are of great learning due to their mastery of the Three Piṭakas. They are called 'dhammadhara' because they bear that very Dhamma of learning (pariyatti-dhamma). Alternatively, they are those of great learning in both pariyatti (scriptural study) and paṭivedha (realization). In this context, the meaning of 'dhammadhara' should be understood as bearing both the pariyatti-dhamma and paṭivedha-dhamma. 'Dhammānudhammapaṭipanna' refers to those who practice the Dhamma of insight (vipassanā) which is in accordance with the noble Dhamma (ariya-dhamma). 'Sāmīcippaṭipanna' refers to those who practice the proper way. 'Anudhammacārī' refers to those who habitually live according to the Dhamma. 'One's own teacher's doctrine' (sakacariya-vāda) refers to the views and doctrines of one's own teachers. All words such as 'they will preach' and so forth are synonyms of one another. 'Sahadhammena' means with a discourse accompanied by reason. 'Sappāṭihāriya' means to the extent of being able to preach the Dhamma so that it leads to liberation from Saṃsāra.

'Brahmacariya' refers to the entire Dispensation (Sāsana) included within the Three Trainings (sikkhā). 'Iddha' means being endowed with the power of the bliss of jhāna. 'Phīta' means reaching prosperity like a tree in full bloom through the power of the perfection of higher knowledge (abhiññā). 'Vitthārika' means being established and widespread in various regions. 'Bāhujañña' means being known by many people, or being penetrated by the power of the attainment of the Dhamma by the masses. 'Puthubhūta' means reaching a state of being widespread in every aspect. How so? 'Well proclaimed among devas and humans' means that as many devas and humans as there are with intelligence, it has been well understood by all of them.

'Appossukka' means being free from concern. The Buddha said, “O Evil Māra, since the eighth week [after enlightenment], you have been wandering around shouting, 'Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna; let the Sugata attain final Nibbāna.' From today onwards, be one who is free from effort; do not strive for my final Nibbāna.”

## Commentary on Relinquishing the Life-Force

'Mindful and clearly comprehending, he relinquished the life-force' (āyusaṅkhāra) means that having firmly established mindfulness and discerning with wisdom, he relinquished and gave up the life-force. In this context, the Buddha did not relinquish the life-force like throwing a stone with his hand; rather, for only three months...
147:
...entering into an attainment (samāpatti), he resolved that he would not enter into an attainment [for the purpose of prolonging life] thereafter. Referring to that, it is said, “he relinquished.” There is also a variant reading “ussajjī.” 'Mahābhūmicāla' refers to a great earthquake. At that time, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. 'Bhiṃsanaka' means causing terror. 'The drums of the devas also burst' means the celestial drums thundered; thunder rolled without rain, and out-of-season streaks of lightning appeared; it means a sudden rain shower fell.

'He uttered an inspired utterance' (udāna)—why did he utter it? Someone might say, “The Buddha, being harassed by Māra who followed him closely again and again saying, 'Venerable Sir, attain final Nibbāna; Venerable Sir, attain final Nibbāna,' relinquished the life-force out of fear.” To show that there is no such opportunity to say so, and that there is no such thing as an inspired utterance for one who is afraid, he uttered this inspired utterance that emerged from the force of joy (pīti).

In that verse, 'tula' refers to the karma of the sensual sphere (kāmāvacara-kamma), which is compared and measured because of its manifest nature to all beings such as dogs and jackals. What is that 'tula'? It is kāmāvacara-kamma. It is called 'atula' because it cannot be compared, or because there is no other mundane karma equal to it. What is that 'atula'? It is sublime karma (mahaggata-kamma). Alternatively, kāmāvacara and rūpāvacara are called 'tula', and arūpāvacara is called 'atula'. Or, karma with small fruit is 'tula', and karma with great fruit is 'atula'. 'Sambhava' means that which is the cause of arising, that which creates an accumulation (of karma). 'Bhavasaṅkhāra' means the karma that conditions further existence. 'Avassaji' means he relinquished. 'Muni' refers to the Sage who is the Buddha. 'Ajjhattarata' means delighting in one's own internal nature. 'Samāhita' means being composed through the power of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). 'Like a coat of mail, he broke it' means breaking it like armor. 'Attasambhava' refers to the defilements (kilesa) arisen within oneself.

This is the meaning: He relinquished the mundane karma called 'tula' and 'atula', which is named 'sambhava' because it is accompanied by fruit, and 'bhavasaṅkhāra' because it conditions existence. Just as a great warrior on a battlefield destroys his armor, he, delighting in his internal nature and having a composed mind, destroyed the defilements arisen within himself.

Alternatively, 'tula' means weighing or deciding. 'Atula and sambhava' refer to Nibbāna and the karma that causes existence. 'Bhavasaṅkhāra' is the karma that leads to existence. 'The Sage relinquished' means that the Buddha-Sage, reflecting by way of “the five aggregates are impermanent; Nibbāna, the cessation of the five aggregates, is permanent,” and so forth, seeing the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna, relinquished that bhavasaṅkhāra-kamma, which is the root cause of the aggregates, by means of the Noble Path (ariya-magga) which is said to “lead to the exhaustion of karma.” How? Delighting in the internal and being composed, he broke it like armor...
148:
...meaning the net of defilements arisen within oneself. Because that Venerable One delights within by the power of insight (vipassanā) and is composed by the power of serenity (samatha), he thus destroyed the entire net of defilements, which is called 'attasambhava' because it arises in oneself and covers the individual existence (attabhāva) like a coat of mail, starting from the preliminary stage through samatha and vipassanā. Because the karma performed in the absence of defilements does not cause rebirth, it is said to be relinquished. Thus, by abandoning defilements, he relinquished karma. For one who has abandoned defilements, there is no such thing as fear; therefore, without fear, he relinquished the life-force. It should be understood that he uttered the inspired utterance to make known that he was without fear.

## Explanation of the Great Earthquake

'Yaṃ mahāvātā' means at the time when great winds blow. When great winds blow, the winds called 'ukkhepaka' (uplifting winds) also arise. When those winds blow, they cut through the wind that supports the water, which is over one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas thick. Then the water in the sky falls; when that water falls, the earth falls. Again, the wind, by its own power, binds and takes up the water like a pair of bellows blowing inside; then the water rises upward; when that water rises, the earth rises. In this way, the trembling water causes the earth to tremble. This trembling occurs even up to the present day, but because the mass of the earth is so great, the sinking and rising are not noticeable.

'Mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo' means 'mahiddhika' because of the greatness of accomplishment, and 'mahānubhāva' because of the greatness of the majesty experienced. 'Parittā' refers to weak devas. 'Appamāṇā' refers to powerful devas. 'So imaṃ pathaviṃ kampeti' means that person causes the earth to tremble, like the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna who wished to cause terror by exercising psychic power, or like the novice Saṅgharakkhita, the nephew of the Venerable Mahānāga Thera, who wished to test it. It is heard that he attained Arahantship while his hair was being shaved (at the very tip of the razor) and thought: “Is there any monk who, having attained Arahantship on the very day of his ordination, has ever shaken the Vejayanta palace?” Then, knowing that there was no one, he thought, “I shall shake it.” He stood on top of the Vejayanta palace by means of higher knowledge (abhiññā) and tried to shake it by treading with his feet, but was unable to do so. Then the dancing girls of Sakka, the king of devas, said, “Son Saṅgharakkhita, do you wish to shake the Vejayanta palace with your foul-smelling head? Dear... the palace is well-constructed; how could you shake it?”
149:
The novice reflected, "These goddesses are mocking me. I have not yet found my teacher. Where is my teacher, the Elder Sāmuddika Mahānāga?" Knowing that the Elder had created a water cave in the great ocean and was spending the day there, he went to that place, paid homage to the Elder, and stood there. Then the Elder said, "Dear Saṅgharakkhita, have you entered the battlefield without learning the art of war?" and asked, "Dear, were you unable to shake the Vejayanta Palace?" The novice replied, "Venerable Sir, I had not found my teacher." Then the Elder said, "Dear, if one like you cannot shake it, who can? Dear, have you ever seen a lump of cow dung floating on the surface of the water? Dear, those who bake pan-cakes define them by the edges; understand by this analogy." The novice said, "Venerable Sir, this is enough," and resolving that the site of the palace should become water, he headed towards the Vejayanta Palace.

When the goddesses saw the novice, they said, "Having gone away once in shame, now the novice has come again, he has come again!" Sakka, the King of Devas, said, "Do not speak thus with my son; now he has found his teacher, and in a moment he will shake the palace." The novice then pressed the pinnacle of the palace with his big toe. The palace tilted towards the four directions. The deities cried out, "Dear, please make the palace stable! Dear, please make the palace stable!" The novice placed the palace back in its original position and, standing on the pinnacle of the palace, uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):

"I have gone forth this very day, and this very day I have reached the destruction of the taints (āsavas). This very day I have shaken the palace; how wonderful is the power of the Great Buddha!
I have gone forth this very day... how wonderful is the power of the Excellent Dhamma!
I have gone forth this very day... how wonderful is the power of the Excellent Saṅgha!" Thus he uttered his inspired utterance.

Apart from this, the words spoken regarding the other six types of earthquakes are just as they were spoken in the Mahāpadāna Sutta.

Thus, among these eight types of earthquakes, the first earthquake is due to the disturbance of the elements; the second is due to psychic power and majesty; the third and fourth are due to the power of merit (puñña-teja); the fifth is due to the power of knowledge (ñāṇa-teja); the sixth is due to the giving of applause (sādhukāra); the seventh is due to the mind of compassion (karuṇā); the eighth is due to weeping. When the Great Being (Mahāsatta) descends into his mother's womb, and when he is born from there, the earth shakes due to the power of merit of that Bodhisatta. When he attains Buddhahood, (the earth shakes) due to the power of knowledge.
150:
(The earth) shakes as if being struck. During the preaching of the Dhammacakka Sutta, it shakes while established in the nature of appreciation (sādhukāra). At the time of relinquishing the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra), it shakes, unable to endure the trembling of the mind, established in the nature of compassion. At the time of Parinibbāna, it shakes as if oppressed by the force of weeping. This meaning should be understood through the power of the earth-protecting deities; as for the great earth comprised of the four great elements, it has no mind and thus does not shake in this way.

In the words, "Ānanda, these eight causes," the word "these" indicates the things being pointed out. By these words, the Venerable Ānanda noted, "Today, it is certain that the Blessed One has relinquished the life-force." Although the Blessed One knew that (Venerable Ānanda) had noted this, without giving him the opportunity, He combined other groups of eight and said, "Monks, these eight (assemblies)," and so forth.

## Explanation of the Eight Assemblies (Aṭṭha Parisā)

In those words, "an assembly of hundreds of khattiyas (kings)" is similar to the meeting with King Bimbisāra, the meeting with relatives, the meeting with the Licchavī kings, and so on; such an assembly can also be found in other world-systems. "Spoken with them before" means having previously engaged in mutual conversation. "Discussed with them" means having previously engaged in Dhamma discussions. "What was their appearance like?" means those people were white, black, or golden-brown; the Blessed One, however, was only of golden appearance. This statement is made with reference to the physical form. The physical form is also apparent only to their intellect; the Blessed One was not like a Milakkha (barbarian), nor did He wear ruby earrings; He stayed only in the form of a Buddha. Those people, however, saw only a physical form similar to their own.

"What was their voice like?" means among them were those with broken voices, trembling voices, or voices like a crow's; the Blessed One, however, had a voice like that of the Great Brahma. This statement is made with reference to other languages. If the Blessed One preached while sitting on the King's throne, they would think, "Today the King preaches with a melodious voice." When the Blessed One had finished preaching and departed, and they saw the King return, the thought would arise, "Who was that?" In the words, "Who was that?", it means they wondered, "Who was this person who just now preached so melodiously in the Magadhan or Sinhalese language and then disappeared? Was it a deva or a human?" Thus, although they investigated, they did not know. Why did He preach to those who did not know?
151:
It is for the purpose of establishing a habitual tendency (vāsanā). This Dhamma heard in this way will surely be a support in the future; thus, He preached with reference to the future. The appearance of the assembly of hundreds of Brahmins, etc., should be understood through the encounters with Soṇadaṇḍa and Kūṭadaṇḍa, or by the power of other world-systems.

For what purpose did the Blessed One bring forth and preach these eight assemblies? It was only to demonstrate His fearlessness. Bringing forth these assemblies, He said: "Ānanda, there is no fear or trembling in the Blessed One who approaches these eight assemblies and preaches the Dhamma. Seeing only a single Māra, who could produce such a perception that the Blessed One would be afraid? Ānanda, the Blessed One, without fear or trembling, mindful and clearly comprehending, has relinquished the life-force."

## Explanation of the Eight Bases of Mastery (Abhibhāyatana)

Abhibhāyatana means the bases of mastery or overcoming. What do they overcome? They overcome opposing states and sense objects. These bases of mastery overcome opposing states because they are contrary to them, and they overcome sense objects because of the person's superior knowledge.

In the phrases such as "perceiving forms internally," one is called "perceiving forms internally" by virtue of performing preliminary work (parikamma) on one's own body. One who wishes to perform preliminary work on the color blue/black on one's own body does so on the hair, the bile, or the pupils of the eyes. One who wishes to perform preliminary work on the color yellow does so on the fat, the skin, the backs of the hands and feet, or the yellow parts of the eyes. One who wishes to perform preliminary work on the color red does so on the flesh, the blood, the tongue, or the red parts of the eyes. One who wishes to perform preliminary work on the color white does so on the bones, the teeth, the nails, or the white parts of the eyes. That color is not an extremely blue, extremely yellow, extremely red, or extremely white color, but only an impure color.

"One sees external forms" means when the preliminary work arises in one's own body and the sign (nimitta) occurs externally, that person, by virtue of performing preliminary work internally and by virtue of absorption (appanā) externally, is said to be "perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms." "Parittāni" means objects that are not developed (limited). "Suvaṇṇa-dubbaṇṇāni" means beautiful or ugly objects. It should be understood that this base of mastery is preached only by virtue of limited (paritta) objects. "Mastering those forms" means, for example, a person with good digestion who receives a ladleful of rice...
152:
Just as one might pull a single morsel of almsfood, thinking, "What food is there here?", so too, a person of sharp wisdom, pre-eminent in the field of knowledge, masters those forms and enters into meditative attainment, thinking, "What meditative attainment is to be entered into in this slight object? This object is not a burden for me." This means that as soon as the sign (nimitta) arises, he attains absorption (appanā) in this object. By the words "I know, I see," his advertence (ābhoga) is expressed. That advertence occurs only to one who has emerged from the attainment, not within the attainment itself. The phrase "is one who has such a perception" means he has such a perception either by way of the perception of advertence or the perception of jhāna. For such a person, the perception of mastery exists even within the attainment, but the perception of advertence occurs only upon emerging from the attainment.

"Immeasurable" means those that are developed, great, and extensive. Regarding the word "mastering," just as a man who eats much, upon receiving a single tray of rice, does not consider that tray of rice as great, thinking, "Let there be another tray of rice; how can this much suffice for me?", so too, a person of sharp wisdom, pre-eminent in the field of knowledge, masters those forms and enters into meditative attainment, thinking, "What meditative attainment is to be entered into here? This object is not immeasurable; it is not a burden for the purpose of establishing my concentration." This means that as soon as the sign arises, he attains absorption in this object.

"One who is non-percipient of form internally" refers to one who is devoid of the preparatory perception (parikamma-saññā) regarding the form within his own continuity, either because of not obtaining it or because of its absence.

"One sees forms externally" means that for whomsoever the preparatory work and the sign arise only externally, that person is said to be "one who, being non-percipient of form internally, sees forms externally" by the power of the preparatory work and the power of absorption. Here, the remaining meaning is exactly as stated in the fourth base of mastery (abhibhāyatana). Among these four, the "slight" object comes by way of the temperament of initial thought (vitakka-carita); the "immeasurable" object by way of the deluded temperament (moha-carita); the "beautiful" object by way of the hateful temperament (dosa-carita); and the "ugly" object by way of the lustful temperament (rāga-carita). For these individuals, these objects are suitable (sappāya). The suitability for these persons has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga, in the Description of Temperaments (Carita-niddesa).

In the fifth base of mastery and those following, the word "blue" (nīla) is spoken by way of encompassing everything. "Blue in color" is spoken by way of the color itself. "Showing a blue color" is spoken by way of appearance; it means they appear as a single sheet of blue, being of a color that is unmixed and without apparent gaps. The word "blue in luster," however, is spoken by way of radiance; it means having a blue radiance, endowed with a blue light. By this statement, the purity of those objects is shown. Pure color...
153:
These four bases of mastery are taught solely by way of the power of mastering (the mind). The flax flower (umā-puppha) is smooth and delicate; when seen, it is of a purely blue color. The butterfly pea flowers (girikaṇṇikā) and others, however, possess a white element (color) when seen. Therefore, only this flax flower should be taken, not those butterfly pea flowers. "Of Bārāṇasī" (Vārāṇaseyyaka) refers to cloth produced in the city of Bārāṇasī. In that city of Bārāṇasī, the cotton is delicate, the spinners and weavers are skilled, and the water is pure and smooth. Therefore, that cloth is smooth on both sides; on both sides, it appears smooth, delicate, and lustrous.

In the case of "yellow in color" and so on, the meaning should be understood in this same way. All details on how to perform the kasina, the preparatory work, and the attainment of absorption—such as "one learning the blue kasina takes the sign in a flower, or in a cloth, or in a color element"—have been taught in detail in the Visuddhimagga. These eight bases of mastery are also brought forth to demonstrate the state of fearlessness (of the Buddha). Having taught these bases of mastery, he said: "Ānanda, whether entering or emerging from such meditative attainments, there is no fear or trembling for the Tathāgata. Who could cause such a perception to arise that the Tathāgata would be afraid upon seeing a single Māra? Ānanda, the Tathāgata, without fear, without trembling, mindful and clearly comprehending, has relinquished the life-formations (āyu-saṅkhāra)."

## Explanation of the Eight Deliverances

The word "Deliverance" (Vimokkha) has a clear meaning. These eight deliverances are also brought forth to demonstrate the state of fearlessness. Having taught these deliverances, he said: "Ānanda, whether entering or emerging from these meditative attainments, there is no fear or trembling for the Tathāgata... (as before) ...has relinquished."

Now, the Blessed One, without giving the Venerable Ānanda an opportunity, began another discourse in the manner starting with "Once, Ānanda, I (ekamidāhaṃ)." In that passage, "First Fully Enlightened" (paṭhamābhisambuddho) refers to the first time during the eighth week after reaching Buddhahood.

"Relinquished" (ossaṭṭho) means the life-span that has been given up and determined. Having said this, he said: "Therefore, this ten-thousandfold world system trembles."

## The Request of Venerable Ānanda

"Enough" (alaṃ) is a word of prohibition. "Bodhi" refers to the penetration of the four path-knowledges. "Do you believe?" (saddahasi tvaṃ) means he asked, "Do you believe in this state of the Tathāgata as described?" Therefore...
154:
"Therefore, Ānanda" (tihānanda) means he showed that because you believe this word, therefore this matter is your fault alone.

Regarding the words "Once, Ānanda, I (ekamidāhaṃ)," the Blessed One began to blame the Elder in various ways to dispel his grief, saying: "I did not call you only at this place; at other times too, I called you and made a clear sign, yet you did not penetrate and understand that sign. This matter is your fault alone."

"From those who are dear and beloved" refers to separation by birth, separation by death, and becoming different by way of another existence from parents, brothers, sisters, and so on. "How can that be obtained?" means that because there is separation from all those who are dear and beloved, therefore, even if one fulfills the ten perfections, attains Enlightenment, turns the Wheel of Dhamma, performs the Twin Miracle, or descends from the celestial realm, it is impossible to say of the Tathāgata's body—which has arisen, is manifest, is conditioned, and is subject to dissolution—"May it not dissolve." Even if one weeps and laments, one cannot obtain that result. "Shall I swallow it back?" means: "Shall I eat again that which has been relinquished and spat out?"

"What is this Dispensation?" means: "What is this noble Dispensation that includes the three trainings?" "Enduring" (addhaniyaṃ) means able to withstand a long period of time (stable). "Long-lasting" (ciraṭṭhitikaṃ) means lasting for a long time by way of occurring for a long duration. All the four foundations of mindfulness and so on are taught by way of both the mundane and the supramundane. The decision regarding these qualities contributing to enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma) has been taught in every aspect in the Visuddhimagga, in the Description of Purification by Knowledge and Vision of the Way (Paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi-niddesa). The remaining words here have clear meanings.

## The Explanation of the Third Recitation Section is Finished.

## Explanation of the Elephant Look

"The Elephant Look" (nāgāpalokita) means that while the bones of ordinary people are joined end to end, and the bones of Paccekabuddhas are linked together, the bones of the Buddhas are not like that.
155:
The neck bones of the Buddhas are joined together like links in a chain; therefore, when they wish to look back, they are unable to turn only the neck. Just as a great elephant turns its entire body when it wishes to look behind, so too does the Buddha turn his whole body to look. While standing at the gate of the city of Vesālī, the thought 'I shall look upon Vesālī' arose in his mind. As if to say, 'Venerable Sir... You who have fulfilled the perfections for more than a hundred thousand eons have never performed the act of turning the neck,' this great earth turned like a potter's wheel, causing the Buddha to face the city of Vesālī. It is in reference to this event that it was said (nāgāpalokita - looking like a great elephant). It is asked: Why did he not look like a great elephant at all those places such as Sāvatthī, Rājagaha, Nāḷandā, Pāṭaligāma, Koṭigāma, and Nādikagāma, even though those were also the last times he would see them? The answer is: because it was not a marvel. Turning his body himself in those places was not a marvel; therefore, he did not look like a great elephant there. Alternatively, the princes of Vesālī were nearing destruction and would perish within three years. Thinking that those princes would establish a shrine named 'Nāgāpalokita' at the city gate and make offerings of perfumes and flowers, and that such offerings would lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time, he looked out of compassion for them. 'Dukkhassantakaro' means one who makes an end to the suffering of the round of rebirth. 'Cakkhumā' means one who is endowed with the five eyes. 'Parinibbuto' means one who is extinguished by the Nibbāna of defilements.

## Catumahāpadesavaṇṇanā
'Mahāpadesa' means a great opportunity or a great reason. It refers to great reasons mentioned in reference to great persons such as the Buddha. One should not first accept it with joy and appreciation; if one does so, later when it is said 'this Dhamma is not consistent,' one might not abandon their view, thinking, 'Was this Dhamma previously correct and only now incorrect?' One should not first reject it, saying, 'What is this fool saying?'; if one says this, the person might not even speak words that ought to be spoken. Therefore, it is said, 'without rejoicing and without rejecting.' 'Padabyañjanānīti' refers to the syllables (letters) called words. 'Sādhukaṃ uggahetvā' means having learned well...
156:
One should note well: 'Here the Pali text is stated, here the meaning is stated, here the connection (anusandhi) is stated, here the sequence of words is stated.' 'Sutte otāretabbāni' means they should be compared with the Suttas. 'Vinaye sandassetabbāni' means they should be compared with the Vinaya.

In this context, 'Sutta' refers to the Vinaya (Vibhaṅga). This is as stated: 'Where was it prohibited? It was prohibited in the Sutta Vibhaṅga in Sāvatthī.' 'Vinaya' refers to the Khandhaka. This is as stated in 'Vinayātisāre.' If said this way, it does not encompass the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. In fact, only if the two Vibhaṅgas are called 'Sutta' and the Khandhaka and Parivāra are called 'Vinaya' does it encompass the entire Vinaya Piṭaka. Otherwise, if the Suttanta Piṭaka is called 'Sutta' and the Vinaya Piṭaka is called 'Vinaya,' it only encompasses two Piṭakas. Or, if the Suttanta Piṭaka and Abhidhamma Piṭaka are called 'Sutta' and the Vinaya Piṭaka is called 'Vinaya,' it still does not encompass all three Piṭakas. This is because there is no Buddha-word that does not receive the name 'Sutta.' These are: Jātaka, Paṭisambhidā, Niddesa, Suttanipāta, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and Apadāna.

However, the Elder Sudinna says: 'There is no Buddha-word that does not receive the name Sutta,' and rejecting all those, he says: 'The three Piṭakas are Sutta, and the Vinaya is the reason (standard).' Then, to show that reason, he brought this Sutta:

'Gotamī, of whatever teachings you may know: "These teachings lead to passion, not to passionlessness; to bondage, not to detachment; to accumulation (of defilements), not to dispersal; to great ambition, not to fewness of wishes; to discontent, not to contentment; to socializing, not to seclusion; to laziness, not to arousal of energy; to being difficult to support, not to being easy to support"—Gotamī, you may definitely hold: "This is not the Dhamma, this is not the Vinaya, this is not the Teacher's instruction." Gotamī, of whatever teachings you may know: "These teachings lead to passionlessness, not to passion; to detachment, not to bondage; to dispersal, not to accumulation; to fewness of wishes, not to great ambition; to contentment, not to discontent; to seclusion, not to socializing..."'
158:
...is answered. This method is the same for the ear and so forth. This is a problem to be answered categorically (ekāṃsavyākaraṇīya). If it is asked, 'Is the eye impermanent?', it should be answered analytically: 'Not only the eye, but the ear is also impermanent, the nose is also impermanent.' This is a problem to be answered analytically (vibhajjavyākaraṇīya). If it is asked, 'As the eye is, so is the ear? As the ear is, so is the eye?', one should ask in return, 'In what sense do you ask?' If he says, 'I ask in the sense of seeing,' it should be answered, 'No.' If he says, 'I ask in the sense of impermanence,' it should be answered, 'Yes.' This is a problem to be answered by counter-questioning (paṭipucchāvyākaraṇīya). If it is asked, 'Is the soul the same as the body?' and so forth, it should be set aside, saying, 'The Blessed One has not declared this.' This problem should not be answered. This is a problem to be set aside (ṭhapanīya). Thus, when problems arise in that manner, these four ways of answering problems are the standard (pamāṇa). The problem should be answered by means of these four.

In the Suttas and so forth, 'Sutta' refers to the three Piṭakas recited in the three Councils. 'Suttānuloma' refers to things that are suitable and conform to the Suttas. 'Ācariyavāda' refers to the Commentaries (Atthakathā). 'Attanomati' refers to one's own opinion known by one's own wisdom through inference. Among these four, the Sutta is not to be rejected; he who rejects the Sutta rejects the Buddha himself. As for what conforms to the Sutta, it should be accepted only if it agrees with the Sutta; if it does not agree, it should not be accepted. The Ācariyavāda should also be accepted only if it agrees with the Sutta; if it does not agree, it should not be accepted. Attanomati is the weakest of all; it too should be accepted only if it agrees with the Sutta; if it does not agree, it should not be accepted. Only the Sutta included in these three Councils—the Council of Five Hundred (Pañcasatikā), the Council of Seven Hundred (Sattasatikā), and the Council of One Thousand (Sahassikā)—is the standard; other censurable Suttas (gārayhasutta) should not be accepted. It should be known that the words and syllables that seem to enter into those censurable Suttas do not enter into the Sutta, nor are they found in the Vinaya.

## Explanation of the Story of Cunda the Smith's Son
'Kammāraputtassa' means to the son of a smith. That Cunda was a wealthy merchant who became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) upon first seeing the Buddha, and he built and offered a monastery in his mango grove. With reference to that monastery, it is said 'ambavane' (in the mango grove).

'Sūkaramaddava' is the meat of a single large pig that is neither too tender nor too tough. That meat is soft and succulent like ghee; having had that meat well prepared...
160:
The Blessed One, seated in a vehicle made of all kinds of gems, departed from the city of Kusinārā and set out on the road, thinking, "I shall go to the city of Pāvā." Referring to this, it is said, "He traveled the long journey from Kusinārā to Pāvā."

Āḷāra is his name. It is said he was called Āḷāra because he was tall and golden-complexioned. Kālāma is the lineage (clan). "Yatra hi nāma" means "such a one as." "Neva dakkhati" means he did not see. Because it is associated with the word "yatra," it is spoken here in the future tense. In such places, the grammatical characteristic is often like this. "Niccharantīsu" means while they were wandering about. "Asaniyā phalantiyā" means while a great sound was thundering, as if nine kinds of thunderbolts were breaking. 

The nine kinds of thunderbolts are: Asaññā, Vicakkā, Saterā, Gaggarā, Kapisīsā, Macchavilolikā, Kukkuṭakā, Daṇḍamaṇikā, and Sukkhāsanī. Among them, Asaññā causes loss of consciousness. Vicakkā creates a circle. Saterā falls like a saw. Gaggarā falls with a "ji-ji" sound. Kapisīsā resembles a frowning monkey. Macchavilolikā is like a wriggling fish. Kukkuṭakā falls like a chicken. Daṇḍamaṇikā falls like a plow-handle. Sukkhāsanī digs up and destroys the place where it falls. 

"Deve vassante" means while it was raining at intervals along with the sound of thunder. "Ātumāyaṃ" means he lived depending on the city of Ātumā. "Bhusāgāre" means in a threshing shed. "Ettheso" means for this reason these people have gathered. "Kva ahosi" means where were you? "So taṃ bhante" means "You, Bhante." "Singīvaṇṇaṃ" means having a color like that of pure gold. "Yugamaṭṭhaṃ" means a pair of smooth cloths, a pair of delicate cloths. "Dhāraṇīyaṃ" means a cloth that I wear from time to time. That Pukkusa used to wear such clothes only on festival days and kept them stored at other times. This refers to such a noble set of auspicious robes. 

"Anukampaṃ upādāya" means out of compassion and care for me. "Acchādehī" is a figurative expression meaning "please clothe me with this"; it means give one to me and one to Ānanda. When asked if Venerable Ānanda accepted that cloth, the answer is: he certainly did. Why? Because the duty of service had reached its peak. Although Venerable Ānanda had previously refused such gifts and only performed service, now that his service had reached its culmination, he accepted it. If people were to say, "Venerable Ānanda could not please the Blessed One"...
161:
...he accepted it also to cut off the opportunity for the words of those who might say, "Although Venerable Ānanda served for twenty-five years, he never received anything from the Blessed One." Furthermore, the Blessed One knew, "Even if Ānanda accepts it, he will not wear it himself; he will offer it only to me. By the Malla prince offering it to Ānanda, it will also be an offering to the Saṅgha; thus, a great mass of merit will accrue to that prince." Therefore, he had one given to the Elder. The Elder also accepted it for that very reason. 

"Dhammiyā kathāyā" means with words of appreciation for the donation of the robes. "Bhagavato kāyaṃ upanāmitaṃ" means placed close by way of wearing or wrapping. The Blessed One used one of the two cloths as an undergarment and one as an upper robe. "Hataccikaṃ viya" means just as an ember whose heat is spent burns only within and has no glow on the outside, so it appeared as if the radiance was covered on the outside. 

"Imesu kho Ānanda dvīsu pi kālesu"—why does it happen like this at these two times? It is due to the excellence of nutriment (āhāra) and due to intense joy (somanassa).
