At these two times, the devas throughout the entire universe infuse essence (ojā) into the food; when that exquisite food enters the stomach, it produces clear material phenomena (rūpa). Due to the clarity of the material phenomena caused by the nutriment, the mind and the six faculties become exceedingly radiant. 

On the day of attaining Buddhahood, intense joy arose in the Blessed One as he reflected, "The mass of defilements I have accumulated for many billions of aeons has been abandoned today." The mind became clear; when the mind is clear, the blood becomes clear; when the blood is clear, the faculties become exceedingly radiant. On the day of his Parinibbāna, when he reflected, "Today I shall enter the city of the Deathless Nibbāna, where many Buddhas have entered," intense joy arose, the mind became clear, the blood became clear, and the faculties became exceedingly radiant. Thus, it should be understood that it happens at these two times due to the excellence of nutriment and intense joy. 

"Upavattane" means in the Sal-grove which is the turning point from the east. "Antarena yamakasālānaṃ" means between the pair of Sal trees. The verses beginning with "Singīvaṇṇaṃ" were inserted at the time of the Council (Saṅgāyana).
162:
In the passage "natvā ca pivitvā ca" (having bathed and drunk), it is said that at the time the Blessed One was bathing, the fish and turtles in the river and the entire forest on both banks of the river appeared golden and bright like the color of gold. "Ambavanaṃ" refers to the mango grove on the bank of that river. "Āyasmantaṃ Cundakaṃ"—at that moment, Venerable Ānanda was left behind as he was wringing out the water-bathing cloth; Venerable Cunda was near the Blessed One. The Blessed One called that Venerable Cunda. These verses beginning with "Gantvāna Buddho nadikaṃ Kakudhaṃ" were also inserted at the time of the Council. 

In those verses, "pavatta bhagavā idha dhamme" means the Blessed One set the Dhamma in motion in this Dispensation; he brought forth the eighty-four thousand groups of Dhamma. "Pamukhe nisīdi" means he sat right in front of the Blessed One. At this time, Venerable Ānanda arrived. When he arrived, the Blessed One called Venerable Ānanda. 

"Alābhā" means the losses consisting of not receiving the benefits said to be the fruits of other offerings. "Dulladdhaṃ" means even the human life obtained through special merit is poorly obtained. "Yassa te" means in which offering of yours. People might criticize, saying, "Who knows if the rice was undercooked or overcooked? What kind of last meal did the Tathāgata consume before he passed away? What kind of meal was it that you offered?"

"Lābhā" means the gains said to be the fruits of the offering in the present life and the life hereafter. "Suladdhaṃ" means your human life is well obtained. "Samasamaphalā" means they are equal in fruit in every respect. Having consumed the meal offered by Sujātā, the Blessed One attained Buddhahood; that meal was consumed at a time when greed, hatred, and delusion were not yet abandoned. Now, the meal offered by Cunda was consumed at a time when greed, hatred, and delusion were already abandoned. Even so, why are these two meals equal in fruit? It is because of the equality of the Parinibbāna, the equality of the attainments (samāpatti), and the equality of the reflection. 

Having consumed Sujātā's meal, the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna element with residue (saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Having consumed Cunda's meal, he attained Parinibbāna with the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu). Because of this equality of attaining Parinibbāna, they are equal in fruit. On the day of becoming Buddha, he entered into two hundred and forty thousand crores of attainments; on the day of Parinibbāna, he also entered into all those same attainments. Because of this equality of entering attainments, they are also equal in fruit. Sujātā also later heard, "This person was not a tree-deity, but a Bodhisatta; having consumed that meal, he attained the peerless Supreme Enlightenment."
163:
It is said that after the Buddha attained Enlightenment (Abhisambuddha), he subsisted on that meal alone for seven weeks. When she (the goddess) heard this, as she repeatedly reflected, 'What a great gain for me!', intense rapture and joy (pīti-somanassa) arose. For Cunda also, when he later heard, 'I have offered the final meal; I have attained the pinnacle of Dhamma; the Buddha, having partaken of my meal, has passed away into the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu),' as he reflected, 'What a great gain for me!', intense joy (somanassa) arose. Since their reflections were similar, it should be understood that the benefits are equal. 'Yasasavaṭṭanika' means having the benefit of producing a retinue. 'Ādhipateyyasaṃvattanika' means having the benefit of producing sovereignty. 'Saṃyamato' means one who is restrained by the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃyama), one who stands in restraint (saṃvara). 'Veraṃ na cīyati' means the fivefold hostilities do not increase. 'Kusalo ca jahāti pāpakaṃ' means the wise person, the possessor of merit, completely abandons base unwholesome states through the Noble Path. 'Rāgadosemohakkhayā sa nibbuto' means that person, having abandoned these base unwholesome states, is extinguished through the Nibbāna of defilements due to the destruction of lust and so forth. Thus, seeing the excellence of Cunda’s offering and the excellence of the recipient (himself), he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna).

## End of the Description of the Fourth Recitation Section

## Description of the Twin Sāla Trees
In the phrase 'together with a great community of monks' (mahatā bhikkhusaṃghena saddhiṃ), there is no specific limit to the number of monks here. From the time he experienced the painful feelings in the village of Veḷuva, monks who had arrived from various places upon hearing 'the Buddha will soon pass away' did not leave. Therefore, they were an innumerable Sangha. 'Upavattanaṃ mallānaṃ sālavanaṃ' means that just as one goes to the Thūpārāma through the Rājamātu-vihāra gate from the banks of the Kaḷamba river, so too is the Sāla grove on the other side of the Hiraññavatī river. That grove in Kusinārā is like the Thūpārāma of Anurādhapura. Just as the road entering the city from the south gate of the Thūpārāma faces east and then turns north, the road going from the garden to the Upavattana Sāla grove also faces east and then turns north. Therefore, that place is called 'Upavattana'.
164:
"Yamaka-sālānam uttarasīsakam" (between the twin Sal trees, with the head to the north) means that there was a row of Sal trees at the head side of the couch and another row at the foot side. In that arrangement, there was one young Sal tree at the head and one young Sal tree at the foot. Alternatively, "Yamaka-sālā" refers to Sal trees that stood with their roots, trunks, branches, and leaves intertwined with one another. "Mañcakaṃ paññapehi" (Prepare the couch) refers to the royal couch used by the royalty for sleeping in that garden; it was with reference to this that He said, "Prepare the couch." Ven. Ānanda prepared that very couch.

When He said, "Ānanda, I am weary, I will lie down," it should be understood that for the Tathāgata—according to the verse stating that among elephants, the ten types: Gocara, Kaḷāpa, Gaṅgeyya, Piṅgala, Pabbateyya, Hemavata, Tamba, Mandākinī, Uposatha, and Chaddanta are the noblest—the strength of ten ordinary (Gocara) elephants equals the strength of one Kaḷāpa elephant. By this decimal increase, all the strength equivalent to the power of a thousand crores of ordinary elephants had become exhausted, like water poured into a filter, from the time He partook of Cunda's meal. Although the distance from the city of Pāvā to the city of Kusinārā is three gāvutas, and He had to travel with great effort, resting at twenty-five places in between, the Buddha was only able to enter the Sāla grove at the time of sunset. Thus, illness comes by oppressing all health. As if to demonstrate this fact, He spoke words that cause spiritual urgency (saṃvega) to all worldlings: "Ānanda, I am weary, I will lie down."

Why did the Buddha come to this place with such great effort? Was it not possible to attain Parinibbāna elsewhere? It was possible to attain Parinibbāna anywhere; however, He came to this place for three reasons. The Buddha foresaw: "If I attain Parinibbāna elsewhere, there will be no occasion for the Mahāsudassana Sutta to arise. Only if I attain Parinibbāna in Kusinārā can I preach, adorned in two sections (bhāṇavāra), how I enjoyed celestial-like glory even in the human realm; upon hearing that Dhamma, many people will realize that merit should be performed."
165:
Furthermore, He foresaw: "If I attain Parinibbāna elsewhere, Subhadda will not have the opportunity to see me. This Subhadda is one who is to be tamed by the Buddha (Buddha-veneyya), not by the disciples; the disciples are not capable of taming him. This Subhadda will approach me while I am attaining Parinibbāna in Kusinārā and ask questions. After I have answered his questions, he will be established in the Refuges, receive ordination in my presence, take up a subject of meditation, and while I am still alive, he will become an Arahant, becoming the last disciple."

Furthermore, He foresaw: "If I attain Parinibbāna elsewhere, a great conflict will arise during the distribution of the relics; blood will flow like a river. If I attain Parinibbāna in Kusinārā, the Brahmin Doṇa will settle that dispute and distribute the relics." It should be understood that for these three reasons, the Blessed One came to this place with such great effort.

Regarding the term "Sīha-seyyā" (the lion's posture), there are four types of postures (seyyā): the posture of the sensualist (kāma-bhogī-seyyā), the posture of the hungry ghost (peta-seyyā), the posture of the lion (sīha-seyyā), and the posture of the Tathāgata (tathāgata-seyyā).

Among these four: "Monks, beings who enjoy sensual pleasures mostly sleep on their left side"—this is the kāma-bhogī-seyyā. Among them, there are almost none who sleep mostly on their right side.

"Monks, hungry ghosts (petas) mostly sleep on their backs"—this is the peta-seyyā. Because they have little flesh and blood and are mostly skeletons, petas cannot sleep on either side; they sleep only on their backs.

"Monks, the lion, the king of beasts, takes up his sleep on the right side... [pe]... he is joyful" (Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.246)—this is the sīha-seyyā. Because of his great power and majesty, the lion, the king of beasts, places his two front paws in one place and his two hind paws in another, tucks his tail between his thighs, notes the position where the front paws, hind paws, and tail are placed, and sleeps with his head resting upon his front paws. Even if he sleeps the whole day, when he wakes up, he wakes without fear; he lifts his head and notes the position where the front paws and other parts are placed. If any part is displaced from its original position, he is displeased, thinking, "This is not suitable for your breed and your courage," and he sleeps again in that very spot, not going out to find food. If they are not displaced, he is joyful, thinking, "This is suitable for your breed and your courage," and he rises...
167:
"Divine (flowers)" refers to flowers born in the Nandā pond in the celestial realm; those flowers are golden in color, have leaves the size of parasols, and carry pollen the size of large jars. Not only Mandārava flowers, but other divine flowers such as Parichattaka and Koviḷāra were also filled into golden baskets and scattered by devas stationed at the edge of the universe, in the Tāvatiṃsā heaven, and in the Brahma realm, falling from the sky. "Upon the body of the Blessed One" means they came without being scattered in the intervening space and covered only the body of the Blessed One with petals, filaments, and pollen dust.

"Divine sandalwood powders also" refers to sandalwood powders used by the devas. Not only those used by devas, but also sandalwood powders used by nagas, garudas, and humans. Not only sandalwood powders, but powders of all kinds of divine fragrances such as Kāḷānusārī and Lohitacandana, as well as powders of orpiment, collyrium, gold dust, silver dust, and all objects scented with divine perfumes, were filled into golden and silver bowls and scattered by devas stationed at the edge of the universe and elsewhere; these fell without being scattered in the intervening space and covered only the body of the Blessed One.

"Divine musical instruments also" refers to musical instruments used by the devas. Not only those, but all instruments of devas, nagas, garudas, and humans from ten thousand universes—classified as stringed instruments, percussion instruments covered with skin, solid instruments, and hollow instruments—assembled in this single universe and were played in the sky.

"Divine songs also" refers to the devas named Varuṇa-vāraṇa who are long-lived. Having heard that "The Great Being (Mahāpurisa) has arisen in the world and will become a Buddha," they thought, "We shall take him away on the day of his conception," and began weaving garlands. While they were weaving, they heard, "The Great Being has already taken conception in his mother's womb." When asked, "For whom are you weaving?" they replied, "It is not finished yet; we shall take him away on the day he leaves the womb (is born)." Again, hearing "He is born," they said, "We shall go on the day of his renunciation." After he lived in the house for 29 years, they heard again, "Today he has renounced," but said, "We shall go on the day he becomes a Buddha." After he practiced for 6 years, they heard again, "Today he has become a Buddha," but said, "We shall go on the day he preaches the Dhammacakka." Hearing again, "Having spent seven times seven days at the Bodhi tree, he went to Isipatana and preached the Dhammacakka," they said, "We shall go on the day he performs the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya)." "Today he has performed the Twin Miracle..."
168:
Even upon hearing, “He has done so,” they thought, “We shall go on the day he descends from the celestial realm.” Again, upon hearing, “Today he has performed the descent from the celestial realm,” they thought, “We shall go when he relinquishes the life-force (āyu-saṅkhāra).” Again, upon hearing, “Today he has relinquished the life-force,” they thought, “It is not yet over; we shall go on the day he attains Parinibbāna.” However, when they heard, “Today, between the twin Sāla trees, the Blessed One has attained the lion’s posture (sīha-seyyā), lying on his right side, mindful and clearly comprehending; he will attain Parinibbāna at the time of dawn; to whom are you going now?”—

They said: “How can this be? ‘On this very day he was conceived in his mother’s womb; on this very day he emerged from his mother’s womb; on this very day he went forth in the Great Renunciation (Mahābhinikkhamana); on this very day he attained Buddhahood; on this very day he preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta; on this very day he performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya); on this very day he descended from the celestial realm; on this very day he relinquished the life-force; and on this very day he will attain Parinibbāna.’ Should he not remain even for the duration of drinking a bowl of rice gruel on the second day? Such an occurrence is not fitting for one who has fulfilled the ten perfections (pāramīs) and attained Buddhahood.” Carrying unfinished garlands and finding no space within the world-system (Cakkavāḷa), they hung onto the edges of the Cakkavāḷa and ran along its perimeter. Clasping hands or embracing each other’s necks, they sang songs based on the Triple Gem, the 32 marks of a Great Man (Mahāpurisalakkhaṇa), the six-colored rays, the ten perfections, the five hundred and fifty Jātaka stories, and the 14 types of Buddha-knowledge. At the end of each song, they exclaimed, “Great is his fame! Great is his fame!” Referring to this, it was said: “To honor the Tathāgata, the singing of deities also arose in the sky.”

The Blessed One, while lying on his right side between the twin Sāla trees, saw the great exertion of the assembly that had gathered from the surface of the earth to the edge of the Cakkavāḷa, and from the edge of the Cakkavāḷa up to the Brahma realm, and addressed the Venerable Ānanda. Therefore, it was said: “Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda... (to honor the Tathāgata, the singing of deities also arose in the sky).” Having shown such a great offering of honor, and wishing to show that he is not truly honored by such an offering, he said: “Ānanda, by such an offering (the Buddha is not yet truly honored),” and so forth.

This is the meaning: “Ānanda, when I was prostrate at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, combining the eight factors to make my aspiration, I did not aspire for flowers, scents, musical instruments, or songs; nor did I fulfill the perfections for that purpose. Therefore, I am not truly honored by such an offering.”
169:
However, why did the Blessed One, who elsewhere praised the fruit of an offering made even with a single barley flower while reflecting on the Buddha’s virtues as being immeasurable even by Buddha-knowledge, reject such a grand offering here? He rejected it because he wished to encourage the assembly and to ensure the long-lasting stability of the Sasana. If the Blessed One had not rejected it in this way, in the future, when it is time to practice virtue (sīla), they would not fulfill virtue; when it is time to develop concentration (samādhi), they would not fulfill concentration; when it is time to develop insight (vipassanā), they would not exert effort in the work of insight. They would live only by urging attendants to make offerings.

This material offering (āmisa-pūjā) cannot sustain the Sasana for even a single day, nor for the time it takes to drink a cup of rice gruel. Even a thousand monasteries like the Mahāvihāra and a thousand stupas like the Mahācetiya cannot uphold the Sasana. If a person performs a wholesome deed, the benefit is for that person alone. Only the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (sammā-paṭipatti) is the offering fitting for the Blessed One. Only that practice is what the Blessed One desires, and it alone can sustain the Sasana. Therefore, wishing to show that practice, he said: “Ānanda, whatever monk...” and so forth.

In that passage, “dhammānudhammapaṭipanna” refers to one who practices the preliminary path (pubbabhāgapaṭipadā), which is the secondary Dhamma (anudhamma) leading to the nine transcendent states (lokuttara-dhamma). Because that practice is fitting and proper, it is called “sāmīci.” Because one practices that fitting practice, one is called “sāmīcippaṭipanna.” Because one practices and fulfills the anudhamma known as the preliminary path, one is called “anudhammacārī.”

This preliminary path should be understood as the right practice (sammā-paṭipada) ranging from virtue (sīla), the rules of conduct (ācārapaññatti), and the undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) up to the stage of change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). Therefore, if a monk, remaining in the six types of disrespect, violates the disciplinary rules and lives by improper livelihood (anesana), this monk is not a dhammānudhammapaṭipanna. If a monk does not violate even slightly all the training rules prescribed for him, nor the boundaries of the Conqueror (jina-vela), the limits of the Conqueror (jina-mariyāda), and the laws of the Conqueror (jina-kāḷasutta), this monk is called a dhammānudhammapaṭipanna. The same applies to bhikkhunīs. If a male lay follower (upāsaka) lives committing the five enmities (breaking the five precepts) and the ten unwholesome courses of action, he is not a dhammānudhammapaṭipanna. One who practices perfectly in the Triple Gem, the five precepts, and the ten precepts; who observes the Uposatha eight days a month; who gives alms; who makes offerings with scents and flowers; who supports his parents; and who supports recluses and brahmins who practice rightly—this person is called a dhammānudhammapaṭipanna. The same applies to female lay followers (upāsikās).
170:
“With the highest offering” means with a magnificent offering. Only this non-material offering (nirāmisa-pūjā or dhamma-pūjā) can sustain my Sasana. He showed that as long as these four groups of followers honor me with this offering, so long will my Sasana shine brightly like the full moon in the middle of the sky.

## Commentary on the Elder Upavāṇa

“Removes” means setting aside. “Move away” means to go elsewhere. With just a single word, the Elder put down his palm-leaf fan and stood in another place. The words “attendant” (upaṭṭhāka) etc. were spoken referring to the fact that he was not a constant attendant during the first period of Enlightenment (paṭhamabodhi-kāla). When the Venerable Ānanda said, “Venerable Sir, this is the Venerable Upavāṇa,” he perceived the Elder Upavāṇa as being at fault. Intending to say, “Now I will explain the faultless state of that Elder,” the Blessed One said, “Ānanda, for the most part,” and so forth. In that passage, “for the most part” was said referring to the fact that the unconscious (asaññasatta) Brahmās and the formless (arūpa) deities and Brahmās were left behind.

“Apphuṭa” means not touched or not pervaded. It is said that ten powerful deities stood in each space the size of the tip of a yak-tail hair near the Blessed One, having created subtle bodies. Behind those deities stood twenty each, then thirty each, then forty each, then fifty each, and then sixty each deities and Brahmās. Those deities did not touch each other with their hands, feet, or clothing. There was no such situation where one had to say, “Move away from me, do not bump into me.” This is consistent with what is stated in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: “Whether they be ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty, they stand even in a space the size of the tip of a needle without touching each other.” “Ovārento” means obstructing or covering. The Elder naturally had a large body like a young elephant. Because the Elder was wearing his refuse-rag robes (pāṃsukūla), he appeared very large.

“To see the Blessed One” means that because they did not get the chance to see the Blessed One’s face, they complained in this manner. Could those deities not see through the Elder? Indeed, they could not. Although deities can see through worldlings (puthujjanas), they cannot see through those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsavas). Due to the Elder’s great psychic power and the sharpness of his majestic aura, they could not even approach him.
171:
Why is only that Elder so great in psychic power and majesty, while other Arahants are not as great? The reason is that he had previously been a guardian deity at the stupa of the Blessed One Kassapa.

It is heard that when the Blessed One Vipassī attained Parinibbāna, a single stupa was built for the sacred relics, which were like a solid mass of gold. For Buddhas with a long lifespan, there is traditionally only one stupa. People built that stupa to a height of one yojana, using golden bricks that were one cubit long, one span wide, and two inches thick; using red arsenic (haritāla) and cinnabar (manosilā) for the mortar work; and using sesame oil for the water requirements. From that point, the earth-dwelling deities (bhummā devā) built another yojana, the space-dwelling deities (ākāsaṭṭhā devā) another yojana, the cloud-deities (uṇhavalāhaka devā) another yojana, the mist-deities (abbhavalāhaka devā) another yojana, the deities of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) another yojana, and the Tāvatiṃsa deities another yojana, respectively. Thus, it became a great stupa seven yojanas high. When people came carrying flowers, perfumes, garments, and so on, the guardian deity would make offerings to the stupa right in their sight.

At that time, this Elder was a wealthy Brahmin (Brāhmaṇa Mahāsāla) and went there taking a bright yellow cloth. A goddess took the cloth from his hand and offered it to the stupa. Seeing this, the Brahmin felt inspired and made a wish: "May I also become a guardian deity at the stupa of such a Buddha in the future." After passing away from that life, he was reborn in the celestial realm. While he was wandering through the celestial and human realms, the Blessed One Kassapa appeared in the world and attained Parinibbāna. The relics of that Buddha were also in a single solid mass. Enshrining those relics, a stupa one yojana high was built. He became a guardian deity at that stupa, and when the Dispensation (Sāsana) disappeared, he was reborn in the celestial realm. In the time of our Blessed One, he passed away from there, took conception in a noble family, went forth into homelessness, became a monk, and attained Arahantship. Thus, because he had been a guardian deity at a stupa, that Elder should be known as one with abundant majesty (Tejussada).

By the words "Ānanda, the deities complain," the intention is to show: "Ānanda, the deities complain; there is no other fault in my son."

Why is it asked, "Venerable Sir, what is the nature of those deities?" When the Blessed One said, "The deities complain," regarding what the nature of those deities was in your minds...
172:
(The deities) asked, "What are they doing? Can you accept the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One?" Then, the Blessed One, wishing to show the state of those deities who could not accept it, said, "I will no longer speak of the reasons for accepting Parinibbāna," and spoke the words beginning with "Santānanda."

In that passage, "ākāse pathavīsaññiniyo" refers to deities who create earth in the sky and have the perception of earth in that very sky. "Kandanti" means they weep. "Chinnapātaṃ papatanti" means they fall down here and there as if they had been cut in the middle. "Āvaṭṭanti" means they roll about and return to the very place where they fell. "Vivaṭṭanti" means they roll from the place they fell to another place. Alternatively, "āvaṭṭanti vivaṭṭanti" refers to rolling about by stretching both legs, once forward, once backward, once to the left, and once to the right. In the phrase "Santānanda, the deities with the perception of earth on the earth," it means that the natural earth cannot support the deities. Like Hatthaka Brahma, the deities would sink into it. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Hatthaka, create a coarse, manifest body." Thus, "pathaviyaṃ pathavīsaññiniyo" is said in reference to the deities who create earth on the earth.

"Vītarāgā" refers to the deities who are Anāgāmīs and Arahants, who have abandoned sorrow and grief and are as firm as stone pillars.

## Catusaṃvejanīyaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā
(Description of the Four Places Arousing Spiritual Urgency)

"Vassaṃvuṭṭhā" means that during the time of the Blessed One, monks would assemble on two occasions: once when the time to enter the rains-retreat (Vassa) was near, to take up a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), and once when the retreat ended, to report the extraordinary attainments they had achieved through their meditation efforts. Just as in the time of the Blessed One, in the island of Sri Lanka (Tambapaṇṇidīpa), the monks on this side of the river would assemble at the Lohapāsāda palace, and the monks on the other side of the river would assemble at the Tissamahāvihāra monastery. Among those monks, those on this side of the river would bring brooms and dustpans, assemble at the Mahāvihāra, perform duties such as applying lime-wash to the stupa, and then make a commitment: "When the rains-retreat ends, come and assemble at the Lohapāsāda." Then, they would live in places where they could reside comfortably, and when the retreat ended, they would come to the assembly of the Five Nikāyas at the Lohapāsāda. Among those monks, those skilled in the Pāḷi would recite and chant the Pāḷi; those skilled in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā) would recite and chant the Commentaries.
173:
If anyone should cause a mistake in either the Pāḷi or the Commentary, they would investigate by asking, 'Under whom did you learn?' and have them learn it correctly after making the necessary corrections. The monks living on the other side of the Ganges river also did the same at the Tissamahāvihāra monastery. Among the monks who arrived and assembled on these two occasions, those who had taken up a meditation subject and departed even before the commencement of the rains-retreat (vassūpanāyikā) and returned to report their attainment of extraordinary Dhamma—it is in reference to such monks that it was said, 'Venerable Sir... those who first entered the rains-retreat,' and so on.

'Manobhāvanīya' refers to those who are to be developed by the mind, or those who are praiseworthy. Alternatively, it means those who develop their own minds, make them flourish, and wash away (abandon) the dust of passion and so forth. An Elder who is perfect in his duties, upon seeing a senior monk, does not remain still but goes out to welcome him, takes the umbrella, bowl, and robes from his hand, brushes off the couch, and offers it. He performs major and minor duties for the monk sitting on that couch and prepares the sleeping place in the monastery. Even upon seeing a new monk, he does not remain silent and seated but stands nearby and performs the duties. That Elder, desiring not to decline in those duties and practices, speaks thus.

At that time, the Blessed One thought: 'Ānanda is thinking that he will no longer have the opportunity to see the inspiring (manobhāvanīya) monks. I will tell him the place where he can see the inspiring monks; staying in that place, he will have the opportunity to see the inspiring monks without wandering here and there.' Thinking thus, he spoke the words beginning with 'These four...'

In that passage, 'saddhassa' refers to one who has a mind of faith in the Buddha and so on, and who is perfect in his duties; such a person is seen performing all duties, starting from the duties of the stupa courtyard in the morning. 'Dassanīyāni' means places worthy of being seen, places that should be visited for the purpose of seeing. 'Saṃvejanīyāni' means places that arouse spiritual urgency (saṃvega). 'Ṭhānāni' means causes, or locations and places.

This statement 'Ye hi keci' was spoken to show the benefit of wandering to the stupa courtyards. In that passage, 'cetiyacārikaṃ āhiṇḍantā' refers to those who wander about performing tasks such as sweeping the stupa courtyard, washing the seating areas, and pouring water on the Bodhi tree in various places; there is no need to even speak of them. It is shown that even those who set out thinking, 'I will worship the stupa in another monastery,' and pass away on the way with a mind of faith, will certainly be established in the celestial realm without any danger.
175:
(Monks,) make an effort. 'Appamattā' means to be those who possess unremitting mindfulness in this Dispensation. By making an effort with energy, be 'ātāpino' (those who possess energy that burns away defilements). Without regard for the physical body or for life, having a self that is surrendered and a mind that is directed (towards Nibbāna), so should you dwell.

'Venerable Sir, how [should it be done]?' means how should those wise kings and others conduct (arrange) themselves? 'Venerable Ānanda, how should we arrange the remains of the Blessed One?'—they will surely ask me this; 'What answer should I give to them?' is the meaning of the question. 'Ahatena vatthena' means (it should be wrapped) with new cloth from the Kāsī country. 'Vihatena kappāsena' means (it should be wrapped) with well-beaten (carded) cotton. Because the cloth from Kāsī is too soft, it cannot absorb oil, whereas cotton can. Therefore, He said 'vihatena kappāsena'. 'Āyasāya' refers to (a vessel) made of gold. In this context, the word 'ayasa' is intended to mean gold.

## Thūpārahapuggalavaṇṇanā

Regarding 'Rājā cakkavattī' (a wheel-turning monarch), why did the Blessed One allow that a stupa be built for a king who lived in the household life and passed away, but not for a virtuous worldling (puthujjana) monk? It is because it would not be a marvel. If permission were given to build stupas for worldling monks, there would be no space left for stupas even in the island of Sīhaḷa, and it would be the same in other places. Therefore, considering that 'those stupas would not be a marvel,' He did not grant permission. A wheel-turning monarch appears only as a single individual; therefore, his stupa is a marvel. However, it is indeed appropriate to perform great offerings and honors to a virtuous worldling monk, just as one would for a monk who has attained Parinibbāna.

## Ānanda-acchariyadhamma-vaṇṇanā

'Vihāraṃ' in this context refers to a circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāla) intended as a dwelling; having entered that dwelling. 'Kapisīsaṃ' is the door-bolt at the top of the doorpost. Regarding 'stood weeping,' it is heard that the Venerable One thought thus: "The Blessed One has told me of a place of residence that is awe-inspiring; He has spoken of the benefits of visiting stupas; He has answered the problem of how to behave towards women; He has instructed on the arrangements for His remains; and He has also spoken of the four persons worthy of a stupa. Today, the Blessed One will surely attain Parinibbāna." While thinking so, intense grief (domanassa) arose in the Venerable Ānanda. Then, this thought occurred to him: "It is not appropriate (not pleasant) to weep in the presence of the Blessed One; in a certain place..."
176: "I shall go and make my sorrow diminish," he thought, and did so. Intending that matter, it is said, "standing and weeping."## "Ahañca vatamhi" means "And I indeed." There is also a variant reading "Ahaṃ vatamhi." "Yo mama anukampako" means "He who has compassion for me, who admonishes and instructs me." He lamented greatly: "From now on, for whom shall I provide water for washing the face? Whose feet shall I wash? Whose cell shall I attend to? Whose bowl and robes shall I carry while wandering?" "Āmanteisi" means the Buddha called the Elder because he did not see him in the midst of the Saṅgha.## "Mettena kāyakammena" means by bodily acts such as providing water for washing the face, which arise by the power of a mind of loving-kindness. "Hitena" means performed for the increase of welfare and benefit. "Sukhena" means performed only with happiness and joy, not with suffering or a bad mind. "Adwayena" means performed without dividing into two parts. Some people perform acts only in one's presence but not in one's absence; some perform only in one's absence but not in one's presence; it means performed without such distinction. "Appamāṇena" means immeasurable. Even the universe is very narrow, even the highest plane of existence (bhavagga) is very low; he showed that "only the bodily acts you have performed are truly vast."## "Mettena vacīkammena" means by verbal acts such as announcing the time for washing the face, which arise by the power of a mind of loving-kindness. Furthermore, the words spoken after receiving an instruction, saying "Very well, Venerable Sir," are also verbal acts associated with loving-kindness. "Mettena manokammena" means by mental acts that arise when, after attending to the physical needs early on, one sits in a secluded place and thinks, "May the Blessed One be free from illness, free from suffering, and be happy." "Katapuññosi"—he showed that "you are one who is endowed with the aspiration for the Perfections (pāramī) for a hundred thousand aeons." Do not remain complacent with just these words "Katapuññosi," do not be negligent; strive only in the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). If you strive thus, you will soon become an Arahat free from taints; you will reach the fruit of Arahatship at the time of the Dhamma Council (Saṅgāyanā). He showed that there is no such thing as service rendered to a Buddha like himself being without fruit.## Having spoken thus, as if spreading out the great earth, as if expanding the sky, as if humbling the Mount Cakkavāḷa, as if lifting Mount Meru, as if taking the great Jambu tree by its trunk and shaking it, the Blessed One addressed the monks to begin proclaiming the virtues of the Venerable Ānanda. In those words—
177: Why did he not say the words, "Monks, at this time also..."? It is because there is no other Buddha. By these words, it should be understood that "there is no other Buddha even in the intervals between universes." "Paṇḍito" means one who is wise and skilled. "Medhāvī" means one who possesses wholesome wisdom regarding the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), and so forth.## "Bhikkhuparisā Ānandaṃ dassanāya" refers to those who approach the Elder wishing to see the Blessed One, and those who come having heard of the Elder's reputation, thinking, "Venerable Ānanda is inspiring in every way; he is handsome, pleasant to behold, very learned, and an ornament to the Saṅgha." Thus it is said, "The assembly of monks approaches to see Ānanda." This should be understood in the same way in all instances. "Attamanā" means they are delighted and joyful in their minds because the reputation they heard matches what they see. "Dhammaṃ" refers to the welcoming and greeting words of Dhamma such as, "Friend, are you healthy? Are you keeping well? Do you perform your duties with proper reflection? Do you fulfill the major and minor duties towards your teachers and preceptors?" In those words, saying to the bhikkhunīs, "Sisters, do you undertake and practice the eight Garudhammas?" is also a special feature. When laymen (upāsakas) come, he does not make greetings such as, "Layman, do you have pain in your head or limbs? Are your sons and brothers healthy?" He only does this: "Laymen, how do you observe the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts? Do you keep the Uposatha eight days a month? Do you fulfill the duty of serving your parents? Do you attend to the recluses and brahmins who live according to the Dhamma?" He greets them thus. It is the same for the laywomen (upāsikās).## Now, wishing to compare the Venerable Ānanda with a Universal Monarch, he spoke the words beginning with "Cattārome bhikkhave." In those words, "Khattiyā" refers to consecrated kings and those of the royal lineage who are not yet consecrated. Those kings, having heard the reputation of the Universal Monarch, thinking, "The Universal Monarch is handsome, pleasant to behold, inspiring, and is a righteous king who rules righteously, traveling through the sky," are delighted, thinking, "What was heard and what is seen are the same." "Bhāsati" means when he speaks—he makes greetings such as, "Friends, how do you fulfill the royal duties? Do you observe the ancestral traditions?" To the brahmins, however, he greets: "Teachers, how do you teach the mantras? How do the students learn the mantras? Do you receive offerings, or clothing, or cows?" To the wealthy merchants: "Friends, is there any oppression against you from the royalty, either by punishment or by taxation?"
178:
“The rain falls well; the crops are flourishing,” in this way he performs the hospitality (towards the people). To the monks, he performs hospitality thus: “Venerable sirs, how easily are the requisites of a monk obtained? Do not be negligent in the Dhamma of a monk.”

## Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta

“Khuddakanagarake” means a small town, a narrow little town. “Ujjaṅgalanagarake” means an uneven or rugged small town. “Sākhānagarake” means small towns that are like the branches of trees, just as branches are small; similarly, they are small towns that are like branches of other great cities (mahānagara). “Khattiyamahāsālā” refers to the great nobles of the Khattiya clan who have attained the status of Khattiyamahāsāla. This method should be understood in all instances.

Among them, a Khattiyamahāsāla is one who has buried wealth amounting to one hundred or one thousand crores, and while one cartload of kahāpaṇas goes out as daily expenses, two cartloads return (as income) in the evening. A Brāhmaṇamahāsāla is one who has buried wealth amounting to eighty crores, and while one jar of kahāpaṇas goes out as daily expenses, one cartload returns in the evening. A Gahapatimahāsāla is one who has buried wealth amounting to forty crores, and while five measures (ambaṇa) of kahāpaṇas go out as daily expenses, one jar returns in the evening.

“Mā hevaṃ, Ānanda, avaca” means: Ānanda, do not say so; this city should not be called a “small town.” The Buddha, to describe the prosperity and abundance of this city, said, “I have come to this place with great effort and great energy, standing and sitting many times,” and then spoke the words beginning with “Bhūtapubbaṃ.” “Subhikkhā” means being endowed with plenty of food and provisions. “Hatthisaddena” means that if one elephant makes a sound, eighty-four thousand elephants join in; thus, it was not silent of the sound of elephants. It was the same with the sound of horses. In that city, meritorious (puññavanta) beings would travel along the main roads, following one another in chariots drawn by four Sindh horses; thus, it was not silent of the sound of chariots. In that city, musical instruments such as drums were constantly played; thus, it was also not silent of the sounds of drums and so on. Therein, “sammassaddo” is the sound of cymbals. “Pāṇitāḷassaddo” is the sound of the square-shaped ambaṇa drum played with the palms. Some also call it “kuṭabherisaddo” (pot-drum sound).
179:
“Asnātha pivatha khādatha” means the sense of “Eat, drink, and chew.” In brief, the city was constantly noisy with this tenth sound, “Eat!” In other cities, sounds such as “Discard the rubbish, take the hoe, take the basket, let us go on a journey, take the bag of rice, take the parcel of food, prepare the wooden weapons, etc.” occur; He shows that in this city, it was not so.

After saying “with the tenth sound,” He concluded the entire Mahāsudassana Sutta with “Ānanda, the royal capital of Kusāvatī was surrounded by seven walls,” and then spoke the words beginning with “Ānanda, you go.” Therein, “abhikkamatha” means approach forward, come here. Did those Malla princes not know that the Blessed One had arrived? They did know. In the place where Buddhas arrive, a great clamor always occurs; however, they could not come because they were seated due to some business to be performed. Intending that “those Malla princes will come and arrange places for the community of monks to stand and sit,” the Blessed One sent (Ānanda) even though it was an unseasonable time.

## Commentary on the Salutation of the Mallas

In “amhākañca no,” the word “no” is merely a particle (nipāta). “Aghāvino” means those who have reached suffering and distress. “Dummanā” means those who are unhappy. “Cetodukkhasamappitā” means those filled with mental distress. “Kulaparivattaso kulaparivattaso ṭhapetvā” means placing them separately, household by household, according to the streets and lanes.

## Commentary on the Story of Subhadda the Wanderer

“Subhaddo nāma paribbājako” refers to a wanderer who went forth from a noble Brāhmaṇamahāsāla family. “Kaṅkhādhammo” means one who has a nature of doubt and uncertainty. Why did he have such (doubt) today? It was because he possessed such a supporting condition (upanissaya). In the past, during the time of performing merit, there were two brothers. They cultivated crops together. Among them, the elder brother had the thought: “When I plant crops once, I will donate the first-fruits (aggadāna) nine times.” At the time of sowing seeds, he donated the first-fruits of the seeds; at the time of the crops being in the bud stage, with the younger brother...
180:
While the two brothers were consulting, the younger brother said, “While it is in the bud stage, let us break open the bud and show it.” The elder brother said, “Do you wish to destroy the young paddy plants?” The elder brother, knowing the younger brother's lack of compliance, divided the field and, from his own portion, broke open the paddy buds, extracted the milky sap, mixed it with ghee and cream, and donated it. At the time of making the first-cakes (puthuka), he made the first-cakes and donated them. At the time of harvest, he donated the first-fruits of the harvest; at the time of binding the sheaves, the first-fruits of the sheaves; and so on, the first-fruits of the sheaves, the first-fruits of the threshing floor, the first-fruits of the pots on the threshing floor, and the first-fruits of the granary—thus, he donated the first-fruit offerings (aggadāna) nine times in a single crop season. The younger brother, however, donated only after the harvest was completed.

Among them, the elder brother became the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña. When the Blessed One looked to see, “To whom shall I first preach the Dhamma?” He thought, “Aññā Koṇḍañña once donated the first-fruit offerings nine times in a single crop season; I shall preach this most noble Dhamma to him first,” and thus He preached the Dhamma first to him. That Venerable one, together with eighteen crores of Brahmas, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). The younger brother, having remained behind and donated later, arrived just as the Blessed One was about to attain Parinibbāna, thinking, “I wish to see the Blessed One.”

In saying, “Do not trouble the Blessed One,” the Elder (Ānanda) thought, “These outsiders (aññatitthiya) are usually attached only to their own views; the Blessed One would have to preach much to make him give up that view, which would cause physical and mental fatigue; the Blessed One is already naturally fatigued,” and thus he spoke. The wanderer (paribbājaka), thinking, “This monk does not give me permission; one who desires benefit should act with compliance,” complied with the Elder and requested two or three times.

“He heard” means He heard the words spoken while standing at the curtain-door even with His natural ear. Having heard, and because He had come with great effort solely for the benefit of Subhadda, He said, “Enough, Ānanda,” and so on. Therein, “alaṃ” is a particle meaning prohibition. “Aññāpekkho va” means only because of desiring to know. “Abbhanyiṃsu” means they acknowledged according to their own claims. This means: if their claim were the way to liberation from defilements, all would know; if not, they would not know. Therefore, whether their claim is the way to liberation or not...
181:
This is indeed the meaning of that problem. At that time, the Blessed One, because there was no benefit in speaking about their doctrines not being the way to liberation from defilements, and because there was no opportunity, prohibited it with “alaṃ” and preached only the Dhamma. The Blessed One had come with the intention: having preached the Dhamma to the Malla princes in the first watch, to Subhadda in the middle watch, and having given exhortation to the community of monks in the last watch, He would attain Parinibbāna at the time of the powerful dawn.

“In that doctrine, a recluse is not found” means that the first recluse, the Stream-enterer, is not there; the second, the Once-returner; the third, the Non-returner; and the fourth, the Arahant, are also not there. Although He spoke indefinitely (aniyama) in the previous discourse as “only in this Dispensation,” He now spoke specifically defining His own Dispensation. “Other doctrines are empty of recluses” means that other doctrines are empty and void of the twelve types of recluses, namely: the four individuals practicing for the sake of the four paths, the four individuals established in the paths, and the four individuals established in the fruits. “Subhadda, these monks” refers to these twelve types of monks. In “if they should practice well,” a Stream-enterer who preaches the Dhamma he has attained to another and makes that person a Stream-enterer is said to “practice well.” The same method applies to the Once-returner and so on. One established in the path of Stream-entry who makes another established in the path of Stream-entry is said to “practice well.” The same applies to those established in the remaining paths. One practicing Vipassanā for the sake of the path of Stream-entry who preaches the meditation subject he is proficient in and makes another a practitioner of Vipassanā is said to “practice well.” The same applies to other practitioners of Vipassanā. With this point in mind, He said, “if they should practice well.” “The world would not be empty of Arahants” means it will continuously exist with Arahants, like a forest of reeds or a forest of Sal trees.

“At the age of twenty-nine” means when he was twenty-nine years old. In “that renunciation,” the word “yaṃ” is merely a particle. “Searching for what is wholesome” means searching continuously for “What is wholesome?” Therein, “What is wholesome?” refers to Omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa); it means searching for that knowledge. “Since I went forth” means He showed that from the time He went forth, more than fifty years have passed within this period. “In the way of the Dhamma” means in the Noble Path (ariyamagga). “One practicing partially” refers to one practicing the path of Vipassanā. “Outside this Dispensation” means outside of My Dispensation.
182:
“Samaṇopi natthi” (There is no recluse) means that there is not even a person with partial Vipassanā, nor even a Sotāpanna, who is the first recluse.

“Ye ettha” (Those who are here) means: You who have received the consecration of discipleship in the presence of the Blessed One in this Dispensation have gained a great gain; you have gained a good gain. In external dispensations, if a teacher says to a disciple, “Ordain this person, discipline this person, give instruction to this person,” it is said that the disciple is placed in the teacher's own position. Therefore, for such a person, these gains of “Ordain this person, discipline this person, give instruction to this person” occur. The wandering ascetic Subhadda, following the custom of those external dispensations, spoke in this manner to the Venerable Ānanda.

“Alattha kho” (He indeed received) means: How did he receive it? The Elder took the wandering ascetic Subhadda to a certain place, moistened his head with water from a water-pot, taught him the meditation on the five parts ending in the skin (tacapañcaka-kammaṭṭhāna), had his hair and beard shaved, clothed him in saffron-dyed robes, gave him the refuges, and then brought him to the Blessed One. The Blessed One granted him full ordination and taught him a subject of meditation. Taking that meditation subject, the bhikkhu Subhadda determined a walking path in a certain part of the garden, and through diligent effort in developing Vipassanā, he attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). He then returned, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down. It is with reference to this that the words beginning with “Acirūpasampanno kho pana” (Not long after his ordination) were spoken.

This bhikkhu Subhadda was the last eye-witness disciple (sakkhisāvaka) of the Blessed One—this is the statement of the Elders who conducted the Council. In this context, anyone who was ordained while the Blessed One was still alive and later attained Arahantship after taking a meditation subject, or who received full ordination while He was alive and later attained Arahantship, or who took a meditation subject while He was alive and later attained Arahantship—all such persons are called the last eye-witness disciples. As for this bhikkhu Subhadda, he underwent novice ordination, full ordination, and took his meditation subject while the Blessed One was still alive, and thus attained Arahantship.

## The Explanation of the Fifth Recitation Section (Pañcamabhāṇavāravaṇṇanā) Ends.

## The Explanation of the Tathāgata’s Last Words (Tathāgatapacchimavācāvaṇṇanā)

Now, the Blessed One began to give his final exhortation to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. To show this, the words beginning with “Atha kho bhagavā” were spoken. In that passage, “Desito paññatto” (taught and prescribed) means the Dhamma that has been taught...
183:
...the Dhamma I have taught and the Vinaya I have prescribed (shall be your teacher). 'Prescribed' has the meaning of being established and made permanent. 'That Dhamma and Vinaya shall be your teacher after my passing' means that the Dhamma and Vinaya will act as the teacher for you after the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna. While I was still alive, I taught the Vinaya consisting of the two Vibhaṅgas, together with the Khandhaka and Parivāra, based on the cases that arose through the seven classes of offenses (āpatti), such as: 'This is a light offense, this is a heavy offense, this is a curable offense, this is an incurable offense, this is a worldly fault (lokavajja), this is a fault by prescription (paṇṇattivajja), this offense is to be cleared before an individual, this offense is to be cleared before a group, this offense is to be cleared before the Saṅgha.' All that Vinaya Piṭaka will perform the duty of the teacher for you after my Parinibbāna.

While I was still alive, I analyzed and taught the Suttanta Piṭaka in various ways, such as: 'These are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.' All that Suttanta Piṭaka will perform the duty of the teacher for you after my Parinibbāna. While I was still alive, I analyzed and taught the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, adorned with the infinite methods of the twenty-four conditions of the Mahāpaṭṭhāna, such as: 'These are the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the four truths, the twenty-two faculties, the nine roots, the four nutriments, the seven contacts, the seven feelings, the seven perceptions, the seven volitions, and the seven consciousnesses'; and further, 'This many dhammas are of the sense sphere, this many are of the fine-material sphere, this many are of the immaterial sphere, this many are included (pariyāpanna), this many are unincluded (apariyāpanna), this many are mundane, and this many are supramundane.' All that Abhidhamma Piṭaka will perform the duty of the teacher for you after my Parinibbāna.

Thus, the words spoken during the forty-five years from the time of becoming a Buddha until Parinibbāna are manifold, consisting of the three Piṭakas, the five Nikāyas, the nine Angas, and the eighty-four thousand Dhamma-groups (dhammakkhandha). Though I alone shall attain Parinibbāna, these eighty-four thousand Dhamma-groups will remain. Now, I alone give you exhortation; after my Parinibbāna, these eighty-four thousand Dhamma-groups will exhort you. Thus, the Blessed One, showing many reasons, gave the exhortation: 'That Dhamma and Vinaya shall be your teacher after my passing.' Then, wishing to show the proper conduct for the future, He spoke the words beginning with “Yathā kho pana”.
185:
The matter concerning the Brahma-punishment (brahmadaṇḍa) has already been decided in the Samantapāsādikā, as it also appears in the Saṅgīti Sutta.

'Kaṅkhā' means being in two minds (doubt). 'Vimati' means the inability to decide. If doubt should arise in anyone as to whether it is the Buddha or not, the Dhamma or not, the Saṅgha or not, the Path or not, or the practice or not, the Blessed One said, “Bhikkhus, ask!” This is the summary of the meaning here. “Do not remain silent merely out of respect for the Teacher” means: We entered the Buddha's Dispensation under the Teacher; the four requisites we have are also those obtained from the Teacher; we have been without doubt for so long, it is not proper to have doubt now at the final moment—do not remain silent without asking due to such respect for the Teacher. “Bhikkhus, let a friend tell a friend” means: Whichever bhikkhu among you is intimate and dear to another, let that bhikkhu tell the other; I will teach that bhikkhu, and by hearing his words, all will be free from doubt. This is what He showed.

“Thus I am clear (pasanno)” means: I believe in this way. “Only knowledge” (ñāṇameva) means it is only the knowledge that realizes the state of being free from doubt; here, it means it is not merely faith (saddhā) in the Tathāgata. “Of these” refers to the five hundred bhikkhus staying in this inner chamber. “He who is the last” means the one who is last in terms of spiritual qualities. This was said with reference to the Venerable Ānanda.

“Strive with diligence (appamādena sampādetha)” means: Accomplish all tasks by not being separated from mindfulness. Thus, the Blessed One, while lying on the couch of the Parinibbāna, condensed all the exhortations He had given for forty-five years into this single word 'appamāda' and delivered it. “These are the last words of the Tathāgata” is the statement of the Elders who conducted the Council (saṅgītikāraka).

## The Explanation of the Account of the Passing (Parinibbutakathāvaṇṇanā)

After this, to show the beginning of the process of attaining Parinibbāna and the manner of the passing, the words beginning with “Atha kho bhagavā paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ” were spoken. Therein, the question “Venerable sir, has the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna?” was asked upon seeing the absence of in-breaths and out-breaths of the Blessed One who had entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). How did the Elder know, “Not yet, friend”? The Elder, entering those various attainments along with the Blessed One, followed Him until He emerged from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), and now...
186: ...the Blessed One entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti); the Elder knew that there is no such thing as passing away (kālaṅkiriyā) within the attainment of cessation. Then, the Blessed One, having emerged from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, entered the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception ...pe... emerged from the third jhāna and entered the fourth jhāna. At this point, the Blessed One entered the first jhāna in 24 instances; the second jhāna in 13 instances; likewise the third jhāna; and the fourth jhāna in 15 instances. To explain: He entered the first jhāna in these 24 instances—the 10 foulness (asubha), the 32 parts of the body, the 8 kasinas, loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, mindfulness of breathing, and limited space. Excluding the 32 parts of the body and the 10 foulness, He entered the second jhāna in the remaining 13 instances; He entered the third jhāna in those same instances. He entered the fourth jhāna in these 15 instances—the 8 kasinas, the divine abode of equanimity, mindfulness of breathing, limited space, and the 4 immaterial states. This is just a summary. The Lord of Dhamma, entering the city of Nibbāna, entered all the attainments numbering two hundred and forty thousand koṭis, and just as a person going to another place embraces his relatives, He experienced all the bliss of the attainments and then entered Nibbāna. In the statement that the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna immediately after emerging from the fourth jhāna, there are two types of 'immediacy': immediacy of jhāna (jhānasamanantara) and immediacy of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇasamanantara). Among them, the passing away of one who emerges from jhāna and descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), occurring within that very life-continuum, is called 'immediacy of jhāna'. The passing away of one who emerges from jhāna, reviews the jhāna factors, and then descends into the life-continuum, occurring within that very life-continuum, is called 'immediacy of reviewing'. Both of these are types of immediacy. As for the Blessed One, He entered jhāna, emerged from it, reviewed the jhāna factors, and then attained Parinibbāna with the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta), which is indeterminate (abyākata) and the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca). Any Buddha, Paccekabuddha, or Noble Disciple, and indeed all beings down to the smallest ants, pass away only with the life-continuum mind which is indeterminate and the truth of suffering. The shaking of the great earth and so on occurred exactly as previously described. 'Bhūtā' means beings. 'Appaṭipuggalo' means the peerless person. 'Balappatto' means the one who has attained the ten powers of knowledge.
187: 'Uppādavayadhammino' means having the nature of arising and passing away. 'Tesaṃ vūpasamo' means the stilling of those conditioned formations; it implies that only the unconditioned Nibbāna is true bliss. 'Nāhu assāsapassāso' means the cessation of inhalation and exhalation. 'Anejo' is so called because of the absence of the agitation (ejā) known as craving. 'Santimārabbha' means by taking as the object, or referring to, the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbāna). 'Yaṃ kālamakari' means the person who has passed away. The meaning is: 'O friends, my teacher the Buddha Sage, aiming for the state of peace, has passed away; for that Noble One of steady mind, there is now no inhalation or exhalation, it is no more, it does not arise.' 'Asallīnena' means with a mind that is not shrinking, not contracted, but well-blossomed. 'Vedanaṃ ajjhavāsayi' means he endured the feeling; he endured it without rolling to and fro according to the dictates of the feeling. 'Vimokkho' means liberation unobstructed by any phenomena; the state of not reaching any designation, which is like the extinguishing of a lamp. 'Tadāsi' refers to the earthquake mentioned below as 'Saha parinibbānā mahābhūmicālo'. That earthquake was hair-raising and terrifying. 'Sabbākāravarūpete' means endowed with all noble attributes. 'Avītarāgā' refers to worldlings (puthujjanas), Stream-enterers (sotāpannas), and Once-returners (sakadāgāmis). They have not yet abandoned grief (domanassa). Therefore, they also weep with their arms raised. They weep with both hands placed upon their heads; all this should be understood according to the previous method. 'Ujjhāyanti' means they complained and criticized, saying, 'The noble ones themselves cannot endure it; how can they make others find relief?' 'Venerable sir, how does the Venerable Anuruddha perceive the devas?' is a question asking, 'Venerable sir, how does the Venerable Anuruddha note the devas? Can those devas endure the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One?' 'Atha tāsaṃ pavattidassanatthaṃ' means then, to show the state of those devas, the Elder spoke the words beginning with 'Santāvuso'. That speech has the same meaning as already stated. 'Rattāvasesaṃ' means because he attained Parinibbāna in the late watch of the night, the remaining small portion of the night...
188: ...refers to the small amount of time remaining. 'With Dhamma talk' does not mean a specific separate sermon, but rather they spent the time with talk related to death, such as: 'Friends, even the peerless Buddha in the world with its devas is not spared by this King of Death; how then would he be ashamed of the common people?' While they were speaking thus, dawn broke in an instant. Seeing the dawn, the Elder said to the other elder: 'With that duty to be done' refers to the duties to be performed upon hearing that the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, such as what kind of offerings with flowers and scents should be made at the site of Parinibbāna, how the place for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha should be, and how the food and provisions should be. ## Description of the Worship of the Buddha's Body (Buddhasarīrapūjāvaṇṇanā) 'All musical instruments' means all various kinds of musical instruments. 'Assemble' means to cause them to gather by beating drums. They did exactly as instructed. 'In the pavilion' means in a pavilion decorated with clothes and ornaments. 'Preparing' means arranging. 'By the south to the south' means through the southern part of the city towards the southern direction. 'By the outside to the outside' means carrying it along the outskirts of the city without entering the city center. 'To the south of the city' means placing it at a location similar to the South Gate of Anurādhapura, and after performing the offerings, it implies they would cremate the body at a location similar to the Jetavana Monastery. 'Eight Malla princes' refers to eight Malla princes of middle age who were endowed with strength. 'Having washed their heads' means those who have bathed and washed their heads. 'To the Venerable Anuruddha' means that because the Elder was famous for possessing the Divine Eye (dibba-cakkhu), they planned and asked him even though other senior elders were present, thinking, 'This Elder will explain it clearly to us.' When they asked, 'Venerable sir, what is the wish of the devas?', they were asking, 'Venerable sir, we know our own wish, but what is the wish of the devas?' The Elder, wishing to show their own wish first, spoke starting with 'Your wish is...'. 'The Malla princes' shrine named Makuṭabandhana' is the name of the festive hall for ornamentation of the Malla princes. Because it was a place of reverence and respect, it is called a 'shrine' (cetiya).
189: In the passage 'between houses, sewers, and rubbish heaps,' 'sandhi' means the space between houses. 'Samala' refers to dung heaps and drainage sewers. 'Saṅkaṭīra' means rubbish heaps. 'With the dances of devas and the dances of humans' means there were dances of devas above and dances of humans below. The same applies to singing and other performances. Furthermore, humans among devas and devas among humans moved along mixed together while performing offerings and worship. 'While carrying through the center of the city'—while the body of the Blessed One was being carried, a lady named Mallikā, the wife of General Bandhula, heard that the Blessed One's body was being brought. She had the Mahālatā ornament, similar to Visākhā's, which she had kept without wearing since her husband's death, brought out. Thinking, 'I shall worship the Blessed One with this ornament,' she had it cleaned, washed with scented water, and stood at the doorway. It is said that this ornament had existed only in three places: with those two women and in the house of the thief Devadāniya. When the Blessed One's body reached the doorway, she said, 'Sirs, please set the Blessed One's body down for a moment,' and she adorned and worshipped the Blessed One's body with that ornament. When the ornament was draped starting from the head, it reached down to the soles of the feet. The golden-hued body of the Blessed One became exceedingly brilliant when adorned with the Mahālatā ornament made of the seven kinds of jewels. Seeing this, with a mind full of faith, she made a wish: 'Lord, for as long as I wander in Saṃsāra, may my body be as if always adorned without needing separate ornaments.' Then, they carried the Blessed One's body along with the seven-jeweled Mahālatā ornament, exited through the East Gate, and placed the Blessed One's body at the Makuṭabandhana Cetiya of the Mallas to the east of the city. ## Description of the Story of the Venerable Mahākassapa (Mahākassapattheravatthuvaṇṇanā) 'From Pāvā to Kusinārā' means being on the road with the intention 'I shall go to Kusinārā' after having finished the alms-round in the city of Pāvā. In the phrase 'sat at the foot of a tree,' why is it not called 'day-rest' (divāvihāra)? Because he did not sit with the purpose of day-rest. The Elder's retinue of monks had grown up in comfort and possessed great merit. They were exhausted from walking barefoot at noon on the ground which was like a hot stone slab. When the Elder saw those monks, he thought: 'The monks are tired, and the destination is not far; let them rest for a moment to relieve their fatigue, and in the evening we shall go to Kusinārā to pay homage to the Blessed One, the Possessor of Ten Powers.'
190:
Stepping off the path, he spread his double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) at the foot of a certain tree, cooled his hands and feet with water from a water-pot, and sat down. The attendant monks also sat at the feet of trees, engaging in meditation with proper attention (yoniso manasikāra) and discussing the virtues of the Triple Gem. Because they sat for the purpose of dispelling fatigue, it is not called "day-rest" (divāvihāra).

Regarding "mandāravapupphaṃ gahetvā": it means he came holding a flower the size of a large tray, placed on a split stick, carrying it like an umbrella. "Addasa kho": he saw that person coming from afar. Having seen him, he reflected: "A Mandārava flower is clearly visible in the hand of this Ājīvaka. This flower does not always appear on the paths of men. It appears when a person of psychic power performs a miracle, or at the descent of the Omniscient Bodhisatta into his mother's womb, and so on. Today, however, no one has performed a miracle. My Teacher, the Buddha, has not descended into a womb, nor was He born from a womb, nor did He attain Buddhahood today, nor did He preach the Dhammacakka, nor did He perform the Twin Miracle, nor did He descend from the celestial realm, nor did He relinquish the life-force. My Teacher, the Buddha, being advanced in years, must surely have attained Parinibbāna."

Then, he formed the intention: "I will ask that man." Thinking, "If I ask while sitting, it would be disrespectful to my Teacher, the Buddha," he rose from his seat. Just as the Chaddanta elephant king wraps himself in his ruby-colored hide, he donned the cloud-colored rag-robe (paṃsukūla) given by the Buddha. Placing his joined palms (añjali) to his forehead, out of respect for the Buddha, he faced the Ājīvaka and asked: "Friend, do you know our Teacher, the Buddha?"

Why did he ask, knowing the Buddha's Parinibbāna, or did he ask without knowing? Some say that the knowledge of Arahants is connected with reflection (āvajjana), and because he did not reflect, he asked without knowing. The Elder was one who frequently dwelt in attainments (samāpatti). Whether in his night-quarters, day-quarters, caves, or pavilions, he always sustained himself through the power of attainment. Entering the village of his supporters, he would enter attainment at the doorway and only upon emerging would he accept alms-food. The Elder thought: "In this final existence, I shall benefit the people. May those who offer me alms-food or worship with scents and flowers receive great merit."
191:
He acted thus. Therefore, some say he did not know because of his frequent entry into attainments. That statement, "He asked while not knowing," should not be accepted.

There is no reason for him not to know. The Buddha's Parinibbāna was made manifest by signs such as the shaking of the ten thousand world systems. Among the followers of Venerable Mahākassapa, some monks had seen the Buddha, while others had not. Among them, those who had seen Him wished to see Him again, and those who had not seen Him also wished to see Him. Among those who had not seen Him, because of their intense desire to see Him, if they were to hear "He has attained Parinibbāna" while traveling and asking "Where is the Buddha?", they would not be able to restrain themselves. They would cast away their robes and bowls and, clad in a single garment or improperly dressed, they would beat their breasts and weep. Then people would see my fault, saying, "These rag-robe-wearing monks who travel with Venerable Mahākassapa are weeping like women; how can they bring us solace?" This place is a secluded forest; even if they weep here, there is no fault. Thinking, "Hearing the news in advance can lessen grief," he asked despite knowing, in order to instill spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in the monks.

"Ajja sattāhaparinibbuto samaṇo gotamo": this means it has been seven days today since the Ascetic Gotama attained Parinibbāna. "Tato me idaṃ": this means I obtained this flower from the place where the Ascetic Gotama attained Parinibbāna.

"Subhaddo nāma vuḍဎပဗ္ဗဇိတော": "Subhadda" was his name. Because he went forth as a monk in his old age, he is called "vuḍḍhapabbajita" (one who went forth when old). Why did he speak thus? It was because of his grudge against the Buddha. It is said that this man was the former barber, an old man in robes, mentioned in the Ātumā story of the Khandhaka. When the Buddha left Kusinārā and was traveling to the city of Ātumā with twelve hundred and fifty monks, hearing that the Buddha was coming, he thought, "I will offer rice-gruel (yāgu) when He arrives." He told his two sons, who were novices: "Dear sons, the Buddha is coming to Ātumā with a Saṅgha of twelve hundred and fifty monks. Dear sons, take your barber's tools, go from house to house, and ask for salt, oil, rice, and snacks."
192:
"We shall offer rice-gruel to the arriving Buddha; collect firewood and so on," he said. They did as they were told.

When people saw those pleasant and well-spoken boys, they made offerings whether they intended to or not. After making the offerings, they asked, "Dear sons, what would you like to take?" The boys replied, "We have no need for anything else; our father wishes to offer rice-gruel when the Buddha arrives." Hearing this, the people gave everything they could carry without limit. What they could not carry themselves, they had others deliver.

Then, when the Buddha arrived at Ātumā and stayed in the chaff-house (thusa-koṭṭhāgāra), Subhadda went to the village gate in the evening and invited the people, saying, "Lay devotees, I expect nothing else from you; the rice and other items my sons have brought are sufficient for the Saṅgha. Just give me your manual labor." Saying, "Take this, take that," he had all the supplies brought and had stoves built in the monastery. Wearing a dark, dye-colored cloth and wrapping himself in the same, he spent the whole night directing them, saying, "Do this, do that." Spending a hundred thousand (kahāpaṇas), he had delicious rice-gruel and honey-lumps prepared. What is called "bhojjayāgu" is a type of gruel that is both eaten and drunk; in that gruel, all kinds of delicacies such as ghee, honey, molasses, fish, meat, flowers, and fruit juices were added. It had such a fragrant scent that it was fit to be rubbed on the heads of those who like to play.

Then, in the early morning, the Buddha performed His personal duties and, surrounded by the community of monks, headed towards the city of Ātumā for alms. People said to Subhadda, "The Buddha has entered the village for alms; for whom have you prepared the rice-gruel?" Still wearing those dark, dye-colored clothes, holding a ladle and a spoon in one hand, he knelt with his right knee on the ground like a Brahmā, paid homage, and said, "Lord, please accept my rice-gruel."

Then, following the method in the Khandhaka where "Tathāgatas ask even though they know," the Buddha questioned him. Having heard the full account, He rebuked the one who went forth in old age. Because of that incident, He prescribed two training rules: the rule on improper acceptance (akappiya-samādāna) and the rule on carrying barber's tools (khurabhaṇḍa-pariharaṇa), saying, "Monks, for incalculable tens of millions of aeons, alms-food..."
193:
...'You have spent your time only in searching; this food of yours is unallowable (akappiya) food obtained through unrighteous means. Those who consume this food will be reborn only in the lower realms for thousands of existences. Discard it; do not take it,' the Buddha said, and then proceeded toward the alms-round. Not a single monk took anything.

Subhadda, being displeased, thought: 'This man wanders around saying, "I know everything." If he did not want us to take it, he should have sent word to inform us. This cooked food can last at most seven days. This food would have been a lifelong search for me. He has destroyed everything; this man wishes for my misfortune.' Thus, he harbored a grudge against the Buddha, but while the Dasabala Buddha was alive, he could not say anything. It is said that he had this thought: 'This is a Great Man (Mahāpurisa) who renounced from a noble family; if I say anything, he will only threaten me.' It was only today, upon hearing that 'the Buddha has attained Parinibbāna,' that this Subhadda spoke thus, as if finding relief and being greatly delighted.

When the Elder Mahākassapa heard those words, he felt as if his heart were being pierced, or as if a thunderbolt had fallen upon his head. Spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in the Elder Mahākassapa: 'It has been only seven days since the Buddha attained Parinibbāna; even today, his golden-hued body still remains. Yet, in this Sāsana for which the Buddha strove with great hardship, such grave impurities and thorns have appeared so quickly. If this wicked person increases and gains such companions, it is certain that he will cause the Sāsana to decline.' Then the Elder considered thus:

'If I were to make this old man wear rags, sprinkle him with ashes, and expel him right here, people would say, "While the remains of the Monk Gotama are still present, his disciples are already quarreling," and they would blame us. Therefore, I will endure for the time being.'

'The Dhamma taught by the Buddha is like a heap of flowers that has not yet been strung together. Just as flowers are scattered here and there when the wind blows, if time passes according to the wishes of such wicked people, one or two training rules (sikkhāpada) in the Vinaya will disappear; one or two cycles of questions (pucchāvāra) in the Sutta will disappear; one or two levels (bhūmantara) in the Abhidhamma will disappear. If they are uprooted in this order, we shall become like hungry ghosts and demons. Therefore, let us perform a Council (Saṅgāyana) of the Dhamma and Vinaya. If we do this...'
195:
When the people heard those words, they said: 'Friends, the monk named Mahākassapa is coming with five hundred monks, saying, "I will pay homage to the feet of the Dasabala Buddha." It is said that the funeral pyre (citaka) will not burn until that Venerable One arrives. Friends, what is the appearance of that monk? Is he dark or fair? Is he tall or short? While such a monk exists, how could the Parinibbāna of the Dasabala Buddha be possible?' Thus, some went to meet him on the way, carrying scented flowers and other offerings. Others decorated the roads and stood watching the path he would come.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa arrived at Kusinārā... and paid homage (to the Buddha's feet) with his head. The Elder circumambulated the pyre to the right and reflected: 'The head is here; the feet are here,' marking the positions. Then, standing near the feet, he entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā). Emerging from it, he made a determination (adhiṭṭhāna): 'May the feet of the Dasabala Buddha, adorned with the thousand-spoked wheel marks, emerge through the five hundred layers of cloth, the golden coffin, and the sandalwood pyre, and rest upon my noble head.' Simultaneously with his thought of determination, those five hundred layers of cloth parted, and the feet emerged like the full moon appearing from between the clouds. The Elder stretched out his hands, which were like newly blossomed red lotuses, and firmly took hold of the golden-hued feet of the Buddha up to the ankles, placing them upon his noble head. It is in reference to this event that it is said, 'He paid homage to the Buddha's feet with his head.'

When the multitude saw that miracle, they all simultaneously let out a great roar. They made offerings of scented flowers and paid homage as they desired.
