Thus, once the Elder, the multitude, and those five hundred monks had paid homage, there was no further need for determination. By the power of the original determination, the soles of the Buddha's feet, which had the color of lac-dye, were released from the Elder's hands and returned to their original place without moving the sandalwood fuel or anything else. They remained exactly as they were in the original place. Neither when the Buddha's feet emerged nor when they returned was a single fiber of cotton, a thread of cloth, a drop of oil, or a piece of wood displaced. Everything remained exactly in its original place. When the Buddha's feet disappeared, like the moon or the sun that has emerged and then retreated, the multitude wept with a great lamentation. A compassion (sorrow) greater than that at the time of the Parinibbāna itself arose.
198:
## Commentary on the Distribution of the Bodhisatta's Relics

'The King has heard'—how did he hear? Firstly, the ministers of that King heard (of the Buddha's Parinibbāna) and thought: 'The Buddha has attained Parinibbāna; it is no longer possible to bring that Buddha back. In terms of the faith of a worldling (puthujjana), there is no one equal to our King. If this King hears of this directly, his heart will likely break. We must protect the King.' Thus they planned. Those ministers brought three golden vats, filled them with the four sweet delicacies (catumadhura), and approached the King, saying: 'Great King, we have had a bad dream. To dispel that bad dream, it is proper for the Great King to wear a dukūla cloth and lie in a vat of catumadhura with only the nostrils visible.' When the King heard the words of the ministers who sought his welfare, he agreed, saying, 'Friends, let it be so,' and did as they suggested.

Then a minister removed his ornaments, disheveled his hair, and facing the direction where the Buddha attained Parinibbāna, he raised his joined palms and addressed the King: 'Great King, there is no being who can escape death. That Buddha, who increased our lives, who is the site of the shrine (cetiya), who is the field for planting the seeds of merit, and who cools us as if pouring anointment, has attained Parinibbāna in the city of Kusinārā.' As soon as the King heard this, he lost consciousness and released heat into the vat of catumadhura. Then, they took the King and placed him in the second vat. When the King regained consciousness, he asked, 'Friends, what did you say?' They replied, 'Great King, the Buddha has attained Parinibbāna.' The King again lost consciousness and released heat into the vat of catumadhura. Then, they took the King from that vat and placed him in the third vat. When the King regained consciousness again, he asked again, 'Friends, what did you say?' They replied, 'Great King, the Buddha has attained Parinibbāna.' The King lost consciousness once more, and then they took the King, bathed him, and poured water over his head from jars.

When the King regained consciousness, he rose from his place, disheveled his hair which had the color of rubies and was anointed with scented water, spreading it over his back which had the color of a gold plate. Beating his chest with his palms, clutching his chest with his beautifully rounded fingers that had the color of coral sprouts as if stitching a golden statue, he descended into the middle of the main road, weeping and lamenting like a madman. That King, surrounded by adorned dancers, left the city and went to Jīvaka's Mango Grove, looking at the places where the Buddha had resided and preached the Dhamma—
199:
"The Blessed One is the Possessor of Omniscient Knowledge; did He not reside and preach the Dhamma here? He has removed the dart of my grief; Venerable Sirs, you have extracted the dart of my grief. I have approached you as my refuge, but now, O Blessed One, You do not utter even a single word to me," thus he lamented and wailed repeatedly. "O Blessed One, at other times I have heard, 'May you travel throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa, accompanied by the community of monks.' But now, I have heard news that is improper and unfitting for You," saying such words and recollecting the virtues of the Blessed One through sixty verses, he thought: "My task will not be accomplished merely by lamenting. I shall have the relics of the Blessed One, the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala), brought to me." Thus it is known. Having heard the news, at the end of such events as losing consciousness, he dispatched a messenger. Referring to that matter, it is stated in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta starting with "Atha kho rājā" (Then the King...).

In that passage, "dispatched a messenger" means sending both a messenger and a royal message. After sending them, he thought, "If they give (the relics), it is well. If they do not, I shall bring them by whatever means necessary," and he prepared the fourfold army and set out himself. Just like King Ajātasattu, other kings such as the Licchavī kings also dispatched messengers and set out themselves with their fourfold armies. Among those kings, the people of Pāveyya lived in a city three gāvutas away from Kusinārā, closer than all the other kings; the Blessed One had also entered the city of Pāvā before proceeding to Kusinārā. If it is asked why they did not arrive first? Those kings had a very large retinue, and because they prepared and came with such a massive force, they were delayed.

Those kings addressed the community of monks thus—the inhabitants of those seven cities arrived and surrounded the city of Kusinārā, saying, "Give us the relics, or else we shall wage war." The Mallas of Kusinārā replied, "This Blessed One (attained Parinibbāna) in our village territory." It is heard that they said: "We did not reject the Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Blessed One, nor did we go and bring Him here. The Blessed One came here of His own accord and sent word to summon us. You also would not give us a treasure that appeared in your own village territory. In the world including the devas, there is no treasure equal to the Buddha-treasure; possessing such a noble treasure, we cannot give it up. You are not the only ones who have drunk mother's milk; we too have drunk mother's milk. You are not the only noble men; we too are noble men." Thus, with rising pride, they exchanged royal messages and spoke defiant words. Had war broken out, only the people of Kusinārā would have been victorious. Why? Because—
200:
The devas and brahmas who had arrived to worship the relics were on the side of those kings. In the Pali text, however, it is only stated: "The Blessed One attained Parinibbāna in our village territory; we shall not give a portion of the bodily relics of the Blessed One."

While they were speaking thus, Dona the Brahmin heard the dispute of those kings and thought, "These kings are quarreling at the place where the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna; this is not proper. There is no benefit in this conflict and anger. I shall appease that dispute." He then went to the assembly of kings and spoke these words. How did he speak? Standing on a high place, he spoke the discourse known as the Doṇagajjita (The Thunder of Dona), which is about the length of two bhāṇavāras. Among those words, during the first bhāṇavāra, those kings did not understand even a single word. At the end of the second bhāṇavāra, however, all the kings became silent, saying, "Friends, it is like the voice of our teacher; friends, it is like the voice of our teacher." It is heard that among the well-born men in the entire island of Jambudīpa, there were almost none who were not pupils of that Dona the Brahmin. Then, Dona the Brahmin, knowing that those kings were listening and remaining silent, spoke again: "Friends, listen!" and uttered these two verses:

In those verses, 'amhākaṃ buddho' means 'our Blessed One.' 'ahu khantivādo' means that while fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) before reaching Buddhahood, in the births as Khantivādī the ascetic, Dhammapāla the prince, Chaddanta the elephant king, Bhūridatta the naga king, Campeyya the naga king, Saṅkhapāla the naga king, Mahākapi the monkey king, and many other Jātaka births, He did not get angry at others but practiced only patience. He praised only the virtue of patience. Now, when He has reached the quality of Tādi (steadfastness) regarding desirable and undesirable objects, it goes without saying; in every aspect, our Blessed One was one who habitually preached patience. Of such a Blessed One.

'na hi sādhu yaṃ uttamapuggalassa, sarīrabhāge siyā sampahāro' means that it is not good for a conflict with weapons to arise because of the portion of the bodily relics of the Supreme Person.

'sabbeva bhonto sahitā' means 'Friends, may you all be united, do not be divided.' 'samaggā' means 'being gathered together in body and speech, may you be in harmony with one voice.' 'sammodamānā' means 'may you also be mutually joyful in mind.' 'karomaṭṭhabhāge' means 'let us make eight portions of the bodily relics of the Blessed One.'
201:
'cakkhumato' means 'of the Blessed One who is endowed with the five eyes.' It is not only you who have devotion; many people also have devotion, and among them, there is no one who is not worthy of receiving the relics. Thus, he spoke many reasons and persuaded them convincingly.

'tesaṃ saṅghānaṃ gaṇānaṃ paṭissutvā' means 'having accepted the words of the groups who had arrived from various places.' In the passage 'bhagavato sarīrāni aṭṭhadā samaṃ suvibhattaṃ vibhajitvā', this is the sequence of events: Dona the Brahmin, having accepted the words of those kings, had the golden urn opened. When the kings arrived and saw the golden-hued relics residing within the golden urn, they lamented and wailed, saying: "The Blessed One was the Possessor of Omniscient Knowledge; formerly, we beheld the golden-hued body of the Lord, adorned with the 32 marks of a Great Man, surrounded by the six-colored Buddha-rays, and radiant with the 80 minor marks. Now, only the golden-hued relics remain; O Blessed One, it is not fitting that this has happened."

At that time, the Brahmin, knowing that the kings were heedless, took the sacred right canine tooth and placed it within his turban. After that, he divided the relics into eight equal portions. All the relics amounted to sixteen nāḷis by the standard measure; those who came from each city received two nāḷis each. While the Brahmin was dividing the relics, Sakka, the King of Devas, looked to see: "Who has taken the sacred right canine tooth of the Blessed One, which is the source of the discourse on the Four Noble Truths, for the sake of cutting off the doubts of the world including the devas?" Seeing that "the Brahmin has taken it," he thought: "This Brahmin will not be able to perform the honor and offerings worthy of the sacred canine tooth; I shall take it." He then took it from the turban, placed it in a golden casket, and conveyed it to the realm of the devas to be enshrined and worshipped in the Cūḷāmaṇi Stupa.

The Brahmin, having finished dividing the relics and not finding the canine tooth because it had been taken, was no longer able to ask, "Who took my canine tooth?" Seeing that he would be blamed, with people saying, "Did you not divide the relics yourself? Did you not know from the start whether the relic you were to receive was there or not?", he was no longer able to say, "Give me my share too." Therefore, he thought: "This golden urn is also the place where the relics resided; with this urn, the relics of the Blessed One were measured; I shall make a stupa for this urn," and he said, "Friends, give this urn to me."
202:
The kings of Pipphalivana and the kings of Moriya, like King Ajātasattu and others, also sent messengers and set out prepared for war.

## Description of the Enshrinement and Worship of the Relics

In the city of Rājagaha, the enshrinement of the Buddha's bodily relics and a festival of worship were conducted. How was this carried out? From the city of Kusinārā to the city of Rājagaha, the distance is twenty-five yojanas. Along this path, a level road eight usabhas wide was constructed. Just as the Mallā kings performed offerings between the Makuṭabandhana Cetiya and the Santhāgāra hall, similar offerings were made along this twenty-five yojana journey. To ensure the people did not grow weary, shops were opened at every location. The relics, placed in a golden casket, were surrounded by a protective enclosure of spears, and people from within a five-hundred yojana radius of the kingdom were gathered. Taking those relics, they departed from Kusinārā amidst cheers and acclamations. Wherever they found golden-hued flowers, they would place the relics within the spear-enclosure and perform offerings. Only when those flowers were exhausted would they continue their journey. When the front of the procession reached the position of the rear (having moved by only one carriage-length), they would offer worship with acclamations for seven days. In this manner, the journey to bring the relics lasted seven years, seven months, and seven days.

Those with wrong views (micchādiṭṭhi) grumbled and became angry, saying, "Since the time the ascetic Gotama attained Parinibbāna, all our work has been ruined because we are forced to perform these ceremonies of worship." Consequently, eighty-six thousand of them were reborn in the lower realms (apāya). The noble Arahants, upon reflection, saw that many people were falling into the lower realms due to their anger. They thought, "We shall have Sakka, King of Devas, make arrangements for the conveyance of the relics." They went to Sakka, informed him of the matter, and said, "Great King, please make arrangements for the conveyance of the relics."

Sakka replied, "Venerable sirs, among worldlings (puthujjana), there is no one with faith as great as King Ajātasattu. He will not listen to my words. However, I will display a frightening sign like the intimidation of Māra; I will cause a great sound to be heard, and cause spirit-possession, sneezing, and loss of appetite. At that time, please say to him, 'Great King, the deities and spirits are angry; have the relics conveyed quickly.' If you say this, he will have them conveyed." Subsequently, Sakka performed all those things.

The Great Elders then approached the King and said, "Great King, the deities and spirits are angry; please have the relics conveyed." The King replied, "Venerable sirs, my..."
203:
"...heart is not yet satisfied; nevertheless, let them be conveyed." On the seventh day, the relics were brought. Receiving the relics thus conveyed, the enshrinement in a stupa and the festival of worship were performed in the city of Rājagaha. The remaining kings also took the relics according to their power and performed the enshrinement in stupas and festivals of worship in their respective regions.

"Thus it happened in the past." The Elders who later conducted the Council (Saṅgāyana) stated that this distribution of relics and the establishment of the ten stupas had occurred in the past in Jambudīpa. After the stupas were established, the Venerable Mahākassapa, foreseeing danger to the relics, approached King Ajātasattu and said, "Great King, it is proper to enshrine the relics together in a single place."

"Very well, venerable sir, I shall perform the act of enshrinement. But how shall I bring the remaining relics?" the King asked. "Great King, bringing the relics is not your responsibility; it is only our responsibility," the Elder replied. "Very well, venerable sir, please bring the relics yourselves; I will perform the enshrinement of the relics," the King submitted. The Great Elder brought the remaining relics, leaving only enough for the respective royal families to worship. At Rāmagāma, however, the relics were protected by the Nāgas, so there was no danger to those relics. Knowing that "In the future, they will be enshrined in the Mahāthūpa of the Mahāvihāra monastery on the island of Sīhala," he did not take those relics but brought the relics from the other seven cities. Standing in the southeast of Rājagaha, he made a resolution (adhiṭṭhāna): "May the stones in this place disappear; may the dust be perfectly pure; may water not emerge."

The King had that place excavated, and with the earth that came out, he had bricks made to build stupas for the eighty Great Disciples (Asītimahāsāvaka). To those who asked, "What is the King doing here?" they replied, "He is building stupas for the Great Disciples," so no one knew about the enshrinement of the Buddha's relics. When they reached a depth of eighty cubits, he had copper flooring laid at the bottom. There, he had a copper chamber built, the size of the relic chamber at Thūpārāma, and had caskets and stupas made of eight kinds of materials, such as white sandalwood.

Then, the relics of the Blessed One were placed in a white sandalwood casket, and that white sandalwood casket was placed inside another white sandalwood casket. That casket was again placed inside another. In this way, eight white sandalwood caskets were made into one. Following this same method, those eight caskets were placed inside eight white sandalwood stupas; those eight white sandalwood stupas inside eight red sandalwood caskets; those eight red sandalwood caskets inside eight red sandalwood stupas; those eight red sandalwood stupas inside eight ivory caskets...
204:
...the eight ivory caskets were placed inside eight ivory stupas; those eight ivory stupas inside eight caskets of various jewels; those eight caskets of various jewels inside eight stupas of various jewels; those eight stupas of various jewels inside eight golden caskets; those eight golden caskets inside eight golden stupas; those eight golden stupas inside eight silver caskets; those eight silver caskets inside eight silver stupas; those eight silver stupas inside eight ruby caskets; those eight ruby caskets inside eight ruby stupas; those eight ruby stupas inside eight cat's-eye caskets; those eight cat's-eye caskets inside eight cat's-eye stupas; those eight cat's-eye stupas inside eight crystal caskets; and those eight crystal caskets were placed inside eight crystal stupas. The crystal stupa at the very top was the size of the Thūpārāma Stupa. Above all these, he had a house made of various jewels constructed. Above that, a house made of gold; above that, a house made of silver; and above that, a house made of copper.

In that place, he had sand made of various jewels spread out, and thousands of water-born and land-born flowers scattered. He had the five hundred and fifty Jātaka stories, the eighty Great Disciples, King Suddhodana, Queen Mahāmāyā, and the seven co-natals (sahajāta) crafted entirely of pure gold. He had five hundred vessels each of gold and silver placed there. Five hundred golden banners were erected. He had five hundred golden lamps and five hundred silver lamps made, filled with fragrant oil, and placed wicks made of dukuṭa cloth in those lamps.

At that time, the Venerable Mahākassapa made a resolution: "May the flowers not wither; may the fragrances not perish; may the lamps not be extinguished." He had an inscription carved on a gold plate: "In the future, a prince named Piyadāsa shall raise the white umbrella and become Asoka Dhammarāja. That king shall propagate these relics far and wide." The King offered worship with all forms of offerings, closed the door from the very beginning, and departed. That King closed the copper door and placed the seal of the key on the chain...
205:
(King Ajātasattu, having enshrined the relics,) placed a large heap of rubies at that very spot and had an inscription carved, saying: "In the future, may a poor king take these rubies and perform offerings to the relics."

Sakka, the king of devas, called Vissakamma, the celestial architect, and sent him, saying: "Friend, King Ajātasattu has enshrined the relics; provide protection at this place." Vissakamma came and fashioned mechanical devices in the form of wild beasts. Inside that relic chamber, he arranged wooden mechanical figures that held crystal-colored swords and revolved with the speed of the wind. These were fastened by a single mechanical bolt. The chamber was surrounded by stone slabs resembling a brick house, covered with another stone slab on top, and then covered with dust to make the ground level, upon which a stone stupa was built. When the enshrinement of the relics was thus completed, the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera, having reached the end of his life span, attained Parinibbāna. The Great King also passed away according to his kamma, and those people also died.

In later times, a prince named Piyadāsa, having assumed the white parasol, became the righteous king named Asoka. He took those relics and caused them to be distributed throughout the island of Jambudīpa. How did he do so? That king, having gained faith in the Sāsana through Nigrodha Sāmaṇera, built eighty-four thousand monasteries and asked the Bhikkhu Saṅgha: "Venerable sirs, I have built eighty-four thousand monasteries; from where can I obtain the relics?" The Saṅgha replied: "Great King, we have heard that there was an enshrinement of relics, but we do not know that they are in such and such a place."

The King had the stupa in Rājagaha dismantled, but not finding the relics, he restored it to its original state. Then, taking the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—he went to the city of Vesālī. Not finding them there, he went to Kapilavatthu. Not finding them there, he went to Rāmagāma. At Rāmagāma, the Nāgas did not allow the stupa to be dismantled; the hoes that struck the stupa were broken into pieces. Thus, not finding them there, he dismantled the stupas in all places such as Allakappa, Veṭhadīpa, Pāvā, and Kusinārā, but not finding the relics, he had them restored to their original state. Returning once more to Rājagaha, he assembled the fourfold assembly and asked: "Has anyone heard that the relics were enshrined in such and such a place?"

Then, a certain Elder who was one hundred and twenty years old said: "I do not know that the relics are enshrined in such and such a place. However, when I was seven years old, my father, a Mahāthera, made me carry a flower basket and said, 'Come, Sāmaṇera, between these bushes...'" (and he used to take me there).
206:
"There is a stone stupa; let us go to that place," he said, and after going there and making offerings, he said, "Sāmaṇera, it is proper to investigate this place." The Elder (who was then a Sāmaṇera) said, "Great King, I only know this much." The King, saying "This is the very place," had the bushes cleared, and after removing the stone stupa and the dust, he saw the lime plaster floor below. Then, having the lime plaster and bricks removed, he descended to the courtyard in order and saw sand filled with the seven kinds of jewels, as well as the wooden mechanical figures revolving while holding swords. Although the King called his yakkha-servants to make offerings, he could not see the end of the mechanism. So, bowing to the deities, he said: "I shall take these relics, enshrine them in eighty-four thousand vihāras, and perform offerings. May the deities not create any obstacles for me."

Sakka, while traveling, saw this matter and called Vissakamma, saying: "Dear son, King Asoka the Righteous is descending to the courtyard, saying 'I will take out the relics.' Go and remove the wooden mechanical figures." Vissakamma went in the guise of a village youth with five top-knots, stood before the King holding a bow, and said: "Great King, I shall remove them." When the King said, "Dear son, remove them," he took an arrow and shot it at the joint, whereupon all the mechanical figures were destroyed and scattered. Then, the King took the key-seal that was fastened to open it and saw the heap of rubies. Seeing again the inscription that read, "In the future, may a poor king take these rubies and perform offerings to the relics," he became angry and said, "It is not proper to call a king like me a poor king." He then opened the door by fitting the parts repeatedly and entered the inner chamber.

Although two hundred and eighteen (218) years had passed, the lit lamps were still burning just as they were. He saw that the blue lotuses were as if they had just been brought and offered, the flower mats were as if they had just been spread, and the perfumes were as if they had just been ground. The King then took the gold plate. Having read the inscription on the gold plate: "In the future, a prince named Piyadāsa will assume the white parasol and become the righteous king named Asoka; that king will cause these relics to be widely distributed," he said, "Friends, the Venerable Mahākassapa Thera has indeed seen me!" He then bent his left arm and struck it with his right hand in a gesture of triumph. The King left only a small portion of the relics for worship at that spot, took the remaining relics, closed the relic chamber as it was before, restored everything to its original state, built a stone stupa on top, and in the eighty-four thousand vihāras...
207:
After enshrining the relics, he paid homage to the Great Elders and asked: "Venerable sirs, am I an heir to the Buddha's Sāsana?" The Elders replied: "Great King, how could you be an heir? You are still outside the Sāsana." The King asked: "Venerable sirs, if I, who have spent ninety-six billion in wealth and built eighty-four thousand vihāras, am not an heir, then who else could be an heir?" The Elders replied: "Great King, you are merely a donor of the four requisites (paccayadāyaka). Only one who causes his own son or daughter to be ordained into the Sāsana is called an heir to the Sāsana." The King then caused his son and daughter to be ordained. At that time, the Elders said: "Great King, now you are an heir to the Sāsana."

"Thus this matter occurred in the past" means that in this way, the enshrinement of the relics on the surface of Jambudīpa also occurred in the past. The Elders who conducted the Third Council also included this passage.

As for the verses beginning with "Aṭṭhadoṇaṃ cakkhumato sarīraṃ" (Eight measures of the remains of the Visionary One), they were spoken by the Elders in the island of Ceylon (Tambapaṇṇidīpa).

## The Commentary on the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta is finished.
208:
## 4. Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Sutta
## Description of the Royal City of Kusāvatī
241-2. In this Mahāsudassana Sutta, beginning with "Thus have I heard," the explanation of unfamiliar terms is as follows: "Sabbaratanamayo" means that in this city wall, one brick is made of gold, one of silver, one of beryl (veḷuriya), one of crystal (phalika), one of red stone (ruby), one of masāragalla stone, and one of all kinds of gems. This wall was sixty cubits in height within all the walls. Some Elders, however, say: "A city should be beautiful for those standing inside and looking out; therefore, the outermost wall is sixty cubits high, and the remaining walls decrease in height in succession." Others say: "It should be beautiful for those standing outside and looking in; therefore, the innermost wall is sixty cubits high, and the remaining walls decrease in height in succession." Still others say: "It should be beautiful for those standing both inside and outside; therefore, the middle wall is sixty cubits high, and the three walls inside and the three walls outside decrease in height in succession."

"Esikā" refers to a gatepost or a pillar at the city gate. "Tiporisaṅgā" means that since the measure of five cubits by the hand of a medium-sized man is called one "porisa," it has a circumference of three "porisa" (fifteen cubits). How are these pillars situated? On the outer side of the city, there is one pillar leaning against each large gatepost, one pillar leaning against each small gatepost, and three pillars between each large gate and small gate. In the phrase "tālapantīsu" (among the rows of palm trees), among the palm trees made of all kinds of gems, it should be understood in the same manner as described for the city wall, such as one being made of gold and so forth. The same applies to the leaves and fruits. These rows of palm trees are eighty cubits in height and stand individually between the walls on a level ground surface strewn with sand.

"Vaggū" refers to a skilled and beautiful sound. "Rajanīyo" is a sound capable of causing passion. "Khamanīyo" is a sound that is pleasant and not wearisome even when listened to all day long. "Madanīyo" is a sound that produces the intoxication of pride and the intoxication of manhood. "Pañcaṅgikassa" refers to musical instruments endowed with these five factors: ātata, vitata, ātatavitata, susira, and ghana. Therein, "ātata" refers to one-sided instruments such as the large drum covered with leather. "Vitata" refers to two-sided instruments. "Ātatavitata" refers to instruments covered with leather all around.
209:
"Susira" refers to hollow instruments such as the flute. "Ghana" refers to solid instruments such as cymbals. "Suvinītassa" refers to an instrument that is well-tuned by tightening or loosening the strings and so forth. "Suppaṭitāḷitassa" refers to an instrument that is well-struck to make the rhythmic measure known. "Sukusalehi samannāhatassa" refers to an instrument played by those who are skilled and proficient in playing. "Dhuttā" refers to gamblers who play with dice. "Soဏ္ဍာ" refers to drunkards. These very people, by virtue of their desire to drink repeatedly, are called "pipāsā" (the thirsty ones). "Paricāresuṃ" means they revelled, dancing and moving their hands and feet.

## Description of the Wheel Treasure
"Sīsaṃ nhātassa" means of one who has bathed his head with scented water. "Uposathikassa" means of one who has undertaken the Uposatha observances. "Upari-pāsāda-vara-gatassa" means of one who has ascended to the upper terrace of the noble palace, eaten excellent food, entered the auspicious chamber (sirigabbha) on the top floor (mahātala), and is reflecting on his virtues (sīla). At that time, it is said that the King, having given a great alms-offering by spending hundreds of thousands of wealth early in the morning, performed the auspicious head-washing with sixteen pots of scented water, and after eating his breakfast, he arranged his clean upper robe over one shoulder and sat cross-legged on the auspicious couch (sirisayana) in the chamber on the upper palace, reflecting on his accumulation of merits such as generosity (dāna) and so forth. This is the customary practice (dhammatā) of all Universal Monarchs (Cakkavatti).

While he was thus reflecting on his merits, the divine Wheel Treasure of the devas appeared, produced by seasonal conditions (utu-samuṭṭhāna) due to the aforementioned causes such as meritorious deeds. It appeared like a mass of blue sapphires, as if splitting the surface of the eastern ocean, and as if decorating the sky. That Wheel Treasure appeared to King Mahāsudassana in the same way. This Wheel Treasure is called "dibba" (divine) because it is endowed with the power and majesty of the devas. It is called "sahassāra" because it has a thousand spokes. It is called "sanemika sanābhika" because it has a rim and a hub. It is called "sabbākāraparipūra" because it is complete in all its aspects.

Therein, it is called "cakkaratana" (Wheel Treasure) because it is both a wheel and a treasure (ratana) in the sense of producing delight. The hub, which is described as "sanābhika," is made of Indanīla sapphire. In the center of that hub, there is a tube made of pure silver; that tube is as beautiful as if it were smiling with a row of pure, smooth teeth. The hole in the center is like the moon's disk. It is rimmed with silver plates on both the inner and outer sides. Among those hubs...
210: In the various parts of the circumference of the hub's tube, the demarcating lines in the appropriate places are well-defined and clearly visible. This is the perfection of all aspects of the hub of that Wheel Treasure. Regarding the spokes, of which it is said, 'It has a thousand spokes,' those spokes are made of the seven gems and are endowed with radiance like the rays of the sun. The demarcating lines of their sockets and beads are also well-defined and clearly visible. This is the perfection of all aspects of the spokes of that Wheel Treasure. Regarding the rim, of which it is said, 'It has a rim,' it is made of coral, extremely red, pure, and smooth, as if bearing the glory of a cluster of rays from the young sun. At the joints, the circular demarcating lines made of red Jāmbūnada gold plates, glorious like the glow of sunset, are well-defined and clearly visible. This is the perfection of all aspects of the rim of that Wheel Treasure. On the back of the rim's circle, between every ten spokes, there is a coral rod that is hollow inside like a flute, adorned with small circular holes, and capable of catching the wind. When the wind blows through it, it produces a sound that is melodious, enchanting, lovely, and intoxicating, like a five-fold musical ensemble played by a skilled musician. Above that coral rod is a white umbrella, and on both sides are two rows of hanging flower garlands. Thus, the circumference of the rim is beautified by a hundred coral rods, each bearing a hundred white umbrellas surrounded by two hundred rows of hanging flower garlands. Inside the two tubes of the hub, there are two lion faces. From these lion faces, two clusters of pearls hang down, the size of palm trunks, glorious like a cluster of rays from the full moon, ending in red woolen balls resembling the young sun, and appearing to carry the beauty of the flow of the celestial Ganges. When these pearl clusters rotate in the sky along with the Wheel Treasure, they appear as if three wheels are rotating together. This is its perfection in every way and in all aspects. That Wheel Treasure, perfect in all aspects, approaches the royal capital, appearing to beautify the sky at a level neither too high nor too low, near the tops of the forest groves, where people who have finished their evening meal are sitting on seats prepared at their doorsteps engaging in conversation, and where children are playing at crossroads and junctions. From a distance of twelve yojanas, the sound (of it brushing against) the tips of the tree branches can be heard...
211: ...delighting the ears of beings with its sweet sound, and from a distance of one yojana, attracting the eyes with its color, brilliant with the accumulation of various radiances, as if proclaiming the power of the merit of the Universal Monarch. Then, upon merely hearing the sound of that Wheel Treasure, among those people who were looking towards the east with hearts wondering, 'Where is this sound coming from? Whose sound is this?', one person said to another: 'Look, sirs, a marvel! Previously, this full moon rose alone, but today it has risen with a second. This pair of full moons, like a pair of royal golden swans, seems to be leaping across the sky one after the other.' Another said: 'What are you saying, friend? Where have you ever seen two full moons rising together? Is this not the sun risen, bearing golden rays and shimmering light?' Another, laughing, said: 'Are you mad? Has not the sun just set? How could it rise again, following this full moon? Surely, this must be the celestial mansion of some meritorious person, brilliant with the accumulation of the radiance of many gems.' Dismissing them all, others said: 'Sirs, why do you talk so much nonsense? This is neither the full moon, nor the sun, nor a celestial mansion. Such things do not possess this kind of glory and prosperity. Indeed, this must be the Wheel Treasure.' While those people were thus conversing, the Wheel Treasure, leaving the orb of the moon, came towards them. Then, when they asked, 'To whom has this appeared?', speakers arose saying, 'To no one else; has not our Great King fulfilled the duties of a Universal Monarch? It is for him that this has appeared.' Then all those people, and whoever else saw it, followed the Wheel Treasure. That Wheel Treasure, as if wishing to make known its arrival for the sake of the King, circled the city seven times along the top of the city walls, then circumambulated the King's palace to the right, and remained as if fixed to an axle at a place like the northern lion-window of the palace, where it could be easily honored with perfumes, flowers, and so on. As it remained thus, seeing the mass of radiance entering through the windows and other openings, decorating the interior of the palace with the brilliance of various multicolored gems, for the purpose of seeing it...
212:
The King became one in whom desire had arisen. His attendants also came to the King with the gift of pleasant words and reported that matter to him. Then the King, his body pervaded with intense rapture and joy, left his throne, rose from his seat, went near the window, and seeing that Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana), thought, "I have indeed heard of this," and so on. For King Mahāsudassana, everything happened in that very way. Therefore it was said: "King Mahāsudassana, having seen... Am I indeed a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavatti)?" In that passage, "that person is a Wheel-Turning Monarch"—to what extent is one a Wheel-Turning Monarch? When the Wheel Treasure rises into the sky even by an inch or two and revolves, now, to show what should be done to make it proceed, [the Buddha] said, "Then indeed, Ānanda," and so forth.

In that passage, "rising from the seat" means getting up from the sitting position and coming near the Wheel Treasure. "Taking a golden water vessel" means lifting a golden vessel (bhinkāra) with a spout like an elephant's trunk. "King Mahāsudassana (follows the Wheel Treasure) together with the fourfold army" means that for all Wheel-Turning Monarchs, immediately after pouring water and saying, "May the noble Wheel Treasure be victorious," the Wheel Treasure rises into the air and revolves. At the very moment it revolves, that King is called a Wheel-Turning Monarch. While the Wheel Treasure is revolving, the King, following it, mounts the excellent vehicle of a Wheel-Turning Monarch and rises into the air. Then his attendants carrying the parasol, yak-tail fan, and so on, as well as the women of the harem, and others such as the viceroy (uparāja) and the general (senāpati), decorated with various ornaments, tunics, and armor, shining with the brilliance of various jewels, and adorned with raised banners and flags, rise into the air together with their respective armies and surround the King.

The royal officials, to gather the people, have drums beaten through the city streets: "Friends, the Wheel Treasure has appeared to our King; assemble, having decorated yourselves according to your wealth." The great multitude, simply by the sound of the Wheel Treasure, abandon all their affairs, take perfumes, flowers, and so on, and having assembled, they all rise into the air and surround the King. Whoever has the thought of wanting to go with the King finds himself in the sky. Thus, there is an assembly twelve yojanas in length and breadth. In that assembly, not even a single man has a cut or broken body, or soiled clothes...
213:
...there was none. For a Wheel-Turning Monarch has a pure retinue. The assembly of a Wheel-Turning Monarch, while traveling in the sky like Vijjādharas, is like jewels scattered upon a floor of sapphire (indanīla). For King Mahāsudassana, it was just so. Therefore it was said: "King Mahāsudassana, together with the fourfold army (followed)."

That Wheel Treasure revolves in the region of the sky above the treetops, neither too high nor too low. Those who desire the flowers, fruits, and shoots of the trees are able to take them easily. Those standing on the ground are able to recognize, "This is the King, this is the Viceroy, this is the General." In postures (iriyāpatha) such as standing, whoever desires to go in whatever manner, goes in that very manner. Those devoted to arts such as painting go while performing their respective tasks right there [in the sky]. Just as on the ground, all their affairs are accomplished even in the sky. Thus, taking the assembly of the Wheel-Turning Monarch, that Wheel Treasure, leaving Mount Sineru on the left, travels over the Great Ocean to the island of Pubbavideha, which is seven thousand yojanas in extent.

In that island, on a delightful piece of ground that is twelve yojanas in diameter and thirty-six yojanas in circumference, sufficient for the assembly to settle, where food and requisites are easily obtained, endowed with shade and water, and having a pure and level surface, that Wheel Treasure stands as if fixed to an axle. Then, by that sign, the great multitude descends and dwells there, performing all their affairs such as bathing and eating as they please. For King Mahāsudassana, everything was just so. Therefore it was said: "Ānanda, in whatever place the Wheel Treasure stays, there King Mahāsudassana takes up residence together with the fourfold army."

When the Wheel-Turning Monarch has thus taken up residence, the kings who are there, even upon hearing that "an enemy army has arrived," do not gather their forces and prepare for war. For immediately upon the appearance of the Wheel Treasure, there is no being who would dare to lift a weapon against that King with the thought of him being an enemy. This is the power of the Wheel Treasure.
214:
By the power of that king's Wheel Treasure, all enemies are brought to submission. Because that lord of men subdues his enemies, his Wheel Treasure is called 'Arindama' (Subduer of Enemies). Therefore, all those kings, taking gifts suitable to their own royal splendor and wealth, approach that king and, with bowed heads, worship his feet with the radiance of the jewels in their crowns. They respond to his commands with words such as 'Come, Great King.' They did the same for King Mahāsudassana. Thus it was said: 'Ananda, those in the eastern direction... [say] "Exhort us, Great King."' 

In that context, 'Svāgataṃ' means 'well come.' When some people come, others grieve; when they leave, others rejoice. When some come, others rejoice; when they leave, others grieve. You are one whose coming brings joy and whose leaving brings grief. Therefore, your coming is called 'well come.' When this is said, the Cakkavatti King does not say, 'Provide me with this much annual tax,' nor does he seize the wealth of one to give to another. Instead, with wisdom suitable to his status as a King of Dhamma, he reflects on the taking of life and so on, and with a loving and sweet voice, he teaches the Dhamma: 'Look, dear ones, the taking of life, when practiced, developed, and frequently done, leads to hell,' and gives advice such as 'Life should not be taken.' King Mahāsudassana did the same. Thus it was said: 'King Mahāsudassana spoke thus: "Life should not be taken... eat as you have eaten before."' Do all people accept this advice of the king? Even the Buddha's advice is not accepted by all; how then would they all accept the king's? Therefore, only those who are wise and discerning accept it. However, all become followers. Thus he said: 'Ananda, those in the eastern direction...' 

Then, after giving advice to the inhabitants of Pubbavideha and after the Cakkavatti's army had finished their morning meal, that Wheel Treasure rose into the sky and plunged into the Eastern Ocean. Whenever it plunged, like a serpent king that smells medicine and contracts its hood, it caused the expansion of the waves to subside, and the water of the great ocean receded to a depth of about one league (yojana), standing like a wall of beryl within the ocean. At that very moment, as if wishing to see the king's merit and glory, at the bottom of the great ocean...
215:
Various scattered jewels arrived from here and there and filled that place. Then the royal retinue, seeing the bottom of the great ocean filled with various jewels, took as much as they desired in their waist-cloths and so on. When the retinue had taken the jewels as they pleased, that Wheel Treasure turned back. As it returned, the retinue was in front, the king in the middle, and the Wheel Treasure at the rear. The water of the great ocean, as if attracted by the glory of the Wheel Treasure and as if unable to bear separation from it, followed continuously, striking against the edge of the rim. In this way, the Cakkavatti King, having conquered Pubbavideha up to the edge of the Eastern Ocean, and wishing to conquer Jambudīpa up to the edge of the Southern Ocean, proceeded toward the Southern Ocean along the path shown by the Wheel Treasure. King Mahāsudassana did the same. Thus it was said: 'Ananda, then the Wheel Treasure, having plunged into the Eastern Ocean and emerged, turned toward the southern direction.' 

The manner of its turning, the encampment of the army, the arrival of rival kings, the giving of advice to them, the plunging into the Southern Ocean, the receding of the ocean water, and the taking of jewels—all should be understood in the same way as previously described. 

Having conquered that Jambudīpa, which is ten thousand leagues (yojana) in extent, and emerging from the Southern Ocean, he went in the same manner as previously described to conquer Aparagoyāna, which is seven thousand leagues in extent. Having conquered it up to the edge of the ocean, he emerged from the Western Ocean and went in the same way to conquer Uttarakuru, which is eight thousand leagues in extent. Having conquered it up to the edge of the ocean, he emerged from the Northern Ocean. 

By this much, the Cakkavatti King attained sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans. Having thus achieved victory, in order to see the perfection of his royal splendor, he leaped into the sky with his retinue and looked upon the four great islands, which were surrounded by five hundred small islands each—like four natural lakes adorned with forests of blooming red, white, and blue lotuses—following the path shown by the Wheel Treasure.
216:
He returned to his royal capital in due course by the road. Then, that Wheel Treasure remained as if beautifying the palace gate.

When the Wheel Treasure was thus established, there was no need for torches or lamps in the king's palace; the radiance of the Wheel Treasure alone dispelled the darkness at night. For those who desired darkness, however, there was only darkness. For King Mahāsudassana, all this happened in that very way. Therefore, it was said: "Having plunged into the southern ocean... etc... such a Wheel Treasure appeared."

## Description of the Elephant Treasure

When the Wheel Treasure had thus appeared, the ministers of the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) prepared the site of the regular auspicious elephant, making the ground level and clean. They had it smeared with fragrant scents such as sandalwood, scattered with fragrant flowers of various colors below, and decorated above with a canopy adorned with delightful garlands of flowers interspersed with golden stars, like a celestial mansion. Then they said, "O King, please contemplate the arrival of such an Elephant Treasure." The king, having given great gifts and undertaken the precepts in the manner previously mentioned, sat reflecting on the perfection of that merit.

Then, urged by the power of the king's merit, a noble elephant—wishing to enjoy that special honor—came from either the Chaddanta clan or the Uposatha clan. It had a pure white body adorned with feet, neck, and face as red as the young sun, stood on seven points (sattappatiṭṭho), had well-proportioned limbs, a trunk as beautiful as a blooming red lotus, was possessed of psychic power, and was capable of traveling through the air like a yogi. It was like a silver mountain with edges tinged with vermilion powder. If it comes from the Chaddanta clan, the youngest one comes. If it comes from the Uposatha clan, the eldest one comes. In the Pali text, however, it only appears as "the elephant king named Uposatha." Since an elephant king is not the property of anyone else, the Commentaries state that the youngest one comes. Such an elephant comes to the Wheel-turning Monarchs who fulfill the duties of a Cakkavatti and contemplate in the manner described. For King Mahāsudassana, it came of its own accord to the site of the regular auspicious elephant, displaced that elephant, and stood there. Therefore, it was said: "Ananda, furthermore... etc... the elephant king."
217:
Seeing the Elephant Treasure that had thus appeared, the elephant keepers and others were joyful and delighted, and they went quickly to inform the king. The king came very quickly, and seeing that Elephant Treasure, with a heart full of faith, he thought, "Friends, this elephant vehicle is truly excellent; if only it would undergo training!" and he stretched out his hand. Then, that Elephant Treasure, like a domestic calf, lowered its ears, showed its docility, and approached the king. The king desired to mount that elephant. Then his attendants, knowing the king's wish, presented the Elephant Treasure after raising golden banners, adorning it with golden ornaments, and covering it with a golden net. The king, without making the elephant crouch, ascended by a ladder made of the seven kinds of jewels, his mind inclined toward traveling through the sky. As soon as the thought arose, that elephant king soared into the blue sky, which had the radiance of an indanīla sapphire, like a king of swans. Then, all the king's retinue followed in the same manner as described for the movement of the Wheel Treasure. Thus, the king together with his retinue traveled over the entire earth and returned to the royal capital before the morning meal. In this way, the Elephant Treasure of a Wheel-turning Monarch possesses great psychic power. For King Mahāsudassana, such an Elephant Treasure had also appeared. Therefore, it was said: "The king saw... etc... it appeared."

## Description of the Horse Treasure

When the Elephant Treasure had thus appeared, the ministers of the Wheel-turning Monarch prepared the regular auspicious horse stable to have level and clean ground. Having decorated it, they exerted effort to make the king contemplate its arrival in the same manner as before. The king, having given gifts and performed honors and offerings in the same manner as before, and being established in the practice of virtue, sat comfortably on the upper floor of the palace and repeatedly recollected his perfection of merit. Then, urged by the power of the king's merit, a horse king named Valāhaka came from the Sindhava breed and stood in that place. It had a beautiful appearance like a mass of white clouds in the autumn season entwined with streaks of lightning, with red feet and a red muzzle. Its body was pure, smooth, firm, and compact like a mass of moonlight. It was called Kaḷasīsa (Black-headed) because it possessed a head as black as a crow's neck or an indanīla sapphire. It was called Muñjakesa (Muñja-maned) because it possessed hair that was soft, round, and straight like muñja grass, as if it had been well-trimmed. It was capable of traveling through the sky. For King Mahāsudassana, this Horse Treasure arrived just like the Elephant Treasure. All the rest...
218:
It should be understood in the same manner as described for the Elephant Jewel. In reference to a Horse Jewel of such nature, the Blessed One said 'Puna ca paraṃ' and so forth.

## Description of the Gem Jewel
To the Universal Monarch for whom the Horse Jewel has appeared, the Gem Jewel arrives from Mount Vepulla. It is four cubits in length and has a circumference equal to the hub of a chariot wheel. It is adorned at both ends with very pure strings of pearls hanging from the tips of the lotuses, and with two golden lotuses. It is surrounded by eighty-four thousand attendant gems, spreading the splendor of the full moon surrounded by a host of stars. When this Gem Jewel that has arrived is placed in a pearl net and raised into the sky to a height of about sixty cubits by a succession of bamboo poles, its radiance spreads to the surrounding area of about one league (yojana) during the night. Because of that radiance, that entire area becomes illuminated as if it were the time of dawn. Then, farmers perform their agricultural work, merchants open their shops, and various artisans carry out their respective tasks, thinking 'it is daytime.' For King Mahāsudassana also, all that happened in the same way. Therefore, it was said, 'Furthermore, Ānanda... the Gem Jewel appeared.'

## Description of the Woman Jewel
To the Universal Monarch for whom the Gem Jewel has appeared, the Woman Jewel appears, which is the cause for the excellence of his sensual pleasures. She is either brought from the royal family of Madra as his chief queen, or she comes of her own accord from Uttarakuru due to the power of merit. The remaining perfections of that Woman Jewel are found in the Pāḷi text itself in the manner beginning with: 'Furthermore, Ānanda, the Woman Jewel appeared to King Mahāsudassana; she was beautiful, lovely to behold...'

In that Pāḷi, she is called 'Abhirūpā' (very beautiful) because she has an extraordinary appearance due to the perfection of her form. She is called 'Dassanīyā' (lovely to behold) because she delights the eyes just by being seen; therefore, she is worthy of being looked at even after setting aside other distracting tasks. She is called 'Pāsādikā' (inspiring/pleasing) because she gladdens the mind through the power of joy just by being seen. 'Paramāya' means supreme because she brings about such clarity of mind. 'Vaṇṇapokkharatāya' means because of the beauty of her complexion. 'Samannāgatā' means endowed with. Alternatively, she is called 'Abhirūpā' because she is neither too tall nor too short. She is called 'Dassanīyā' because she is neither too thin nor too fat.
219:
She is called 'Pāsādikā' because she is neither too dark nor too fair. Because she is endowed with supreme beauty of complexion, she surpasses the appearance of humans and approaches the appearance of the devas. Indeed, the radiance of the complexion of humans does not emanate outwards, but the radiance of the devas emanates even to a great distance.

The radiance of that queen's body illuminates an area of about twelve cubits. Among the descriptions such as 'neither too tall,' her perfection of height is stated by the first pair, her perfection of girth by the second pair, and her perfection of complexion by the third pair. Alternatively, the absence of bodily defects is stated by these six, and her bodily perfection is stated by the phrase 'surpassing the appearance of humans.' 'Silk-cotton or cotton' means it is as soft as silk-cotton or cotton that has been beaten a hundred times and placed in clarified butter. 'When it is cold' means when it is cold for the king (she is warm). 'When it is hot' means when it is hot for the king (she is cool). 'Scent of sandalwood' means the scent of fresh yellow sandalwood (haricandana), which has been well-ground and mixed with the four types of fragrances, constantly wafts from her body. 'Scent of blue lotus wafts' means that when she laughs or speaks, an extremely fragrant scent, like that of a blue lotus that has just blossomed, wafts from her mouth.

To show the conduct appropriate to the bodily perfection of that queen who is thus endowed with the excellence of appearance, touch, and scent, the passage beginning with 'Taṃ kho pana' was said. In that text, she is called 'one who rises first' (pubbuṭṭhāyinī) because, upon seeing the king, she rises first from her seat as if she were being burned by fire. She is called 'one who lies down last' (pacchānipātinī) because, when the king is seated, she performs tasks such as fanning him with a palm-leaf fan and only afterwards lies down or sits. She is called 'one who asks what is to be done' (kiṃkārapaṭissāvinī) because she responds with the words, 'O King, what shall I do?' She is called 'one who acts pleasingly' (manāpacārinī) because she behaves and acts only according to the king's wishes. She is called 'one who speaks endearingly' (piyavādinī) because she speaks only what is pleasing to the king.

Now, to show that 'the conduct of that queen is due only to the purity of her nature and not due to deceit,' the passage beginning with 'Taṃ kho pana' was said. In that text, 'does not transgress' (no aticarī) means she does not behave in a way that oversteps; it means that, setting aside the king, she does not desire another man even in her mind.

In that text, the qualities mentioned at the beginning, such as 'beautiful,' and at the end, such as 'one who rises first,' are her natural qualities. However, those such as 'surpassing the appearance of humans' should be understood as having arisen through the power of past kamma, depending on the merit of the Wheel-turning King, from the time the Wheel Treasure appeared.
220:
Her beauty and other qualities reached perfection from the moment the Wheel Treasure (Cakkaratana) appeared. Therefore, it is said: "Such a Woman Treasure (Itthiratana) appeared."

## Explanation of the Householder Treasure

After the Woman Treasure had appeared to the Wheel-Turning Monarch, the Householder Treasure (Gahapatiratana) appeared so that matters concerning wealth and property might proceed according to his wishes. This householder was naturally very wealthy and born into a wealthy family. He was a great merchant-householder who increased the King's wealth. Along with the power of the Wheel Treasure, a divine eye (dibbacakkhu) born of kamma-result (kamma-vipākaja) appeared to him, through which he could see buried treasure within a league (yojana) inside the earth. Seeing that wealth, with a joyful mind, he would go and invite the King with wealth, fulfilling all financial matters. He did the same for King Mahāsudassana. Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore, Ānanda... such a Householder Treasure appeared."

## Explanation of the Counselor Treasure

After the Householder Treasure had appeared to the Wheel-Turning Monarch, the Counselor Treasure (Parināyakaratana), capable of managing all affairs, appeared. This counselor was the King's eldest son. He was naturally wise, skilled, intelligent, and discerning. Relying on the King's merit and through the power of his own kamma, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittañāṇa) arose in him. With that knowledge, he was able to know the thoughts of the King's retinue within twelve leagues and determine what was beneficial or harmful to the King. Seeing his own power, with a joyful heart, he invited the King to let him advise on all matters. He did the same for King Mahāsudassana. Therefore, it is said: "Furthermore... the Counselor Treasure appeared." In that context, "to place those who should be placed" means to appoint people to their respective positions.

## Explanation of the Possession of the Four Psychic Powers

"Samavepākinī" means that which digests food evenly. "Gahaṇī" refers to the kamma-born heat element (digestive fire). In that regard, for one person, the food consumed is digested as soon as it is eaten; for another...
221:
Otherwise, it remains in the stomach like a bundle of food; both of these [the old and the new food] are not endowed with even digestion. For whomsoever the desire for food arises again at the next mealtime, that person is endowed with even digestion.

## Commentary on the Dhamma Palace Ponds

"He created" does not mean that he had drums beaten in the city to gather the people and then created them; rather, as soon as the King's thought arose, eighty-four thousand ponds appeared, breaking through the ground. It is in reference to those ponds that this was said. "With two tiers of walls" means that it was surrounded by one tier of walls at the very edge of the bricks, and by another tier of walls at the edge of the boundary of the precinct. 

Why did "such a thought occur"? It is said that one day, the Great Being, the King, saw the great multitude of people going about after bathing and drinking, and he thought, "These people are going about in a state like that of madmen. If there were flowers for them to wear here, it would be good." Then, such a thought occurred to that King. In that passage, "blooming in all seasons" means that flowers usually bloom in only one season. I, however, thought, "I will make them bloom in all seasons."

"He caused to be planted" does not mean that he had lotus seeds of various colors brought from various places and then had them planted; rather, everything was accomplished for that King as soon as his thought arose. The people of the world thought that the King had planted them. Therefore, it is said, "He caused to be planted." From that time on, the multitude of people went about as if playing at a festival, wearing various kinds of water-born and land-born flowers.

Then the King, desiring to make the people even more endowed with happiness, thought of the provision of happiness for the people, saying, "What if I, on the banks of these ponds..." and so on, and he did everything. In that passage, "they gave baths" means that one person rubbed the body, another prepared scented powders, another brought water for the person bathing on the bank, and another both received and gave the clothes.

"He truly established" means how did he establish it? He had ornaments suitable for women and men made, and placing only the women there for the purpose of service, and placing everything else for the purpose of charity, King Mahāsudassana gave gifts; he had drums beaten, saying, "Enjoy those gifts." The multitude of people came to the banks of the ponds, bathed, changed their clothes, anointed themselves with various scents, and wore exquisite flowers...
222:
Going to the alms-hall, whatever one desired among the various kinds of gruel, rice, hard food, and the eight kinds of drinks, they ate and drank. Wearing various fine linen clothes from the Khoma country, they enjoyed prosperity. Those who already possessed such clothes and ornaments left them and went away. Those who did not possess them took them and went away. Even with elephants, horses, chariots, and so on, after riding and traveling a little, those who had no need for them left them behind, while those who had need took them and went away. After sleeping on noble beds and enjoying prosperity, those who had no need for them left them behind, while those who had need took them and went away. After enjoying prosperity with women, those who had no need for them left them behind, while those who had need took them and went away. After adorning themselves with the seven kinds of jewel ornaments and enjoying prosperity, those who had no need for them left them behind, while those who had need took them and went away. That alms-giving was also provided with constant and persistent effort. The inhabitants of Jambudīpa had no other work; they went about only enjoying the King's alms.

Then the Brahmins and householders thought: "Although this King gives such alms, he does not have anything brought to him, saying, 'Give me rice and so on, or milk and so on.' However, it is not proper for us to remain silent just because the King does not have things brought." Thinking thus, they collected much wealth and offered it to the King. Therefore, it was said: "Then, Ānanda, the Brahmins and householders..." and so on. They thought thus equally. Why did they think thus? Some brought a little from their houses, some brought much. When offering, disputes might arise: "Is only what is brought from your house good, and not what is brought from mine? Is only what is brought from your house much, and not what is brought from mine?" To prevent such sounds of quarreling, they thought thus equally.

"Come, friend" means "Come, friend." He gave the order by assigning the name "Dhamma Palace" to the palace. When Vissakamma asked, "O King, how large should the palace be?", although he was told, "Let it be one league in length and half a league in width, and let it be made entirely of jewels," Vissakamma replied, "So be it, your words are excellent," and after having the King accept it, he created it. In that context, "Evaṃ bhadraṃ tavāti kho Ānanda" means "Ānanda, may it be well with you in this way." "Paṭissutvā" means having accepted, having the meaning of "vatvā" (having said). By silence...
223:
Wishing, "I will have the opportunity to practice the Dhamma of a recluse," he accepted by remaining silent. "Sāramayo" means made of the heartwood of sandalwood.

In the phrase "dwīhi vedikāhi" (with two railings), one railing was at the upper edge of that palace, and one railing was at the lower boundary edge.

"Duddikkho ahosi" means it was difficult to look at; it means it was difficult to look at because it was full of brilliance. "Musati" means it attracts, it makes one tremble, it does not allow one to remain still. "Viddhe" means high, or distant because of the absence of clouds. "Deve" means in the sky.

"Māpesi kho" means he did not create it by saying, "I will create a pond in this place, destroy your houses." It was not created in that way. By the mere arising of a thought, the earth split and such a pond appeared. "Te sabbakāmehi" means he satisfied them with all desired objects—monks with monks' requisites, and Brahmins with Brahmins' requisites.

## The Explanation of the First Recitation Section is finished.

## Explanation of the Attainment of Jhana

"Mahiddhiko" means being endowed with great psychic power, which is described as the creation of eighty-four thousand ponds by the mere arising of a thought. "Mahānubhāvo" means being endowed with great majesty because of the greatness of those things to be experienced. "Seyyathidaṃ" is an indeclinable; its meaning is "Which three?". "Dānassa" means the meaning of perfect generosity. "Damassa"—in the Āḷavaka Sutta, wisdom is referred to as "dama." Here, however, it is the act of Uposatha performed by restraining oneself. "Saṃyamassa" means the meaning of virtue (sīla).

## Explanation of the Bodhisatta's Previous Practice

Standing here, the previous practice (pubbayoga) of that King should be known—it is said that in the past, the King was born in a householder's family. At that time, during the dispensation of the living Kassapa Buddha, a certain elder lived in the forest. The Bodhisatta...
224: A lay devotee, entering the forest on his own business, saw the Elder, approached and paid homage to him. Looking at the Elder's dwelling place and walking path, he asked, "Venerable Sir, does the Noble One reside here?" Hearing the reply, "Yes, lay devotee," he thought, "It is fitting to build a leaf-hut (paṇṇasālā) for the Noble One right here." Abandoning his own work, he cut timber and bamboo, built a leaf-hut, roofed it, plastered the walls with smooth clay, fitted doors, and made a wooden floor. Thinking, "Will he use it or not?" he sat to one side watching. The Elder, returning from the village, entered the hut and sat on the wooden floor. The lay devotee also approached, paid homage, and sitting nearby, asked, "Venerable Sir, is the leaf-hut comfortable?" "It is comfortable, good man, and suitable for a renunciant," the Elder replied. When asked, "Venerable Sir, will you reside here?" the Elder said, "Yes, lay devotee." Knowing by his manner of acceptance that he would reside there, the devotee made him promise to come to his house door regularly and said, "Venerable Sir, please grant me a boon." The Elder replied, "Lay devotee, renunciants have transcended the granting of boons." He pleaded, "Venerable Sir, I ask only for a boon that is allowable and faultless." The Elder said, "Speak, lay devotee." He said, "Venerable Sir, in a place of permanent residence, people desire your presence for both auspicious and inauspicious occasions; they get angry if you do not come. Therefore, even if you go to another invited place, please complete your meal only after entering my house." The Elder accepted. That lay devotee spread a coarse mat in the leaf-hut, prepared a couch and a stool, placed a backrest, and a footstool. He dug a pond, made a walking path, and scattered sand. Seeing wild animals coming to rub against the walls and causing the clay to fall, he surrounded it with a thorn fence. Seeing them descend into the pond and make the water muddy, he lined the inside with stones, surrounded the outside with a thorn fence, and planted rows of palm trees along the edge of the fence. Seeing the swept area of the great walking path being disturbed, he also surrounded the path with a fence and planted rows of palm trees along its edge. Having thus completed the monastery residence, he offered the Elder the three robes, alms-food, medicine, utensils, a thorn-remover, a mortar, nail-cutters, a needle, a walking staff, sandals, a water-gourd, an umbrella, a lamp-stand, a cleaning tool, a water-strainer, a regulation water-pot (dhammaka-raṇa), an alms-bowl, a platter, and whatever other requisites are used by renunciants. There was no requisite that the Bodhisatta had not offered to the Elder. That Bodhisatta, observing the precepts and keeping the Uposatha...
225:
He attended to the Elder for the rest of his life. The Elder, residing in that very place, attained Arahantship and passed into Parinibbāna.

The Bodhisatta also, having performed meritorious deeds for the duration of his life, was reborn in the celestial realm; passing away from there and coming to the human world, he was reborn in the royal city of Kusāvatī and became King Mahāsudassana.

"Thus, even a merit that is not very great,
When performed in the field (āyatana) [of the Sasana],
Has a great result (vipāka);
Therefore, the wise person should perform that merit."

Mahāviyūha is a great gabled mansion (kūṭāgāra) made of silver. Having a desire to reside there, he went; with this much, sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) [shall cease]. These three types of sensual thoughts are to be turned back by this much. "The place beyond this is not your ground; this is a hall for jhāna; this is not a place for residing with you"—thus he turned back the three types of thoughts at the very door of the gabled mansion.

In the first jhāna and so forth, there is no separate task of kasina preliminary work (parikamma). When there is a need for the blue kasina, a blue gem appears; when there is a need for the yellow kasina, gold appears; when there is a need for the red kasina, a ruby appears; when there is a need for the white kasina, silver appears—wherever he looks, only the kasina is manifest.

Everything that should be said regarding the phrases "with loving-kindness" and so forth has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Thus, in the Pali text, only the four jhānas and the four immeasurables (appamaññā) are mentioned. The Great Being (Mahāpurisa), however, having produced all eight attainments (samāpatti) and the five higher powers (abhiññā), and entering the attainments in fourteen ways such as in forward and reverse order, spends his time with the bliss of the attainments, just as a bee that has entered a honeycomb enjoys the taste of honey.

## Commentary on the Eighty-Four Thousand Cities

Kusāvatī-rājadhāni-pamukhāni means that the royal city of Kusāvatī is the chief and most excellent of those cities. Bhattābhihāro means the offering of food to be brought.
226:
Why did he think like this: "A hundred years, a hundred years"? It was because he was weary of their sound. For it is said (in Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.72), "Sound is a thorn to one who has entered an attainment." Therefore, the Mahāpurisa was weary of the sound. If so, why did he not say, "Do not come"? He did not say it because [he thought], "Now the King no longer looks [at them], they will not receive their regular duties; let that [loss] not happen to them" (out of compassion).

## Subhaddādevī-upasaṅkamana-vaṇṇanā

When did this thought occur? It occurred on the day the King passed away. At that time, it is said the deities thought, "Let the King not pass away without a protector; let him pass away only while surrounded by many harem women, daughters, and sons." Then, influencing the Queen, they caused such a thought to arise in her. "Yellow garments" means those garments were naturally pleasing to the King; therefore, she said, "Wear those garments." "Queen, stay right here" means "Queen, this so-called meditation hall (jhānāgāra) is not a place for living with you; it is a place for me to enjoy the bliss of jhāna; do not enter here."

Regarding "this thought occurred": in the world, beings shine exceedingly at the time of death; therefore, seeing the King's clear faculties, this thought occurred. Then, not wishing for the King's death, thinking "Let the King not pass away; I will now speak of the King's virtues and act as if staying," she said, "Great King, these are your possessions," and so on. In that speech, "arouse desire" means arouse love, create delight. "Regard for life" means having regard, attachment, or craving for life.

"Queen, you [should speak] to me in this way" means when the Queen, thinking "This person has become a monk," said to the King, "Great King, we women do not know the proper way to address monks; how should we speak to the Great King?", the King said, "Queen, address me in this way," and so on. "Censured" means censured by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples, and other wise and learned people. Why? Because dying with attachment is the cause of being reborn in one's own house as a yakkha, a dog, a python, an ox, a buffalo, a rat, a chicken, a louse, a gnat, or other such unfortunate states.
227:
Ānanda, "Then Queen Subhaddā, having wiped away her tears" means the Queen went to a certain place, wept and wailed, and then, having wiped away her tears, spoke these words.

## Brahmalokūpagama-vaṇṇanā

Why is it said "or a householder's (meal)"? It is because they have great wealth like the son of the treasurer Soṇa and others. It is said that a single meal of the treasurer's son Soṇa was worth two hundred thousand. Thus, for those who eat such a meal, there occurs for a moment dizziness caused by food, stupor caused by food, and exhaustion caused by food.

"At that time, I lived in which (city)" means the place where I lived was only one city; in the remaining cities, sons, daughters, and servants lived. The same applies to the palaces and gabled houses (kūṭāgāra). Among the thrones and so on, he used only one throne; the remaining thrones were for the use of sons and others. Among the women, only one woman attended him; the rest were merely attendants. "Wears" means he wore only one pair of garments; the remaining garments belonged to the sixteen hundred thousand men, plus eighty thousand more, who moved about as attendants. "Eats" means he ate only about one measure (nāḷi) of rice, the supreme amount; he shows that the remaining food belonged to the eight hundred thousand men, plus forty thousand more, who moved about as attendants. Indeed, one pot of rice is sufficient for ten people.

These eighty-four thousand cities, palaces, and gabled houses arose as the result of offering a single leaf-roofed hut. The eighty-four thousand thrones arose as the result of giving a couch for sleeping. The eighty-four thousand elephants, horses, and chariots arose as the result of giving a stool for sitting. The eighty-four thousand jewels arose as the result of offering a single lamp. The eighty-four thousand ponds arose as the result of offering a single pond. The eighty-four thousand women, sons, and householders, along with the usable items—cups, plates, water-pitchers, water-filters, needles, nail-clippers, keys, ear-cleaners, foot-washing stools, sandals, umbrellas, and walking sticks—arose as the result of those gifts. The eighty-four thousand cows arose as the result of offering milk. The eighty-four thousand crores of garments [arose] as the result of offering garments for wearing and covering...
228:
(Those possessions) appeared. It should be understood that eighty-four thousand pots of rice appeared as a result of the offering of food.

In this way, the Blessed One, having taught the prosperity of King Mahāsudassana in detail from the beginning, and wishing to show all that prosperity to be like children playing with sandcastles, spoke the words beginning with "Ananda, look," while lying on the couch of his Parinibbāna. In that context, "vipariṇatā" means reaching a state that cannot be designated, like a lamp that has gone out by abandoning its original nature. "Ananda, in this way, indeed, formations are impermanent" means they are impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having come into being.

By this much, the Blessed One is like a man who, having tied a ladder to a jasmine tree one hundred cubits high, climbed it, took a jasmine flower, and then descended while letting go of the ladder. In the same way, as if tying a ladder, he ascended to the prosperity of King Mahāsudassana, which was many hundreds of millions of years high, and then, as if letting go of the ladder, he descended by taking the characteristic of impermanence that stands at the peak of prosperity. For that very reason, in ancient times, King Vasabha, upon hearing the Dīghabhāṇaka elders reciting this sutta at Ambalaṭṭhikā on the eastern side of the Lohapāsāda, thought: "Friends, what did my grandfather say here? He is only speaking of the prosperity in the place where he ate and drank." But when the words "Ananda, in this way, indeed, formations are impermanent" were spoken, he bent his left hand and struck it with his right hand, saying: "Friends, having seen this state, the One with five eyes, the Buddha, spoke thus." With a joyful heart, he gave the cry of "Sādhu, Sādhu."

"In this way, they are not lasting" means they are devoid of a permanent nature, like bubbles on water. "In this way, they are not a source of solace" means they are devoid of solace (refuge), like water drunk in a dream or like applied sandalwood paste.

"One should discard the body" means to abandon the body. "Ananda, now that defilements are exhausted, for the Tathāgata, there is no other body to discard or to look after," he said. Having said this, he addressed the Elder again: "The majesty of a Cakkavatti king disappears on the seventh day after the king has gone forth. In the case of King Mahāsudassana, however, on the seventh day after his death, the walls made of seven kinds of jewels, the palm trees made of seven kinds of jewels, the eighty-four thousand lotus ponds, the Dhamma Palace, the Dhamma Pond, and the Wheel Treasure—all these disappeared." Regarding treasures such as elephants, it is the natural law that they die together (with the king) when their lifespan is exhausted.
230:
## 5. Janavasabhasutta-vaṇṇanā
## Nātikiya-ādibyākaraṇa-vaṇṇanā
273-275. "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Janavasabha Sutta. In that sutta, the explanation of obscure terms is as follows: "Parito parito janapadesu" means in the various surrounding districts. "Paricārake" means those who serve the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha. "Upapattīsu" means in the arisings (destinations) of knowledge, destiny, and merit. "Kāsikosalesu" means in Kāsī and Kosala, meaning in the kingdom of Kāsī and the kingdom of Kosala. This method should be understood in all places. However, he did not declare (the destiny) in these six kingdoms: Aṅga, Magadha, Yonaka, Kamboja, Assaka, and Avanti. Among these sixteen Great Kingdoms (Mahājanapadas), he only declared it in the first ten. "Nātikiyā" means the residents of Nātika village.

"Tenā" means because of that state of being an Anāgāmī and so forth.
