"Sutvā" means having heard the answer to the question from the Blessed One, who declared it by distinguishing with his Omniscient Knowledge, they became free from doubt regarding those states of Anāgāmī and so forth, and were joyful because of that state of Anāgāmī and so forth. In the Commentary, however, the word "tenā" is explained as "te nātikiyā" (those people of Nātika). In this sense, the letter "na" is merely a particle.

## Ānandaparikathā-vaṇṇanā
"Bhagavantaṃ kittayamānarūpo" means he passed away while praising thus: "Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the Saṅgha! Oh, the Dhamma is well-expounded!" "Bahujano pasīdeyya" means many people would attain clarity of faith, thinking: "Our parents, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, and friends used to eat together with us, used to sleep together with us; we did such and such pleasant things for them; they are said to be Anāgāmīs, Sakadāgāmīs, and Sotāpannas. Oh, how wonderful! Oh, how excellent!"

"Gatiṃ" means the destiny of knowledge. "Abhisamparāyaṃ" means the future state of knowledge itself. In the phrase "addasā kho," how many people did he see? He saw two million four hundred thousand (2,400,000) people.
231:
"Upasantapadisso" means one with a peaceful vision (upasantadassano). "Bhātiriva" means shines exceedingly, glows exceedingly. "Indriyānaṃ" means of the faculties, with the mind as the sixth. "Ānanda, I have seen" means he said he saw not ten, nor twenty, nor a hundred, nor a thousand, but exactly twenty-four hundred thousand (2,400,000) beings.

## Janavasabhayakkhavaṇṇanā

Seeing that "so many people have been freed from suffering depending on me," a powerful joy (somanassa) arose; the mind became clear; because the mind was clear, the blood originating from the mind became clear; because the blood was clear, the faculties with the mind as the sixth became clear. After saying all this, he said, "At that time, Ānanda," and so on. In those words, because that person (Janavasabha) became a Sotāpanna after hearing the Buddha's Dhamma and becoming the leader of one hundred and ten thousand people, he was named "Janavasabha."

"Seven times from here" means passing away from this deva world seven times. "Seven times from there" means passing away from that human world seven times. "Fourteen rounds of saṃsāra" means all fourteen sequences of the aggregates (khandhas). "Knows the dwelling" means knowing the dwelling by way of the sequence of births. "Where I dwelt before" refers to the place where I dwelt even before this current existence, by reaching the company of King Vessavaṇa among the devas and by being a king among humans. Because of having dwelt thus in the past, and because of having performed much merit towards the Triple Gem as a Sotāpanna now, although he is capable of being reborn in higher planes by the power of that merit, he was reborn in this very place due to a strong attachment (nikanti) to the place where he had dwelt for a long time.

"My aspiration stands" shows that he does not let time pass by being negligent with just the mere knowledge that "I am a Sotāpanna," but has undertaken insight (vipassanā) for the sake of the path of Sakadāgāmi, living with such effort as "Today, even today, I shall penetrate [the truth]." "Since the day" refers to the day he became a Sotāpanna upon first seeing [the Buddha] in the Laṭṭhivana Garden. "Venerable Sir, since that day I know I am one who will not fall into states of woe (avinipāta)" means that starting from that day, "Venerable Sir, I know the state of non-falling (avinipātadhamma) attained through the path of Stream-entry in the Laṭṭhivana Garden, as well as the long duration of non-falling into states of woe characterized by the previous fourteen existences."
232:
"Anacchariya" means anu-acchariya, which is wonderful. Seeing the Blessed One on the way while going on some business is indeed a wonder to be contemplated repeatedly. It is also a wonder that what was heard in the presence of the Blessed One was exactly the same as what King Vessavaṇa himself was saying to his own assembly. The two reasons are: the fact of seeing the Blessed One on the way, and the desire to report what was heard in the presence of King Vessavaṇa.

## Devasabhāvaṇဏနာ

Regarding "sannipatitā" (assembled), why did they assemble? It is said that those devas assemble for four reasons: to support the commencement of the rains retreat (vassūpanāyika), to support the Pavāraṇā ceremony, to hear the Dhamma, and to enjoy the games of the Pāricchattaka flowers. Among those reasons, on the day of the rains retreat called "Tomorrow the rains must be entered," on the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, the devas of the two deva worlds assemble in the Sudhammā assembly hall and deliberate: "In such-and-such a monastery, one monk has entered the rains; in such-and-such a monastery, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, or a thousand monks have entered the rains; in these various places, provide well-arranged protection for the noble ones." In this way, the support for the rains retreat is carried out.

At that time too, they assembled for this very reason. "Idaṃ tesaṃ hoti āsanasmiṃ" means this is the seat of those four Great Kings. When those Great Kings are seated thus, then afterwards it is our seat.

"Yenatthena" means for the purpose related to the rains retreat. "Thinking of that purpose, consulting on that purpose" means thinking for the sake of the protection of the forest-dwelling Saṅgha of monks. They consult with the four Great Kings, saying, "Arrange protection for the Saṅgha of monks who have entered the rains in these various places." "Vuttavacanāpi taṃ" means the Great Kings accept what the thirty-three gods (Tāvatiṃsa devaputtā) say. Likewise, the thirty-three gods further instruct, and the other devas accept those instructions. In both phrases, "taṃ" is merely a particle. "Avipakkantā" means those who have not yet departed.

"Uḷāro" means extensive or great. "Devānubhāvaṃ" refers to the radiance that spreads for twelve yojanas from the clothes, ornaments, mansions, and bodies of all the deities. However, the bodily radiance of those with great merit spreads for a hundred yojanas. It means the radiance that surpasses that divine power of the [ordinary] devas.
233:
"Brahmuno hetaṃ pubbanimittaṃ" means that just as the dawn is the precursor to the rising sun, this radiance is shown to be the precursor to the arrival of the Great Brahmā.

## Commentary on the Talk of Sanankumara

"Anabhisambhavanīyo" means inaccessible. It implies that the Tāvatiṃsa devas cannot see that Brahmā. "Cakkhupathasmiṃ" means within the range of the eye-sensitivity or the visual field. It means that the Brahmā cannot be reached or overwhelmed by the visual range of the devas. Indeed, lower deities can only see the coarse forms created by higher deities. "Vedapaṭilābhaṃ" means obtaining joy and delight. "Adhunābhisitto rajjena" means one who has just been anointed in kingship. This meaning should be illustrated by the story of King Duṭṭhagāmaṇi Abhaya.

It is said that after defeating thirty-two Tamil kings and being anointed in Anurādhapura, the king could not sleep for a whole month due to intense joy and satisfaction. Therefore, he informed the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, saying, "Venerable sirs, I cannot sleep." Then they said, "Great King, if so, observe the Uposatha today." So the king observed the Uposatha. The Saṅgha went and sent eight monks who were experts in the Abhidhamma, saying, "Recite the Cittayamaka." They went and said, "Great King, please lie down," and began the recitation. While listening to the recitation, the king fell asleep. The elders said, "Do not wake the king," and departed. The king woke up at sunrise the next day and, not seeing the elders, asked, "Where are the venerable ones?" They replied, "They left after knowing you had fallen asleep." Then the king said, "Friends, my masters know not only the medicine known even to children but also the medicine that causes sleep."

"Pañcasikho" means having created a form similar to the Gandhabba Pañcasikha. It is said that all deities cherish the form of the deva-son Pañcasikha. Therefore, Brahmā also manifested by creating such a form. "Pallankena nisīdi" means sitting cross-legged.

"Vissaṭṭho" means well-released and unhindered. "Viññeyyo" means easy to understand the meaning. "Mañjū" means sweet and gentle. "Savanīyo" means worthy of listening to and pleasant to the ear.
234:
Bindu means having a compact sound. Avisārī means being very clear and distinct, without scattering. Gambhīra means a sound arising deeply from the base of the navel, not a sound arising merely from the striking of the tip of the tongue, lips, and palate. Indeed, a sound arising in such a way [from the tongue-tip, etc.] is unpleasant and cannot be heard at a distance. Ninnādī means being resonant like the sound of a great rain cloud or a large drum. Furthermore, it should be understood here that each subsequent word is the meaning of each preceding word. Yathāparisaṃ means making it known to the entire assembly, however large that assembly may be. That sound revolves only within the assembly; it does not spread outside. 

The words beginning with "Whoever they may be" are spoken to show the fact that he practiced for the benefit of the many. "Taken refuge" (saraṇaṃ gatā) does not refer to those who have taken refuge in any which way, but refers to those who have taken refuge with a mind free from doubt. "They fill the host of Gandhabba deities" means they fill the group of Gandhabba devas. Thus, it means that from the time our Teacher, the Buddha, appeared in the world, an uninterrupted assembly has arisen in the six deva worlds and so on, like a measure filled with pounded rice, or like a forest of reeds or a forest of Sal trees.

## Commentary on the Developed Bases of Power

"How well-prescribed these are by the Blessed One" means how well-prescribed and how well-spoken they are by my Teacher, the Blessed One. In the term "Iddhipāda," it should be understood that it is called "Iddhi" in the sense of accomplishment, and "Pāda" in the sense of foundation. "Due to the capability of power" (iddhipahutāya) means due to the state of being able to exercise power. "Due to the pervasiveness of power" (iddhivisavitāya) means due to the state of the expansion of power; it means the state of having mastery (vasībhāva) practiced by way of repeated cultivation. "Due to the transformability of power" (iddhivikubbanatāya) means due to the state of being able to transform power, for the purpose of demonstrating it in various ways.

In the terms beginning with "endowed with the formations of effort and concentration of desire" (chanda-samādhi-padhāna-saṅkhāra-samannāgataṃ), concentration caused by desire or where desire is predominant is "chanda-samādhi"; it is a designation for the concentration obtained by making the desire to act (kattukamyatā-chanda) the dominant factor. Formations that are primary are "padhāna-saṅkhāra"; it is a designation for the right effort (sammāppadhāna-vīriya) that accomplishes the four tasks. "Endowed with" (samannāgataṃ) means being possessed of both chanda-samādhi and padhāna-saṅkhāra. 

"Iddhipāda" means the remaining group of consciousness and mental factors (citta-cetasika) which serve as the foundation (pāda) for the chanda-samādhi and padhāna-saṅkhāra associated with the mind of direct knowledge (abhiññā-citta), which have reached the designation of "Iddhi" either in the sense of accomplishment by way of fruition, or by the method that "by this, beings accomplish, prosper, and reach excellence." For it is said: "The base of power (iddhipāda) is the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness of one who has become so" (Vibhaṅga 434).
235:
In this way, the meaning of the remaining terms should also be understood. Just as concentration obtained by making desire the predominant factor is called 'concentration of desire' (chanda-samādhi), so too, concentration obtained by making energy, consciousness, or investigation the predominant factor is called 'concentration of investigation' (vīmaṃsā-samādhi), and so on. Alternatively, access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) is called the 'base' (pāda), and the first absorption (pathama-jhāna) is called 'power' (iddhi). The first absorption together with its access is called the 'base', and the second absorption is called 'power'. Thus, the preceding part is the 'base' and the subsequent part is 'power'; in this way, the meaning here should be understood. The discussion on the bases of power (iddhipāda-kathā) has been stated in detail in the Visuddhimagga and the Vibhaṅga-aṭṭhakathā.

Some say, 'The completed state is power (iddhi), and the incomplete state is the base of power (iddhipāda)'. To refute their view, the Uttara-cūḷika-vāra was brought forth in the Abhidhamma: 'There are four bases of power: the base of power consisting of desire, the base of power consisting of energy, the base of power consisting of consciousness, and the base of power consisting of investigation. Therein, what is the base of power consisting of desire? Here, a monk, at a time when he develops supramundane absorption that is leading out (to Nibbāna), leading to the diminution (of rebirth), for the abandoning of wrong views, and for the attainment of the first stage (Sotāpatti), secluded from sense pleasures, enters and dwells in the first absorption, which is difficult practice and slow intuition. At that time, whatever desire, state of desiring, wish to act, wholesome desire for the Dhamma (dhammacchanda) there is—this is called the base of power consisting of desire. The remaining states are states associated with the base of power consisting of desire' (as stated in the Vibhaṅga). These states are mentioned only in terms of the supramundane. In that regard, the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla Thera brought about the supramundane state by making desire the principal factor. The Venerable Soṇa Thera by making energy the principal factor, the Venerable Sambhūta Thera by making consciousness the principal factor, and the Venerable Mogharāja by making investigation the principal factor.

An analogy therein: Among four sons of ministers who live depending on the King, desiring a high position, one becomes full of desire for service. Knowing the King's intention and preference, he serves day and night, pleases the King, and attains the position. Like him, one who brings about the supramundane state with desire as the principal factor should be understood. Another one thinks, 'Who can serve every single day? I will please him with effort when a task arises.' When the border region revolts, being sent by the King, he suppresses the enemy with effort and attains the position. Like him, one who brings about the supramundane state with energy as the principal factor should be understood.
237:
Regarding the term "oḷārika" (gross): The bodily formations (kāya-saṅkhāra) and verbal formations (vacī-saṅkhāra) are indeed gross, but how are mental formations (citta-saṅkhāra) gross? Because they have not yet been abandoned. Bodily formations are abandoned by the fourth absorption, verbal formations by the second absorption, and mental formations by the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Thus, even when bodily and verbal formations are abandoned, those mental formations still remain; therefore, in comparison to those abandoned, they are called "gross" because they are not yet abandoned. "Happiness" (sukha) refers to the happiness of the attainment of fruition associated with the fourth absorption that arises for one emerging from the attainment of cessation. "Joy greater than happiness" (sukhā bhiyyo somanassaṃ) refers to the repeated joy (somanassa) for one who has emerged from the attainment of fruition. "The second attainment of opportunity" (dutiyo okāsādhigamo) is so called because the fourth absorption stands having removed pleasure and pain and having taken its own opportunity. In this context, when the fourth absorption is taken, the second and third absorptions are also taken; therefore, they are not mentioned separately.

In the phrases "This is wholesome" (idaṃ kusalaṃ), etc., "wholesome" refers to the ten wholesome courses of action (kamma-patha). "Unwholesome" refers to the ten unwholesome courses of action. The dyads such as "blameworthy" (sāvajja-duka), etc., should also be understood by way of these wholesome and unwholesome states. All these states are called "dark and bright with counterparts" (kaṇha-sukka-sappaṭibhāga) because they are dark, bright, and have counterparts. Nibbāna alone is "without counterpart" (appaṭibhāga). "Ignorance is abandoned" (avijjā pahīyati) means the ignorance that conceals the round of rebirth is abandoned. "Knowledge arises" (vijjā uppajjati) means the knowledge of the path of Arahantship arises. "Happiness" (sukha) refers to both the happiness of the path of Arahantship and the happiness of fruition. "Joy greater than happiness" refers to the repeated joy for one who has emerged from the attainment of fruition. "The third attainment of opportunity" (tatiyo okāsādhigamo) is so called because the path of Arahantship stands having removed all defilements and having taken its own opportunity. The remaining paths are included within that path of Arahantship; therefore, they are not mentioned separately.

These three attainments of opportunity should be explained in detail by way of the thirty-eight meditation objects. How? Having defined all meditation objects by way of access and absorption according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga, the first absorption in twenty-four places should be explained as "the first attainment of opportunity". The second and third absorptions in thirteen places, and the fourth absorption and the attainment of cessation in fifteen places, should be explained as "the second attainment of opportunity". The ten access concentrations, which are the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the path, belong to the third attainment of opportunity. Furthermore, among the three trainings (sikkhā), the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) belongs to the first attainment of opportunity, the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā) to the second, and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā) to the third; thus it should also be explained by way of the trainings. In the Sāmaññaphala Sutta as well, from the minor section on virtue up to the first absorption is the first...
238:
...is called the attainment of opportunity (okāsādhigama). From the second jhāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called the second attainment of opportunity. From insight (vipassanā) up to the fruit of arahantship (arahattaphala) is called the third attainment of opportunity. Thus, it is also taught by way of the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. Among the three Piṭakas, the Vinaya Piṭaka is included in the first attainment of opportunity, the Suttanta Piṭaka in the second, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka in the third; thus it is also taught by way of the Piṭakas.

In ancient times, the Great Elders (Mahātheras) used to begin their teaching with this very sutta during the Rains Retreat (vassa). Why? It was to have the opportunity to teach by analyzing the three Piṭakas. It cannot be said of one who teaches by coordinating with the three Piṭakas that it is "badly taught." Only this sutta, taught by including it within the three Piṭakas, is called "well taught."

## Commentary on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Catusatipatthānavannanā)
"Kusalassādhigamāya" means for the purpose of attaining the wholesome states of the Path (magga) and the Fruit (phala). Both are indeed "wholesome" (kusala) because they are faultless and secure. In this context of the foundations of mindfulness, "sammāsamādhiyati" means being concentrated with a one-pointed mind on that internal body. "Bahiddhā parakāye ñāṇadassanaṃ abhinibbatteti" means directing knowledge towards the body of another, external to one's own body. This method is the same in all instances. In all instances, the word "satimā" refers to mindfulness that grasps the body and so forth. By the word "loko," the body and so forth that are grasped are themselves called the "world" (loka). It should be understood that these four foundations of mindfulness are taught as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

## Commentary on the Seven Requisites of Concentration (Sattasamādhiparikkhāravannanā)
In the term "samādhiparikkhārā," there are three types of requisites (parikkhāra). In the passage "The chariot has virtue as its equipment (sīlaparikkhāro)," "parikkhāra" means ornament (alaṅkāra). In the passage "well-fortified with seven city-requisites (nagaraparikkhārehi)," "parikkhāra" means retinue or surroundings (parivāra). In the passage "medicinal requisites for the sick (gilānapaccayajīvitaparikkhāro)," "parikkhāra" means necessities or equipment (sambhāra). Here, however, "seven requisites of concentration" is said by way of the "retinue" (parivāra) requisite. "Parikkhatā" means surrounded. "Ayaṃ vuccati so ariyo sammāsamādhi" means this concentration, like a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) surrounded by the seven jewels, is [surrounded] by the seven factors...
239:
Concentration that is surrounded [by other factors] is called "Noble Right Concentration." It is also called "sa-upanisa" because it has a basis, and "sa-parivāra" (or sa-upanissaya) because it is accompanied by requisites; the meaning is that it exists only together with its requisites. "Sammādiṭṭhissa" means for one who is established in Right View. "Sammāsaṅkappo pahoti" means Right Intention arises. This method should be understood for all terms. Furthermore, this meaning should be understood by way of the Path (Magga) and by way of the Fruit (Phala). How? For one established in Path Right View, Path Right Intention arises... for one established in Path Knowledge, Path Liberation (Vimutti) arises. Similarly, for one established in Fruit Right View, Fruit Right Intention arises... for one established in Fruit Knowledge, Fruit Liberation arises.

The terms beginning with "Svākkhāto" have already been explained in the Visuddhimagga. "Apārutā" means opened. "Amatassa" means of Nibbāna. "Dvārā" means the Paths which are the means of entry. "Aveccappasādena" means with unwavering confidence. "Dhammavinitā" means those who are led out by the true liberating Dhamma.

The phrase "Atthāyaṃ itarā pajā" is spoken with reference to Non-returners (Anāgāmīs); the meaning is that Non-returners exist. "Puññabhāgā" means those who are arisen through a portion of merit. "Ottappaṃ" refers to one who possesses moral dread. By that statement, he shows: "I am unable to count them because of the fear of false speech, thinking 'perhaps at some time there might be a falsehood'; it is not that I lack the power to count."

With the words "Taṃ kiṃ manyati bhavaṃ," he is merely questioning King Vessavaṇa. It is not that he holds the view that such a Teacher did not exist or will not exist. This is because there is no difference in the realization (abhisamaya) of all Buddhas.

"Sayaṃparisāyaṃ" means in one's own assembly. "Tayidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ" means this entire holy life of the three trainings (sikkhā). The remaining words are clear. These words were established by the Elders who performed the Dhamma Recitation.

## The Commentary on the Janavasabha Sutta is finished.
240:
## 6. Commentary on the Mahāgovinda Sutta

"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Mahāgovinda Sutta. In that sutta, the explanation of the obscure terms is as follows: "Pañcasikha" means one with five topknots or five earrings. It is said that in his human life, at the time of performing meritorious deeds, while he was a young boy with five topknots, he was a leader of cowherds. Taking other boys with him, he wandered about performing such merits as building rest houses at crossroads outside the village, digging ponds, constructing bridges, leveling uneven roads, and removing trees that obstructed the axles of carts, and he passed away while still young. That existence (attabhāva) of his was dear, pleasant, and delightful. After passing away, he was reborn in the Cātumahārājikā celestial realm with a lifespan of nine million years. His physical form was three gāvutas in height and resembled a mass of pure gold. He wandered about adorned with ornaments equivalent to a thousand carts, anointed with perfumes equivalent to nine new jars, wearing celestial red cloth, wearing red-gold earrings, and with five earrings surrounding his back, just like the appearance of a young boy with five topknots. Therefore, they know him as "Pañcasikha."

"Abhikkantāya rattiyā" means when the night had passed, or when the first watch of the night had passed. "Abhikkantavaṇṇo" means one who has an extremely dear, pleasant, and delightful complexion. By nature, this deity had a beautiful complexion, but because he came adorned, he became one of surpassing beauty. "Kevalakappaṃ" means entirely, in the whole surroundings without remainder. Here, the word "kevala" means without remainder, as in the term "kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ." The word "kappa" means surroundings, as in the terms "kevalakappaṃ Jetavanaṃ" and so forth. "Obhāsetvā" means having suffused with radiance, making the whole area a single mass of radiance and a single light, like the moon or the sun.

## Description of the Celestial Assembly

"Sudhammāyaṃ sabhāyaṃ" refers to the assembly hall arisen from the essence of a jewel-like Kaṇikāra tree belonging to a woman named Sudhammā. It is said that the floor of that hall is made of crystal and the pillars are made of rubies.
243:
The seat of the Great King of Gods is prepared. Then the seats of the thirty-three celestial youths are prepared, followed by the seats of other powerful deities. For other deities, however, the flower pollen itself serves as their seat.

The deities enter the celestial assembly and sit down. Then, masses of pollen emerge from the flowers, strike the pinnacle above, and fall down, making the three-gāvuta-tall bodies of the deities appear as if they were adorned with lac dye. Their play lasts for four months. Thus, the assembly gathers to enjoy the play of the Pāricchattaka flowers.

On the eighth day of each month, a proclamation for hearing the Great Dhamma is made in the celestial realm. In that Sudhammā assembly hall, either the Mahābrahmā Sanatkumāra, or Sakka the King of Gods, or a Dhamma-preaching monk, or another Dhamma-preaching celestial youth delivers a Dhamma discourse.

On the eighth day of the waxing and waning moon, the ministers of the Four Great Kings; on the fourteenth day, their sons; and on the fifteenth day, the Four Great Kings themselves go out, taking golden plates and cinnabar, and wander through villages, market towns, and royal capitals. They record on the golden plates with cinnabar: "Such a woman or man has gone to the Buddha for refuge, has gone to the Dhamma for refuge, has gone to the Saṅgha for refuge. They observe the five precepts. They keep the eight Uposatha days each month. They support their mother; they support their father. In such a place, an offering was made with a hundred handfuls of lotuses. A thousand lamps were lit. They listened to the Dhamma at an improper time. They donated tiered umbrellas, flower altars, enclosure walls, lion thrones, and lion-staircases. They fulfill the three types of good conduct. They undertake and practice the ten courses of meritorious action." They then bring these and place them in the hands of the celestial youth Pañcasikha. Pañcasikha places them in the hands of Mātali. Mātali the charioteer gives them to Sakka, the King of Gods.

When those who perform meritorious deeds are not many, the golden book is small. Seeing that, the gods are displeased, thinking, "Alas, sirs, the great multitude of people live heedlessly; the four woeful states will be filled, and the six celestial realms will be empty." But if the book is large, seeing that, the gods rejoice, thinking, "Alas, sirs, the great multitude of people live heedfully; the four woeful states will be empty..."
244:
...the six celestial realms will be filled. They will rejoice, thinking, 'We shall have the opportunity to celebrate the festival of the stars, surrounded by those of great merit who have come after performing meritorious deeds in the Buddha's Dispensation.' Sakka, the king of devas, takes that book and reads it. His voice, speaking normally, spreads for twelve yojanas. When he speaks with a loud voice, it remains covering the entire ten-thousand-yojana city of the devas. Thus, they assemble to hear the Dhamma. However, it should be understood that here they have assembled to support the Pavāraṇā. 'Paying homage to the Tathāgata' means paying homage to the Tathāgata through nine reasons. 'The goodness of the Dhamma' refers to the excellence of the Dhamma, such as its being well-proclaimed (svākkhāta). 'The good conduct of the Saṅgha' refers to the good practice of the Saṅgha, such as practicing uprightly (ujuppaṭipanna).

## Commentary on Yathābhuccha

Yathābhuccha means as it truly is, according to its nature. Vaṇṇa means virtue or quality. Payirudāhāsi means he spoke. 'He practiced for the benefit of many'—how did he practice? Even while making the aspiration (abhinīhāra) for Buddhahood by combining the eight factors at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, he was practicing for the benefit of many. While fulfilling these ten perfections (pāramīs)—the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramī), virtue (sīla-pāramī), renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī), wisdom (paññā-pāramī), energy (viriya-pāramī), patience (khanti-pāramī), truthfulness (sacca-pāramī), determination (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī), loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī), and equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī)—for four incalculable periods (asankhyeyyas) and a hundred thousand aeons (kappas), he was indeed practicing for the benefit of many.

While performing such difficult deeds during his lives as the ascetic Khantivādī, Prince Cūḷadhammapāla, the elephant king Chaddanta, the naga kings Bhūridatta, Campeyya, and Saṅkhapāla, and the monkey king Mahākapi, he was indeed practicing for the benefit of many. While existing in the life of Vessantara, giving the great gift of seven hundred items, causing the earth to shake in seven places, and reaching the pinnacle of the perfections, he was indeed practicing for the benefit of many. Furthermore, while staying in the Tusita heaven for the full lifespan in the life immediately following that, he was indeed practicing for the benefit of many. Having seen the five preliminary omens there, being requested by the devas and brahmas of the ten thousand world-systems, having conducted the five great investigations (mahāvilokana), and giving his promise to support the devas and brahmas...
245:
...while passing away from the Tusita heaven and taking conception in his mother's womb, he was indeed practicing for the benefit of the many. While staying in his mother's womb for ten months and emerging from it in the Lumbinī grove; while living as a householder for twenty-nine years, departing on the Great Renunciation, and ordaining on the banks of the Anomā River; while exhausting himself through six years of austerities (dukkharacariyā), ascending the Bodhi-seat (pallanka), and penetrating the Knowledge of Omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa); while spending the seven weeks (satta-sattāha) at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); while going to Migadāya and turning the peerless Wheel of Dhamma; while performing the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya); while descending from the celestial realm; while remaining for forty-five years after becoming a Buddha; while relinquishing the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra); and while entering Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu) between the twin Sal trees—he was indeed practicing for the benefit of the many. It should be understood that as long as his relics, even as small as mustard seeds, remain, he is practicing for the benefit of the many. The remaining terms are synonyms of this phrase 'practiced for the benefit of the many' (bahujanahitāya paṭipanno). In this context, each subsequent term explains the meaning of the preceding one.

'We see neither in the past nor now' means that in the past, we see no one other than the Buddha; in the future, we see no one; and as for the present, because there is no other Teacher (Satthu), we see no one else besides that Blessed One. This is the meaning here. For in the Commentary, it is said: 'The Buddhas of the past and future are just like our Teacher; what is Sakka saying?' Having reflected thus, it is stated: 'At present, there is no other teacher who practices for the benefit of the many except our Teacher; therefore, he says "we do not see".' Just as in this instance, the meaning should be understood in the subsequent terms as well. Terms like 'well-expounded' (svākkhāta) and 'wholesome' (kusala) have the meanings already mentioned.

'As the water of the Ganges (is compared) with the water of the Yamunā' means that at the confluence of the Ganges and Yamunā, the waters coincide and merge in color, smell, and taste; they become of a single nature like molten gold in the middle, not dissimilar as when mixed with the water of the great ocean. The path (paṭipadā) to the pure Nibbāna is also pure. Indeed, one cannot see Nibbāna in old age after having performed medical work and the like in one's youth and frequented improper places; rather, the path leading to Nibbāna must be pure, like the sky. Just as the sky is unattached and pure, and just as the moon and sun travel to whatever place they desire in the sky, so too the path of a monk going to Nibbāna, whether in a family or a group...
247:
“We shall get our turn; we shall provide the meal there” (Mahāvagga 282). In this way, many stories in other Khandhakas and the Vinaya should be understood.

In the Asadisa-dāna (Incomparable Alms-giving), however, this gain and honor reached the pinnacle. On one occasion, after the Blessed One had wandered through the countryside and arrived at Jetavana Monastery, the King invited Him and offered alms. On the second day, the citizens offered alms. Then, the King gave more than they did, and the citizens gave more than the King; in this manner, as many days passed, the King thought: “These citizens are doing more and more every day. Although I am the King who rules the earth, it will be a matter of reproach if I am defeated by the citizens in alms-giving.” Then, Queen Mallikā told the King of a plan. The King had a pavilion built in the palace courtyard with precious Sal wood, covered it with blue lotuses, and arranged five hundred seats. He placed five hundred elephants behind the seats and had each elephant hold a white umbrella over each monk. Between every two seats, a princess adorned with all kinds of ornaments ground four types of fragrant perfumes. Whenever the grinding was finished, she put it into a perfume jar in the center, and another princess stirred it with a bunch of blue lotuses. In this way, each monk was attended by three princesses. Another woman adorned with all kinds of ornaments held a palm-leaf fan and fanned them; another held a water-strainer and filtered the water; another brought water from the bowl. For the Blessed One, there were four priceless items: a footstool, a stand, a backrest, and a gem for the umbrella handle; these four were priceless items. The gift for the youngest monk in the order of the Saṅgha was worth one hundred thousand. In that alms-giving, Elder Aṅgulimāla was the youngest in the order of the Saṅgha. The elephant brought near the Elder’s seat did not dare to approach the Elder. They reported this matter to the King. The King asked, “Is there no other elephant?” They replied, “There is a fierce elephant, but it is not possible to bring him.” The Blessed One asked, “Great King, who is the youngest monk in the order of the Saṅgha?” “It is Elder Aṅgulimāla, Blessed One,” he replied. “Great King, if that is so, adorn that fierce elephant and bring him to stay there.” They adorned the elephant and brought him. Due to the Elder’s power and majesty, that elephant did not even dare to let air out of its nose. In this way, alms were given continuously for seven days. On the seventh day, the King paid homage to the Blessed One and said, “Blessed One, please preach the Dhamma to me.”
248:
In that assembly, there were two ministers named Kāḷa and Juṇha. The minister Kāḷa thought: “The property of the royal family is being destroyed. What will so many people do? After eating, they will just go to the monastery and sleep. If a single royal servant received this property, what could he not do? Oh, the King’s property is indeed being destroyed!” The minister Juṇha, however, thought: “This kingship is truly great. Who else would be able to give such an alms? How can one be called a king if, even while established in kingship, he cannot give such an alms?” When the Blessed One looked into the inclinations of the assembly, He knew the inclinations of those two ministers and thought: “If I preach the Dhamma today according to Juṇha’s inclination, Kāḷa’s head will split into seven pieces. I have fulfilled the Perfections out of compassion for living beings. Juṇha will penetrate the Paths and Fruits when I preach the Dhamma on another day; for now, I will show consideration for Kāḷa.” Thus, He preached to the King a discourse consisting of only one verse:

“The miserly do not go to the world of the gods,
Fools indeed do not praise giving,
But the wise man, rejoicing in giving,
Through that very act, becomes happy hereafter.” (Dhammapada 177)

The King, being displeased, thought: “I have given a Great Alms (Mahādāna), yet the Teacher preached only a little Dhamma to me. I suppose I was unable to win the heart of the One of Ten Powers.” After eating his morning meal, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Blessed One, and asked: “Blessed One, I have given a great alms, but the rejoicing (Anumodanā) was not made great for me. Blessed One, what is my fault?” “Great King, there is no fault in you; it is only that the assembly was not pure. Therefore, I did not preach the Dhamma,” He said. When asked, “Blessed One, why was the assembly not pure?” the Teacher told him of the thoughts of the two ministers. The King asked Kāḷa, “Dear Kāḷa, is it true that you thought this?” “It is true, Great King,” he replied. “While I am giving my own property, which part of you is hurting? I no longer wish to see you; banish him from my country!” he ordered. Then he had Juṇha called and asked, “Dear son, is it true that you thought this?” “It is true, Great King,” he replied. “Let it be according to your heart’s desire,” the King said, and having five hundred monks sit on the seats arranged in that very pavilion, surrounded by those same princesses, he took wealth from the royal house and...
249: "Give an offering similar to the one I have given for seven days," (he said). He gave accordingly. Having given on the seventh day, he requested, "Venerable Sir, please preach the Dhamma." The Blessed One, performing the appreciation (anumodanā) for both offerings together, preached a great Dhamma discourse like two great rivers overflowing with a swift current. At the end of the discourse, Juṇha became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). The King, being inspired with faith, offered an external gift called bāhiravatthu to the Dasabala Buddha. Thus, it should be understood that gain and honor arose specifically for that Blessed One. "Abhinnapphanno siloko" means the praising of virtues and qualities. That reputation also arose specifically from the time the Blessed One turned the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattana). From then on, kings spoke of the Blessed One's virtues. Brahmins, householders, Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Gandhabbas, Devas, and Brahmās also spoke of his fame, starting with "Itipi so bhagavā..." Other sectarians gave a thousand coins to Vararoja and sent him, saying, "Speak blame of the ascetic Gotama." He took the thousand coins and looked at the Dasabala Buddha from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair, but seeing not even a fault the size of a louse's egg, he thought: "The mouth of one who speaks blame of this faultless body—adorned with the 32 marks of a Great Man and the 80 minor characteristics, surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance, resembling the Nandana Grove beautiful with diverse flowers, the sky shining with clusters of stars, and the fully blossomed Pāricchattaka tree—would be twisted, and his head would split into seven pieces. There is no way to speak blame; I will only speak praise." Thus, from the soles of the feet to the tips of the hair, he spoke only praise with more than a thousand verses. At the time of the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), however, this praise reached its pinnacle. This is the meaning of "Abhinnapphanno siloko." "Yāva maññe khattiyā" means that kings, brahmins, vessas, suddas, Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Yakkhas, Asuras, Devas, and Brahmās all live joyfully and delighted, with an appearance of affection. "Vigatamado kho pana" means that the Blessed One does not consume food out of intoxication or heedlessness, thinking, "So many people live with an appearance of affection for me," nor for the sake of play; rather, that Blessed One consumes food entirely free from intoxication.
250: "Yathāvādī" means that as one speaks with words, so is one's bodily action. As one acts with the body, so is one's verbal action. The body does not contradict the speech, nor the speech the body; speech conforms to the body, and the body to speech. For example: "With the left side, he is like a pig; With the right side, like a goat; With the voice, like a calf; With the horns, like an old ox." This Pig-Ogre (Sūkarayakkha), seeing pigs, shows his left side which resembles a pig and catches and eats them. Seeing goats, he shows his right side which resembles them and catches and eats them. Seeing calves, he makes a sound like a calf and catches and eats them. Seeing oxen, he creates horns resembling theirs, and when they approach from afar thinking "He looks like an ox," he catches and eats them. It is also like the crow in the Dhammikavāyasa Jātaka who was questioned by birds. That crow said, "I feed only on wind; because I feed on wind, I keep my mouth open; fearing the death of small creatures, I stand on only one leg. Therefore, you too: 'Practice the Dhamma; may it be well with you. O kinsmen, practice the Dhamma. One who practices the Dhamma sleeps happily in this world and the next.'" Thus he inspired confidence in the birds. Then: "This bird is truly good; This bird is supremely righteous; Standing on one leg, He speaks, 'Dhamma, Dhamma.'" In this way, he ate the birds who had come to trust him. Their speech did not conform to their body, nor their body to their speech. It is not so with the Blessed One. It shows that the Blessed One's speech truly conforms to his body, and his body to his speech. One who has crossed over and transcended lack of faith (vicikicchā) is called "Tiṇṇavicikiccho." One who is free from doubt (kathaṅkathā) in the form of "How is this? How is that?" is called "Vigatakathaṅkatho." For the general public [asks]: "This is a tree; what is a tree? This is a village; this is a district; this is a country; what is a country? Why is this tree's trunk straight and this one's crooked? Why are some thorns straight and some crooked? Why are some flowers fragrant and some foul-smelling? The fruit..."
251:
"Some things are sweet, some are not sweet"—others have such doubts, but not the Teacher. Indeed, the Teacher is one who has removed all doubt, [knowing] "Because of the predominance of these elements, this is so." It is like those who have attained the first jhāna etc., having doubt regarding the second jhāna etc. Even for Paccekabuddhas, because they lack the definitive realization of Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa), there is still doubt in terms of conventional usage; but not so for the Buddha. This shows that the Blessed One has removed all doubt in all matters.

"One whose intentions are fulfilled" (Pariyosita-saṅkappa) means: some reach the end of their intentions and have their desires fulfilled through mere virtue, some through mere insight, some through the first jhāna... (p)... some through the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, some through the mere state of a stream-enterer... (p)... some through Arahatship, some through the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa), and some through the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa). But my Teacher is not like that. It shows that my Teacher has reached the end of his intentions through Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).

"Ajjhāsayaṃ ādibrahmacariyaṃ" is in the nominative case with the sense of instrument. It means one who has crossed over doubt, is free from doubt, and has reached the end of his intentions through a noble aspiration which is a supreme support, and through the Noble Path (Ariyamagga) which is the ancient holy life. Because of the statement, "He himself fully realized the Truths among dhammas never heard before, and therein attained Omniscience and mastery over the Powers," the fulfillment of the Blessed One's intentions is also accomplished through the Noble Path.

"Just like the Blessed One" (Yathariva Bhagavā) means exactly like the Blessed One. Thus, people speak with longing, "Oh, if only four Victors (Jinas) were wandering in the four directions on this surface of Jambudīpa and teaching the Dhamma, it would be wonderful!" Then others, desiring them to wander together in the three regions (maṇဍala), spoke of three Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas. Others, thinking, "Having fulfilled the ten perfections, the arising of four or three is very difficult; but if one Buddha were to reside permanently and teach the Dhamma, and another were to wander, in this way Jambudīpa would be beautiful and many would attain benefit and happiness," said, "Friends, it would be very good!"

In the phrase "Aṭṭhānametaṃ anavakāso yaṃ," both "ṭhāna" and "avakāsa" are synonyms for "cause" (kāraṇa). A cause is called "ṭhāna" because the result stays there, depending on it. It is called "avakāsa" because it is like an opportunity, as the result cannot occur elsewhere without that cause. "Yaṃ" is in the nominative case with the sense of instrument. This is the meaning...
252:
...it means: "There is no cause or reason why two Buddhas should arise together in a single world system (loka-dhātu)."

And here—
"As far as the sun and moon revolve, illuminating the quarters with their radiance, so far does the thousandfold world extend; therein your power is exercised." (M. Ni. 1.503)—
In this verse, a single world system (cakkavāḷa) is called one world system (loka-dhātu). In the passage, "The thousandfold world system (sahassī loka-dhātu) shook" (A. Ni. 3.126), a thousand world systems are called one world system. In the passage, "Ānanda, if the Tathāgata wishes, he could make his voice heard throughout the three-thousandfold great thousand world system (ti-sahassī-mahā-sahassī loka-dhātu) and pervade it with his radiance" (A. Ni. 3.81), the three-thousandfold great thousand (one hundred billion world systems) is called one world system. In the passage, "This is the ten-thousandfold world system" (M. Ni. 3.201), ten thousand world systems are called one world system. Referring to that (ten thousand world systems), he said "in a single world system." This much is called the "birth-field" (jāti-khetta). Even in that birth-field, Buddhas do not arise anywhere else except in the Middle Country (Majjhima-desa) of Jambudīpa in this world system. Outside of the birth-field, the place of arising for Buddhas is not known (does not exist). "Yenathena" means by the sense of invitation and support.

## Commentary on the Talk of Sanankumāra
"Vaṇṇena ceva yasasā ca" means with the retinue of ornaments and with the glory of merit.

In the phrase "Sādhu mahābrahme," the word "Sādhu" is used in the sense of appreciation (sampasādana). "Saṅkhāya modāmā" means we rejoice having known.

## Commentary on the Story of Govinda the Brahmin
"Yāva dīgharattaṃ mahāpañño va so Bhagavā" means it is not possible to limit it by saying "only this much"; rather, the Blessed One has been one of great wisdom for a very long time. "No" means "What do you think?" Then, wishing to answer the question himself, he said, "Friends, it is not a wonder that now..."
253:
Having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) and crushed the heads of the three Māras (or five Māras) upon the throne of enlightenment (bodhi-pallaṅka), and having penetrated the uncommon knowledge (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), it is no wonder that the Blessed One is of great wisdom. 'O friends, I shall show you how I was of great wisdom even during the time when I was still possessed of passion and established in partial knowledge (padesa-ñāṇa) before the enlightenment had matured,' he said, bringing forth the hidden cause of his past life, beginning with 'Bhūtapubbaṃ bhoti' (Once upon a time...).

'Purohita' refers to the advisory chaplain (anusāsanī-purohita) who instructs in all matters. 'Govinda' refers to one who has been consecrated with the Govindiya-consecration; his original name was different, but from the time of his consecration, he became known as 'Govinda.' 'Jotipāla' is so named because of his shining (jotana) and his protecting (pālana). On the day he was born, all weapons shone brightly. The King, seeing his auspicious weapons glowing at dawn, stood in fear. Govinda went to attend the King in the early morning and asked if he had slept well. The King replied, 'Teacher, how could I have slept well?' and told him the reason. Govinda said, 'Great King, do not fear; a son has been born to me, and by his power, the weapons throughout the city are glowing.' The King thought, 'Will this boy become my enemy?' and became even more afraid. When asked, 'Great King, what are you thinking?' he told him the reason. Then Govinda reassured him, 'Great King, do not fear; this boy will not harm you. Indeed, in the whole of Jambudīpa, there will be no one equal to him in wisdom. By my son's words, the doubts of the multitude will be severed, and he will advise you in all matters.' The King was pleased and gave a thousand coins, saying, 'Let this be for the boy's milk-money,' and added, 'Show the boy to me when he is grown.' The boy grew up in due course. Because of his shining and his ability to protect, they named him 'Jotipāla.' Thus it is said, 'He is called Jotipāla because of his shining and his protecting.'

'Sammā vossajjitvā' means having relinquished well. There is also such a reading. 'Alamatthadasataro' means one who is capable and sees the benefit (alamatthadasa); because he can decide better than those who see the benefit, he is called 'alamatthadasatara.' 'Jotipālassēva māṇavassa anusāsaniyā' indicates that he too consults only Jotipāla for instruction.
254:
'Bhava-m-atthu bhavantaṃ Jotipālaṃ' means may there be prosperity, the attainment of distinction in Dhamma, and all goodness and auspiciousness for the venerable Jotipāla. 'Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ' (courteous talk)—what is it? It means concluding the consoling conversation that dispels grief related to death, in this manner: 'Enough, Great King, do not worry; this is the constant law for all beings,' and so on. 'Mā no bhavaṃ Jotipālo anusāsaniyā paccabyāhāsī' means do not speak back; it means when asked to 'instruct,' do not refuse our instruction by saying 'I cannot instruct.' 'Abhisambhosi' means he arranged and established. 'Manussā evamāhaṃsu' (people spoke thus): seeing that he was wiser than his father, instructing in all matters and accomplishing all tasks, they were pleased and said, 'O friends, the Brahmin Govinda is wonderful indeed! O friends, the Brahmin Mahāgovinda is wonderful indeed!' The meaning is: 'O friends, this one's father was the Brahmin Govinda, but this one is indeed the Brahmin Mahāgovinda (Great Govinda).'

## Description of the Division of the Kingdom

'Yena te cha khattiyā' refers to those six nobles who were called 'friends.' It is said they were the younger brothers of King Reṇu, born of the same father. Therefore, Mahāgovinda, thinking, 'Will this king divide the kingdom for them after his consecration or not? It would be better if I send them to King Reṇu beforehand to obtain a promise,' approached the place where those six nobles were. 'Rājakattāro' refers to the ministers who appoint the king.

'Madanīya kāmā' refers to the sensual pleasures that cause intoxication and negligence. As time goes by, one might not even be able to remember this matter; therefore, it means 'Come, sirs, please come.'

'Sarāmahaṃ bho' (I remember, sir): that was a time when people spoke the truth. Therefore, without saying what was untrue like 'When did I say it? Who saw it? Who heard it?', he said, 'Friend, I remember.' 'Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ' is the courteous talk of this nature: 'Great King, do not worry when the King has passed away; this is the constant law for all beings; conditioned things (saṅkhāras) are of such a nature.' 'Sabbāni sakaṭamukhāni paṭṭhapesi' means all the...
255:
He established the six kingdoms like the front of a wagon (facing the center). Each king's kingdom was three hundred yojanas in extent; the area where they met with King Reṇu's kingdom was ten gāvutas, and in the center, King Reṇu's kingdom was like a canopy. Why was it established in this way? It was with the intention that when they came to see the King from time to time, they would come and go through their own territories without encroaching on another's kingdom. For one who enters another's kingdom and says, "Give me food, give me an ox," the people complain, "These kings do not travel through their own domains but oppress us." But for one who travels through his own domain, the people do not consider it oppression, thinking, "This person should indeed receive this and that from us." Considering this benefit, Mahāgovinda established it thus, saying, "May the kings rule their kingdoms for a long time in harmony."

"Dantapura of the Kaliṅgas, Potana of the Assakas,
Māhissati of the Avantis, Roduka of the Sovīras,
Mithilā of the Videhas, Campā built among the Aṅgas,
And Bārāṇasī of the Kāsīs—these were built by Govinda."

These seven cities were built by Mahāgovinda himself for the benefit of those kings.

"Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, Vessabhū together with Bharata,
Reṇu, and the two Dhataraṭṭhas—these were the seven Bhāradhas at that time."

These are the names of those seven kings. Among them, one was named Sattabhū, one Brahmadatta, one Vessabhū, one Bharata along with him, one Reṇu, and two were named Dhataraṭṭha. These seven were the Great Kings (Mahārājas) who took responsibility for the kingdoms on the surface of Jambudīpa.

## The Explanation of the First Recitation Section is Finished.
257:
"Approached where King Reṇu was" means he approached for the purpose of cutting off obstacles, thinking, "In this way, there will be no one who wishes to see me or talk to me in the interval; since the obstacles and anxieties are cut off, I shall live happily." This method applies to all places.

Sādisiyo means those of similar appearance and similar birth.

Having a new hall (santhāgāra) built means having a wonderful dwelling built that is equipped for staying during the night, staying during the day, and for walking meditation; suitable for living throughout the four months of the rainy season; and surrounded by reeds on the outside. "Meditates on the jhāna of compassion" means he meditates on the third and fourth jhānas through compassion. Here, with compassion as the lead, the other three divine abodes (brahmavihāras) are also included. "Anxiety and longing" means for one established in the stage of jhāna, there is no anxiety from dissatisfaction or trembling from fear; it means there was only the longing for the Brahma's coming, the craving for him to come.

## The Explanation of the Conversation with Brahma

Fear means the fear of mental agitation. "Not knowing" means those who do not know. "How shall we know him?" means "How shall we know him? Where does this person live? What is his name? What is his clan?"—among such aspects, "By what aspect shall we recognize him?" is the meaning.

"They know me as Kumāra" means they know me as "Kumāra" (the Youth) or as "the Young One." "In the Brahma world" means in the noble world. Sanaṃtana means ancient or old. It shows, "I am that ancient Kumāra, the Brahma named Sanaṅkumāra." "Govinda, know thus" means "O wise Govinda, you should know thus; recognize me in this way."

"Seat, water, foot-washing water, and vegetables mixed with honey (are offered) to the Brahma.
We ask the Venerable One about the offering; may the Venerable One accept our offering."

Here, aggha refers to the gift to be presented before a guest. Therefore, "This seat has been prepared; please sit here. This water is pure; drink the drinking water from here. Wash your feet. This foot-washing water (pajja) is oil prepared for the benefit of the feet; anoint the feet with this oil. This is vegetables mixed with honey." The holy life (brahmacariya) of a Bodhisatta is not like the holy life of others. That Bodhisatta does not think, "This will be for tomorrow, this will be for the third day"...
259:
"One who practices" refers to one who is practicing these dhammas. This is a brief explanation here; the detailed version was already spoken above by Mahāgovinda and the Brahmā.

In that verse, "not knowing these things" means "I do not know, I do not understand these āmagandha (foul smells/defilements)." "O wise one, tell me here" means "O wise and learned sir, tell me, speak to me of those things here." "By what is it covered? Why do beings smell foul?" is a question asking: by what kind of hindrance of defilements are beings covered so that they emit a putrid odor? "Bound for states of woe" means one who goes to the states of deprivation (apāya). "One for whom the Brahma-world is closed" means the Brahma-world is closed and obstructed for that person. It is a question asking: by what kind of defilement is the path of beings to the Brahma-world closed, obstructed, and concealed?

"Anger, falsehood, deceit, and treachery" refers to kodha characterized by anger, musāvāda characterized by deceiving others, nikati characterized by trickery through showing something similar, and dubbha characterized by betraying friends. "Stinginess, arrogance, and envy" refers to kadariyatā characterized by harsh miserliness, atimāna characterized by thinking oneself superior to others, and usūyā characterized by the desire to destroy the prosperity of others. "Desire, selfishness, and oppressing others" refers to icchā characterized by craving (taṇhā), vivicchā characterized by stinginess (macchariya), and paraheṭhanā characterized by violence (vihiṃsā). "Greed, hatred, pride, and delusion" refers to lobha characterized by attachment to anything, dosa characterized by destructiveness, mada characterized by intoxication, and moha characterized by bewilderment. "Those associated with these things are not free from foul smells (āmagandha)" means that beings associated with these fourteen defilements are not free from foul smells; they are indeed those with foul smells, smelling like a rotting corpse, having a putrid odor. "Bound for states of woe, for whom the Brahma-world is closed" means that such a person is both bound for states of deprivation and has the path to the Brahma-world concealed. When teaching this sutta, it should be explained by comparing it with the Āmagandha Sutta, and the Āmagandha Sutta should also be explained by comparing it with this sutta.

"Those things are not easily subdued" means those āmagandha (defilements) are not easily subdued or abandoned; they are difficult to give up and difficult to conquer. "Now, Lord Govinda, whatever time you deem fit" means "Lord Govinda, whatever time you deem fit for renunciation, let it be so. In this way, my coming to you will be a good coming, and the Dhamma talk spoken will be well-spoken. Dear..."
260:
“The foremost man in the whole of Jambudīpa, remaining in the first stage of life, thus renouncing such great wealth, prosperity, and glory—your renunciation is exceedingly noble, like a state elephant breaking its iron chains and departing. This is the way to Buddhahood.” Having thus strengthened the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), the Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra returned to the Brahma-world.

## Explanation of the Address to King Reṇu

The Great Being also thought, “It is not proper for me to depart directly from here and renounce. I am the one who advises the royal family on their welfare; therefore, I will inform the King. If the King also follows and renounces, it would be very good. If he does not renounce, I will hand back the position of chaplain (purohita) and then renounce.” He then approached the King. Referring to that, it was said: “Then, sirs, Mahāgovinda... I do not delight in the chaplaincy,” and so on.

In those words, “Tvaṃ pajānassu rajjena” means “You yourself look after (manage) your kingship.” “Nāhaṃ porohicce rame” means “I do not delight in the state of being a chaplain; I am weary of it. Look for another advisor; I do not delight in the chaplaincy.”

Then the King thought, “The wealth in the house of the brahmin who has been in seclusion for four months must surely have become depleted,” and inviting him with wealth, he said, “If you are in need of sensual pleasures and wealth, I shall fulfill them for you.” Then again he thought, “Could this man have been harassed by someone while living alone?” and said—

“I shall prevent whoever harasses you; I am the commander of the earth (the King).
You are my father and I am your son; O Govinda, do not forsake us.”

The meaning of that verse is: I shall prevent whoever harasses you; you just tell me, “It is this person,” and I will know what must be done in this matter. “Bhūmisenāpati ahaṃ” means, alternatively, “I am the lord of the earth; as such, I shall hand over this kingdom to you yourself.” “Tuvaṃ pitā ahaṃ putto” means “You shall stand in the place of a father, and I shall stand in the place of a son.” Being so, O Govinda, lead my mind and drive (manage) it according to your own mind; let it be as you wish. As for me, I will follow only your mind, and consuming the alms-food given by you, I will serve you, even holding a sword and shield in my hand, or I will drive the chariot for you. “Mā no govinda pajahi” also means...
261:
This is the text. The meaning of that text is: "You stand in the place of a father; I shall stand in the place of a son. O Lord Govinda... do not forsake us, do not abandon us." Then, the Great Being (Mahāpurisa), wishing to show that what the King thought did not exist in him, said:

"I have no lack of sensual pleasures, and there is no one who harms me. Having heard the word of a non-human (amanussa), I cannot delight in the home."

In that verse, 'na matthi' means 'na me atthi' (I have not). 'Gahe' means 'gehe' (in the house). Then the King questioned that Brahmin Govinda:

"What is the appearance of the non-human? What beneficial words did he speak to you? Hearing which, do you completely abandon us, the home, and the entire Jambudīpa?"

In that verse, 'jahāsi no, gehe amhe ca kevalī' means that the King, regarding the Brahmin's house filled with wealth as his own house, says: "Hearing what word do you completely abandon our house, us, and all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa without exception?"

Then the Great Being, wishing to tell the King, spoke the words beginning with "upavutthassa me pubbe." In that context, 'upavutthassa' means for one who has reached the state of living in solitude for four months. 'Yiṭṭhakāmassa me sato' means while I was one desiring to make an offering. 'Aggi pajjalito āsi, kusapattaparitthato' means the fire was lit, being spread with kusa grass, and having added ghee, curd, honey, and so on, the fire was made to blaze. The meaning here is: for me who stood thinking, "I will give gifts to the great multitude," after having thus kindled the fire.

'Sanantano' refers to Sanankumāra Brahmā. Then the King, desiring to ordain himself, spoke the words beginning with "saddahāmi." In that context, 'kathaṃ vattetha aññathā' means how would you act in any other way? 'Te taṃ anuvattissāma' means we also will follow only you and practice; we will follow you and ordain. There is also a variant reading "anuvajissāma," the meaning of which is: we will follow. 'Akāco' means faultless, not rough. 'Govindassānusāsane' means in your teaching, Govinda. He says that they will practice having the Venerable Govinda alone as their teacher.
262:
## Commentary on the Addressing of the Six Khattiyas
'Where those six Khattiyas were, there they approached' means they approached King Reṇu and encouraged him, saying, "Noble Great King, it is very good. While beings take kingship by killing even their mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters, and so on, for the Great King to desire to ordain after abandoning such great royal glory is a noble deed performed by the Great King." Thus, they approached him, making his effort even firmer. 'Thus they thought together' means they thought together in the same manner as the King, perhaps thinking that at some time the Brahmin's wealth might have declined. 'We will entice with wealth' means we will persuade or support him. 'Let that much wealth be brought' means let that much wealth be caused to be brought or taken; it means, "Take as much as you desire."

'It is only because of you sirs' means taking you as the cause; it is only because of what was given by you that much wealth has arisen.

'If you abandon sensual pleasures' means if you renounce both objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma) and defiled sensuality (kilesa-kāma). 'In which the worldling is attached' means the worldling is stuck or clinging to those sensual pleasures. 'Exert effort, stand firm' means in this case, start the energy; having determined upon unslacked effort, be firm. 'Be endowed with the strength of patience' means be possessed of the strength of patience; thus he generates effort in the kings.

'This path is the straight path' means this path of the Jhana of Compassion (karuṇā-jhāna) is called the straight path. 'This path is unsurpassed' means this alone is the incomparable path, the supreme path for rebirth in the Brahma world. 'The Dhamma protected by the virtuous' means this is the Dhamma protected by the virtuous ones, namely the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples. Thus, by speaking of the virtues of the Jhana of Compassion, he makes their resolve firm so that they do not turn back.

'Sirs, who indeed knows the life of beings?' means, sirs, life is like a water bubble, like a dewdrop on the tip of a blade of grass, having the nature of perishing in a moment. Who knows its destination? At what moment will it break? 'The hereafter must surely be gone to' means the next world must certainly be gone to; in that regard, a wise son of a good family should understand with wisdom. 'Mantā' refers to wisdom (paññā); the meaning is that one should consult, understand, investigate, and know with that wisdom. Or, it is the locative case used in the sense of the instrumental. 'Should be understood with wisdom' means it should be understood by wisdom, known by knowledge. What should be understood? The fact that life is difficult to know...
263:
Knowing the certainty of having to go to the afterlife, one should cut off all obstacles and perform merit; one should practice the holy life. Why? Because for a being who is born, there is no such thing as immortality.

## Commentary on the Addressing of the Great Wealthy Brahmins and Others
'Having few followers and few gains' means, friends, that the state of a monk has very little fame. From the time of renunciation, even one who renounces the throne is oppressed and spoken of as a lowly, helpless person. Gains are also very few; even after wandering through an entire village, it is difficult to obtain food. This state of a Brahmin, however, brings great fame due to having a large following, and great gains due to being endowed with offerings and honor. At present, you are the supreme chaplain in the entire island of Jambudīpa, receiving the best seat, the best water, the best food, the best scent, and the best flowers in all places.

'Like a king among kings' means: 'At present, I am like a Wheel-turning Monarch among ordinary kings.' 'Like a Brahma among Brahmas' means: 'I am like Mahābrahmā among ordinary Brahmas.' 'Like a deity among householders' means: 'I am like Sakka, the king of devas, among the remaining householders.'

## Commentary on the Addressing of the Wives
'There are forty equal wives' means there are forty wives of equal status; furthermore, there are many dancing women in the three stages of life.

## Commentary on the Renunciation of Mahāgovinda
'He wanders on tour' means he wanders on tour through villages and towns in succession. Wherever he goes, there is a commotion like the appearance of a Buddha. When people hear that 'the wise Mahāgovinda is coming,' they build pavilions in advance, decorate the roads, and go out to welcome and receive him. Great gains and honors arise, overwhelming like a great flood. 'To the chaplain of the seven kings' means he was the chaplain to seven kings. Just as now, when some suffering arises in such places, people say 'Homage to the Buddha,' at that time they said, 'Homage to the Brahmin Mahāgovinda, homage to the chaplain of the seven kings.'
264:
Although the Divine Abodes (Brahmavihāra) starting with 'accompanied by loving-kindness' are the only ones mentioned in the Pali text, the Bodhisatta (Mahāpurisa) actually developed all eight meditative attainments and five supernormal powers. 'He showed his disciples the way to companionship with the Brahma world' means he taught the path for the sake of being with Brahma in the Brahma world.

'In every way' refers to those who developed the eight meditative attainments and five supernormal powers. 'Those who did not understand the teaching in every way' refers to those who did not know even one of the eight meditative attainments and were unable to develop them. 'Not fruitless' means being accompanied by its result. 'Not in vain' means it is not empty. 'Produces the lowest result' means it leads to rebirth in the Gandhabba realm. 'Fruitful' means it is beneficial through rebirth in the remaining deva worlds. 'Accompanied by increase' means it is accompanied by growth through rebirth in the Brahma world.

'I, Pañcasikha, remember'—by this phrase, this Sutta is known as the word of the Buddha (Buddhabhāsita). 'Not for disenchantment' means not for the sake of disenchantment with the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa). 'Not for dispassion' means not for the sake of dispassion toward the round of rebirths. 'Not for cessation' means not for the sake of the cessation of the round of rebirths. 'Not for peace' means not for the sake of the calming of the round of rebirths. 'Not for higher knowledge' means not for the sake of knowing the round of rebirths with higher knowledge. 'Not for enlightenment' means not for the sake of awakening from the round of rebirths by dispelling the sleep of defilements. 'Not for Nibbāna' means not for the sake of the deathless Nibbāna.

'For absolute disenchantment' means for the sake of absolute disenchantment with the round of rebirths. Here, 'for disenchantment' refers to insight (vipassanā). 'For dispassion' refers to the Path (magga). 'For cessation' and 'for peace' refer to Nibbāna. 'For higher knowledge' and 'for enlightenment' refer to the Path. 'For Nibbāna' refers to Nibbāna itself. Thus, the definitive explanation should be understood as: insight is mentioned in one place, the Path in three places, and Nibbāna in three places. Figuratively, however, all of these are synonyms for both the Path and Nibbāna. What should be said regarding Right View and so on has already been stated in the 'Explanation of the Truths' in the Visuddhimagga.

'Those who did not know in every way' refers to those who did not know how to fulfill all four Noble Paths, but developed only three, two, or one. 'To all these sons of good family' refers to the sons of good family who practiced the holy life. He concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship, saying 'Not fruitless... fruitful, accompanied by increase.'
267:
"What will they do to us?" they said. They went and told the ministers appointed to that task, and the ministers told the royal families. Then the Sakyans, saying, "We will show our strength and power to those who live with our sisters," went out prepared for war. The Koliyans also, saying, "We will show our strength and power to those who live in the Kol tree," went out prepared for war.

The Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of Great Compassion at dawn, surveyed the world and saw them thus departing prepared for war. Seeing them, he reflected, "If I go, will this quarrel be settled or not?" and concluded, "I will go there and, for the sake of settling the quarrel, I will tell three Jātakas; then the quarrel will be settled. Then, to illustrate unity, I will tell two Jātakas and preach the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. After hearing the teaching, the inhabitants of both cities will each give two hundred and fifty princes (totaling five hundred); I will ordain them, and then there will be a Great Assembly (Mahāsamāgama)." Therefore, while they were departing prepared for war, without informing anyone, he took his bowl and robes and went by himself, sitting cross-legged in the air between the two armies, emitting six-colored rays.

When the inhabitants of Kapilavatthu saw the Blessed One, they thought, "Our noble kinsman and Teacher has come. Has he seen the cause of our quarrel?" and they considered, "It is not proper for us to strike the bodies of others with weapons while the Blessed One has come. Let the inhabitants of the city of Koliya kill us or cook us if they wish." They discarded their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down. The inhabitants of the city of Koliya thought likewise, discarded their weapons, paid homage to the Blessed One, and sat down.

The Blessed One, though he already knew, asked, "Great Kings, why have you come?" They replied, "Venerable Sir, we have not come for water-sports, mountain-sports, river-sports, or to see the hills; we have come to this place having prepared for battle." "Great Kings, on account of what are you quarreling?" "Venerable Sir, on account of water." "Great Kings, how much is water worth?" "Venerable Sir, it is of little value." "Great Kings, how much is the earth worth?" "Venerable Sir, it is invaluable." "Great Kings, how much are khattiyas worth?" "Venerable Sir, khattiyas are invaluable." "Great Kings, why do you destroy invaluable khattiyas on account of water which is of little value? There is no satisfaction in quarreling. Great Kings, by the power of quarreling, having harbored a grudge in an improper place, a certain tree deity once harbored a grudge against a black lion..."
268:
"...It has followed [you] throughout this entire aeon," he said, and told the Phandana Jātaka. Then he said, "Great King, one should not be a believer in others' words. For, by being a believer in others' words, on account of the words of a single rabbit, the herds of four-footed animals in the Himālaya, which is three thousand yojanas in extent, jumped into the great ocean. Therefore, one should not be a believer in others' words," and he told the Pathavīundriya Jātaka. Then he said, "Great King, sometimes the weak see the flaw or opening of the strong, and sometimes the strong see that of the weak. Even a small quail once caused the death of a noble elephant," and he told the Laṭukika Jātaka. Having thus told three Jātakas for the sake of settling the quarrel, he told two Jātakas to illustrate unity. How? "Great King, no one can find an opportunity against those who are united," he said, and told the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka. Then he said, "Great King, while they were united, no one could see a flaw. But when they quarreled with one another, then the hunter's son took their lives and carried them away. There is no satisfaction in quarreling," and he told the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka. Having thus told these five Jātakas, he finally preached the Attadaṇḍa Sutta.

The kings, being filled with faith, said, "If the Teacher had not come, we would have killed one another with our own hands and caused a river of blood to flow. We would not have seen our sons and brothers at the doors of our houses; there would have been no one even to bring news. We have gained our lives because of the Teacher. If the Teacher had lived the household life, the sovereignty over the four great islands surrounded by two thousand small islands would have come into his hands, and he would have had over a thousand sons; then he would have moved about surrounded only by khattiyas. Now, however, he has renounced that prosperity, gone forth, and attained Enlightenment; let him even now move about surrounded only by khattiyas." Thus, the inhabitants of both cities gave two hundred and fifty princes each (totaling five hundred). The Blessed One ordained those princes and went to the Mahāvana forest. Because they had ordained only out of deep respect and not by their own desire, dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arose in those monks. Their former wives also sent messages, saying, "Noble lords, be weary [of the monkhood]; the household life does not remain stable," and so on. Those monks became even more dissatisfied.

The Blessed One, reflecting, knew their state of dissatisfaction and thought, "These monks are dissatisfied while living together with a Buddha like me. Come, I will tell them the beauty of Kunāla Lake and, having led them there, [remove] their dissatisfaction..."
269:
Thinking, "I shall dispel their dissatisfaction," the Blessed One spoke of the Kunāla Lake. The monks desired to see it. "Monks, do you wish to see the Kunāla Lake?" he asked. "We do, Bhante," they replied. "If so, come, let us go," he said. "Bhante, how shall we go to the place where the Blessed One, possessed of psychic power, goes?" they asked. "Just have the desire to go; I shall take you there by my psychic power," he said. "Very well, Bhante," they replied.

Then the Blessed One, taking the five hundred monks, rose into the air and, alighting at Kunāla Lake, addressed the monks: "Monks, whatever fish in this Kunāla Lake you do not know by name, ask their names." The monks asked, and the Blessed One answered every question. Not only the names of the fish, but he also had them ask and then explained the names of the trees in that forest, and the two-footed and four-footed creatures and birds at the foot of the mountains.

Then, the Kunāla bird king came, seated on a stick held in the beaks of two birds, surrounded by a flock of birds on the front, back, and both sides. Seeing the bird king, the monks said, "Bhante, this bird must be the king of these birds; we think these are his retinue." "Monks, it is so. This bird king is also of my lineage, my tradition," he said. "Bhante, now we have seen these birds. We wish to hear the account of what the Blessed One said: 'This bird king is also of my lineage, my tradition'." "Monks, do you wish to hear it?" he asked. "We do, Bhante," they replied.
