"Then listen," he said, and he dispelled their dissatisfaction by preaching the Kunāla Jātaka, adorned with three hundred verses. At the conclusion of the teaching, all the monks were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), and psychic powers (abhiññā) came to them along with the Path. The Blessed One thought, "Let this much of the higher Dhamma be for these monks," and rising into the air, he went to the Mahāvana forest. Although those monks had gone by the psychic power of the Blessed One, upon returning, they descended into the Mahāvana forest surrounding the Blessed One by their own psychic power.

The Blessed One sat on the prepared seat and addressed the monks: "Come, monks, sit down. I shall teach you the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) for the abandoning of your defilements (kilesas) which are to be eradicated by the three higher paths." He then taught the meditation subject. The monks thought, "The Blessed One, knowing our dissatisfaction, took us to Kunāla Lake and dispelled it. To us who attained the fruit of Stream-entry there, he has now given the meditation subject for the three higher paths here. It is not proper for us to spend time being complacent, thinking 'We are Stream-enterers.' We should strive to be like the Great Men (uttamapurisa)." Having paid homage at the feet of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala), they rose, shook out their sitting mats, and went to sit individually in mountain caves and at the feet of trees.
270:
The Blessed One thought: "These monks, by nature, do not abandon their meditation subject. For a monk who has obtained the method, there is no such thing as exhaustion. As they go about, they will develop insight (vipassanā), reach Arhatship, and come to me, thinking, 'We shall report the special qualities we have individually attained.' When they arrive, the deities from the ten thousand world systems will assemble in this single world system. There will be a Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya). It is proper for me to sit in a secluded place." Then, having had the Buddha-seat prepared in a secluded spot, he sat down.

The elder who first took the meditation subject and departed reached Arhatship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Then another, and another—all five hundred blossomed like lotuses in a lotus pond. The monk who first attained Arhatship thought, "I will report this to the Blessed One." He uncrossed his legs, shook out his sitting mat, stood up, and approached the Ten-Powered One. In this manner, one after another, all five hundred came in succession, as if entering a refectory. The first to arrive paid homage, prepared a seat, sat to one side, and wishing to report the quality he had attained, looked back at the path he had come to see if anyone else was there. He saw another, and then another. Thus, all of them arrived and sat to one side. Out of mutual respect, one did not speak to the other, and the other did not speak to the first. It is said that for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), two dispositions occur: the thought arises, "Oh, may the world with its devas quickly realize the quality I have attained!" Yet, like a man who has found a hidden treasure, there is also the disposition of not wishing to tell others of the state one has attained.

While that assembly of Noble Ones (ariya-maṇဍala) remained thus, the full moon disk—beautiful like a great silver mirror held up in the eastern direction, or like a silver wheel being turned by its rim—emerged and ascended into the sky, free from the five defilements of clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu, so that the loveliness of the world adorned by the appearance of a Buddha might be seen from the summit of Mount Yugandhara in the east. At such a moment, in such a brief instant, the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans in the Mahāvana forest at Kapilavatthu, together with a great community of monks, about five hundred monks, all of whom were Arhats.

There, the Blessed One was born in the lineage of Mahāsammata, and those five hundred monks were also born in the clan of Mahāsammata. The Blessed One was born in a Khattiya womb, and those monks...
271:
They were born into the Khattiya (noble) class. Just as the Blessed One renounced the world from the Khattiya class, these monks also renounced the world from the Khattiya class. Just as the Blessed One renounced the status of a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch) that was within his reach and went forth, these monks also renounced the royal wealth within their reach and went forth. Thus, the Blessed One, in a pure place, during a pure time of night, being pure himself, had a pure retinue. Being free from lust, he had a retinue free from lust. Being free from hatred, he had a retinue free from hatred. Being free from delusion, he had a retinue free from delusion. Being free from craving, he had a retinue free from craving. Being free from defilements, he had a retinue free from defilements. Being peaceful, he had a peaceful retinue. Being disciplined, he had a disciplined retinue. Being liberated from defilements, he had a liberated retinue. He shone with exceeding magnificence. This is the field of praise; one should speak words of praise as much as one is able. Thus, referring to those monks, it was said: "With about five hundred monks, and all of them were indeed Arahants."

"Yebhuyyena" means that the vast majority had assembled. A few deities from the Asaññasatta and Arūpa realms, and those deities who were in meditative absorption (samāpatti), did not come to the assembly. The order of the deities' assembly was as follows: Deities in the vicinity of the Mahāvana forest stirred, saying, "Friends, come! Beholding the Buddha is of great benefit; hearing the Dhamma is of great benefit; beholding the Saṅgha is of great benefit. Come, come!" Making a great sound, they arrived, and after paying homage to the Blessed One and to the Khīṇāsava (taintless) monks who had attained Arahantship at that very moment, they stood to one side. In this same manner, hearing the voices of those deities, and through successive distances—across the Himavantā mountains which are three thousand yojanas wide, in sixty-three thousand cities, nine million nine hundred thousand market towns (doṇamukha), nine million six hundred thousand ports, and fifty-six million jewel mines—deities from the entire Jambudīpa, Pubbavideha, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and the two thousand small islands, thus from the entire Cakkavāḷa (world system), and from the second and third Cakkavāḷas, up to ten thousand Cakkavāḷas, it should be understood that the deities assembled. Here, ten thousand Cakkavāḷas are intended as the ten thousand world elements (lokadhātu). Therefore, it was said: "Deities from the ten thousand world elements had mostly assembled."

With the deities thus assembled, the entire interior of the Cakkavāḷa, up to the Brahma realm, was as crowded as a needle case packed with needles without any gap. The height of that Brahma realm should be understood thus: If a stone the size of the seven-pinnacled pavilion of the Lohapāsāda were dropped from the Brahma realm,
272:
it would reach the ground only after four months. In such a vast space, the deities were so densely packed that there was no room for flowers or smoke thrown from below to rise upwards, nor for mustard seeds dropped from above to descend downwards. However, just as the place where a Cakkavatti king sits is not congested and the arriving powerful nobles always find a place, while it is only further away that it becomes very crowded; in the same way, the place where the Blessed One sat was not congested, and the arriving powerful deities and Mahābrahmas always found a place. Furthermore, in the immediate vicinity of the Blessed One, just as described in the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, even in a space the size of a hair-tip, ten, twenty, thirty, or even sixty deities, having created subtle forms for themselves, stood there.

"Suddhāvāsakāyikānaṃ" refers to those living in the Suddhāvāsa (Pure Abodes). The Suddhāvāsa are the five Brahma realms which are the abodes of the pure Anāgāmīs (Non-returners) and Khīṇāsavas (Arahants). "To those Brahmas, this thought occurred"—why did it occur? It is said that those Brahmas, having entered meditative absorption (samāpatti) and emerged at the predetermined time, looked upon the Brahma realm and saw it empty, like a dining hall after lunch. Then, reflecting, "Where have the Brahmas gone?", they realized there was a great assembly and thought: "This assembly is great; we have been left behind. For those left behind, it is difficult to find a place. Therefore, let us not go empty-handed, but let us each compose a verse and go. By that verse, we shall make our arrival known in that great assembly and also speak in praise of the Dasabala (the Ten-Powered One)." Thus, because they reflected after emerging from meditative absorption, this thought occurred to them.

"They appeared before the Blessed One"—although the Pali text says they descended as if right in the presence and in front of the Blessed One, this meaning should not be taken literally here. Those Brahmas, while still in the Brahma realm, composed the verses; then one descended at the eastern rim of the Cakkavāḷa, one at the southern rim, one at the western rim, and one at the northern rim. Then, the Brahma who descended at the eastern rim of the Cakkavāḷa entered the blue kasina (nīlakasiṇa) and emitted blue rays, making his arrival known to the deities of the ten thousand world systems as if covering them with a jeweled net.
273: The Buddhavīthi (the range of the Buddha's authority) is something that no one can overwhelm or obstruct. Therefore, that Brahma came only through the open Buddhavīthi, paid homage to the Blessed One, and stood at a suitable place. Standing at a suitable place, he recited a verse composed by himself. The Brahma who descended to the southern edge of the world-system also entered the yellow kasina (pītaka-kasiṇa) attainment and, emitting golden rays as if covering the deities of the ten thousand world-systems with a golden cloth, made his arrival known and stood in the same manner. The Brahma who descended to the western edge of the world-system also entered the red kasina (lohitaka-kasiṇa) attainment and, emitting red rays as if wrapping the deities of the ten thousand world-systems with a noble red blanket, made his arrival known and stood in the same manner. The Brahma who descended to the northern edge of the world-system also entered the white kasina (odātaka-kasiṇa) attainment and, emitting white rays as if covering the deities of the ten thousand world-systems with a noble white cloth, made his arrival known and stood in the same manner. In the Pali, however, it is said: "They appeared before the Blessed One. Then those deities paid homage to the Blessed One and stood at a suitable place." Thus, their appearance before him and their standing after paying homage are spoken of as if occurring in a single moment. Although it happened in the sequence mentioned above, it is shown collectively. The recitation of the verses, however, is stated separately for each individual in the Pali. In those verses, "Mahāsamaya" means a great assembly (a great gathering). "Pavana" refers to a forest grove. By both terms, the Blessed One said that today there is a great gathering, a great assembly in this forest grove. Then, to show whose assembly it was, he said, "The hosts of deities have assembled." There, "devakāyā" means groups of deities. "We have come to this Dhamma assembly"—seeing the groups of deities thus assembled, we too have come to this gathering of the Dhamma. For what reason? To see the "aparājitasangha" (the unconquered Sangha), whom no one can defeat; to see this unconquered Sangha who has today crushed the three Maras and won the battle—this is the meaning. That Brahma, having recited this verse and paid homage to the Blessed One, stood at the eastern edge of the world-system itself. Then the second Brahma came and recited in the same manner as described. In that verse, "tatra bhikkhavo" means the monks in that place of assembly. "Samādahaṃsu" means they composed themselves with concentration. "Cittamattano ujuṃ akaṃsu" means they removed all crookedness, distortion, and deviousness from their minds and made them straight. Like a charioteer [holding] the reins...
274:
In the phrase "as if taking hold...", it means that just as a charioteer who has placed the goad upon swift-running horses stands holding all the reins without urging or restraining them, even so, these five hundred monks, who are endowed with six-factored equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) and have guarded sense-doors, are wise and guard their sense faculties. "O Blessed One, we have come here to see those monks." That Brahma also went and stood in his own place.

Then the third Brahma came and spoke in the same manner as previously mentioned. In that verse, "having cut the stake" (chetvā khīlaṃ) means having cut the stake of lust, hatred, and delusion. "The bolt" (palighaṃ) means the bolt of lust, hatred, and delusion itself. "The city-pillar" (indakhīlaṃ) also means the city-pillar of lust, hatred, and delusion itself. "Having uprooted, unstirred" (ūhacca maneja) means these monks are unstirred (aneja) due to the absence of the stirring (ejā) of craving; having uprooted and destroyed the city-pillar. "They wander" (te caranti) means those monks wander in the four directions with unobstructed movement. "Pure" (suddhā) means free from the defilements. "Stainless" (vimalā) means without stain; this is a synonym for the word "pure." "By the one with vision" (cakkhumatā) means by the Blessed One who is endowed with the five eyes. "Well-tamed" (sudantā) means tamed in regard to the eye, and also tamed in regard to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. "Young noble elephants" (susunāgā) refers to monks who are like young noble elephants. "O Blessed One, we have come to see these monks, who are like young noble elephants tamed by such an unsurpassed trainer of those to be tamed (yogācariya)." That Brahma also went and stood in his own place.

Then the fourth Brahma came and spoke in the same manner as previously mentioned. In that verse, "gone" (gatāse) means those who have gone to the refuge through a doubt-free taking of refuge. That Brahma also went and stood in his own place.

## Devatāsannipāta-vaṇṇanā (Description of the Assembly of Deities)

Then the Blessed One, looking out, saw the assembly of deities and Brahmas from the surface of the earth up to the edge of the world-system and up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm, and he thought: "This assembly of deities is vast. The monks, however, do not know that there is such a vast assembly of deities. Let me inform them." Having thought thus, the whole account should be expanded according to the Pali: "Then the Blessed One addressed the monks." Therein, "at most this many" (etaparamā) means this is the maximum number of those deities. Now, because Buddhas are no longer present, the third turn, "Monks, even now...", is not mentioned. Why did he say, "Monks, I will tell you"? It was to cause joy in the minds of the deities. For it is said that the deities thought: "In such a vast assembly, the Blessed One will mention the names and clans of only the powerful deities; what will he say for the deities of little power?"
276:
"They too are unable," he saw and thought, "If it were a Paccekabuddha, would he be able?" He knew, "Even that Paccekabuddha would not be able." He reflected, "Among Sakka, Suyāma, and others, would anyone be able?" If any of them were able, he would have them ask and he himself would answer; however, not even one among them was able.

Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One: "Only a Buddha like me would be able. Is there another Buddha anywhere else?" Spreading his infinite knowledge throughout the infinite world systems and looking, he did not see another Buddha. And this is not surprising, that he would not see one equal to himself now; even on the day of his birth, in the manner stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta Commentary, not seeing anyone equal to himself, he uttered the irreversible lion's roar: "I am the foremost in the world."

Thus, not seeing anyone else equal to himself, he thought: "If I ask and I myself answer, these deities and Brahmās will not be able to penetrate the meaning. But if another Buddha asks and I answer, it will be wonderful, and the deities and Brahmās will be able to penetrate the meaning. Therefore, I will create a Created Buddha (Nimmitabuddha)." He entered the meditative absorption (jhāna) which is the basis for higher knowledge (abhiññā), and after emerging, he performed the preliminary work (parikamma) with sense-sphere consciousness (kāmāvacara citta), resolving: "Let the holding of the bowl and robes, the looking ahead and looking aside, and the bending and stretching be just like mine." Then, with fine-material sphere consciousness (rūpāvacara citta), he determined the creation as if the moon's orb were emerging, breaking through the peak of Mount Yugandhara in the east.

The host of deities, seeing that form, said, "Friends, has another moon arisen?" Then, when it surpassed the moon and came closer, they said, "It is not the moon; the sun has arisen." Again, when it came closer, "It is not the sun; it is a celestial mansion." Again, when it came closer, "It is not a celestial mansion; it is a son of the gods (devaputta)." Again, when it came closer, "It is not a son of the gods; it is a Great Brahmā." Again, when it came closer, they said, "It is not a Great Brahmā; friends, another Buddha has come!" There, the worldling deities thought, "For just one Buddha, there is such a gathering of deities; if there are two, how great will it be!" The noble (ariya) deities, however, thought, "In a single world system, there are never two Buddhas; surely the Blessed One has created another Buddha similar to himself."

Then, while that host of deities was looking on, the Created Buddha came and, without bowing to the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala), sat on a created seat made equal to the Buddha's in his presence. The Blessed One possessed the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and the Created Buddha also possessed only the thirty-two marks.
277:
From the body of the Blessed One, the six-colored rays (chabbannaraṃsi) emerged; they also emerged from the body of the Created Buddha. The rays from the Blessed One's body struck the body of the Created Buddha, and the rays from the Created Buddha's body struck the body of the Blessed One. The rays emerging from the bodies of those two Buddhas spread as far as the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm, and from there they returned, descending upon the heads of the deities and Brahmās, and remained at the edge of the universe (Cakkavāḷa). The entire interior of the universe shone like a shrine-house encircled by circular golden rafters. The deities from ten thousand universes gathered in this single universe, entering and standing within the radiance of the two Buddhas. While still seated, the Created Buddha, wishing to praise the destruction of defilements at the throne of enlightenment (Bodhipallaṅka) of the Possessor of Ten Powers, spoke this verse:

"I ask the Sage of extensive wisdom,
Who has crossed over, reached the far shore, is extinguished, and is firm of self;
Having gone forth from the home and discarded sensual pleasures,
How should a bhikkhu rightly wander in the world?"

The Blessed One, thinking, "I will speak the names and clans of the deities who have arrived to gladden their minds," said, "Bhikkhus, I shall announce..." and so on.

In that passage, "I will recite the verse" means "I will bring forth a collection of words regulated by syllables and feet." "Yattha bhummā tadassitā" means "In whatever places the earth-dwelling deities reside, depending on those bhikkhus." With "Ye sitā girigabbharaṃ" and so on, he spoke of the virtues of those bhikkhus; it means the bhikkhus who live depending on mountain caves and clefts. "Pahitattā" means those with resolute minds. "Samāhitā" means those with undistracted minds.

"Puthū" means many people. "Sīhāva sallīnā" means they stay close together in one place like lions. "Lomahaṃsābhisambhuno" means those who stand having overcome horripilation; it means those who are without fear. "Odātamanasā suddhā" means being of pure mind, they are purified. "Vippasannāmanāvilā" means those who are exceedingly clear and free from turbidity.

"Knowing more than five hundred bhikkhus" means knowing more than five hundred bhikkhus together with the Fully Enlightened One. "Vane Kāpilavatthave" means in the forest grove located near Kapilavatthu. "Tato āmantayī satthā" means at that time the Teacher addressed them.
278: It means they are called 'disciples' (sāvaka) because they listen to his Dhamma teaching, and 'delighting in the teaching' (sāsane rate) because they delight in the teaching of the three trainings. He speaks all this as if it were spoken by another, starting from the words 'Silokamanukassāmi'. 'Monks, the hosts of devas have arrived; know them, monks' was said for the purpose of inducing the knowledge of the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) in those monks. Those monks, having heard the Buddha's instruction, immediately exerted effort for that purpose. To those monks who thus exerted effort, the knowledge of the divine eye, which can see non-humans (amanussa), appeared. That knowledge was not produced by preliminary work (parikamma) at that moment; rather, it was accomplished through the Noble Path (ariya-magga) itself. For the purpose of seeing non-humans, they only had to make an effort. The Teacher, referring to this very meaning—'You have the knowledge; bring forth that knowledge and know them'—said, 'Monks, know them.' Among those monks, some saw a hundred non-humans. Some saw a thousand, some seventy thousand. Some monks saw a hundred thousand. Some saw without limit (ananta). It means they saw in great numbers without boundary, such as by hundreds or thousands. Why? Because all directions were pervaded and filled with them. Having known all that was seen by each of them. 'Vavatthitvāna cakkhumā' means the Teacher, endowed with the five eyes, discerned them clearly as if seeing the lines on the palm of a hand. After that, he spoke the previously mentioned verse for the purpose of proclaiming their names and clans (gotta). 'Know these devas whom I shall proclaim; look, observe'—this is the connection here. 'Girāhi' means with words. 'Anupubbaso' means in order. 'Seven thousand are those Yakkhas, terrestrial ones of Kapilavatthu' means that here, there are seven thousand terrestrial Yakkhas who arose depending on Kapilavatthu.
279: He says: 'Possessing power' (iddhimanto) means those endowed with divine power. 'Possessing majesty' (jutimanto) means those endowed with splendor. 'Possessing beauty' (vaṇṇavanto) means those endowed with physical beauty and complexion. 'Possessing fame' (yasassino) means those endowed with a retinue. They came with joyful hearts. 'Bhikkhūnaṃ samitiṃ vanaṃ' means they came to this Mahāvana forest, to the presence of the monks, to see the monks. Alternatively, taking 'samitiṃ' as an assembly, it means they came to see the assembly of monks. There are six thousand Yakkhas born in the Hemavata mountains; all of them have various colors, such as blue and so on. There are three thousand Yakkhas born in the Sātāgiri mountains. All these mentioned so far are sixteen thousand. There are five hundred born in the Vessāmitta mountains. The Yakkha named Kumbhīra, born in the city of Rājagaha. His residence is Mount Vepulla. More than a hundred thousand Yakkhas attend to him. Kumbhīra of Rājagaha also came to this forest with his retinue to see the assembly of monks. King Dhataraṭṭha rules the eastern direction. 'Gandhabbānaṃ adhipati' means he is the chief of the Gandhabbas in all four directions. All of them follow his will. This Great King has a large retinue. He, Dhataraṭṭha, has many powerful sons, all named 'Inda', bearing the name of Sakka, the king of devas. King Virūḷhaka rules that direction.
280:
“The sons of that king also exist” means that king also has such sons (of great power). In the Pali text, however, they write “Mahabbalā”. In the Commentary, in all instances, there is only the reading “Mahābalā”.

“Dhataraṭṭha in the eastern direction, Virūḷhaka in the south,
Virūpakkha in the west, and Kuvera in the north.
These four Great Kings stood in the four directions all around,
shining brilliantly in the Great Forest of Kapilavatthu,” so it was said.

These verses are spoken in an all-inclusive sense. The meaning here is: In the ten thousand world-systems, there are Great Kings named Dhataraṭṭha. All of them, accompanied by hundreds of thousands of crores of Gandhabba devas, having come and starting from the Great Forest of Kapilavatthu in the eastern direction, stood filling the entire interior of the world-system. In this same way, Virūḷhaka and others stood in the southern direction and so on. Therefore, it is said: “They stood in the four directions all around, shining brilliantly.” This means: “Having come from the multitude of world-systems, they stood in the four directions, shining brightly like great bonfires on mountain peaks.” Because those kings came specifically referring to the Kapilavatthu forest, although they stood filling the world-system and were equal in size to the world-system, it is said “in the forest of Kapilavatthu.”

“The deceptive, crafty, and crooked servants of those kings have come” means those Great Kings have servants who are crooked in conduct and possessed of deception (māyā), characterized by concealing their own faults. Because they deceive the world with deception in one's presence or behind one's back, they are called “vañcanika” (deceivers), and because they are endowed with craftiness and hypocrisy, they are called “saṭha” (crooked ones); the meaning is that these servants also have come. “Māyā, Kuṭeṇḍu, Viṭeṇḍu, Viṭucca, and Viṭuṭo have come together” means all these servants are indeed deceivers. By name, one here is named Kuṭeṇḍu, one is named Viṭeṇḍu. In the Pali text, they write “Veṭeṇḍu”. One is named Viṭucca, one is named Viṭuṭo. “Saha” (together) means that Viṭuṭo also came together with them.
283:
“Venerable Sir, it is now the time” means may there be good for you; it is the time to approach the forest where the monks are meeting to see the Saṅgha of monks.

“The devas of Water, Earth, Fire, and Air also came” means the devas named Water and so on, who were reborn after performing preliminary work (parikamma) on the water-kasiṇa and so on, have come. “The Varuṇa and Vāraṇa devas, and Soma together with his retinue” means the devas named Varuṇa, Vāraṇa, and Soma came together with the deva named Yasa (Retinue). “The devas of the groups of Loving-kindness and Compassion” are those devas reborn after performing preliminary work on the meditations of loving-kindness and compassion. These devas of great fame also came.

“These ten groups of devas exist in ten ways; all are of various colors” means those ten groups of devas standing in ten ways all came with various colors such as blue and so on.

“The Veṇḍu devas, the Sahali devas, and the two devas Asama and Yama” have come. The devas dependent on the moon came, placing the moon in front. Likewise, the devas dependent on the sun came, placing the sun in front; and the devas dependent on the stars came, placing the stars in front. “The Mandavalāhaka devas also came” means the Wind-clouds, the Mist-clouds, and the Heat-clouds; all these cloud-group devas are called “Mandavalāhaka”. The meaning is that they also came. “Vāsava, the best of the Vasu devas, Sakka, Purindada, also came” means Vāsava, the chief of the Vasu devas, who is also called Sakka and Purindada, has also come.

“These ten groups of devas came in ten ways. All are of various colors” such as blue and so on.

“Then the devas named Sahabhū came. They were blazing like flames of fire.” It is also said that Jala, Maggi, and Sikhārī are the names of those devas. The Ariṭṭhaka devas and the Roja devas, and the Umapuppha devas who have the color of the flax flower (umā), also came.
285:
In the Pali text, however, they write "Jātināmā". The Āsā deities are called "Āsavā" by virtue of their desire (chanda). The Nimmānaratī deities arrived, and then the Paranimmita deities arrived. These ten groups of deities also arrived in ten ways.

"These sixty groups of deities" means the sixty groups of deities consisting of six sets of ten, starting with the Āpo deities; all of them have various colors such as blue, etc. They arrived according to their names and groups. "Others similar to them also arrived" means deities from other world-systems who are similar in color and name also arrived. Thus, with a single term, [the Buddha] refers to all deities as if making a bundle or a package.

Having thus indicated the groups of deities in the ten thousand world-elements, he now spoke the verse beginning with "Pavuṭṭhajātiṃ" to show the purpose for which they came. The meaning of that verse is: Because they have birth (jāti) that is departed (pavuṭṭha), the Ariya Saṅgha is called "Pavuṭṭhajāti". We shall behold the Ariya Saṅgha who are "Pavuṭṭhajāti", who are "Akhila" (without spikes) because of the absence of the spikes of lust, hatred, and delusion, who are "Oghatiṇṇa" because they stand having crossed the four floods, and who are "Anāsava" because of the absence of the four taints. We shall also behold the Dasabala Buddha, who is "Oghatara" because of having crossed those very floods, who is "Nāga" because of not committing evil, and who shines with glory like the moon, having transcended the state of darkness (impurity). For this purpose, all those [deities] arrived according to their names and groups, along with others who are similar.

Now, wishing to show the Brahmas, he spoke the words beginning with "Subrahmā Paramatto ca". Therein, Subrahmā is one Brahma. Paramatta is also a Brahma. The Ariya Brahmas, who are the sons of the Blessed Buddha endowed with psychic power, arrived together. Sanaṅkumāra Brahma and Tissa Mahābrahma also arrived. He also arrived.

"A Mahābrahma rules over a thousand Brahma worlds; he has appeared endowed with splendor and a formidable body, accompanied by a retinue and fame."
287:
[Māra] retreated. Being extremely angry and unable to bring [the assembly] under his control, he followed only the will of his own anger and retreated unwillingly. The Blessed One knew: "This Māra, seeing this great assembly (Mahāsamāgama), is thinking 'I will create an obstacle to the realization of the Dhamma,' and is sending the army of Māra at intervals to show terrifying things." This is the nature of the Blessed One: in a place where the realization of the Dhamma (abhisamaya) will not occur, he does not prevent Māra from showing terrifying things. But in a place where the realization of the Dhamma will occur, he resolves so that the assembly neither sees the form of Māra nor hears his voice. In this assembly, a great realization of the Dhamma will occur; therefore, he resolved so that the deities neither saw Māra's form nor heard his voice. Thus it is said: "Then he retreated, extremely angry and unable to have his way."

The Blessed One, who knows and distinguishes all that with his special knowledge (abhiññā) and eye of wisdom, said:

"O monks, the armies of Māra have approached; recognize them." This means: "O monks, the armies of Māra have approached; recognize them appropriately for yourselves and enter into Fruit Attainment (phalasamāpatti)." They exerted effort to enter Fruit Attainment. Māra and his army moved far away from the Ariyas who are free from passion. They could not move even a single hair of those passionless ones. Then Māra spoke this verse referring to the Saṅgha of monks:

"All are victors in battle, they have transcended fear and possess fame and a retinue; your disciples, well-known among people, rejoice together with the Ariyas."

Therein, "modanti saha bhūtehi" means they rejoice together with the Ariyas who have arisen in the Dispensation of the Dasabala Buddha. "Janesutā" means they are famous, well-known, and recognized among people.

This Mahāsamaya Sutta is dear and pleasing to the deities; therefore, when one wishes to speak auspicious words in new places, this very sutta should be recited. It is said that the deities wander about with attentive ears, thinking, "We will listen to this sutta." At the conclusion of the teaching...
288:
While this sutta was being preached, one hundred billion deities and Brahmās attained the fruit of Arahantship; the number of those who became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) and so forth was beyond counting.

Regarding the deities' love and appreciation for this sutta, there is this story: It is said that a goddess lived in a Nāga tree (Nāgarukkha) at the entrance of the Nāga Cave in the Koṭipabbata Vihāra. A young monk was reciting this sutta inside the cave. Having listened to it, the goddess uttered the word 'Sādhu' (Well done) in a loud voice at the end of the sutta. When the monk asked, "Who is this?", she replied, "Venerable sir, I am a goddess." When asked, "Why did you utter 'Sādhu'?", she replied, "Venerable sir, I heard this sutta on the day the Blessed One sat and preached it in the Mahāvana forest, and I have heard it again only today. You, venerable sirs, have learned this Dhamma well, without omitting even a single syllable, exactly as it was preached by the Blessed One."

When asked, "Did you personally hear it when the One Possessing Ten Powers (Dasabala) was preaching?", she replied, "Yes, venerable sir." When asked, "I have heard that there was a very large assembly of deities at that time; where were you standing to listen?", she replied:

"Venerable sir, I am a goddess residing in the Mahāvana forest. However, when the powerful deities arrived, I found no space in Jambudīpa and had to come to this island of Lankā (Tambapaṇṇidīpa). Although I tried to stand and listen at the port of Jambukola, as powerful deities arrived there in succession, I had to retreat. Eventually, I stood in the sea behind the village of Mahāgāma in the Rohana district, immersed in water up to my neck, and listened from there."

When asked, "Goddess, did you see the Teacher from such a great distance from where you stood?", she replied, "Venerable sir, what are you saying? While the Teacher was preaching the Dhamma in the Mahāvana forest, I felt as if he was constantly looking only at me. Thus, feeling fearful and respectful, I remained hidden among the waves."

When asked, "It is said that on that day, one hundred billion deities attained the fruit of Arahantship. Did you also attain Arahantship then?", she replied, "No, venerable sir." When asked, "I suppose you attained the fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi)?", she replied, "No, venerable sir." When asked, "I suppose you attained the fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi)?", she replied, "No, venerable sir." When the monk said, "It is said that the deities who attained the three higher paths are beyond counting; I suppose you became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna)?", the goddess, having attained the fruit of Stream-entry on that day, felt shy and said, "Venerable sir, you are asking what should not be asked." Then the monk asked, "Goddess, can you show your form to us?", she replied, "I cannot, venerable sir."
290:
## 8. Sakkapañhasutta-vaṇṇanā
## Nidāna-vaṇṇanā
This sutta beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the Sakkapañha Sutta. In this sutta, the explanation of obscure terms is as follows: Regarding the Brahmin village named Ambasaṇḍa, it is called "Ambasaṇḍa" because it is situated not far from mango groves (ambasaṇḍa). Regarding 'on the Vediyaka Mountain', that mountain is surrounded on all sides by a dark green forest at its base, resembling a jeweled pedestal (maṇivedikā); therefore, it is known as "Vediyaka Mountain". Regarding 'in the Indasāla Cave', even in ancient times, it was a cave located between two mountains, with an Indasāla tree (Terminalia chebula) at its entrance; thus, it was known as "Indasāla Cave". Later, people enclosed it with walls, installed doors and windows, and having made it a cave decorated with well-finished plasterwork, floral designs, and vine patterns, they offered it to the Blessed One. However, by its former name, it is still known as "Indasāla Cave". Referring to that cave, it is said, "in the Indasāla Cave".

"Ussukkaṃ udapādi" means a righteous zeal (enthusiasm) arose. Indeed, this Sakka was one who frequently visited the Blessed One; there was no assembly of deities where he had not previously attended, and there was no son of the gods who lived as heedfully as Sakka. Yet, why did such zeal for the vision of the Buddha (Buddhadassana) arise in him as if he had never seen the Buddha before? It was because he was threatened by the fear of death. At that time, his life span was nearly exhausted. Seeing the five prior omens (pubbanimitta), he realized, "Now my life span is exhausted." Among the sons of the gods in whom the omens of death appear, those who were reborn in the celestial realm through small meritorious deeds fall into fear and trembling, wondering, "Where will we be reborn now?" However, those who have established a refuge against fear by performing many meritorious deeds do not fear, relying on the gifts they have given (dāna), the virtue they have guarded (sīla), and the meditation they have developed (bhāvanā), thinking, "We shall enjoy prosperity in the higher celestial realms."

As for Sakka, the king of gods, when he saw the prior omens, he felt anxiety (at the thought of leaving) the celestial city of ten thousand yojanas, the Vejayanta Palace of one thousand yojanas in height, the Sudhammā celestial hall of three hundred yojanas, the Pāricchattaka tree of one hundred yojanas in height, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat of sixty yojanas, the retinue of twenty-five million celestial dancers in the two celestial realms, and the Nandana Grove.
291:
Looking at all these splendors—the Cittalata Grove, the Missaka Grove, and the Phārusaka Grove—he was overcome by fear, thinking, "Alas, friends, this prosperity of mine will surely perish."

Then, searching for someone, he thought, "Is there any ascetic or brahmin, or the Great Brahmā, the grandfather of the world, who can pull out the arrow of grief lodged in my heart and make this prosperity stable?" Seeing no one, he realized again, "Only the Fully Enlightened One is capable of pulling out the arrow of grief that has arisen in hundreds of thousands of beings like me." At that moment, while he was reflecting thus, the desire arose in Sakka, the ruler of the gods, to see the Blessed One.

"Where is the Blessed One staying now? In which district, depending on which town, using whose four requisites, and to whom is he preaching the Deathless Dhamma?" (he wondered). "Addasā kho" means he saw, he understood with penetration. "Mārisā" is a term of endearment, a specific usage among deities. It also means "those free from suffering." Why did Sakka address the deities? He did so for the sake of having companions. It is said that previously, when the Blessed One was staying at the Saḷalaghara, Sakka went alone to see him. The Teacher thought, "His wisdom is not yet mature. After a few days, while I am staying in the Indasāla Cave, he will see the five portents and, fearing death, will approach me with deities from two deva worlds. He will ask fourteen questions, and at the end of the explanation of the questions on equanimity, he will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry along with eighty thousand deities." Thus, the Teacher did not grant him an opportunity.

That Sakka thought, "Because I went alone before, the Teacher did not grant me an opportunity. It is true that I do not have the supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Path and Fruit. However, if even one person has the supporting condition, the Blessed One will surely preach the Dhamma to an assembly as large as the universe. There will certainly be some deity in the two deva worlds who has the supporting condition; the Teacher will preach the Dhamma with reference to that person. By hearing that Dhamma, I too shall appease my own distress." Thinking thus, he addressed the deities for the sake of having companions.

"Evam bhaddam tava" means the Tāvatiṃsa deities said, "Great King, let it be so. Let us go to see the Blessed One. The appearance of a Buddha is rare. May it be a blessing to you, who, instead of saying 'Let us go for mountain-play or river-play,' urges us toward such a place." "Paccassosuṃ" means they accepted his words, placing them on their heads.
292:
Sakka, the ruler of the gods, addressed Pañcasikha, the son of the Gandhabba. Even though he had already addressed the deities, why did he address Pañcasikha separately? It was to gain an opportunity (for an audience). This was Sakka's thought: "It is not appropriate to approach the Teacher with a host of deities from two deva worlds, like someone striking with a vanguard. But this Pañcasikha is an attendant of the One of Ten Powers and is beloved. He goes at any desired moment, asks questions, and listens to the Dhamma. I will send him ahead to request an opportunity, and when the opportunity is granted by him, I will approach and ask my questions." Thus, he addressed him to gain an opportunity.

"Very well, your majesty," said Pañcasikha. "Great King, let it be so. May it be a blessing to you, who, instead of saying 'Come, dear friend, let us go to see garden-play or theatrical performances,' says 'We shall see the Buddha, we shall hear the Dhamma.'" Supporting Sakka's words very firmly, he accepted them and joined him in going together.

In that context, 'Beluvapaṇḍu' refers to a lute with a pale yellow color like a ripe wood-apple. It is said that its sounding box was made of gold, its neck of sapphire, its strings of silver, and its pegs of coral. The arm of the lute was one gāvuta, the place where the strings are tied was one gāvuta, and the upper neck was one gāvuta; thus, it was a lute three gāvutas in size. So, taking that lute, tuning it to the fifty musical scales, and striking it with his fingertips, he produced a sweet song. Signaling to the other deities the time of Sakka's departure, he stood to one side. When the host of deities had assembled by the signal of his singing and playing, then Sakka, the ruler of the gods... (pe)... appeared on Mount Vediyaka.

'It became exceedingly radiant' means that on other days, the place would be radiant with the light of a single deity, or Māra, or a Brahmā. But on that day, it became exceedingly radiant with the light of the deities from two deva worlds, becoming a single mass of light, like the time when a thousand moons and suns have risen. 'People in the surrounding villages' refers to the people from the villages all around. It is said that at the usual time of the evening meal, while children were playing in the middle of the village, Sakka arrived there. Therefore, the people saw and said: "Indeed, do not deities approach the Blessed One at the middle watch of the night? But this one..."
293:
Why did he come even in the earlier part of the first watch? Because he was threatened by the fear of death.

'What is this?' means: 'Friends, what indeed is this? Which powerful deity or Brahma is approaching the Blessed One today to ask questions and listen to the Dhamma? How indeed will the Blessed One answer the questions and teach the Dhamma? It is a gain for us that the Teacher, who dispels the doubts of deities like us, dwells in a monastery not far away, where we have the opportunity to offer alms-food given by the small bowl or by the ladle.' (Thus the deities thought). Those deities, being struck with awe and with their hair standing on end, placed their hands, shining with the union of ten fingernails, in a gesture of salutation (añjali) upon their heads and stood worshipping.

'Difficult to approach' means difficult to attend upon. I am possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion. The Teacher is free from lust, hatred, and delusion. Therefore, it is difficult for one like me to attend upon the Tathāgata. 'Meditator' (Jhāyī) means one who meditates through both meditation on characteristics (lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna) and meditation on objects (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna). 'Delighting in that very Jhana' means one who delights in Jhana. 'Secluded within' means secluded within that state or secluded just now. Therefore, he is difficult to approach not only because he is a meditator delighting in Jhana, but also because he is secluded just now. 'Make him pleased' means you should propitiate him; it means 'request him to grant me an opportunity.' 'Taking the Beluva-paṇḍu lute'—if it is asked, 'Was it not already taken?' Yes, it was taken. However, while traveling, it was hung on the shoulder; now, placing it in the left hand and preparing it for playing, he took it up. Therefore, it is said 'taking.'

## Commentary on the Verses of Pañcasikha's Song

'Made him hear' means he caused him to hear. 'Connected with the Buddha' means (speech) that proceeded by taking the Buddha as the object and as the support. The same method applies to the remaining words.

In the verse, 'I salute your father, O auspicious Sūriyavacchasā, Timbaru,' 'Sūriyavacchasā' means one whose body is like the sun. It is said that a radiance arises from the toes of that daughter of a deity and ascends to the tips of her hair; therefore, she appears like the orb of the young sun. Thus, they recognize her as 'Sūriyavacchasā.' Referring to that, he said: 'O auspicious Sūriyavacchasā, I salute your father, Timbaru, the king of the Gandhabba deities.' 'By whom you were born, O beautiful one' means...
294:
By which cause, depending on which King of Deities, Timbaru, you were born, O Kalyāṇī, beautiful in all limbs. (That birth) is the generator of joy to me because it increases my delight and happiness.

'As the wind is dear to one who is sweating' means that just as the wind is desired, dear, and pleasing to those who are sweating for the purpose of removing the sweat, so it is in this case. 'As drinking water to one who is thirsty' means like drinking water to one who desires to drink, being thirsty and overcome by thirst. 'Aṅgīrasī' means she is called Aṅgīrasī because there are rays (rasmiyo) in her limbs (aṅge); he speaks addressing her by that very name. 'As the Dhamma is to Arahants' means as the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is to the Arahants.

'To one who is hungry' means to one who desires to eat, being overcome by hunger. 'As if quenching a blazing fire with water' means just as someone might extinguish a blazing fire with a pot of water, even so, he says, 'Extinguish the fever of my sensual lust that has arisen because of you.'

'Mixed with the pollen of filaments' means mixed with the pollen of the filaments of a lotus. 'Like an elephant oppressed by the heat' means like an elephant who is burning due to the heat of the sun. 'I wish to descend into your breast and belly' means just as that elephant, having descended into a lotus pond and drunk water, remains submerged with only the tip of its trunk visible and experiences happiness and pleasure, even so, he says, 'When shall I descend into the middle of your breasts and your belly and obtain happiness and pleasure?'

'Like an elephant beyond the hook, I have conquered the goad and pike; I do not know the reason, being intoxicated by you of the beautiful thighs.'—

Here, 'tutta' refers to the iron rod used for piercing at the base of the ear. 'Tomara' refers to the pike-staff used for piercing the feet and other parts. 'Aṅkusa' refers to the curved hook used for piercing the head. An elephant that is in musth goes beyond the hook, exceeding the hook; even when being pierced by the hook, it does not come under control. That elephant, with the pride of intoxication, does not understand any reason, thinking, 'I have conquered the goad and pike, I who do not even come under the control of the hook.' Just as that elephant beyond the hook does not know any reason, saying 'I have conquered the goad and pike,' even so, I too, being intoxicated (sammattā) by you who have thighs endowed with auspicious marks (lakkhaṇūruyā)—intoxicated, heedless, like one insane—do not know any reason. Or else, like an elephant beyond the hook, I too, being intoxicated by you of the beautiful thighs, [do not know] any...
295:
From that time on, I no longer know the cause of detachment (from her). Why? Because just as that noble elephant is conquered by the goad and the pike, I too have been conquered (unable to resist desire); I no longer listen to anyone's words.

"Tayī gedhitacittosmi" means: O one with thighs of beautiful features, my mind is bound to you. Alternatively, "gedhitacitta" means one whose mind has reached a state of longing. "Cittaṃ vipariṇāmitaṃ" means existing in a state that has abandoned its natural condition. "Paṭigantuṃ na sakkomi" means being unable to turn back (from that longing). "Vaṅkaghasthova ambujo" means like a fish that has swallowed a hook. There is also a variant reading "ghaso," which has the same meaning.

"Vāmūrū" means one with beautifully shaped thighs, or it means thighs like the trunk of a banana tree. "Sajā" means embrace me. "Mandalocanā" means: Women do not look intensely but look gently; therefore, they are called "mandalocanā" (one with gentle eyes). "Palissajā" means embrace me from all sides. "Etaṃ me abhipatthitaṃ" means I have desired this repeatedly.

"Appako vata me santo" means being one who has very little (merit) by nature. "Vellitakesiyā" means: One whose hair, when loosened and spread over the back, moves like a snake is called "vellitakesī"; it means (towards) that Vellitakesiyā. "Aneka-bhāvo samuppādī" means it has arisen in many various ways. There is also a variant reading "aneka-bhāgo." "Arahanteva dakkhiṇā" means it is distinguished in various ways, like an offering given to the Arahants.

"Yaṃ me atthi kataṃ puññaṃ" means whatever merit I have performed exists. "Arahantesu tādīsu" means (merit performed) towards Arahants endowed with such qualities. "Tayā saddhiṃ vipaccataṃ" means may all that merit bear fruit only together with you.

"Ekodī" means having reached a state of oneness (concentrated). "Nipako sato" means: "Nepakka" is called wisdom; because of being endowed with that wisdom, one is called "nipako." Because of being endowed with mindfulness, one is called "sato." "Amataṃ muni jigīsāno" means: Just as that Muni, the Buddha, desires and seeks Nibbāna, the deathless, so too, O Suriyavacchasā, I desire and seek you. Alternatively, it means just as that Muni wanders seeking and searching for the deathless, so too I wander seeking and searching for you.

"Yathāpi muni nandeyya, patvā sambodhimuttamaṃ" means: Just as the Muni, the Buddha, sitting upon the Bodhi-throne, rejoices and is delighted upon attaining supreme omniscience. Evaṃ... (In this way...)
296:
"Nandeyyaṃ" means: "In this way, I too would rejoice upon being united with you; I would be filled with joy and happiness," he says.

In the phrase "tāhaṃ bhadde vareyyāhe," "ahe" is a term of address. "O beautiful Suriyavacchasā, even if Sakka, the king of gods, offered a boon saying, 'Suriyavacchasā, will you take the kingship of the gods in the two deva worlds?', I would renounce that kingship and say, 'I will take only Suriyavacchasā.' Thus I would request, desire, and take you."

"Sālaṃva na ciraṃ phullaṃ" means: Near your father's city gate, there is a Sāl tree that has recently blossomed. That Sāl tree is extremely delightful. Like that recently blossomed Sāl tree, I pay homage and bow down to your very glorious father. It means I pay homage to the father who has such a daughter.

In the word "saṃsandati," why did [the Buddha] praise the quality of the song and the sound of the lute? Was there lust (sārāga) in the Blessed One? No. The Blessed One is equanimous with six-fold equanimity (chaḷaṅgupekkhā) in such matters; He only knows the pleasant and unpleasant as they are, but has no attachment there. It is also stated thus: "Friends, the Blessed One has eyes, He sees forms with the eyes, but there is no desire or lust in the Blessed One; His mind is well-released. Friends, the Blessed One has ears," etc. (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.232). If He did not praise the quality, Pañcasikha would not know "I have been given an opportunity." Then Sakka might think "The Blessed One has not given Pañcasikha an opportunity," take the deities, and return from there; if so, it would be a great loss. The Blessed One praised the quality to let them know "The Blessed One has given Pañcasikha an opportunity." Knowing that by praising it, they would approach with the deities, ask questions, and at the end of the explanation, 80,000 deities would be established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), He praised the quality.

In that context, "kadā saṃyūḷhā" means at what time did you meet or gather? "Tena kho panāhaṃ, bhante, samayena" means "Venerable Sir, at that time" refers to the eighth week after Your attainment of Enlightenment. "Bhaddā nāma suriyavacchasā" means named Bhaddā by name, and called Suriyavacchasā because of her physical perfection. "Bhaginī" is just a term of address; it means a goddess. "Parakāminī" means desiring or longing for another.
297:
"Upanaccantiyā" means to the one who is dancing. This person (the goddess Bhūjatī) once went with the devas of the Four Great Kings to perform a dance for Sakka, the king of devas. At that moment, Sakka proclaimed the eight true qualities of the Tathāgata. While going and dancing on that day, she heard those qualities.

## Commentary on the Approach of Sakka

"Paṭisammodati" means the Blessed One rejoices, saying "It is consistent with you," etc., and Pañcasikha also rejoices in return. When reciting the verses, Pañcasikha rejoices, and the Blessed One rejoices in return. "Āmantesi" means he made it known. It is said that Sakka had this thought: "This Pañcasikha was sent by me for my business, but he is doing his own business. Standing before such a Teacher (the Buddha), he speaks unfitting words connected with sensual pleasures. Those called actors are shameless; while speaking, he might even show improper behavior. Let me make him aware of my business." Thinking thus, he called him.

"Evañca pana tathāgatā," etc., are words established by the Elders who were Reciters of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhakas). "Abhivadantī" means they speak with words of joyful greeting. "Abhivadito" means spoken to with words of greeting.

"Urundā samapādi" means it became greatly opened; the darkness within the cave disappeared. "Āloko udapādi" means the darkness that was naturally in the cave vanished, and light arose. All these are the words of the Dhamma Reciters.

"Cirapaṭikāhaṃ bhante" means "Venerable Sir, I have desired to see you for a long time." "Kehici kehici kiccakaraṇīyehi" means the sons and daughters of the devas are born in their laps; the women who serve at their feet are born upon their beds; the devas who decorate them are born surrounding the bed; the attendants are born within the celestial mansion. For these, there is no legal dispute. However, for those born in the boundaries between mansions, they cannot decide "Is this yours or mine?" and thus a dispute arises. They ask Sakka, the king of devas. He says, "To whichever mansion it is closer, let it belong to that person."
298:
If the distance is equal to both mansions, he says, "Whichever mansion she stands looking at, let her belong to that person." If she looks at neither, he takes her as his own to settle their quarrel. Activities such as playing are also duties to be performed. Referring to such duties, he said, "due to some various duties."

"Salalāgārake" means in the scented hut made of Salala wood. "Aññatarena samādhinā" means at that time, the Blessed One, knowing that Sakka's wisdom had not yet matured and wishing to create an opportunity, sat in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti). Not knowing this, he (Pañcasikha or the narrator) said, "by a certain concentration." "Bhūjatī ca nāma" means Bhūjatī is the name of that goddess. "Paricārikā" means a celestial maiden who serves at the feet. It is said that she had attained two fruits (Sotāpatti-phala), and thus she no longer had any delight in the deva world. She would constantly come to the Blessed One, place her hands together in reverence on her head, and stand worshiping the Blessed One. "Nemisaddena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhito" means one should not ask, "Does one in attainment hear sound?" Did the Blessed One not say to Sakka, the lord of devas, "I have arisen from that concentration by the sound of the wheel-rim of your [chariot]"? Setting aside the sound of the wheel-rim, one in attainment does not hear even the sound of a pair of conch shells being blown near the ear, nor even the sound of a thunderbolt. However, the Blessed One entered the attainment of fruition for a determined duration, thinking, "I will not give Sakka an opportunity for this much time." Sakka, thinking, "The Teacher does not give me an opportunity now," circumambulated the scented hut to the right, turned the chariot, and headed toward the deva world. The courtyard of the scented hut became as if five types of musical instruments were being played due to the sound of the chariot. When the Blessed One arose from the attainment according to the determined time, the first advertence (āvajjanā) arose precisely because of the sound of the chariot; therefore, he spoke thus.

## Commentary on the Story of Gopaka

"Sīlesu paripūrakārinī" means one who fulfills the five precepts completely. "Itthittaṃ virājetvā" means having become disgusted with being a woman. Remaining in the state of a woman, it is not possible to enjoy the glory of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), nor the glory of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā, nor to reach Paccekabodhi or Sammāsambodhi; thus, she became disgusted with womanhood. Thinking, "This state of manhood is great, noble, and supreme; only by staying in this state of manhood can these attainments be reached..."
299:
## 
In this way, it is said that she 'developed manhood.' That Gopikā also did this. Therefore, it is said: 'Having discarded womanhood and developed manhood.' 'The lowly Gandhabba group' refers to the inferior and base assembly of Gandhabbas. Why were those of pure virtue born there? It was due to past attachment (nikanti). It is said that even in the past, this was their dwelling place; thus, through the power of attachment, they were born there. 'Upaṭṭhāna' refers to the assembly hall (attendance hall). 'Pāricariya' refers to the state of service or ministration. They come with the intention: 'We shall serve them with song and music.'

'Exhorted' means he reminded them. It is said that when the deva-son Gopaka saw them, he reflected: 'These deva-sons are exceedingly radiant and beautiful; what karma did they perform to come here?' and he saw that 'they had been monks.' Then, reflecting: 'If they were monks, they must have been fulfillers of virtue,' he saw that they were indeed 'fulfillers of virtue.' Reflecting further: 'If they were fulfillers of virtue, is there any other special quality?' he saw that they were 'attainers of jhāna.' Reflecting: 'If they were attainers of jhāna, where did they live?' he saw that 'they were the neighboring monks who came to my house for alms.' Those of pure virtue may be born wherever they wish within the six deva worlds. However, these were not born in the higher deva worlds. Those who attain jhāna are born in the Brahma world, yet these were not born in the Brahma world. He thought: 'I, having established myself in their instruction, was born as a son on the throne of Sakka, the lord of devas, while they were born in the lowly Gandhabba group. These are persons who deserve to be pierced (admonished) repeatedly and severely with words that pierce the bone,' and so he exhorted them with words such as 'Where are you facing?' and so on.

In those words, 'Where are you facing?' means: 'While the Blessed One is preaching the Dhamma right before you, where are you facing? Are you looking here and there while doing other things, or are you sleeping?' 'Bad appearance' refers to an unseemly nature, an appearance unfit to be seen. 'Sahadhammika' refers to fellow practitioners of merit who practiced the same Dhamma in the dispensation of the same Teacher. 'To them, Venerable Sir' means that after the deva-son Gopaka spoke thus and exhorted them further with words such as 'Oh, you are truly shameless and fearless,' the two devas regained mindfulness in that very life.

'The Brahmapurohita group' means they reflected thus: 'Dancers, singers, and musicians who come should indeed receive an inheritance, but this...
300:
## 
Indeed, for us, from the moment we saw [the situation], it was as if we were crackling like a furnace into which salt has been thrown (out of burning shame); they reflected, 'What is this?' They saw their own state of being monks, their pure virtue, their attainment of jhāna, and the fact that they had been the neighboring monks of that deva-son Gopaka. They realized: 'Those of pure virtue are born in their place of choice within the six deva worlds; those who attain jhāna are born in the Brahma world. We were unable to be born in either the higher deva worlds or the Brahma world. This woman, who established herself in our instruction, was born in a higher existence, while we, being monks and having practiced the noble life (brahmacariya) in the Blessed One's dispensation, were born in the lowly Gandhabba group. This is why this deva-son Gopaka rebukes (exhorts) us in this way.' While listening to the words of the deva-son Gopaka, those two persons regained mindfulness of the first jhāna. Using jhāna as a basis and contemplating conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), they established themselves in the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmiphala). At that moment, their lowly sensual-sphere (kāmāvacara) existence could no longer sustain that quality. Therefore, passing away at that very instant, they were reborn among the Brahmapurohita Brahmas. That Brahma-body of theirs appeared while they were still standing there. Thus it was said: 'Venerable Sir, those two devas exhorted by the deva-son Gopaka regained mindfulness in that very life and reached the Brahmapurohita group.'

In those words, 'in that very life' means they regained jhāna-mindfulness in that very same existence. It should be understood that while standing there, they passed away and obtained the Brahmapurohita group (the Brahmapurohita body). One deva-son, however, being unable to cut off attachment, remained obsessed with sensual pleasures and became a permanent resident there.

'Served the Saṅgha' means 'I served the Saṅgha.' 'Sudhammatā' is due to the excellent nature of the Dhamma. 'Tidivūpapanna' means reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. 'Reaching the lowly Gandhabba group' refers to those who have reached and become residents of the Gandhabba group. The words 'We who were formerly humans' should be understood by connecting them with the words 'served with food and drink.'

'Grasping the feet' refers to worshipping and paying homage by performing tasks such as washing the feet and providing oil for the feet. 'In one's own dwelling' means in one's own house. This phrase also connects with 'served.' 'To be known by oneself' means it must be realized by oneself. 'The well-spoken words of the Noble Ones' refers to the well-spoken words of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, which were spoken by you.
301: "Tumhe pana seṭṭhamupāsamānā" means those who attend upon the most excellent Buddha or the unsurpassed Dispensation of the Buddha (Buddha Sāsana). "Brahmacariyaṃ" is the noble practice. "Bhavatūpapatti" is the arising in the existence of beings. "Agāre vasato mayhaṃ" means "for me who lives in the house." "Svajjā" means "that person today." "Gotamasāvakenā" means here the cowherd is called a disciple of the Buddha Gotama. "Samecca" means "having met." "Handa viyāyāma byāyāmā" means "Come, let us strive, let us exert effort." In the sentence "Mā no mayaံ parappessā ahumhā," "no" is just a particle. It means "May we not become the servants or messengers of others." "Gotamasāsanāni" means here the first jhāna, which is realized as it is, is called the teachings of the Buddha Gotama. "Taṃ anussaraṃ" means "reflecting on that Dhamma repeatedly." "Cittāni virājayitvā" means "having detached the mind from the five cords of sensual pleasure." "Kāmesu ādīnavaṃ" means they saw the danger in sensual pleasures through the first jhāna by way of abandonment by suppression (vikkhamphana-pahāna), and through the third path (Anāgāmi-magga) by way of abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna). "Kāmasaṃyojanabandhanāni" refers to the fetters of sensuality and the bonds of sensuality. "Pāpimayogāni" refers to the yokes or bonds of the Evil One, Māra. "Duraccayāni" means things that are difficult to overcome. "Saindā devā sapajāpatikā" means the deities sitting with Sakka as their chief are called "Saindā"; those sitting with Pajāpati, the king of devas, as their chief are called "Sapajāpatikā." "Sabhāyupaviṭṭhā" means those sitting in the assembly hall or rest house. "Vīrā" means the brave ones. "Virāgā" means those free from passion. "Virajaṃ karontā" means those producing the stainless Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-magga). "Nāgovo sannāni guṇāni" means just as a great elephant breaks its bonds, they have cut the bonds of sensual fetters and surpassed the Tāvatiṃsa devas. "Saṃvegajātassa" means "for Sakka who has been moved by spiritual urgency (saṃvega)." "Kāmābhibhū" is the conqueror of both types of sensual pleasures. "Satiyā vihīnā" means those devoid of the mindfulness of jhāna. "Tiṇṇam tesaṃ" means "among those three persons." "Āvasinettha eko" means "among them, one became a resident in an inferior body." "Sambodhipathānusārino" means those who follow the path to the Path of Non-returning. "Devepi hīḷentī" means they even despise the devas; the two...
302:
In the celestial realm, they went flying into the sky, looking down upon and disparaging (other devas), with minds concentrated through access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), scattering the dust from their feet onto the heads of the devas. In this Dispensation, such a proclamation of the Dhamma is called 'Dhamma-pakkāsana.' Through that Dhamma, the disciples become endowed with these virtues. Among those disciples, not even a single disciple has any doubt regarding the Buddha and so forth, or regarding the state of being unobstructed in the four directions, thinking, 'He dwells unattached and unhindered in all directions.' Now, wishing to praise the virtues of the Blessed One, he said: 'We pay homage to the Buddha, the Victor, the Lord of people, who has crossed the flood and cut off doubt.'

In that verse, 'vicikiccha-chinna' means one who has cut off doubt. 'Janinda' means the supreme one in all the worlds. 'Yam te dhammam' means 'that Dhamma of yours.' 'Ajjhagamsu te' means 'those sons of devas have attained.' 'Kāyam brahmapurohitam' means 'the body of the Brahmapurohita devas even while we were watching.' The meaning is this: Having known your Dhamma, among those three persons, those two distinguished individuals attained the Brahmapurohita body and reached the distinction of the paths and fruits even while we were watching. 'O Dear Sir, we too have come to attain that Dhamma.' 'Āgatamhase' means 'we have arrived.' 'O Dear Sir, if the Blessed One gives us the opportunity, we wish to ask a question' means that if the Blessed One grants permission, then having received the Blessed One's permission, we shall ask the question.

## The Story of Magha the Young Man

'This yakkha has been pure for a long time' means he has been pure since a long time ago. Since how long ago? Since the time he was the young man Magha in the village of Macala in the kingdom of Magadha, before the Buddha had appeared. At that time, it is said that one day, having risen early in the morning, he went to the place where the people of the village worked in the center of the village, and at the spot where he would stand, he cleared away the dust and rubbish with his feet to make it pleasant. Another person came and stood in that spot. Through just that much, he regained mindfulness, cleared a space the size of a threshing floor in the center of the village, scattered sand, brought wood, and made a fire during the cold season. Young and old people would come and sit there.
303:
Then one day, this thought occurred to that youth Magha: "Let us go to the city and see the king, the princes, the great ministers, and so forth. Regarding this moon and sun, people say, 'There is a divine son named Canda, and a divine son named Suriya.' By performing what kind of merit did they attain such prosperity?" Then, reflecting, "It is by nothing else but by performing meritorious deeds," he thought, "I too should perform only such meritorious deeds that grant such prosperity."

He rose early, drank his gruel, and taking a billhook, an axe, a hoe, and a pestle in his hand, went to the crossroads. He moved stones with the pestle and rolled them away. He removed trees that struck the axles of carts. He leveled uneven ground. He built a rest house at the crossroads. He dug a pond. He constructed a bridge. Thus, having worked all day, he returned home at sunset. Another person asked him, "Friend Magha, you go out early in the morning and return from the forest only in the evening; what work do you do?" (Magha) replied, "I am performing meritorious deeds; I am clearing the path to heaven." "Friend, what is this called 'merit'?" (the other asked). "Do you not know?" (he asked back). "Indeed, I do not," (the other said). "When you went to the city, did you see the king, the princes, the great ministers, and so forth?" (he asked). "Yes, I have seen them," (the other said). "Those people attained those positions by performing meritorious deeds. I too am doing work that can grant such prosperity. Have you heard of the 'divine son named Canda' and the 'divine son named Suriya'?" (he asked). "Yes, I have heard of them," (the other said). "I am clearing the path to that heaven," (he said). "Is this meritorious deed suitable only for you, or is it not suitable for others as well?" (the other asked). "This merit is not forbidden to anyone," (he said). "If so, when you go to the forest tomorrow, please call me too," (the other said). On the next day, he took him along. In this way, thirty-three young men in that village all became his followers. They, being of one mind, went about performing meritorious deeds. Wherever they went, they leveled the roads, completing them in a single day. They finished digging ponds, building rest houses, and constructing bridges in a single day.

Then their village headman (Gāmabhojaka) thought: "Formerly, when these men drank liquor and committed acts such as killing living beings, I obtained wealth through coins and fines. Now, since the time they began performing merit, there is no such income. I will create a rift between them and the royal family." Approaching the king, he said, "Great King, I see thieves." "Friend, where?" (the king asked). "In my village," (he said). "Friend, what kind of thieves?" (the king asked). "They are offenders against the king, Your Majesty," (he said). "Of what class are they?" (the king asked). "They are of the householder class, Your Majesty," (he said). "What do the householders do?" (the king asked).
304:
"Why did you not tell me, knowing this?" (the king asked). "Great King, I did not tell out of fear. Now, please do not hold it against me," (the village headman replied). Then the king, believing that "This man is crying out the truth to me," said, "In that case, go and bring them yourself," and sent him with a force of men.

The headman went, and while they were consulting together—having worked in the forest all day, eaten their evening meal, and sat in the middle of the village—saying, "What work shall we do tomorrow? Which road shall we level? Shall we dig a pond or build a bridge?"—he surrounded them and said, "Do not move! It is the king's command!" He bound them and led them away. Then their wives, hearing that "Your husbands have been bound and taken away as 'thieves who have offended the king'," said, "For a long time these deceivers have been staying in the forest every day saying 'We are performing merit.' All work has been neglected, and nothing prospers at home. They are well bound; they are well caught."

The village headman brought them and showed them to the king. The king, without investigating, said, "Have them trampled by an elephant." While they were being led away, Magha said to the others, "Friends, will you be able to follow my word?" "It is because we followed your word that we have reached this danger. Even so, we will follow your word. Speak, friend, what shall we do?" (they replied). "Friends, for those wandering in the cycle of rebirth, such danger is constant. Are you thieves?" he asked. "We are not thieves," they replied. "In this world, the Act of Truth (Saccakiriya) is the only refuge. Therefore, all of you, make an Act of Truth: 'If we are thieves, let the elephant trample us; but if we are not thieves, let it not trample us.'" They did so.

The elephant could not even approach them; it ran away trumpeting. Even though they struck the elephant with goads, spears, and hooks, they could not bring it near. They reported to the king, "We cannot bring the elephant near." "In that case, cover them with mats and have them trampled," he ordered. Even when they were covered with mats, the elephant ran away trumpeting twice as loudly.

The king, hearing this, summoned the slanderer and said, "Friend, the elephant does not wish to trample them." "True, Your Majesty, the leader of the youths knows a mantra; this is the power of that mantra," he replied. The king summoned him and asked, "Is it true that you have a mantra?" "Your Majesty, I have no mantra. However, we performed an Act of Truth: 'If we are the king's thieves, let it trample us; but if we are not thieves, let it not trample us.' This is the power of our Act of Truth." "Friend, what work do you do?" he asked. "Your Majesty, we level roads, and at the crossroads, rest houses..."
305:
## 
"We shall perform meritorious deeds; we shall dig a pond; we shall build a bridge; we go about performing such meritorious deeds as these," they replied. "Why did you slander these people?" he [the King] asked. "When we are negligent, this man obtains such and such things; when we are not negligent, he does not obtain them. For that reason, I slandered them," he replied. "Friend, even this elephant, though an animal, knows your virtues. I, being a human, did not know. I return your residential village to you; let this elephant also belong to you, and let the slanderer be your slave. From today onwards, perform meritorious deeds for me as well," he said, and having given them wealth, he dismissed them. 

Taking the wealth and riding the elephant in turns, they consulted: "Friends, although meritorious deeds are performed for the sake of future lives, for us, they have yielded fruit in this very life, like a blue lotus blooming in the water. Now, let us perform even greater merit." "What shall we do?" they asked. "Let us build a strong rest-house at the crossroads for the public to rest, but let us do it without giving a share to women," they said. The reason was: "While we were being led away as thieves, not a single woman had even a thought of helping; instead, they rose up saying, 'Bind them well, hold them fast.' Therefore, we will not give them a share." 

They returned to their homes and gave the elephant thirty-three balls of rice and thirty-three bundles of grass, and the elephant's belly became full. They entered the forest and cut trees; the elephant dragged each cut tree and placed it on the cart-track. They planed the wood and began the work on the rest-house. 

In Magha's house, there were four wives: Sujātā, Sudhammā, Cittā, and Nandā. Sudhammā asked the carpenter: "Father, these friends go early and return in the evening; what work are they doing?" "Mother, they are building a rest-house." "Father, please let me have a share in the rest-house too." "They say they will do it without giving a share to women," the carpenter said. Then Sudhammā gave the carpenter eight kahāpaṇas and said, "Father, by some means or another, make it so that I have a share." The carpenter agreed, saying, "Very well, mother." Taking his adze and carpenter's tools early, he stood in the middle of the village and shouted loudly, "Friends, have you not come out even at this time today?" Knowing that all had reached the road, he said, "You go ahead first; I have some lingering work to do."
311:
## 
In this context, due to stinginess regarding dwellings (āvāsa-macchariya), one becomes a yakkha or a peta and wanders about carrying the rubbish of that very dwelling on one's head. Due to stinginess regarding families (kula-macchariya), when one sees others giving alms to that family and thinks, "Alas, my supporting family is ruined," blood may gush from the mouth, diarrhea may occur, and the intestines may come out in pieces. Due to stinginess regarding gains (lābha-macchariya), if one is stingy with gains belonging to the Saṅgha or a group and uses them as personal property, one is reborn as a yakkha, a peta, or a great python. Due to stinginess regarding physical appearance or virtues (vaṇṇa-macchariya) and stinginess regarding the Dhamma (dhamma-macchariya), if one praises only one's own qualities and not those of others, finding fault by saying "What is his appearance like?", and does not teach the Dhamma to anyone, one becomes ugly and mute. 

Furthermore, due to āvāsa-macchariya, one is cooked in the Iron House Hell (Lohageha). Due to kula-macchariya, one becomes a person of few gains. Due to lābha-macchariya, one is reborn in the Excrement Hell (Gūthaniraya). Due to vaṇṇa-macchariya, when reborn in a new existence, one lacks beauty. Due to dhamma-macchariya, one is reborn in the Hot Ashes Hell (Kukkuḷaniraya). Now, these fetters of envy (issā) and stinginess (macchariya) are abandoned by the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). As long as they are not abandoned, even if devas and humans desire freedom from enmity and so on, they cannot escape from the danger of enmity. 

When it is said, "My doubt is crossed in this question," it means "My doubt is cleared by hearing your words"; it does not indicate the crossing of doubt by the power of the Path. "Perplexity (kathaṅkathā) is gone" means the wandering thoughts of "How is this? How is that?" have vanished. 

The introduction (nidāna) and so forth have the meanings already stated. "Rooted in the pleasant and unpleasant" (piyāppiya-nidāna) means stinginess rooted in pleasant beings and formations, and envy rooted in unpleasant beings and formations. Or, both are rooted in both. For a monk, fellow residents and so on, and for a layperson, children and so on, or animals like elephants and horses, are loved beings; they are cherished and considered "mine," and one cannot bear not seeing them even for a moment. When such a person sees another obtaining a similar loved being, he feels envy (issā).
