When others request, "We have some business with this person; please give him to us for a moment," he shows stinginess (macchariya) by saying, "I cannot give him; he will be tired or bored," and so on. Thus, both are rooted in loved beings. For a monk, requisites such as the bowl and robes, and for a layperson, utensils such as ornaments, are loved and cherished; that person...
312:
Seeing such prosperity arising for another, one feels envy (issā), thinking, "O, may such prosperity not happen to him!" Or when asked, one feels stinginess (macchariya), thinking, "We too, out of love for this, do not dare to use it; we are unable to give it." Thus, both envy and stinginess are rooted in dear formations (piya-saṅkhāra). Regarding unloved beings and formations, even if one obtains those aforementioned beings and formations and they are unpleasant to oneself, due to the perverted nature of the defilements, one might feel envy, thinking, "Apart from me, who else should obtain such a gain?" Or when asked, one might feel stinginess by not giving even for a moment. Thus, both are rooted in unloved beings and formations.

In the phrase "rooted in desire" (chanda-nidāna), there are five types of desire (chanda): the desire for seeking, the desire for obtaining, the desire for enjoying, the desire for hoarding, and the desire for spending.

What is the desire for seeking? In this world, a certain person, being insatiable and filled with intense desire, seeks forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles; he seeks wealth. This is the desire for seeking.

What is the desire for obtaining? In this world, a certain person, being insatiable and filled with intense desire, obtains forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles; he obtains wealth. This is the desire for obtaining.

What is the desire for enjoying? In this world, a certain person, being insatiable and filled with intense desire, enjoys forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles; he enjoys wealth. This is the desire for enjoying.

What is the desire for hoarding? In this world, a certain person, being insatiable and filled with intense desire, hoards wealth, thinking, "It will be useful when danger arises." This is the desire for hoarding.

What is the desire for spending? In this world, a certain person, being insatiable and filled with intense desire, spends and gives wealth to elephant-riders, horse-riders, charioteers, and archers, thinking, "These people will protect me, look after me, cherish me, and surround me." This is the desire for spending. These are the five types of desire. Here, only craving (taṇhā) is intended; it is said thus with reference to that craving.

In the phrase "rooted in thought" (vitakka-nidāna), the decisive thought (viniccaya-vitakka) which is said to be "decision based on gain" is called thought (vitakka). Decision (viniccaya) is of two kinds:
313:
They are craving-based decision (taṇhā-viniccaya) and view-based decision (diṭṭhi-viniccaya). The 108 modes of craving are called craving-based decision. The 62 views are called view-based decision. By the power of this craving-based decision, there can be no definitive distinction between what is pleasant and what is unpleasant, or what is dear and what is not dear. This is because a certain thing may be pleasant for one person but unpleasant for another, just as it is with the kings of the border regions and the kings of the middle country regarding earthworms and the meat of wild animals. In an object obtained after deciding through that craving-based decision, the distinction made as, "This much will be for forms, this much for sounds, this much for smells, this much for tastes, this much for tangibles, this much will be for me, this much for others, this much I will store, and this much I will give to others," occurs through decisive thought (vitakka-viniccaya). Therefore, He said, "Sakka, Lord of Devas, desire is rooted in thought (vitakka-nidāna)."

In the phrase "rooted in the conceptual proliferation of perceptions" (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā-nidāna), there are three kinds of conceptual proliferation (papañca): the conceptual proliferation of craving (taṇhā-papañca), the conceptual proliferation of conceit (māna-papañca), and the conceptual proliferation of views (diṭṭhi-papañca). Among them, the 108 modes of craving are called the conceptual proliferation of craving. The nine kinds of conceit are called the conceptual proliferation of conceit. The 62 views are called the conceptual proliferation of views. Here, the conceptual proliferation of craving is intended. In what sense is it called papañca? It is called papañca in the sense of leading to a state of heedlessness. Perception associated with that papañca is called papañca-saññā. The term saṅkhā means a portion or category, as in the phrase "papañca-saṅkhā rooted in perception." Thus, papañca-saññā-saṅkhā-nidāna means thought rooted in the category of the conceptual proliferation of perceptions.

In the phrase "leading to the suitability for the cessation of the conceptual proliferation of perceptions" (papañca-saññā-saṅkhā-nirodha-sāruppa-gāminī), the cessation and calming due to the exhaustion of these conceptual proliferations of perceptions is called nirodha. He asks about the Path (magga) along with insight (vipassanā) which is both suitable for that cessation and leads to that cessation.

## Explanation of the Meditation Subject of Feeling (Vedanā-kammaṭṭhāna-vaṇṇanā)

Then the Blessed One began teaching the three feelings, starting with "somanassampāhaṃ" (I say joy...). Did the Blessed One teach what was asked or what was not asked? Was it connected or unconnected? He taught only what was asked, not what was not asked. He taught only what was connected, not what was unconnected. For devas, mental phenomena (nāma) are more evident than material phenomena (rūpa), and among mental phenomena, feeling (vedanā) is more evident. Why is that? The physical bodies of devas are subtle, and the results of their kamma are powerful. Because their bodies are subtle and the results of kamma are powerful, they cannot survive if they miss even a single day's meal.
314:
The entire meaning—that [wrong views] disappear just as a lump of butter placed on a hot stone melts—should be understood in the same manner as stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta. Therefore, the Blessed One taught Sakka, the King of Devas, by taking the three types of feeling (vedanā) as the basis. Indeed, there are two kinds of meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna): the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) and the meditation subject of mentality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna). These are also called the comprehension of materiality (rūpa-pariggaha) and the comprehension of mentality (arūpa-pariggaha). Among these two, for one to whom materiality is clear, the Blessed One teaches the meditation subject of materiality by expanding on the definition of the four elements (catudhātu-vavatthāna), either by way of a brief reflection or a detailed reflection. For one to whom mentality is clear, He teaches the meditation subject of mentality. Even when teaching it, He does so only after showing the meditation subject of materiality, which is the physical basis for that mentality. However, since the meditation subject of mentality is clear to the devas and brahmas, He taught it by taking feeling as the basis through the power of the meditation subject of mentality.

Indeed, there are three ways of entering into the meditation subject of mentality: by way of contact (phassa), by way of feeling (vedanā), and by way of consciousness (citta). How? For some, when the meditation subject of materiality has been comprehended either briefly or in detail, contact (phassa) becomes clear—which arises as the first impact of the mind and mental factors upon that object, touching that object. For some, feeling (vedanā) becomes clear, arising while experiencing that object. For some, consciousness (viññāṇa) becomes clear, arising while comprehending and cognizing that object.

Among them, for the one to whom contact is clear, it is not that contact alone arises; along with that contact, feeling also arises experiencing that same object, perception (saññā) also arises marking it, volition (cetanā) also arises coordinating it, and consciousness (viññāṇa) also arises cognizing it. Thus, he comprehends the group of five factors starting with contact (phassapañcamaka). For the one to whom feeling is clear, it is not that feeling alone arises; along with that feeling, contact also arises touching that same object, perception also arises, volition also arises, and consciousness also arises. Thus, he comprehends the group of five factors starting with contact. For the one to whom consciousness is clear, it is not that consciousness alone arises; along with that consciousness, contact also arises touching that same object, feeling also arises, perception also arises, and volition also arises. Thus, he comprehends the group of five factors starting with contact.

When that person reflects, "On what do these five factors starting with contact depend?", he understands, "They depend on the physical base (vatthu)." The physical base refers to the physical body (karajakāya), in reference to which...
315:
It is stated [in the Sutta]: "And this consciousness of mine is supported here, bound here." In terms of meaning, that [physical body] consists of the great elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādā-rūpa). Thus, in this context, he sees only mentality and materiality (nāmarūpa), seeing the physical base as 'materiality' and the five factors starting with contact as 'mentality'. In this regard, materiality is the aggregate of materiality (rūpakkhandha), and mentality consists of the four immaterial aggregates; thus, there are only the five aggregates (pañcakkhandha). There are no five aggregates apart from mentality and materiality, nor is there mentality and materiality apart from the five aggregates. When he investigates, "What is the cause of these five aggregates?", he sees, "They have causes such as ignorance (avijjā) and so forth."

Thereafter, he dwells contemplating with the three characteristics [of existence], based on mentality and materiality together with their causes, thinking: "This is merely the cause and the result of the cause; there is no other being or person; it is merely a heap of pure formations (suddha-saṅkhāra-puñja)." Following the sequence of insight (vipassanā), he wanders about contemplating them as "impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta)." Desiring penetration [of the truth] this very day, and having obtained suitable climate (utu-sappāya), suitable person (puggala-sappāya), suitable food (bhojana-sappāya), or suitable hearing of the Dhamma (dhammasavana-sappāya) on such a day, he brings insight to its peak while sitting in a single cross-legged posture and becomes established in the fruit of Arahantship. In this way, the meditation subject was taught to these three types of persons up to the attainment of Arahantship.

In this particular context, however, when the Blessed One taught the meditation subject of mentality, He taught it with feeling (vedanā) as the primary focus. If it were taught by way of contact or by way of consciousness, it would not be clear to this person; it would appear as if in darkness. But by way of feeling, it is clear. Why? Because the arising of feelings is distinct. Indeed, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is very clear. When a pleasant feeling arises, it arises as if shaking, kneading, pervading, and drenching the entire body, like being made to eat butter washed a hundred times, or being anointed with oil cooked a hundred times, or like extinguishing a fever with a thousand jars of water, even causing one to utter the words, "Oh, what bliss! Oh, what bliss!" When a painful feeling arises, it arises as if shaking, kneading, pervading, and drenching the entire body, like inserting a heated iron plate, or like being poured over with molten copper, or like throwing a bundle of wooden torches into a forest of dry grass and trees, even causing one to lament, "Oh, what pain! Oh, what pain!" Thus, the arising of pleasant and painful feelings is clear.

However, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā) is difficult to demonstrate; it is as if overwhelmed by darkness. That feeling becomes clear to one who grasps it through the method of the neutral mode, which is the absence of pleasure and pain, by rejecting both the agreeable and the disagreeable. How? Just as [one might track] the footprints of a deer that has fled after climbing onto a flat rock...
316:
Just as a hunter, while traveling, sees footprints on this side and that side of a flat rock, and even though he does not see them in the middle, he knows by way of inference: "He climbed up from here, he went down from there; in the middle, on the flat rock, he must have gone by this path." In this way, the arising of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) is evident like the footprint at the place of climbing up, and the arising of painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā) is evident like the footprint at the place of going down. Just as one grasps by inference, "Having climbed up from here and gone down from there, he went thus in the middle," so too, for one who grasps by way of inference the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukkha-vedanā)—which is of a neutral nature by way of rejecting both the pleasant and the unpleasant where pleasure and pain have disappeared—it becomes evident. Thus, the Blessed One first taught the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) and then showed the meditation subject of immateriality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna) by switching over by way of feeling (vedanā).

Not only in this [Sakkapañha Sutta] did He show it thus, but also in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, the Cūḷataṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Mahātaṇhāsaṅkhaya Sutta, the Cūḷavedalla Sutta, the Mahāvedalla Sutta, the Raṭṭhapāla Sutta, the Māgaṇ膽iya Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, the Āneñjasappāya Sutta, and the entire Vedanā Saṃyutta, etc.—in many such discourses, He first taught the meditation subject of materiality and then showed the meditation subject of immateriality by switching over by way of feeling. Just as He showed in those various discourses, so too in this Sakkapañha Sutta, He first taught the meditation subject of materiality and then showed the meditation subject of immateriality by switching over by way of feeling. However, in this sutta, materiality is merely the object of feeling and is thus taught in brief; therefore, it might not appear directly in the Pali text.

To show the entry point of immaterial meditation that is evident to that person by way of feeling, He said: "Sakka, Lord of Devas, I say that joy (somanassa) is also of two kinds," and so on. Therein, "duvidhena" means in two ways, or in two portions. "Such joy should not be pursued" means that such joy based on the household life (gehasita-somanassa) should not be pursued. Joy based on the household life is as follows: "Therein, what are the six kinds of joy based on the household life? Joy arises in one who obtains, or sees as obtaining, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, charming, and connected with worldly baits; or in one who recollects such forms that were previously obtained, which are now past, ceased, and changed. Such joy is called joy based on the household life." Thus, it is the joy based on the five cords of sensual pleasure as taught regarding the six sense doors.
317:
"Such joy should be pursued" means that such joy based on renunciation (nekkhammasita-somanassa) should be pursued. Joy based on renunciation is as follows: "Therein, what are the six kinds of joy based on renunciation? Having known the impermanence of forms, and seeing their change, fading away, and cessation, joy arises in one who sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'Formerly as well as now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.'" (M. iii. 308). In this way, when a desirable object (iṭṭhārammaṇa) appears at the six sense doors, it is the kind of joy that arises when one is filled with gladness, thinking, "My insight has gained strength," after having applied insight (vipassanā) by way of impermanence and so on. "Should be pursued" means that joy arising by way of such renunciation, by way of insight, by way of recollection (anussati), and by way of the first jhāna and so on, should be pursued.

Therein, "that which is with initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra)" means that within that very joy based on renunciation, one should understand the joy with initial and sustained thought that arises by way of renunciation, insight, recollection, and the first jhāna. "That which is without initial thought and without sustained thought" means that one should understand the joy without initial and sustained thought that arises by way of the second and third jhānas. "Those joys without initial and sustained thought are more sublime" means that between these two types, the joy without initial and sustained thought is more sublime.

What is shown by these words? Two ways of attaining Arahantship are shown. How? It is said that a certain monk, having applied insight to joy with initial and sustained thought, contemplates, "On what does this joy depend?" and understands, "It depends on the physical base (vatthu)." In this way, following the method mentioned regarding the five factors starting with contact (phassapañcamaka), he gradually established himself in Arahantship. Another monk, having applied insight to joy without initial and sustained thought, established himself in Arahantship by the same mentioned method. Among those joys thus firmly contemplated, joy without initial and sustained thought is more sublime than joy with initial and sustained thought. Insight that contemplates joy without initial and sustained thought is also more sublime than insight that contemplates joy with initial and sustained thought. The attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) associated with joy without initial and sustained thought is also more sublime than the attainment of fruition associated with joy with initial and sustained thought. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Those joys without initial and sustained thought are more sublime."
318:
The statement 'such mental distress (domanassa) should not be cultivated' means that such household-based (gehasita) mental distress should not be cultivated. Household-based mental distress is defined as: 'Therein, what are the six household-based mental distresses? Mental distress arises in one who does not obtain, or who perceives the non-obtaining of, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, charming, and connected with worldly baits; or in one who, recollecting the past forms that were previously not obtained, or have ceased and changed, experiences distress. Such mental distress is called household-based mental distress' (M. iii, 307). This refers to the mental distress rooted in sensual pleasures that arises in one who thinks regarding the six sense doors: 'I have not experienced, I will not experience, or I do not experience the desired object.'

The statement 'such mental distress should be cultivated' means that such renunciation-based (nekkhammasita) mental distress should be cultivated. Renunciation-based mental distress is defined as: 'Therein, what are the six renunciation-based mental distresses? Having understood the impermanence of forms, and having seen with right wisdom as it really is that all those forms, both formerly and now, are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, one conceives a longing for the unsurpassed liberations (vimokkha), thinking: "When shall I enter upon and dwell in that sphere (āyatana) which the Noble Ones now enter upon and dwell in?" In one who thus conceives a longing for the unsurpassed liberations, mental distress arises because of that longing. Such mental distress is called renunciation-based mental distress' (M. iii, 307). Thus, when a desired object appears at the six sense doors, one conceives a longing for the Noble Fruition (ariya-phala) known as the unsurpassed liberation; and while practicing insight (vipassanā) through the perception of impermanence etc. to attain that state, if one is unable to arouse energy, mental distress arises in the one who grieves: 'I have not been able to arouse energy in insight for this fortnight, this month, or this whole year, and thus have not reached the stage of the Noble Ones (ariya-bhūmi).' The term 'should be cultivated' means that mental distress arising by way of renunciation, insight, recollection (anussati), or the first jhāna etc., should be cultivated.

In that context, regarding the phrase 'that which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra)', among those two types of mental distress, only household-based mental distress is called mental distress accompanied by initial and sustained thought. However, mental distress arising by way of renunciation, insight, recollection, or the first and second jhānas should be understood as mental distress without initial and sustained thought. In the ultimate sense (nippariyāyena), however, there is no mental distress without initial and sustained thought. For the faculty of mental distress (domanassindriya) is invariably unwholesome and accompanied by initial and sustained thought. Nevertheless, it is spoken of as 'accompanied by initial and sustained thought' and 'without initial and sustained thought' by way of this monk's perception (maññana).
319:
In this matter, the method is as follows: In this Dispensation, a monk, by seeing the practice of others, takes as 'mental distress' the states accompanied by initial and sustained thought and the states without initial and sustained thought which are the causes of mental distress, as well as the states of the Path and Fruit which have arisen precisely because of mental distress. He thinks: "When will I be able to establish insight in mental distress accompanied by initial and sustained thought? When in mental distress without initial and sustained thought?" and "When will I be able to produce the attainment of the fruit (phala-samāpatti) of mental distress accompanied by initial and sustained thought? When the attainment of the fruit of mental distress without initial and sustained thought?" Thinking thus, he undertakes a practice for three months, six months, or nine months. Having undertaken the three-month practice, in the first month he stays awake for one watch (yāma) and allows himself to sleep for two watches. In the middle month, he stays awake for two watches and allows himself to sleep for one watch. In the final month, he spends his time only in walking and sitting. If he reaches Arahantship by practicing thus, it is well. If he does not reach it, he specially undertakes the six-month practice. In that six-month period also, having practiced each two-month block according to the aforementioned method, if he is still unable to reach Arahantship, he specially undertakes the nine-month practice. In that nine-month period also, having practiced each three-month block in the same way, mental distress arises in that monk who, being unable to reach Arahantship, reflects: "Alas, I have not obtained the chance to perform the Invitation of Purity (visuddhi-pavāraṇā) together with my fellow Dhamma-farers (sabrahmacārī)." Streams of tears flow from him, just as they did for the Elder Mahāsīva who resided at Gāmanta-pabbhāra.

## The Story of Elder Mahāsīva
It is said that the Elder taught eighteen great groups of students. Established in his instruction, thirty thousand monks reached Arahantship. Then a certain monk, reflecting: "In me, the internal virtues are immeasurable; I wonder what the virtues of my teacher are?" saw the teacher's state as a worldling (puthujjana). Thinking: "Our teacher is a refuge for others, but cannot yet be a refuge for himself; I will give him an exhortation," he traveled through the air, descended near the monastery, and having approached the teacher who was sitting in his daytime resting place, performed his duties and sat at one side.

The Elder asked: "Friend Piṇḍapātika (Alms-food eater), for what reason have you come?" "Venerable Sir, I have come to learn a single appreciation (anumodanā)," he replied. "Friend, there will be no opportunity," said the Elder. "Venerable Sir, I will ask when you are standing at the Vitakka-māḷaka (Thought-terrace)," he said. "Others ask at that place," said the Elder. "Venerable Sir, I will ask on the alms-round path," he said. "Others ask there too," said the Elder. "Venerable Sir, I will ask at the place of putting on the inner robe, the place of donning the outer robe, or the place of taking out the bowl..."
321:
"I have come, and though I have practiced for three months, I have not been able to succeed; yet my fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārīs) perform the Visuddhi Pavāraṇā," he thought. As the Elder thought thus, streams of tears flowed. Then, thinking, "The Path and Fruit will not arise for me through these four postures; as long as I have not reached Arahantship, I will not stretch my back on a couch, nor will I wash my feet," he set the couch aside. Again, when the rainy season arrived, he was still unable to attain Arahantship. Streams of tears flowed until the twenty-ninth Pavāraṇā. Village children used thorns to sew the cracks in the Elder's soles; even while playing, they would say, "May [our feet] be like those of the Venerable Mahāsīva Thera."

On the day of the Great Pavāraṇā marking thirty years, the Elder stood leaning against a wooden support and thought, "Now it has been thirty years since I have been practicing the Dhamma of a recluse, yet I have not been able to reach Arahantship. Surely, in this existence, there is neither Path nor Fruit for me. Alas, I cannot perform the Visuddhi Pavāraṇā together with my fellow practitioners." While he was thinking thus, grief (domanassa) arose, and streams of tears flowed. Then, a goddess stood nearby, weeping. When asked, "Who is weeping here?" she replied, "Venerable sir, I am a goddess." When asked, "Why are you weeping?" she replied, "Venerable sir, I have heard that through weeping, the Path and Fruit can be produced; therefore, I also weep, wishing to produce one or two Paths and Fruits."

Then the Elder admonished himself, "O Venerable Mahāsīva, even the deities are mocking you. Is this [weeping] suitable for you?" He then developed insight (vipassanā) and attained Arahantship together with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Thinking, "Now I will lie down," he prepared his lodging, spread out the couch, placed water ready at the washing place, and sat on the steps, thinking, "I will wash my feet."

His disciples also reflected, "It has been thirty years since our teacher went to practice the Dhamma of a recluse. Has he been able to produce the extraordinary Dhamma, or not?" Seeing him sitting to wash his feet after reaching Arahantship, they thought, "While disciples like us are present, it is not fitting that our teacher should wash his own feet. I myself will wash them! I myself will wash them!" Thus, thirty thousand monks came through the air, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, we will wash your feet..."
322:
"Venerable sir," they said. "Friends, it has now been thirty years that my feet have not been washed. Stay where you are; I myself will wash them," he said.

Sakka, the King of Gods, also reflected: "My master, the Venerable Mahāsīva Thera, has reached Arahantship. He does not allow the thirty thousand disciples who came saying 'We will wash your feet' to wash them. While an attendant like me exists, it is not fitting that my master should wash his own feet. I will wash them." Having made this resolution, he appeared before the Saṅgha of monks together with the goddess Sujātā. Sakka, placing the Asura maiden Sujā in front, cleared the way saying, "Move aside, venerable sirs, a woman is coming." He approached the Elder, paid homage, sat in a crouching position before him, and said, "Venerable sir, I will wash your feet." "Kosiya, it has now been thirty years that my feet have not been washed. To the deities, the natural odor of a human body is loathsome; even to those standing a hundred yojanas away, it is like a rotting corpse hanging from the neck. I myself will wash them," he said. "Venerable sir, this odor is not apparent; rather, the fragrance of your virtue (sīla) has surpassed the six celestial realms and reached the pinnacle of existence (bhavagga). Venerable sir, there is no fragrance superior to the fragrance of virtue. I have come because of the fragrance of your virtue," he said. Taking the ankle joint with his left hand, he rubbed the sole with his right hand. The feet became like those of a young boy. Sakka, having washed the feet and paid homage, returned to the celestial realm.

Thus, based on the grief (domanassa) that arose in the monk who reflected, "I have not had the opportunity to perform the pure Pavāraṇā with my fellow practitioners," through the power of the monk's perception, the object of insight, the insight itself, the Path, and the Fruit are said to be "grief with initial and sustained thought" (savitakka-savicāra-domanassa) and "grief without initial and sustained thought" (avitakka-avicāra-domanassa).

Among those types of grief, one monk, having established insight on grief with initial and sustained thought, investigates, "On what does this grief depend?" and realizes it depends on the physical base (vatthu). In this manner, following the method mentioned regarding the five factors starting with contact (phassa-pañcamaka), he gradually becomes established in Arahantship. Another monk, having established insight on grief without initial and sustained thought, becomes established in Arahantship by the same method. Among those persistent types of grief, grief without initial and sustained thought is more sublime than grief with initial and sustained thought. Insight into grief without initial and sustained thought is also more sublime than insight into grief with initial and sustained thought. The attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti) of grief without initial and sustained thought is also...", plastic_terms: ["Sakka", "Sujātā", "Sīla", "Bhavagga", "Savitakka Savicāra", "Avitakka Avicāra", "Phalasamāpatti"],
323:
It is more sublime. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Those states which are without thought and without examination are more sublime."

Regarding the statement "Such equanimity should not be pursued," it means that such household-based equanimity (gehasita-upekkhā) should not be pursued. What is household-based equanimity? "Among them, what are the six household-based equanimities? When a foolish, deluded worldling, who has not overcome defilements, has not overcome the results of kamma, does not see the danger, and is uninstructed, sees a form with the eye, equanimity arises. Such equanimity does not transcend the form; therefore, that equanimity is called household-based." In this way, when a desirable object comes into range at the six sense doors, like a fly stuck to a lump of molasses, one cannot transcend the forms and other objects, but remains attached and stuck to them. Such equanimity based on the cords of sensual pleasure should not be pursued.

Regarding the statement "Such equanimity should be pursued," it means that such renunciation-based equanimity (nekkhammasita-upekkhā) should be pursued. What is renunciation-based equanimity? "Among them, what are the six renunciation-based equanimities? Having known the impermanence of forms, their change, fading away, and cessation, one sees with right wisdom as it really is: 'Formerly and now, all these forms are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change.' To one seeing thus, equanimity arises. Such equanimity transcends the form; therefore, that equanimity is called renunciation-based" (M. Ni. 3.308). Thus, when desirable or undesirable objects come into range at the six sense doors, equanimity associated with insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) arises by not being delighted by the desirable, not being offended by the undesirable, and not being deluded by observing with neutrality. Furthermore, equanimity as specific neutrality (tatramajjhattūpekkhā), which is of the same nature as the feeling, is also considered equanimity here. Therefore, "should be pursued" means that equanimity arising by power of renunciation, by power of insight, by power of the bases of recollection, and by power of the first, second, third, and fourth jhānas should be pursued.

In this context, by the words "There is also that which is with thought and with examination," one should understand the equanimity with thought and examination (savitakka-savicāra-upekkhā) that arises through renunciation, insight, the bases of recollection, and the first jhāna, using that same renunciation-based equanimity. By the words "There is also that which is without thought and without examination," one should understand the equanimity without thought and examination (avitakka-avicāra-upekkhā) that arises by power of the second jhāna and so forth. Regarding "Those states which are without thought and without examination are more sublime," it means that between these two, the equanimity without thought and examination is more sublime. What is being taught by these words?
324:
What is the case? Two types of Arahantship were taught. Indeed, one monk, having established insight (vipassanā) through equanimity with thought and examination, and reflecting, 'On what does this equanimity depend?', understands, 'It depends on the physical base (vatthu).' In this way, following the method mentioned in the five factors beginning with contact (phassapañcamaka), he gradually becomes established in Arahantship. Another monk, having established insight through equanimity without thought and examination, becomes established in Arahantship by the same mentioned method. Among those equanimities that have been attained, equanimity without thought and examination is more sublime than equanimity with thought and examination. Insight through equanimity without thought and examination is also more sublime than insight through equanimity with thought and examination. The attainment of the fruit (phalasamāpatti) of equanimity without thought and examination is also more sublime than the attainment of the fruit of equanimity with thought and examination. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Those states which are without thought and without examination are more sublime."

"O Sakka, Lord of Devas, a monk who practices in this way is practicing the path leading to the cessation of the perceptions and categories of conceptual proliferation (papañcasaññāsaṅkhānirodhasāruppagāminī paṭipadā)." Thus, the Blessed One concluded the teaching with Arahantship as the summit. Sakka, however, attained the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). The intention of the Buddhas is never low; it is always exalted. Whether teaching the Dhamma to one person or to many, they always take Arahantship as the summit. Beings, however, established in their own suitable supporting conditions (upanissaya), some become Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), some Non-returners (Anāgāmī), and some Arahants. The Blessed One is like a king, and those to be tamed (veneyya) are like princes. Just as a king, when eating, lifts a portion of food according to his own capacity and gives it to the princes, and those princes take mouthfuls only according to the size of their own mouths; in the same way, the Blessed One, with a teaching suitable to his own intention, takes Arahantship as the summit. Those to be tamed, according to the capacity of their own supporting conditions, take from that teaching only the fruit of stream-entry, or the fruit of once-returning, non-returning, or Arahantship. Sakka, however, became a Stream-enterer. Having become a Stream-enterer, he passed away right in front of the Blessed One and was reborn as a young Sakka (taruṇa sakka). The place of departure and arrival of the individualities (attabhāva) of passing devas is not apparent; it is like the movement of a lamp flame. Therefore, the remaining devas did not know. Only two persons knew: Sakka himself, because he had passed away, and the Blessed One, because of his unimpeded knowledge (appaṭihatañāṇa). Then Sakka thought: "The Blessed One has taught me only the benefit that should be produced in the three stages. This Path or Fruit, however, cannot be seized by flying up like a small bird; there must be a preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapaṭipadā) that must be undertaken to arrive there. Let me now ask about the preliminary practice for one who will later be one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava)."
325:
## Explanation of the Restraint of the Pātimokkha

Furthermore, desiring to question the Blessed One, he spoke starting with, 'Venerable sir, how should one practice?' and so forth. In that passage, 'pātimokkhasamvarāya' means for the sake of the highest and foremost restraint of virtue (sīlasamvara). The passage beginning with 'kāyasamācārampi' is spoken to show the restraint of the Pātimokkha by way of bodily conduct (kāyasamācāra) that should be cultivated and so forth. This talk on virtue (sīlakathā) should be explained either by way of the courses of action (kammapatha) or by way of prescriptions (paṇṇatti).

In this regard, one who wishes to explain by way of the courses of action should first explain bodily conduct that should not be cultivated (asēvitabba-kāyasamācāra) through killing living beings, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct. One who wishes to explain by way of prescriptions should explain it by way of the transgression of training rules prescribed for the body-door. Bodily conduct that should be cultivated (sēvitabba-kāyasamācāra) should be explained by way of abstinence from killing living beings and so forth, and by way of the non-transgression of training rules prescribed for the body-door. Verbal conduct that should not be cultivated (asēvitabba-vacīsamācāra) should be explained by way of verbal misconduct such as false speech and so forth, and by way of the transgression of training rules prescribed for the speech-door. Verbal conduct that should be cultivated (sēvitabba-vacīsamācāra) should be explained by way of abstinence from false speech and so forth, and by way of the non-transgression of training rules prescribed for the speech-door.

Seeking (pariyesanā), however, is only seeking through body and speech. Although that seeking is already included by taking bodily and verbal conduct (kāyavacīsamācāra), because what is called virtue with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamakasīla) arises only in these two doors and not in the air, it is taught separately to show virtue with livelihood as the eighth. In that seeking, seeking that should not be cultivated is explained as the ignoble search (anariyapariyesanā). Seeking that should be cultivated is explained as the noble search (ariyapariyesanā). Thus it was also said:

'Monks, there are these two kinds of search: the ignoble search (anariyapariyesanā) and the noble search (ariyapariyesanā). And what, monks, is the ignoble search? Here, monks, someone, being himself subject to birth (punabbhava), seeks only what is subject to birth; being himself subject to aging, subject to sickness, subject to death, subject to sorrow, and subject to defilement, seeks only what is subject to defilement.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to birth (punabbhava)? Children and wife, monks, are subject to birth; male and female slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; poultry and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth.'
326:
'Monks, these acquisitions (upadhi) are subject to birth. Being tied to, infatuated with, and addicted to these, one who is himself subject to birth seeks only what is subject to birth.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to aging? Children and wife, monks, are subject to aging... [pe]... seeks only what is subject to aging.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to sickness? Children and wife, monks, are subject to sickness; male and female slaves are subject to sickness; goats and sheep are subject to sickness; poultry and pigs are subject to sickness; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to sickness. Monks, these acquisitions are subject to sickness. Being tied to, infatuated with, and addicted to these, one who is himself subject to sickness seeks only what is subject to sickness.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to death? Children and wife, monks, are subject to death... [pe]... seeks only what is subject to death.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to sorrow? Children and wife... [pe]... seeks only what is subject to sorrow.

And what, monks, do you say is subject to defilement? ... [pe] ... Gold and silver are subject to defilement. Monks, these acquisitions are subject to defilement. Being tied to, infatuated with, and addicted to these, one who is himself subject to defilement seeks only what is subject to defilement. Monks, this is called the ignoble search (anariyapariyesanā).'

Furthermore, all forms of wrong livelihood (anesanā) that occur in five ways by way of scheming (kuhanā) and so forth, in six ways by way of wrong resorts (agocara), and in twenty-one ways by way of medical practice (vejjakamma) and so forth, should be understood as the ignoble search only.

'And what, monks, is the noble search (ariyapariyesanā)? Here, monks, someone, being himself subject to birth, having known the danger in what is subject to birth, seeks the unborn, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. Being himself subject to aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and defilement, having known the danger in defilement, [seeks] the undefiled...'
327:
...seeks the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna. This is called the Noble Quest (ariya-pariyesanā).

Furthermore, it should be understood that seeking alms righteously and fairly, while avoiding the five kinds of deceit (kuhanā) and so forth, the six improper resorts (agocara), and the twenty-one types of wrong livelihood (anesana), is also indeed the Noble Quest.

In this context, whatever is stated as 'not to be associated with' is indeed not to be associated with from the very beginning—starting from the time of seeking the requisites, making an effort, performing the act, and going about for the sake of killing living beings and so forth. As for the other (the good), it should be associated with from the start; if one is unable to do so, one should at least generate the intention. Furthermore, bodily conduct like that of Devadatta and others, who strive for the sake of causing a schism in the Saṅgha and so forth, should not be associated with. Bodily conduct like that of the General of the Dhamma (Ven. Sāriputta), Ven. Mahāmoggallāna, and other elders, which proceeds by way of going to attend upon the Three Jewels two or three times a day and so forth, should be associated with. Verbal conduct like that of Devadatta and others, who break their word by way of sending messages like an archer and so forth, should not be associated with. Verbal conduct like that of the General of the Dhamma, Ven. Mahāmoggallāna, and other elders, which proceeds by way of praising the virtues of the Three Jewels and so forth, should be associated with. A quest like that of Devadatta and others, who seek the ignoble quest (anariya-pariyesanā), should not be associated with. A quest like that of the General of the Dhamma, Ven. Mahāmoggallāna, and other elders, who seek only the Noble Quest, should be associated with.

'One who practices thus' means one who practices to fulfill the conduct that should be associated with, having abandoned the bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and quest that should not be associated with. O Sakka, Lord of Devas, a monk is said to be one practicing for the sake of the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the highest and foremost restraint of virtue. Thus, the Blessed One taught the preliminary practice of the path to be attained by an Arahant.

## Description of the Restraint of the Faculties (Indriyasaṃvara-vaṇṇanā)

In the second question, 'for the restraint of the faculties' (indriyasaṃvarāya) means for the closing of the faculties, for the state of having guarded doors, and for the state of having restrained doors. In the explanation, however, it was spoken by way of forms cognizable by the eye and so forth that should be associated with, in order to show the restraint of the faculties. In that passage, 'when this was said' (evaṃ vutte) refers to Sakka, who, having heard the answers to the questions on joy (somanassa) and so forth below, had the intuition arise that 'it must be of such a nature,' and when the Blessed One spoke thus...
328:
Sakka, Lord of Devas, addressed the Blessed One with these words: 'Venerable Sir, I [understand] this meaning...' and so forth. The Blessed One, having given him the opportunity, remained silent. Indeed, the Blessed One does not give an opportunity to one who wishes to speak but is unable to accomplish the meaning, or to one who is able to accomplish the meaning but does not wish to speak. But because this Sakka both wished to speak and was able to accomplish the meaning, the Blessed One gave him the opportunity.

In the passages such as 'such a form should not be associated with,' the summary of the meaning is: whatever form one looks at and lust and so forth arise, that form should not be associated with, should not be looked at, and should not be stared at. But whatever form one looks at and the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) becomes established, or confidence (pasāda) arises, or the acquisition of the perception of impermanence (anicca-saññā) occurs, that form should be associated with.

Whatever sound with ornate syllables and ornate phrases one listens to and lust and so forth arise, such a sound should not be associated with. But whatever sound based on the meaning and based on the Dhamma—even the song of a water-carrying maid—one listens to and confidence arises or revulsion (nibbidā) becomes established, such a sound should be associated with.

Whatever scent one smells and lust and so forth arise, such a scent should not be associated with. But whatever scent one smells and the acquisition of the perception of foulness and so forth occurs, such a scent should be associated with.

Whatever taste one savors and lust and so forth arise, such a taste should not be associated with. But whatever taste one savors and the perception of repulsiveness in food (paṭikūla-saññā) arises, and by relying on the bodily strength obtained from such consumption, one is able to enter the Noble Plane (ariya-bhūmi), or like the novice Sīva, the nephew of Elder Mahāsīva, the destruction of defilements (kilesakkhaya) occurs even while consuming, such a taste should be associated with.

Whatever tangible one touches and lust and so forth arise, such a tangible should not be associated with. But whatever tangible one touches and the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) occurs, as in the case of Ven. Sāriputta and others, and energy is well-exerted, and posterity is benefited by providing an example to follow, such a tangible should be associated with. It is said that Ven. Sāriputta did not stretch his back on a couch (did not lie down) for thirty years. Likewise, Ven. Mahāmoggallāna. Ven. Mahākassapa did not stretch his back on a couch for one hundred and twenty years. Ven. Anuruddha for fifty years. Ven. Bhaddiya for thirty years. Ven. Soṇa...
329:
Eighteen years (vassa). The Elder Raṭṭhapāla, twelve years. The Elder Ānanda, fifteen years. The Elder Rāhula, twelve years. The Elder Bākula, eighty years. The Elder Nāḷaka did not stretch his back on a couch (did not lie down to sleep) until his final passing (Parinibbāna).

When one attends to certain mental objects known by the mind, lust and so forth arise; covetousness (abhijjhā) and so forth come into focus in such ways as, "Oh, may the wealth and possessions of others become mine!" Such mental states should not be cultivated. Mental states that arise through the power of loving-kindness (mettā) and so forth, such as "May all beings be free from enmity," or the mental states of the three Elders, should be cultivated. It is said that the three Elders made a pact on the day of entering the Rains Retreat (Vassa) that they would not entertain unwholesome thoughts such as sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka). Then, on the day of the Pavāraṇā ceremony, the senior Elder of the Saṅgha asked the junior monk, "Friend, within these three months, how far have you allowed your mind to wander?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I did not allow it to wander outside the monastery grounds." He asked the second Elder, "And you, friend?" He replied, "Venerable Sir, I did not allow it to wander outside the house." Then the two Elders asked the senior Elder, "And what about you, Venerable Sir?" He replied, "Friends, I did not allow my mind to wander outside of my own five aggregates (khandhas)." They remarked, "Venerable Sir, you have performed a very difficult task." Such mental objects known by the mind should be cultivated.

"Ekantavādā" means those who have only one conclusion to their doctrine; thus they are called Ekantavādā. He asks whether they are not those whose doctrine goes in two different ways. "Ekantasīlā" means those who have a single practice. "Ekantachandā" means those who have a single belief (laddhi). "Ekanta-ajjhosānā" means those who have a single finality.

Sakka, Lord of Devas, this world has many inclinations (ajjhāsaya) and diverse inclinations. When one wishes to go, another wishes to stay. When one wishes to stay, another wishes to sleep. It is rare for two beings to have the same inclination. In this world of many elements and diverse elements, whatever element or whatever inclination beings adhere to and grasp, they firmly hold onto that very thing through effort and wrong interpretation, saying, "Only this is the truth, other views are empty," and they speak of it, demonstrate it, and praise it.
331:
...is not complete. "Venerable Sir, as for me," and so forth, he makes known his status as a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna).

## Somanassapaṭilābhakathāvaṇṇanā

"Vedapaṭilābha" means the attainment of joy and satisfaction. "Devāsurasaṅgāma" means the war between the Devas and the Asuras. "Samupabyūḷho" means reaching a state of intense confrontation, as if clashing forehead to forehead. It is said that these Devas and Asuras sometimes battle on the surface of the great ocean; in that battle, there is no actual killing of one another by cutting or piercing; like a fight between wooden rams, there is only victory and defeat. Sometimes the Devas win, and sometimes the Asuras win. Regarding those battles, referring to the specific battle in which the Devas defeated the Asuras so that they would not return, he said, "Venerable Sir, at that time," and so forth. "Ubhayametanti" means both of these. Thinking, "The Devas alone shall enjoy both kinds of essence (ojā) here in the celestial realm," powerful rapture and joy (pīti-somanassa) arose in that Sakka as he reflected thus. "Sadaṇḍāvacaro" means being together with the taking up of sticks and weapons; it shows that he had not laid down his weapons. "Ekantanibbidāya" means for the sake of absolute weariness with the round of suffering (vaṭṭa). Let everything be understood as stated in the Mahāgovinda Sutta.

"Pavedesi" means he spoke or demonstrated. "Idheva" means in this very place. "Devabhūtassa me sato" means to me who has become a Deva. "Punarāyu ca me laddho" means "I have obtained life (jīvita) again through another result of kamma (kammavipāka)"; by this, he reveals both his passing away (cuti) and his rebirth (upapatti).

"Diviyā kāyā" means celestial bodies (attabhāva). "Āyuṃ hitvā amānusaṃ" means having abandoned the celestial life-span. "Amūḷho gabbhamessāmī" means because his destination (gati) is fixed, he will enter the womb without confusion. "Yattha me ramatī mano" means "wherever my mind shall delight, there in the families of kings and so forth, I shall enter the womb"; this explains the meaning that he will be reborn seven times among Devas and humans.

"Ñāyena viharissāmī" means that even when reborn among humans, because he is incapable of such acts as killing his mother, he will live according to the right method, reason, and fairness.
332:
The phrase "Sambodhi ce bhavissati" is spoken with reference to the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmimagga). It indicates, "If I shall become a Once-returner." "Aññātā viharissāmi" means "I will live as one desiring to know (the Dhamma)." "Sveva anto bhavissati" means "This very human world will be my end (final birth)."

Furthermore, "Devo bhavissāmi, devalokasmim uttamo" means "I will once again become the supreme lord of the devas, Sakka, the king of gods, in the celestial realm."

"Antime vattamānamhi" means "while existing in the final birth." "So nivāso bhavissati" means "The abode of the Akaniṭṭha Brahmas—who are the eldest in age and wisdom and more excellent than all other devas—will be my final home." It is said that this Sakka, after passing away from that state of being Sakka, will attain the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga) in that very existence. Thus, becoming an Akaniṭṭha-goer (akaniṭṭhagāmī) with an upward-flowing stream (uddhaṃsota), he will be reborn in the realms such as Aviha and finally be reborn in the Akaniṭṭha realm. With reference to this, it was spoken thus. This person will live for one thousand aeons in the Aviha realm, two thousand in Atappa, four thousand in Sudassa, eight thousand in Sudassī, and sixteen thousand in Akaniṭṭha, thus enjoying the lifespan of the Brahmas for a total of thirty-one thousand aeons. Sakka the king of gods, Anāthapiṇḍika the householder, and Visākhā the great female lay follower—these three have equal lifespans. Among beings who delight in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa), there are none who enjoy happiness comparable to these.

"Apariyosita-saṅkappo" means one whose desires are not yet fulfilled. "Yassu maññāmi samaṇe" means "I think of those monks who live in seclusion."

"Ārādhanā" means accomplishment. "Virādhanā" means non-accomplishment. "Na sampāyanti" means they are unable to speak in a way that achieves fulfillment.

"Ādiccabandhunaṃ": The Sun is of the Gotama lineage, and the Blessed One is also of the Gotama lineage; therefore, it was spoken thus. "Yaṃ karomasi" means the homage we used to pay to Brahma in the past. "Samaṃ devehi" means together with the devas. He shows that from now on, there is no more paying homage to Brahma for us. "Sāmaṃ karoma" means we shall pay homage (to the Buddha).
333:
"Parāmasitvā" means that with a joyful heart, as if striking a friend's hand with one's own, he struck the earth, or he struck it to act as a witness, meaning: "Just as you are immovable, so am I (immovably devoted) to the Blessed One." "Ajjiṭṭhapafñhā" means the questions that were requested or the questions that were desired. All the remaining words are clear in their meaning.

## The Commentary on the Sakkapañha Sutta is finished.
334:
## 9. Mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutta-vaṇṇanā
## Commentary on the Section of the Summary
"Evaṃ me sutaṃ" and so forth is the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. Herein, this is the sequential explanation of the words: "Bhikkhus, this path is the only way." Why did the Blessed One teach this sutta? Because the inhabitants of the Kuru country were capable of receiving profound teachings. It is said that the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen living in the Kuru country, being endowed with suitable climate and resources, always possessed healthy bodies and clear minds by using the suitable climate and resources of that country. Because of their physical and mental health, they possessed the strength of wisdom that was nurtured, making them capable of receiving profound discourse. Therefore, the Blessed One, seeing their capability to receive profound teachings, taught this Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta of deep meaning, incorporating the subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) in twenty-one places leading up to Arahantship. Just as a man, having obtained a golden flower-basket, would place various flowers in it, or having obtained a golden casket, would place the seven gems in it, even so, the Blessed One, having obtained the audience of the Kuru inhabitants, taught this profound discourse. For this very reason, other suttas of profound meaning were also taught there: the Mahānidāna Sutta in the Dīgha Nikāya; and in the Majjhima Nikāya, the Satipaṭṭhāna, Sāropama, Rukkhopama, Raṭṭhapāla, Māgaṇḍiya, and Āneñjasappāya Suttas.

Furthermore, in that district, the four assemblies naturally lived devoted to the practice of the development of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā); even the servants, laborers, and attendants spoke only words connected with mindfulness. Even at places such as water-drawing points and weaving sheds, no useless talk occurred. If a woman was asked, "Mother, which mindfulness meditation do you reflect upon?" and she replied, "None at all," they would rebuke her, saying, "Shame on your life! Though living, you are like the dead." Then, after admonishing her, "Do not do this again from now on," they would teach her one of the mindfulness practices. But if she said, "I reflect upon such-and-such mindfulness," they would applaud her, saying, "Sādhu! Sādhu!" and praise her, saying, "Your life is well-lived; you have truly attained the human state; it is for your sake that the Fully Enlightened One arose."

Not only were the human beings here devoted to the reflection on mindfulness, but even the animals that lived depending on them were also so devoted.
335:
In this regard, there is this story—it is said that a certain performer (naṭa) traveled around training a young parrot. Having stayed near a nunnery, he forgot the young parrot and left. The novice nuns (sāmaṇerīs) took it and cared for it. They named it "Buddharakkhita." One day, seeing the parrot sitting in front of her, the Mahātherī called out, "Buddharakkhita!" "What is it, My Lady?" (the parrot replied). "Do you have any meditative reflection (bhāvanā-manasikāra)?" she asked. "No, My Lady," it replied. "Friend, one who lives in the presence of monastics should not live with a negligent body; some form of reflection is desirable. If you cannot do anything else, practice the recitation: 'Bones, bones' (aṭṭhi, aṭṭhi)." Following the Therī's advice, the parrot lived reciting "Bones, bones."

One day, early in the morning, while it was sitting on top of the gateway basking in the sun, a hawk seized it with its talons. The parrot cried out, "Kiri! Kiri!" Hearing this, the novice nuns said, "My Lady, Buddharakkhita has been seized by a hawk! Let us rescue him!" and they chased after it with stones and such, and rescued him. When he was brought back and placed before her, the Therī asked, "Buddharakkhita, what were you thinking when the hawk seized you?" "My Lady, I thought of nothing else; I thought only that a heap of bones is carrying away a heap of bones, and wondered where they would be scattered. Thus, My Lady, I thought only of the heap of bones." "Sadhu! Sadhu! Buddharakkhita, in the future, this will be a condition (paccaya) for the end of existence (Nibbāna) for you." In this way, even animals in that place were endowed with the reflection of Satipaṭṭhāna. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to generate the wisdom of Satipaṭṭhāna in those people, spoke this sutta.

In that context, "ekāyano" means a single path (ekamagga). Indeed, there are many names for a path: "magga, pantha, patha, pajja, añjasa, vaṭuma, ayana, nāvā, uttarasetu, kulla, bhisi, saṅkama." Here, it is spoken of by the name "ayana." Therefore, in the phrase "Bhikkhus, this path is a single path (ekāyano)," it should be understood to mean "Bhikkhus, this path is a single path; it is not a two-forked road." Alternatively, it is called "ekāyana" because it must be traveled by one alone. "By one alone" means leaving the crowd and living alone with a secluded mind. It is called "ayana" because it must be traveled (paṭipajjitabba), or because one goes by means of this path.
336:
The meaning is that they go from Saṃsāra to Nibbāna. It is called "ekāyana" because it is the path of a single person. "A single person" refers to the most excellent person. Since the Blessed One is the most excellent of all beings, it means the path of the Blessed One. Although others also travel by this path, it is still the Blessed One's path because it was brought forth by Him. As it is said: "Brahmin, that Blessed One is the arouser of the unarisen path," and so on. Or, it is called "ayana" because it goes; the meaning is that it proceeds or occurs. It is called "ekāyana" because it occurs in a single dispensation; it means it occurs only in this Dhamma-Vinaya and not elsewhere. As it is said: "Subhadda, only in this Dhamma-Vinaya is the Noble Eightfold Path found." This is merely a difference in the manner of teaching; in meaning, it is only one. Furthermore, it is called "ekāyana" because it goes to the one Nibbāna. It means that although it proceeds by various methods of meditation in the preliminary stage, in the later stage it goes only to the single Nibbāna. As Sahampati Brahmā said:

"The One who sees the end of the destruction of birth, the Compassionate One who seeks the welfare of beings, knows the Sole Way (Ekāyana). By this path, they crossed in the past, they will cross in the future, and they are crossing the floods (oghas) now."

Some teachers say it is called "ekāyana" because it goes to Nibbāna only once, following the method of the verse "They do not go to the further shore twice." That is not appropriate. For that meaning, the wording should be "sakiṃ ayano." If one takes the meaning as "it has a single way of going," the wording would be appropriate, but the meaning is inappropriate in both cases. Why? Because here the preliminary path (pubbabhāga-magga) is intended. For the preliminary path of Satipaṭṭhāna, which proceeds with the four objects such as the body, is intended here, not the supramundane path (lokuttara-magga). And that preliminary path is traveled many times, and its goings are many.

In the past, there was a discussion among the Great Elders regarding this term. Elder Tipitaka Cūḷanāga said it is the "preliminary path of Satipaṭṭhāna." However, his teacher, Elder Tipitaka Cūḷasuma, said it is the "mixed path" (missaka-magga). When asked, "Venerable Sir, is it not the preliminary path?" he replied, "Friend, it is only the mixed path." When the teacher spoke thus repeatedly...
337:
He remained silent without objecting. They rose from their seats without having settled the problem. Then, the teacher elder, while going to the bathhouse, reflected: "I have taught the Mixed Path (missaka-magga), but Cūḷanāga speaks taking it as the Preliminary Path (pubbabhāga-magga). What is the correct conclusion here?" While reviewing the Sutta from the beginning, he noticed this point: "Monks, should any person develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this way for seven years..." He realized: "There is no such thing as the supramundane path (lokuttara-magga) arising and lasting for seven years. The Mixed Path I spoke of is not applicable; only the Preliminary Path seen by Cūḷanāga is applicable." Knowing this, he went when the announcement for the Dhamma preaching was made on the eighth day.

It is said that the ancient elders (porāṇakattherā) cherished listening to the Dhamma; as soon as they heard the sound, they would gather at once, saying, "I first, I first!" On that day, it was the turn of the elder Cūḷanāga. When that elder had sat on the Dhamma-seat, taken the fan, and recited the introductory verses, the teacher, standing behind the seat, thought: "I will not speak while sitting in private." Indeed, the ancient elders were not envious. They did not go about carrying their own views like a bundle of sugarcane; they accepted only what was reasonable and rejected what was unreasonable. Therefore, the elder called out, "Friend Cūḷanāga!" Cūḷanāga, recognizing it as his teacher's voice, stopped the sermon and asked, "What is it, venerable sir?" The teacher said, "Friend Cūḷanāga, the Mixed Path I spoke of is not applicable; only the Preliminary Path of the foundations of mindfulness that you spoke of is applicable."

The elder Cūḷanāga thought again: "Our teacher is one who has mastered all the scriptures, a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, and a man of great learning. Yet, even for such a bhikkhu, this problem was confusing. In the future, my brothers will also be confused by this problem. I will make this problem firm by citing the Sutta." Thinking thus, he cited from the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "The 'One-way Path' (ekāyana-magga) refers to the Preliminary Path of the foundations of mindfulness."

Of paths, the Eightfold Path is the best; of truths, the Four Truths are the best.
Detachment (virāga) is the best of states; and of two-legged beings, the One with Vision (the Buddha) is the best.
This is the only path; there is no other for the purification of vision.
Follow this path, for it is the confounding of Māra's host.
Following this path, you will make an end of suffering.

Thus, he brought forth and presented the Sutta.
338:
In what sense is it called 'Magga'? It is called 'Magga' because it goes to Nibbāna, and because it is to be sought by those desiring Nibbāna. 'For the purification of beings' (sattānaṃ visuddhiyā) means for the sake of the purification of beings whose minds are defiled by stains such as lust (rāga) and by impurities (upakkilesa) such as covetousness and unrighteous greed (abhijjhā-visamalobha).

Indeed, by this very path, starting from the Buddhas named Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara, who appeared in a single aeon more than four asankhyeyyas and a hundred thousand aeons ago, down to the Buddha Sakyamuni—many Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, many hundreds of Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples (ariyasāvaka) beyond counting—all these beings have washed away the stains of the mind and reached supreme purification. However, in terms of the stains of the body (rūpa), there is no such designation as defilement or purification. Thus it is said:

"The Great Sage did not teach that beings are defiled because the body is defiled, or that they are purified because the body is purified.
The Great Sage taught that beings are defiled because the mind is defiled, and they are purified because the mind is purified."

As He said: "Monks, beings are defiled by the defilement of the mind; they are purified by the purification of the mind." And that purification of the mind occurs through this path of the foundations of mindfulness. Therefore, He said, "For the purification of beings."

'For the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation' (sokaparidevānaṃ samatikkamāya) means for the purpose of transcending and abandoning both sorrow and lamentation. For this path, when developed, leads to the overcoming of sorrow, as in the case of the minister Santati and others, and to the overcoming of lamentation, as in the case of Paṭācārā and others. Therefore, He said, "For the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation." Indeed, the minister Santati, upon hearing only this verse:

"Dry up what is past, let there be nothing for you in the future. If you do not grasp what is in the middle, you will wander at peace."

reached Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). Paṭācārā also, hearing:

"Sons are no protection, nor father, nor kinsmen; for one overcome by the Ender (Death), there is no protection among relatives."

...
339:
Upon hearing this verse, they were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry. Because there is no meditation without contemplating one of the phenomena—body, feeling, mind, or mental objects—it should be understood that they too overcame sorrow and lamentation through this very path.

'Dukkha-domanassānaṃ atthaṅgamāya' means for the cessation and vanishing of these two: physical suffering (dukkha) and mental distress (domanassa). Indeed, when this path is developed, it leads to the cessation of suffering, as in the case of Elder Tissa and others, and to the cessation of distress, as in the case of Sakka, King of Devas, and others.

To explain the meaning here: In Sāvatthī, a son of a wealthy man named Tissa renounced forty crores of gold, ordained, and lived in a forest far from any village. The wife of his younger brother sent five hundred robbers, saying, 'Go, take his life.' They went, surrounded the Elder, and sat down. The Elder asked, 'Lay devotees, why have you come?' 'We have come to take your life,' they replied. 'Lay devotees, give me one night of life by taking a guarantee from me,' he said. 'O recluse, who will be a guarantee for you in such a place?' they asked. The Elder took a large stone, broke both his thigh bones, and said, 'Lay devotees, is the guarantee not obtained?' The robbers moved away, lit a fire at the head of the walking path, and fell asleep. The Elder, suppressing the pain and reflecting on his virtue, felt joy and rapture (pīti-pāmojja) based on his pure virtue. From there, gradually developing insight and practicing the recluse's Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night, he attained Arahantship at dawn and uttered this inspired verse:

'Having broken both my legs, I give you my guarantee,
I am repulsed and ashamed of dying with lust.
Having thought thus, I contemplated things as they really are,
When dawn arrived, I attained Arahantship.'

Another thirty monks took a meditation subject from the Blessed One and entered the rains retreat in a forest monastery. They agreed, 'Friends, we must practice the recluse's Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night; we should not come to one another.' While they were practicing and nodding off toward dawn, a tiger came and snatched the monks one by one. Not a single monk even uttered the words, 'A tiger is seizing me.' After five or ten monks had been eaten in this way, on the Uposatha day, the other monks...
340:
...asked, 'Friends, where are they?' Upon finding out, they agreed, 'From now on, the one who is seized must say, "I am seized by a tiger."' Then, a tiger seized another young monk in the same manner as before. He said, 'Venerable sirs, a tiger is dragging me away!' The monks, holding walking sticks and torches, followed him, saying, 'We will rescue him.' The tiger climbed an inaccessible cliff where the monks could not go and began eating the monk starting from his big toe. The other monks said, 'O good man, there is nothing we can do now. The extraordinary quality of monks is known in such a situation.' While lying in the tiger's mouth, the monk suppressed the pain and developed insight. By the time he was eaten up to the ankles, he became a Stream-enterer. By the time he was eaten up to the knees, a Once-returner. By the time he was eaten up to the navel, a Non-returner. Before his heart-base was eaten, he attained Arahantship along with the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā) and uttered this inspired verse:

'Possessed of virtue and vows, wise and well-concentrated,
Due to a moment's negligence, my mind is oppressed by a tiger.
Being seized in its jaws, as if placed upon a stone slab,
Let the tiger eat my flesh and bones as it pleases,
I shall exhaust the defilements and touch the fruit of liberation.'

Another Elder named Pītamalla was a standard-bearer for three kings during his lay life. Having come to the island of Tambapaṇṇi and seen the King, he received the King's patronage. One day, while passing by the door of a mat-shop, he heard the 'Na Tumhāka' (Not Yours) sentence: 'Bhikkhus, form is not yours; abandon it. Your abandoning of it will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.' He thought, 'Indeed, form is not one's own, nor is feeling.' Taking that very thought as an object, he left, went to the Mahāvihāra, requested ordination, and became a monk. After mastering the two Mātikās, he took thirty monks and went to the Gabalavāliya courtyard to practice the recluse's Dhamma. When his feet could no longer walk, he walked the meditation path on his knees. One night, a hunter searching for deer mistook him for a deer and stabbed him with a spear. The spear pierced through to the other side. The Elder had the spear removed, plugged the wound with a clump of grass, sat on a stone slab, and taking the opportunity, developed insight...
341:
Elder Tissa, having attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā), gave a declaration to the monks who had arrived at the sound of his clearing his throat, and uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):

“This form is not yours, as taught by the Buddha, the best of beings, who speaks of the highest in all the world. O monks, you should abandon that form. Impermanent indeed are formations (saṅkhāra), subject to arising and passing away; having arisen, they cease. The stilling of them (Nibbāna) is bliss.”

In this way, this path (of Satipaṭṭhāna) leads to the cessation of suffering, just as it did for Elder Tissa and others.

Sakka, the King of Devas, having seen his own five premonitory signs (pubbanimitta) and being threatened by the fear of death, became dejected and approached the Blessed One to ask a question. At the conclusion of the answer to the question on equanimity, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) along with eighty thousand deities. His rebirth was clearly manifest just as before.

The young deva Subrahmā was also enjoying heavenly bliss, surrounded by a thousand nymphs. At that time, five hundred nymphs, while picking flowers from trees, passed away and were reborn in hell. When that young deva reflected, “Why are these nymphs taking so long?”, he realized they had been reborn in hell. Examining “How long is my own life span?”, he realized his life was coming to an end and saw that after passing away, he would be reborn in that very same hell. Terrified and deeply dejected, he thought, “No one but the Teacher can remove this dejection of mine.” Taking the remaining five hundred nymphs, he approached the Blessed One and asked this question:

“This mind is always terrified, this heart is always agitated, by troubles that have not yet arisen and by those that have already appeared. If there is a state free from terror, please tell me when asked.”

Then the Blessed One said to him:

“Other than through the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and austerity (tapa), other than through the restraint of the faculties (indriya-saṃvara), and other than through the relinquishing of all (sabba-nissagga), I see no safety for living beings.”
342:
At the conclusion of the teaching, that young deva, together with the five hundred nymphs, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), making that attainment firm and stable, and returned to the deva world. Thus, it should be understood that this path, when developed, leads to the cessation of dejection, just as it did for Sakka and others.

“Ñāyassa adhigamāya”: the Noble Eightfold Path is called “ñāya”; it means for the sake of attaining that path. For when this mundane path of mindfulness (lokiya-satipaṭṭhāna-magga), which belongs to the preliminary stage, is developed, it leads to the attainment of the supramundane path. Therefore, he said, “ñāyassa adhigamāya.”

“Nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya”: because it is free from the bond (vāna) of craving, it is called Nibbāna. It means for the sake of realizing the Deathless (amata), for witnessing it for oneself. For when this path is developed, it gradually achieves the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, he said, “nibbānassa sacchikiriyāya.”

In that (Satipaṭṭhāna teaching), although by saying “for the purification of beings,” the overcoming of sorrow and so forth are already established in meaning, they are not clear to others except for those skilled in the logic of the Dispensation (sāsana-yutti). The Blessed One does not first make people skilled in the logic of the Dispensation and only then teach the Dhamma. Rather, he makes the respective meanings known through the respective discourses. Therefore, in this Dispensation, whatever benefit the Direct Path (ekāyana-magga) achieves, he said “for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation” and so forth, wishing to show those benefits clearly.

Alternatively, the purification of beings that occurs through the Direct Path happens through the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation. The overcoming of sorrow and lamentation happens through the cessation of pain and dejection. The cessation of pain and dejection happens through the attainment of the Noble Path. The attainment of the Noble Path happens through the realization of Nibbāna. Therefore, wishing to show this sequence, he said “for the purification of beings” and then “for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation” and so forth.

Furthermore, this is a praise of the virtues of the Direct Path. Just as the Blessed One spoke praise with eight phrases in the Chachakka teaching: “Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; I will reveal the holy life that is entirely complete and pure, namely, the Six Sets of Six” (M. iii. 420). And just as in the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta: “Monks, these four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa) are supreme, of long standing, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated...” and so forth (he spoke praise).
343:
The Blessed One praised the virtues [of the Dhamma] with nine phrases: "Wise ascetics and brahmins do not revile, have not reviled, and will not revile [these teachings]" (A. IV. 28). Similarly, he praised the virtues of this One-way Path with seven phrases, beginning with "for the purification of beings." Why did he speak thus? It was to arouse enthusiasm (ussāha) in those monks. For upon hearing the praise of these virtues, those monks would think: "This path dispels the four afflictions—sorrow (soka), which is the burning of the heart; lamentation (parideva), which is the wailing of the voice; pain (dukkha), which is bodily unpleasantness; and grief (domanassa), which is mental unpleasantness. It brings about three distinct benefits: purification, the noble method (ñāya), and Nibbāna." Thus, being filled with enthusiasm, they would consider that this Dhamma teaching should be learned, studied, mastered, taught, and that this path should be developed. Thus, he praised the virtues to arouse enthusiasm in those monks, just as a blanket merchant praises the quality of blankets and so forth.

For example, even when a merchant selling a pale yellow woolen blanket (paṇḍukambala) worth a hundred thousand cries out, "Buy this blanket!", people do not yet know what kind of blanket it is. This is because blankets made of hair or animal tails, which are foul-smelling and rough to the touch, are also called "blankets." But when he cries out, "This is a red blanket from the Gandhāra region, fine, brilliant, and pleasant to the touch," then those who can afford it buy it, and even those who cannot afford it desire to see it.
