In the same way, even when it is said, "Monks, this path is a one-way path," it is not yet clear what kind of path it is. This is because various wrong paths that do not lead out of Saṃsāra are also called "paths." However, when it is said, "for the purification of beings," etc., they will think: "This path dispels the four afflictions and brings about the three distinct benefits." Thus, being filled with enthusiasm, they will consider that this Dhamma teaching should be learned, studied, mastered, taught, and that this path should be developed. Intending this, he praised the virtues and said, "for the purification of beings," and so forth. Just like the example of the merchant of the pale yellow woolen blanket worth a hundred thousand, the examples of merchants selling red Jambūnada gold, water-clearing gems, highly pure pearls, coral, and so forth, should also be applied here.

"Yadidaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta); its meaning is "namely these four." "Cattāro" (four) is a numerical limitation. By this limitation, he shows that the foundations of mindfulness are neither fewer than four nor more than four. "Satipaṭṭhāna" refers to the three foundations of mindfulness, the object of mindfulness (sati-gocara), the Teacher's freedom from aversion and attraction towards disciples who practice in three ways, and mindfulness itself.
344:
“Monks, I will teach the origin and the disappearance of the four foundations of mindfulness. Listen to that... Monks, what is the origin of the body (kāya)? With the origin of nutriment (āhāra), there is the origin of the body.” In such passages (S. V. 408), the object of mindfulness is called "Satipaṭṭhāna." Likewise, in passages such as: “The body is the establishment (upaṭṭhāna), not mindfulness; but mindfulness is both the establishment and mindfulness” (Paṭis. M. 3.35). The meaning of that term is: it is called a foundation (paṭṭhāna) because mindfulness stands (patiṭṭhāti) in this object. What stands? Mindfulness stands. The foundation of mindfulness is "Satipaṭṭhāna." Alternatively, "paṭṭhāna" means a principal station. The station of mindfulness is "Satipaṭṭhāna," just like an elephant station (hatthiṭṭhāna) or a horse station (assaṭṭhāna).

“There are three foundations of mindfulness which the Noble One resorts to, and resorting to which the Teacher is worthy of instructing the group” (M. III. 311). Here, the Teacher's state of having transcended aversion (paṭigha) and attraction (anunaya) towards disciples who practice in three ways is called “Satipaṭṭhāna.” Its meaning is: it is called “paṭṭhāna” because it should be set forth (paṭṭhapetabbato), meaning it should be set in motion. By what should it be set forth? By mindfulness. Being set forth by mindfulness, it is called “Satipaṭṭhāna.” However, in passages such as: “The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment” (M. III. 147), mindfulness itself is called “Satipaṭṭhāna.” Its meaning is: it is called “paṭṭhāna” because it stands forth (paṭṭhāti), meaning it occurs by plunging into, entering into, and spreading through [the object]. Mindfulness itself is “Satipaṭṭhāna.” Or alternatively, it is “sati” in the sense of remembering, and “paṭṭhāna” in the sense of standing forth. Thus, because it is both mindfulness and a foundation, it is “Satipaṭṭhāna.” This is the meaning intended here.

If that is so, why is the plural “Satipaṭṭhānā” used? Because of the plurality of mindfulness. These mindfulnesses are many due to the diversity of objects. Then why is “maggo” (path) used in the singular? Because of the oneness in the sense of a path. For these four mindfulnesses reach oneness in the sense of a path. For it is said: “In what sense is a path a path? In the sense of going to Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna.” These four, while performing their function regarding objects such as the body in the subsequent stage, go to Nibbāna; and from the beginning, they are sought by those who desire Nibbāna. Therefore, even though they are four, they are called “one path.” In this way, by the connection of words, the teaching is one with its sequence (sānusandhika), as in: “Monks, I will teach you the path that crushes the army of Māra. Listen to that... And what, monks, is the path that crushes the army of Māra? It is these seven factors of enlightenment” (S. V. 224). Just as “the path that crushes the army of Māra” and “the seven factors of enlightenment” are one in meaning, and only the phrasing here...
345:
It is distinctive. In this way, the expression "ekāyanomaggo" and the expression "cattāro satipaṭṭhānā" are identical in meaning. Only the phrasing (vyañjana) differs here. Therefore, it should be understood that the singular is used because it is one in the sense of the path, and the plural is used because mindfulness is manifold due to the diversity of objects.

Why did the Blessed One say there are exactly four foundations of mindfulness, neither more nor less? It was said for the benefit of those to be led (veneyya). Among those to be led, who are divided into two types—those of dull (manda) and sharp (tikkha) faculties—among those of craving temperament (taṇhācarita) and view temperament (diṭṭhicarita), and those of the vehicle of serenity (samathayānika) and the vehicle of insight (vipassanāyānika):
For one of craving temperament with dull faculties, the coarse contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) is the path to purity. For one of sharp faculties, the subtle contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā) is the path to purity. For one of view temperament with dull faculties, the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā), which is not very diversified, is the path to purity. For one of sharp faculties, the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā), which is highly diversified, is the path to purity. For one of the serenity vehicle with dull faculties, the first foundation of mindfulness, which has a sign (nimitta) to be attained without difficulty, is the path to purity. For one of sharp faculties, the second is the path to purity, because they do not settle on a coarse object. For one of the insight vehicle with dull faculties, the third foundation of mindfulness, which has an object not very diversified, is the path to purity. For one of sharp faculties, the fourth, which has a highly diversified object, is the path to purity. Thus, he said there are exactly four, neither more nor less.

Alternatively, they were stated as four to abandon the perversions (vipallāsa) of beauty (subha), happiness (sukha), permanence (nicca), and self (atta). Although the body is unattractive (asubha), beings are perverted by the perversion of beauty regarding it. To abandon that perversion by showing the unattractive nature of the body, the first foundation of mindfulness was taught. Although feelings and so on are taken as happy, permanent, and self, feelings are suffering (dukkha), the mind is impermanent (anicca), and phenomena are non-self (anattā). To abandon the perversions of happiness, permanence, and self in those who are perverted, the remaining three foundations of mindfulness were taught. Thus, it should be understood that exactly four were taught, neither more nor less, to abandon the perversions of beauty, happiness, permanence, and self. Not only to abandon the perversions, but also to abandon the four floods (ogha), the four yokes (yoga), the four taints (āsava), the four ties (gantha), the four clingings (upādāna), the four wrong courses (agati), and for the full understanding of the four nutriments (āhāra), it should be understood that exactly four were taught. This is the method of the exposition (pakaraṇa).

In the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā), however, it is said that the foundation of mindfulness is only one in terms of refuge (saraṇa) and in terms of converging into a single state (ekattasamosaraṇa), but four in terms of objects. Just as in a city with four gates, those coming from the east take goods produced in the east and enter the city through the east gate. Those coming from the south, west, and north take goods produced in the north and enter the city through the north gate. This should be understood in the same way. The city
346:
is like the great city of Nibbāna. The supramundane Eightfold Path is like the gate. The body and so on are like the east and other directions.

Just as those coming from the east take goods produced in the east and enter the city through the east gate, so too, those coming through the door of contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) develop the fourteen-fold contemplation of the body and, by means of the noble path arisen through the power of the development of contemplation of the body, converge into the single Nibbāna. Just as those coming from the south take goods produced in the south and enter the city through the south gate, so too, those coming through the door of contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā) develop the nine-fold contemplation of feeling and, by means of the noble path arisen through the power of the development of contemplation of feeling, converge into the single Nibbāna. Just as those coming from the west take goods produced in the west and enter the city through the west gate, so too, those coming through the door of contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā) develop the sixteen-fold contemplation of the mind and, by means of the noble path arisen through the power of the development of contemplation of the mind, converge into the single Nibbāna. Just as those coming from the north take goods produced in the north and enter the city through the north gate, so too, those coming through the door of contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) develop the five-fold contemplation of phenomena and, by means of the noble path arisen through the power of the development of contemplation of phenomena, converge into the single Nibbāna. Thus, it should be understood that the foundation of mindfulness is only one in terms of refuge (saraṇa) and in terms of converging into a single state, but four in terms of objects.

"Which four?" is a question asked with the desire to explain. "Idha" (here) means in this Dispensation (sāsana). "Bhikkhave" (O monks) is an address to those who receive the Dhamma. "Bhikkhū" (monks) is an illustration of those who fulfill the practice. Although other deities and humans also fulfill the practice, he said "bhikkhū" because the practice is noble and to show the state of a monk through practice. Among those who receive the instruction of the Blessed One, a monk is the best, because he is like a vessel capable of receiving all forms of instruction. Therefore, because of being the best, he said "bhikkhū." When a monk is mentioned, the rest are also included, just as when a king's departure is mentioned, his retinue is also included. Also, whoever undertakes this practice is called a monk; thus, he said "bhikkhū" to show the state of a monk through practice. Whether it be a deity or a human, one who practices is indeed reckoned as a monk. Thus it was said:
347:
Even if he is adorned, if he should live in equanimity, peaceful, tamed, established in the Dhamma, leading a holy life, and has laid down the rod towards all beings, he is a Brahmin, he is an ascetic, he is a monk. (Dhp. 142)

'Kāye' refers to the physical body (rūpakāya). Here, the physical body is intended as 'kāya' in the sense of a collection of parts and phenomena such as hair, etc., just like a collection of elephants or a collection of chariots. It is called 'kāya' both in the sense of a collection and in the sense of being the place of origin of loathsome things. Because it is the place of origin of those things which are extremely loathsome, it is called 'kāya'. 'Āya' means the place of origin. Here is the word-definition: they come (āyanti) from there, thus it is 'āya'. What come? The loathsome things like hair, etc. Thus, it is 'kāya' because it is the place of origin (āya) of loathsome things (kucchita).

'Kāyānupassī' means one who has the habit of repeatedly contemplating the body, or one who is repeatedly contemplating the body. Even though 'kāye' (in the body) has been said, the second mention of 'kāya' in 'kāyānupassī' should be understood as being done to show the determination without mixing and the breaking up of the compact (ghana-vinibbhoga). By doing so, it is shown that one is not a contemplator of feelings, or a contemplator of mind or mental objects in the body, but rather a contemplator of the body only; by showing only the mode of body-contemplation in the object called 'body', the determination without mixing is shown.

Similarly, one is not a contemplator of a single phenomenon separate from the limbs and parts in the body, nor a contemplator of a woman or a man separate from hair, body hair, etc. Even in this body, which is called a collection of primary elements and derived matter such as hair, body hair, etc., one is not a contemplator of a single phenomenon separate from the primary elements and derived matter. Rather, like one who contemplates the components of a chariot, like one who contemplates the parts of a city, like one who peels the layers of a banana trunk, and like one who opens an empty fist, one is a contemplator of the collection of primary elements and derived matter only. Thus, by showing the object called 'body' through the power of the collection in various ways, the breaking up of the compact is shown. For here, there is no body, woman, man, or any other phenomenon seen separate from the aforementioned collection; it is only in the mere collection of the aforementioned phenomena that beings wrongly adhere in such and such ways. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

'What he sees, that is not the seen; what is seen, that he does not see. Not seeing, the fool is bound; being bound, he is not released.'
348:
It was said, 'to show the breaking up of the compact, etc.' By the word 'ādi' (etc.), this meaning should also be understood. It means that in this body, one is a contemplator of the body only, not a contemplator of other phenomena. Unlike those who see water in a mirage which is not water, one does not see permanence, pleasure, self, and beauty in this body which is actually impermanent, suffering, non-self, and foul. Rather, it means that as a contemplator of the body, one is a contemplator of the collection of the modes of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and foulness.

Alternatively, later on, it is said: 'Here, monks, a monk in this Dispensation, having gone to the forest... he, mindful, breathes in,' and so on, the body is described starting from the in-breath and out-breath and ending with the collection of bones. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga also, it is said: 'Here, someone contemplates the collection of the earth element as impermanent; he contemplates the collection of the water element, the fire element, the air element, hair, body hair, outer skin, inner skin, flesh, blood, tendons, bones, and bone marrow.' Because of contemplating all that in this very body, the meaning should be understood as 'kāye kāyānupassī' in this way as well.

Alternatively, the meaning should be regarded as 'a contemplator of the body called the collection of various phenomena such as hair, etc.', because of not contemplating any phenomenon that might be grasped as 'I' or 'mine' in the body, but contemplating only the collection of various phenomena such as hair, body hair, etc.

Furthermore, the meaning should also be regarded as 'kāye kāyānupassī' because of contemplating the body called the collection of modes such as the characteristic of impermanence, etc., according to the entire method that comes in the Paṭisambhidāmagga in sequence: 'In this body, he contemplates as impermanent, not as permanent,' and so on. Only when it is so, the monk who has entered upon the practice of contemplation of the body in the body contemplates this body as impermanent by the power of the seven contemplations starting with the contemplation of impermanence; he does not contemplate it as permanent. He contemplates it as suffering, not as pleasure. He contemplates it as non-self, not as self. He becomes weary, he does not delight. He becomes dispassionate, he is not lustful. He causes cessation, he does not cause arising. He relinquishes, he does not grasp. That monk, contemplating it as impermanent, abandons the perception of permanence; contemplating it as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure; contemplating it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self; being weary, he abandons delight (nandī)...
349:
He abandons; it should be understood that one who is dispassionate (*virajjanto*) abandons lust (*rāga*), one who causes cessation (*nirodhento*) abandons the origin (*samudaya*), and one who relinquishes (*paṭinissajjanto*) abandons grasping (*ādāna*).

*(Viharati)* 'He dwells' means he maintains himself through the postures. *(Ātāpī)* 'Ardent' means *ātāpa* (heat) because it burns up the defilements in the three realms of existence; this is a name for energy (*vīriya*). One who possesses this ardent energy is 'ardent' (*ātāpī*). *(Sampajāno)* 'Clearly comprehending' means one endowed with the knowledge known as clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). *(Satimā)* 'Mindful' means one endowed with the mindfulness that grasps the body. Since this person, having grasped the object with mindfulness, contemplates it repeatedly with wisdom—for there is no such thing as contemplation (*anupassanā*) for one devoid of mindfulness—therefore the Blessed One said: "Mindfulness, O monks, I say is useful in all things." Thus, by saying "dwells contemplating the body in the body" (*kāye kāyānupassī viharati*), the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body (*kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna*) is meant.

Alternatively, because for one who lacks energy, internal contraction (*thina-middha*) causes obstacles; one who lacks clear comprehension is confused about grasping the right means and avoiding the wrong means; and one who is forgetful is unable to relinquish the wrong means and grasp the right means, the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) does not succeed for him. Therefore, to show the qualities by whose power that meditation succeeds, it is said: "ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful" (*ātāpီ sampajāno satimā*).

Having thus shown the foundation of mindfulness of contemplation of the body and its associated factors, now to show the factor of abandonment, it is said: "having removed covetousness and grief regarding the world" (*vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ*). In that phrase, *(vineyya)* 'having removed' means having removed by means of 'removal by substitution of opposites' (*tadaṅga-vinaya*) or 'removal by suppression' (*vikkhambhana-vinaya*). *(Loke)* 'In the world' means in that very body (*kāya*). For here, the body is intended as 'the world' in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating. However, covetousness and grief are not abandoned by this person only regarding the body; they are also abandoned regarding feelings and so forth. Therefore, in the Vibhaṅga, it is said that all five aggregates of clinging are 'the world.' Or else, because those states are called 'the world,' this is said by way of extracting the meaning. As for the statement: "Therein, what is the world? That very body is the world," this is the meaning here. The connection should be understood as: "having removed covetousness and grief in that world." Since by taking 'covetousness' (*abhijjhā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is included, and by taking 'grief' (*domanassa*), ill will (*byāpāda*) is included, it should be understood that the abandonment of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is stated by showing the two powerful states included among the hindrances.
350:
In this mindfulness of the body, specifically, by the removal of covetousness (abhijjhā), there is the abandoning of attraction rooted in bodily perfection; by the removal of distress (domanassa), there is the abandoning of aversion rooted in bodily misfortune. By the removal of covetousness, delight in the body is abandoned; by the removal of distress, lack of delight in the development of the body is abandoned. By the removal of covetousness, the attribution of non-existent qualities such as beauty and happiness to the body is abandoned; by the removal of distress, the removal of existing qualities such as impurity and suffering from the body is abandoned. Through such abandoning, the power of yoga and the proficiency in yoga of the practitioner (yogāvacara) become manifest. For this is the power of yoga: when one is free from attraction and aversion, able to endure both delight and lack of delight, and free from attributing what is non-existent or removing what is existent. One who is free from attraction and aversion, enduring both delight and lack of delight, not attributing what is non-existent and not removing what is existent, is proficient in yoga.

In another way, in the phrase "contemplating the body in the body," the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) is stated by "contemplation." In the word "dwells," the maintenance of the body by the one practicing the meditation subject through the aforementioned dwelling is stated. In the words such as "ardent," right effort (sammappadhāna) is stated by "ardency"; the meditation subject for all purposes is stated by "mindfulness and clear comprehension," or else the means of maintaining the meditation subject. It should be understood that through mindfulness, serenity (samatha) obtained by the power of repeated contemplation of the body is stated; through clear comprehension, insight (vipassanā) is stated; and through the removal of covetousness and distress, the power of mental development (bhāvanā) is stated.

In the Vibhaṅga, regarding the word "contemplating": "What is contemplation? It is wisdom, understanding, investigation, deep investigation, investigation of states, marking, close marking, very close marking, sagacity, skill, cleverness, discrimination, reflection, examination, breadth of wisdom, guidance, leadership, insight, clear comprehension, a goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the splendor of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of states, right view. This is called contemplation." One who is endowed with, possessed of, reached by, attained to, and gifted with this contemplation is called "one who contemplates."

"Dwells" means he moves, proceeds, guards, keeps going, maintains, wanders, dwells; therefore, it is said "he dwells."

In the word "ardent," "What is ardency? It is the mental inception of energy, exertion, endeavor, effort, striving, zeal, fortitude, vigor, courage, the state of unfaltering endeavor, the state of not laying down the task, the state of not abandoning the burden, the upholding of the burden, energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, right effort. This is called ardency." One who is endowed with... this ardency is called "ardent."

In the word "clearly comprehending," "What is clear comprehension? It is wisdom, understanding, investigation, deep investigation, investigation of states, marking, close marking, very close marking, sagacity, skill, cleverness, discrimination, reflection, examination, breadth of wisdom, guidance, leadership, insight, clear comprehension, a goad, wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the sword of wisdom, the palace of wisdom, the light of wisdom, the radiance of wisdom, the splendor of wisdom, the jewel of wisdom, non-delusion, investigation of states, right view. This is called clear comprehension." One who is endowed with... this clear comprehension is called "clearly comprehending."

In the word "mindful," "What is mindfulness? It is mindfulness, recollection, calling to mind, mindfulness, the state of remembering, the state of bearing in mind, the state of non-drifting, the state of non-forgetfulness, mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness..."
351:
Right mindfulness (sammā-sati); this is called mindfulness. One is endowed with this mindfulness... [pe]... because of being associated with mindfulness, one is called 'mindful.'

In the phrase 'having removed covetousness and grief in the world,' what is 'the world'? This very body is called the world. The five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā) are also called the world. This is called the world. Among those states, what is covetousness (abhijjhā)? It is whatever lust, intense lust, infatuation, compliance, delight, passionate delight, or intense passion of the mind there is. This is called covetousness. Among those states, what is grief (domanassa)? It is whatever mental unpleasantness, mental pain, or unpleasant and painful feeling born of mental contact (phassa) there is. This is called grief.

Thus, this covetousness and this grief are removed in this world, repeatedly removed, calmed, quieted, fully quieted, ceased, completely ceased, made not to arise, made to disappear, dried up, specially dried up, and brought to an end. Therefore, it is said, 'having removed covetousness and grief in the world.' (Vibhaṅga, 357-362). Thus, the meaning of these words has been stated. It should be understood how this method of the commentary corresponds with that Pāḷi text. This is the explanation of the meaning (atthavaṇṇanā) of the summary (uddesa) of the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) in the foundations of mindfulness.

Now, regarding 'contemplating feelings in feelings... in the mind... in mental qualities... having removed covetousness and grief in the world,' the purpose of repeating the words 'feelings in feelings' and so on should be understood in the same way as stated in the contemplation of the body. In the phrases 'contemplating feelings in feelings,' 'mind in the mind,' and 'mental qualities in mental qualities,' 'feelings' refers to the three types of feelings, and those are only mundane (lokiya) feelings. The mind is also mundane, and likewise, the mental qualities (dhammas). Their classification will become clear in the section of detailed exposition (niddesavāra). However, here, just as feelings should be contemplated, one who contemplates them in that way should be known as 'one who contemplates feelings in feelings.' This method applies to the mind and mental qualities as well. How should feelings be contemplated? Firstly, pleasant feeling should be contemplated as suffering (dukkha), painful feeling as a dart (salla), and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent (anicca). As the Blessed One said:
352:
“He who sees pleasure as suffering, and sees suffering as a thorn, and sees the peaceful neutral feeling as impermanent; that monk, seeing rightly, will live in peace.” (Saṃ. Ni. 4.253). All these [feelings] should also be contemplated as “suffering.” For it was said: “Whatever is felt, I say that is included in suffering.” (Saṃ. Ni. 4.259). They should also be contemplated as pleasure and pain. As it is said: “Pleasant feeling is pleasant in its persistence and painful in its change” (Ma. Ni. 1.465); this should be understood in detail. Furthermore, they should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations, such as impermanence. The rest will become clear in the Exposition Section (Niddesavāra).

Regarding mind (citta) and mental objects (dhamma): mind should be contemplated as impermanent, etc., through its diversity such as object (ārammaṇa), predominance (adhipati), conascence (sahajāta), plane (bhūmi), kamma, result (vipāka), and functional (kiriya), as well as through the states of being with lust (sarāga), etc., mentioned in the Exposition Section. Mental objects (dhamma) should be contemplated through individual characteristics (salakkhaṇa), general characteristics (sāmaññalakkhaṇa), emptiness (suññata-dhamma), and the seven contemplations such as impermanence, as well as through the states of being peaceful (santa), etc., mentioned in the Exposition Section. The rest is as previously described. Indeed, for one who has abandoned greed (abhijjhā) and distress (domanassa) in the world called the body (kāya), they are also abandoned in feelings and so forth. However, this is taught in all sections for the sake of various individuals and by way of the development of the foundations of mindfulness occurring in various moments of consciousness. Alternatively, it should be understood that this is taught to show that when they are abandoned in one place, they are abandoned in the rest as well.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Summary Section (Uddesavāra).

## Contemplation of the Body: Explanation of the Section on Breathing (Ānāpānapabba)

Now, just as a skilled bamboo-worker, wishing to make various utensils such as coarse mats, fine mats, baskets, boxes, and caskets, might obtain a large bamboo, divide it into four parts, and then taking each piece of bamboo, split it to make those various utensils; in the same way, the Blessed One, wishing to enable beings to attain various kinds of distinction through the teaching of the foundations of mindfulness, [divided] the single Right Mindfulness (sammā-sati) as “the four foundations of mindfulness.”
353:
What are the four? Here, monks, in this Dispensation, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, and so forth. Having divided the foundations of mindfulness into four by way of the objects, and taking each one of them to analyze the body, the Blessed One began the Exposition (Niddesavāra) with the words, "And how, monks?"

In this context, the word "And how" (kathañca) is a question asked with the desire to explain in detail. The summary of its meaning is: Monks, in what manner does a monk dwell contemplating the body in the body? This method applies to all sections of questioning. "Here, monks, a monk" (idha bhikkhave bhikkhu) means a monk in this Dispensation (Sāsana). Here, the word "here" (idha) serves to point out the Dispensation which is the support for the person who produces the contemplation of the body in all its aspects, and it serves to exclude other dispensations from having such a quality. For it has been said: "Monks, only here is there a recluse... other doctrines are empty of recluses" (M. Ni. 1.139). Therefore, it is said, "a monk in this Dispensation."

"Gone to the forest, or gone to the root of a tree, or gone to an empty hut"—this indicates his acquisition of a lodging (senāsana) suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness. For the mind of this monk, having long been scattered among objects such as visible forms, does not wish to enter the path of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna); it runs only off the track, like a chariot yoked to an untrained ox. Therefore, just as a cowherd, wishing to tame a wild calf that has grown up drinking all the milk of a wild cow, would take it away from the cow and, having driven a large post into the ground at one side, would tie it there with a rope. Then that calf, struggling this way and that and being unable to escape, would eventually sit down or lie down right by that post. In the same way, this monk, wishing to tame his corrupt mind which has long grown up drinking the taste of objects such as visible forms, should take it away from objects such as visible forms and, having entered the forest, the root of a tree, or an empty hut, should tie it to the post of the object of the foundations of mindfulness with the rope of mindfulness. Thus, even if that mind struggles this way and that, when it does not find its previously frequented objects and is unable to break the rope of mindfulness and escape, it eventually sits down and lies down right in that object by way of access concentration (upacāra) and absorption concentration (appanā). Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"Just as a man here would tie a calf to a post to tame it,
So should one firmly tie one's own mind to the object with mindfulness."
354:
Thus, this lodging is suitable for his meditation. Therefore, it is said, "This indicates his acquisition of a lodging suitable for the development of the foundations of mindfulness."

Furthermore, because this meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) is the pinnacle of the contemplation of the body, and is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the attainment of distinction and for dwelling in happiness in the present life for all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples; and because it is not easy to accomplish without leaving the vicinity of a village crowded with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses, and so forth—since sound is a thorn to jhāna—but it is easy for a meditator (yogāvacara) in a forest where there are no villages to grasp this meditation subject, produce the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing, and making that very jhāna the basis, to comprehend the formations (saṅkhāra) and reach the highest fruit, Arahantship; therefore, the Blessed One, showing the lodging suitable for him, said, "Gone to the forest," and so forth.

For the Blessed One is like a master of site-divining (vatthuvijjā-ācariya). Just as a master of site-divining, having seen and thoroughly examined a site for a city, instructs, "Build the city here," and when the city is safely completed, he receives great honor from the royal family; in the same way, the Blessed One, having examined the lodging suitable for the meditator, instructs, "The meditation subject should be practiced here." Then, when the yogi practicing the meditation subject in that place reaches Arahantship in due course, the Blessed One receives great honor (through praise), such as, "The Blessed One is indeed the Fully Enlightened One."

This monk is also said to be like a leopard. Just as a great king of leopards in the forest, depending on a thicket of grass, a thicket of trees, or a mountain cleft, lies in wait and catches wild buffaloes, deer, bears, wild boars, and other animals; in the same way, this monk practicing the meditation subject in the forest and so forth, catches (attains) the four paths and the four noble fruits in due course. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

"Just as the leopard, so-called, catches animals by lying in wait,
Even so, this son of the Buddha, a meditator with yoked effort, an insight-practitioner,
Having entered the forest, catches the supreme fruit."

Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the forest lodging as the proper ground for his exertion and for swift realization, said, "Gone to the forest," and so forth. What remains to be said in this section on mindfulness of breathing from this point on has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. The passage, "Monks, just as a skilled turner," is merely a simile, and the passage, "or internally in the body," refers only to absorption (appanā). Only these points are not included there (in the Visuddhimagga), while the rest are already included.
355:
One who is skilled in what is to come is called 'dakkha' (expert). 'Drawing long' refers to the act of stretching out the hands and feet to draw long when making large drum-heads and the like. 'Drawing short' refers to the act of drawing slowly and short when making small ivory needles and the like.

In the same way, this monk, by means of the in-breaths and out-breaths occurring over a long duration or a short duration, when breathing in long, understands, 'I breathe in long'... [and so on]... he trains himself, 'I shall breathe out.' To one who trains in this way, the four jhānas arise based on the sign (nimitta) of the in-breaths and out-breaths. Emerging from the jhāna, he discerns either the in-breaths and out-breaths or the jhāna factors.

Among them, the one whose meditation subject is the breaths discerns materiality thus: "On what do these in-breaths and out-breaths depend? They depend on the physical base (vatthu). The physical base is the karajakāya (the body). The karajakāya consists of the four great elements and derived materiality." Thereafter, he discerns as 'mentality' (nāma) the states beginning with contact (phassa) as the fifth, which have that materiality as their object. Having thus discerned mentality-materiality, while searching for its cause, he sees dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) beginning with ignorance (avijjā) and, having crossed over doubt, thinking, "This is merely a phenomenon of causes and effects; there is no other being or person," he applies the three characteristics to mentality-materiality along with its causes. As he develops insight (vipassanā), he gradually reaches Arahatship. This is the path of exit (niyyānamukha) up to Arahatship for one monk.

The one whose meditation subject is the jhāna also defines mentality-materiality thus: "On what do these jhāna factors depend? They depend on the physical base. The physical base is the karajakāya. The jhāna factors are mentality, and the karajakāya is materiality." Having thus defined mentality-materiality, while searching for its cause, he sees the mode of causes (paccayākāra) beginning with ignorance and, having crossed over doubt, thinking, "This is merely a phenomenon of causes and effects; there is no other being or person," he applies the three characteristics to mentality-materiality along with its causes. As he develops insight, he gradually reaches Arahatship. This is the path of exit up to Arahatship for another monk.

'Thus, internally' means he dwells contemplating the body in his own group of in-breaths and out-breaths. 'Or externally' means in the group of in-breaths and out-breaths of another. 'Or internally and externally' means at one time in his own, and at another time in another's group of in-breaths and out-breaths. By this, the period of moving back and forth without abandoning his proficient meditation subject is described. However, at one single moment, both cannot be obtained.
356:
'Or contemplating the nature of arising' means—just as air moves back and forth depending on the blacksmith's bellows, the tube, and the appropriate effort, so too the group of in-breaths and out-breaths moves back and forth for the monk depending on the physical body, the nostrils, and the mind. Phenomena such as the body are 'nature of arising' (samudayadhamma); one who sees these is said to 'dwell contemplating the nature of arising in the body.'

'Or contemplating the nature of vanishing' means—just as when the bellows are removed, the tube is broken, and the appropriate effort is absent, that air does not occur, in the same way, when the body is broken, the nostrils are destroyed, and the mind has ceased, the group of in-breaths and out-breaths does not occur. Thus, seeing that the cessation of the in-breaths and out-breaths is due to the cessation of the body and so on, one is said to 'dwell contemplating the nature of vanishing in the body.' 'Or contemplating the nature of both arising and vanishing' means contemplating arising at one time and vanishing at another.

Alternatively, his mindfulness is established as 'There is only a body.' There is only a body; there is no being, no person, no woman, no man, no self, nothing belonging to a self, no 'I', no 'mine', no someone, and no one belonging to someone. Thus is his mindfulness established.

'Only for the sake of knowledge' means this is the determination of the limit of the purpose. This is what is meant: that established mindfulness is not for any other purpose. Rather, it is only for the sake of further and further measures of knowledge and measures of mindfulness, and for the growth of mindfulness and clear comprehension (satisampajañña). 'And he dwells independent' means he dwells independent of the influence of the supports of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). 'And he does not cling to anything in the world' means he does not grasp anything in the world, whether materiality... [and so on]... or consciousness, as "This is my self" or "This belongs to my self." In the phrase 'In this way also' (evampīti), the word 'also' (pi) serves to connect and include the preceding meaning. With this phrase, the Blessed One shows the conclusion of the teaching on the section on breathing.

In that context, the mindfulness that discerns the in-breaths and out-breaths is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca). The prior craving that originates that mindfulness is the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca). The non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca). The Noble Path that fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object is the Truth of the Path (maggasacca). Thus, having striven by way of the Four Truths, he reaches Nibbāna. This is the path of exit up to Arahatship for a monk who has applied himself by way of in-breaths and out-breaths.

## The Section on Breathing is Finished.
357:
## Commentary on the Section on Postures

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of in-breathing and out-breathing, the Teacher now says, "And again, monks," and so forth, to analyze it by way of the postures. In this regard, although jackals, foxes, and the like also know "we are going" when they go, this [instruction] is not spoken with reference to such knowing. For such knowing does not abandon the perception of a being, does not uproot the notion of a self, and is neither a subject of meditation nor the development of mindfulness. But the knowing of this monk abandons the perception of a being, uproots the notion of a self, and is both a subject of meditation and the development of mindfulness. This is spoken with reference to clear comprehension (sampajāna) such as: "Who goes? Whose going is it? For what reason does one go?" The same method applies to standing and other postures.

In that regard, as to the question "Who goes?"—no being or person whatsoever goes. As to "Whose going is it?"—it is not the going of any being or person. As to "For what reason does one go?"—one goes because of the diffusion of the air element (vāyodhātu) born of the mind's activity. Therefore, that monk knows thus: the thought "I will go" arises; that thought produces air; the air produces intimation (viññatti). The movement of the whole body forward through the diffusion of the air element born of the mind's activity is called "going." The same method applies to standing and other postures.

In the case of standing, the thought "I will stand" arises; that thought produces air; the air produces intimation. The state of the whole body remaining upright from the feet upwards through the diffusion of the air element born of the mind's activity is called "standing." The thought "I will sit" arises; that thought produces air; the air produces intimation. The bending of the lower body and the upright state of the upper body through the diffusion of the air element born of the mind's activity is called "sitting." The thought "I will lie down" arises; that thought produces air; the air produces intimation. The stretching out of the whole body horizontally through the diffusion of the air element born of the mind's activity is called "lying down."

To that monk who knows in this way, the thought occurs: "People say 'a being goes, a being stands,' but in the ultimate sense, there is no being at all who is going or standing. For example, people say 'the cart goes, the cart stands,' yet there is no such thing as a 'cart' that goes or stands. When four oxen are yoked and a skilled driver drives them, people say 'the cart goes, the cart stands.'"
358:
It is a mere conventional expression. In the same way, the body is like the cart because it lacks the faculty of knowing; the air-currents born of the mind are like the oxen; and the mind is like the driver. When the thought "I will go, I will stand" arises, the air element that produces intimation arises. Through the diffusion of the air element born of the mind's activity, going and other movements proceed. Then, there is the mere conventional expression: "A being goes, a being stands; I go, I stand." Therefore, it is said:

"Just as a ship goes by the force of the wind,
And an arrow goes by the force of the bowstring,
So this body goes, struck by the wind [of the mind].

Just as a puppet moves only by the power of strings,
So this body-puppet, directed by the power of the mind-string,
Goes, stands, and sits.

What being is there here who, without causes and conditions,
Could stand or go by its own power?"

Therefore, it should be understood that this monk, who notes going and other movements as occurring only by the power of causes and conditions, "knows 'I am going' when going, or knows 'I am standing, sitting, or lying down' when lying down."

Furthermore, the statement "However his body is disposed, he knows it" is an all-inclusive expression. This means: in whatever manner his body is positioned, he knows it in that very manner. When it is positioned in the manner of going, he knows "it goes." When it is positioned in the manner of standing, sitting, or lying down, he knows "it is lying down."

"Thus he dwells contemplating the body in the body internally" means he dwells contemplating the body in the body by grasping his own four postures. "Or externally" means by grasping the four postures of another. "Or both internally and externally" means he dwells contemplating the body in the body by grasping his own postures at one time and another's postures at another time. In the passage "contemplating the nature of arising," etc., the arising and vanishing of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha) should be extracted by way of the five factors, such as "with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form." It is with reference to this meaning that "contemplating the nature of arising," etc., is spoken. The passage "Or the mindfulness that 'there is a body'" and so forth is just as previously explained.
360:
Herein, the comparison is as follows: This body, composed of the four great elements (caturmahābhūta), is like a bag with openings at both ends. The various grains mixed and placed inside that bag are like the thirty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa) such as hair and so forth. The yogī who practices insight is like a person with good eyesight. Just as the various grains become clear to that person when he opens the bag and examines them, the time when the thirty-two parts become clear to the yogī should be understood. Thus, by discerning hair and so forth, one dwells contemplating the body repeatedly in one's own body, or in the body of another, or alternately in one's own and another's body. From this point onwards, it is exactly as previously described. Only here, it should be understood that the mindfulness which discerns the thirty-two parts is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca), and in this way, it is connected to the door of liberation (Nibbāna). The remaining words are the same as those mentioned before.

## The Section on Attention to Repulsiveness is Finished.

## Explanation of the Section on Attention to Elements

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of attention to repulsiveness, the Buddha now said "Again, further" (puna caparaṃ) and so forth, to analyze it by way of attention to the elements. Herein, the explanation of the meaning along with the comparison is: Just as a butcher or a butcher's apprentice hired for wages, having slaughtered a cow and carved it up, might sit at a crossroads where four main roads meet, having divided it into portions; in the same way, a bhikkhu reflects on this body, however it is placed and however it is disposed, according to its posture among the four postures, thinking: "In this body there is the earth element... etc... the air element."

What is meant is this: Just as when a butcher is feeding the cow, or bringing it to the slaughterhouse, or tying it up there, or slaughtering it, or looking at the slaughtered dead cow, the perception of "cow" does not disappear as long as he has not carved it up and divided it into parts. However, when he has carved it up and sits there, the perception of "cow" disappears, and the perception of "meat" arises.
361:
He no longer thinks, "I am selling a cow" or "These people are taking away the cow." Instead, he thinks only, "I am selling meat" or "These people are taking away meat." In the same way, for this bhikkhu, whether as a layman in the past or as a foolish worldling (bālaputhujjana) who has recently ordained, the perception of "being" (satta) or "person" (puggala) does not disappear as long as he does not reflect on this very body, however it is placed and however it is disposed, by way of the elements, after breaking down the perception of compactness (ghanavinibbhoga). But when he reflects by way of the elements, the perception of "being" disappears, and his mind becomes established solely by way of the elements. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "He reflects on this very body, however it is placed and however it is disposed, by way of the elements: 'In this body there is the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.' Just as, monks, a skilled butcher... etc... the air element."

In this comparison, the butcher is like the yogī; the perception of "cow" is like the perception of "being"; the crossroads is like the four postures; and sitting after dividing into parts is like reflecting by way of the elements. This is the explanation of the Pali text here. The discussion on the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), however, is explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.

Thus, by discerning the four elements, one dwells contemplating the body repeatedly in one's own body, or in the body of another, or alternately in one's own and another's body. From this point onwards, it is exactly as previously described. Only here, it should be understood that the mindfulness which discerns the four elements is the Truth of Suffering, and in this way, it is connected to the door of liberation. The remaining words are the same as those mentioned before.

## The Section on Attention to Elements is Finished.

## Explanation of the Section on the Nine Charnel Grounds

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of the body by way of attention to the elements, the Buddha now said "Again, further" and so forth, to analyze it by way of the nine charnel ground (sivathika) sections. Therein, "seyyathāpi passeyya" means "as if one were to see." "Sarīraṃ" refers to a dead corpse. "Sivathikāya chaḍḍitaṃ" means a corpse cast away in a cemetery. "Ekāhaṃ matassa assa" means a corpse one day dead. "Dvīhaṃ matassa assa" means a corpse two days dead. "Tīhaṃ matassa assa" means a corpse three days dead. It is called "uddhumāta" (bloated) because it is swollen up by the wind like a blacksmith's bellows, rising gradually after the cessation of life. "Uddhumāta" itself is "uddhumātaka." Or, because it is repulsive, it is called "uddhumātaka," meaning miserably bloated. "Vinīlaṃ" (discolored)...
362:
A corpse that has a discolored and ruined appearance, or is very dark blue/black, is called 'vinīlaka'. Or, because it is loathsome and censurable, a dark blue corpse is called 'vinīlaka'. This is a designation for the body which, due to having a red color in places where flesh is abundant, a white color in places where pus collects, and generally a blue color in blue areas, appears like a corpse wrapped in a blue cloth. A corpse with pus trickling from ruptured places or from the nine openings of wounds is called 'vipubba'; that same 'vipubba' is also called 'vipubbaka'. Or, because it is loathsome and censurable, a corpse with pus is called 'vipubbaka'. A corpse that has become full of pus and reached such a state is called 'vipubbakajāta'.

'That monk [compares] this very body of his own' means that the monk compares his own body with that (dead) body through knowledge; he brings it close. How? (He compares:) 'This body of mine also is of such a nature, is of such a constitution, and cannot escape this state.' The meaning is: while these three things—life (āyu), heat (usmā), and consciousness (viññāṇa)—exist, this body is capable of standing, walking, and so on. But when these things depart, this body also, being of such a nature, is merely of a putrid nature; being of such a constitution, it will reach various states such as bloating (uddhumātaka); being unable to escape this state, it cannot surpass states such as bloating. Thus, by discerning bloating and so on, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in the body of another, or at times in his own body and at times in the body of another.

'Eaten' means being eaten by [creatures] perching on the abdomen and so on, and plucking out the flesh of the abdomen, the lips, the eye-sockets, and so on. 'With flesh and blood' means joined with remaining flesh and blood. 'Without flesh but smeared with blood' means that although the flesh is gone, the blood is not yet dry; referring to that state, it is said 'without flesh but smeared with blood'. 'Other' means in another direction. 'Hand bones' means the sixty-four types of hand bones scattered individually. The same method applies to foot bones and so on.

'More than a year old' refers to bones that have passed a year. 'Rotten' means those situated in the open air, which become rotten after more than a year due to contact with wind, sun, and rain; however, those inside the earth remain for a much longer time. 'Become powder' means scattered as fine dust. In all instances, the connection should be made according to the method stated for 'that monk [compares] this very body' by way of the eaten corpse and so on. Thus, by discerning from the eaten corpse up to the state of powder, he dwells contemplating the body in his own body, or in the body of another, or at times in his own body and at times in the body of another.
363:
Standing at this point, the nine cemetery contemplations (nava sīvathika) should be summarized and shown. (1) All corpses mentioned by the method beginning with "a corpse dead for one day" are one type; (2) those beginning with "being eaten by crows" are one type; (3) "a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by tendons" is one type; (4) "a skeleton without flesh, smeared with blood, held together by tendons" is one type; (5) "a skeleton without flesh and blood, held together by tendons" is one type; (6) "bones disconnected and scattered" and so on are one type; (7) "bones white, like the color of a conch shell" are one type; (8) "bones more than a year old, heaped up" are one type; (9) "bones rotted and become powder" are one type (thus making nine types).

"Thus, monks," he spoke this word, wishing to conclude the contemplation of the body after showing the nine cemetery contemplations. In that context, the mindfulness that grasps the nine cemetery contemplations is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); the prior craving that causes that mindfulness to arise is the Truth of the Origin (samudaya-sacca); the non-occurrence of both is the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-sacca); the Noble Path that fully understands suffering, abandons the origin, and has cessation as its object is the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). Thus, having made an effort by way of the Four Noble Truths, one reaches Nibbāna, the state of peace. This is the door to liberation up to Arahantship for monks who grasp the nine cemetery contemplations.

## The Section on the Nine Cemetery Contemplations is Finished.

With this much, the fourteen sections of the contemplation of the body—namely, the section on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), the section on postures (iriyāpatha), the section on the fourfold clear comprehension (catusampajañña), the section on the reflection on repulsiveness (paṭikūlamanasikāra), the section on the reflection on the elements (dhātumanasikāra), and the nine cemetery sections—are completed. Among these fourteen sections, only these two—the section on mindfulness of breathing and the section on the reflection on repulsiveness—are absorption meditation subjects (appanā-kammaṭṭhāna). As for the cemetery contemplations, because they are taught by way of contemplating the danger (ādīnavānupassanā), the remaining twelve are only access meditation subjects (upacāra-kammaṭṭhāna).

## Contemplation of the Body is Finished.

## Explanation of the Contemplation of Feeling

Thus, the Blessed One, having taught the fourteenfold contemplation of the body in the foundations of mindfulness, now speaks the words beginning with "And how, monks," in order to teach the ninefold contemplation of feeling. Therein, "a pleasant feeling" means when experiencing a pleasant feeling, whether bodily or mental, one understands, "I experience a pleasant feeling." In that context—
364:
Even infants lying on their backs know when they experience pleasure at times such as while suckling, "We experience a pleasant feeling." However, the Buddha did not teach with reference to such kind of knowing. This kind of knowing cannot abandon the perception of a being, cannot remove the notion of a self, is not a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), and is not the development of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna-bhāvanā). But the knowing of this bhikkhu abandons the perception of a being, removes the notion of a self, and is both a meditation subject and the development of the foundations of mindfulness. Indeed, this was taught with reference to experiencing with clear comprehension (sampajāna-vediyana) in this way: "Who feels? To whom does the feeling belong? For what reason does the feeling arise?"

Among those questions, "Who feels?" means that no being or person feels. "To whom does the feeling belong?" means that the feeling does not belong to any being or person. "For what reason does the feeling arise?" means that the feeling arises only because of a physical basis (vatthu) and an object (ārammaṇa). Therefore, that bhikkhu knows: "Depending on various bases and objects of pleasure and so on, only the feeling itself feels; and based on the occurrence of that feeling, it is merely a conventional expression to say 'I feel'." This bhikkhu, who notes that only the feeling itself feels based on the physical basis and the object, should be understood as one who "knows that he feels a pleasant feeling," like a certain Elder on Cittalapabbata Mountain.

It is said that when the Elder was unwell, he was groaning and rolling back and forth due to intense pain. Then a young monk asked, "Venerable sir, which part of you hurts?" The Elder replied, "Friend, there is no such thing as a separate place that hurts; it is only the feeling itself that is feeling, based on the physical basis and the object." The young monk then said, "Venerable sir, from the time of knowing this, should you not endure it?" The Elder replied, "Friend, I shall endure it." The young monk said, "Venerable sir, endurance is indeed noble." The Elder then endured it. The wind (internal air element) cut through as far as his heart, and his intestines lay in a heap on the couch. The Elder showed this to the young monk, saying, "Friend, look; this much endurance is appropriate." The young monk remained silent. The Elder, having balanced his energy (vīriya), attained Arahatship together with the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) and, becoming a Samasīsī (one who simultaneously ends defilements and life), attained Parinibbāna.

Just as he knows pleasure, so too pain... [as before] ... when experiencing an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he knows, "I experience an unworldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling." In this way, the Blessed One, having taught the meditation subject of materiality (rūpa-kammaṭṭhāna), wished to teach the meditation subject of mentality (arūpa-kammaṭṭhāna). When taught by way of contact (phassa) or by way of consciousness (citta), it is not clear and appears like darkness; however, because the arising of feelings is clear, it becomes clear when taught by way of feeling. Therefore, just as in the Sakkapañha Sutta, in this Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta also, He taught the meditation subject of mentality by way of feeling. In that teaching—
365:
## "Meditation subjects are of two kinds: materiality meditation and mentality meditation," and so forth—this method of exposition should be understood exactly as taught in the Sakkapañha Sutta.

In those words "a pleasant feeling" (sukhaṃ vedanaṃ) and so on, this is another method of knowing: "He knows that he feels a pleasant feeling" means that because painful feeling is absent at the moment of pleasant feeling, when he feels a pleasant feeling, he knows, "I feel only a pleasant feeling." By knowing thus, because the painful feeling that existed previously does not exist now, and because this pleasant feeling did not exist before this moment, he is one who has clear comprehension (sampajañña) regarding that feeling, knowing that feeling is impermanent (anicca), unstable (adhuva), and subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma). This point was also taught by the Blessed One as follows:

"At whatever time, Aggivessana, one feels a pleasant feeling, at that time one does not feel a painful feeling, nor does one feel a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; at that time one feels only a pleasant feeling. At whatever time, Aggivessana, one feels a painful feeling... [as before] ... feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, at that time one does not feel a pleasant feeling, nor does one feel a painful feeling; at that time one feels only a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. A pleasant feeling, Aggivessana, is impermanent, conditioned (saṅkhata), dependently arisen (paṭiccasamuppanna), subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. A painful feeling also... [as before] ... Aggivessana, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is also impermanent... [as before] ... subject to cessation. Seeing thus, Aggivessana, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, becomes disenchanted with painful feeling, and becomes disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there comes the knowledge: 'It is liberated.' He knows: 'Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.'" (Majjhima Nikāya 2.205).

## In the words "or a worldly pleasant [feeling]" (sāmisaṃ vā sukhaṃ) and so on, worldly pleasant feelings (sāmisa-sukha) are the six kinds of joy based on the household life (gehasita-somanassa-vedanā) which are dependent on the fleshly baits of the five cords of sensual pleasure. Unworldly pleasant feelings (nirāmisa-sukha) are the six kinds of joy based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita-somanassa-vedanā). Worldly painful feelings (sāmisa-dukkha) are the six kinds of grief based on the household life (gehasita-domanassa-vedanā). Unworldly painful feelings (nirāmisa-dukkha) are the six kinds of grief based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita-domanassa-vedanā). Worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings (sāmisa-adukkhamasukha) are the six kinds of equanimity based on the household life (gehasita-upekkhā-vedanā). Unworldly...
366:
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling refers to the six types of equanimity based on renunciation (nekkhamma-sita-upekkhā). The classification of these feelings has already been stated in the Sakkapañha Sutta.

Thus, by discerning pleasant feelings and so forth in the manner of "internally (ajjhattaṃ vā)," etc., one dwells contemplating feelings in one's own feelings, or in the feelings of others, or at times in one's own feelings and at times in the feelings of others. In the passage "or contemplating the nature of arising and vanishing (samudaya-vaya-dhammānupassī vā)," it should be understood that one dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings, or contemplating the nature of vanishing in feelings, or at times the nature of arising and at times the nature of vanishing, by seeing the arising and vanishing of feelings through the five modes each, such as "with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling."

From this point onwards, the method is the same as that stated in the Contemplation of the Body (Kāyānupassanā). However, in this Contemplation of Feeling, it should be understood that the mindfulness which discerns feeling is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). By making this connection, the way of exit for the monk who discerns feeling should be understood; the rest of the sequence of words is just the same.

## The Contemplation of Feeling is Finished.

## Commentary on the Contemplation of Mind

Having thus taught the Contemplation of Feeling in its ninefold division, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with "And how, bhikkhus (kathañca, bhikkhave)," to teach the Contemplation of Mind (Cittānupassanā) in its sixteenfold division. Therein, "with lust (sarāgaṃ)" refers to the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. "Without lust (vītarāgaṃ)" refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate (abyākata) consciousness. Since this Contemplation of Mind is purely for insight (vipassanā) and not for the grouping of dhammas, not even a single supramundane (lokuttara) state is obtained in this context. The remaining four unwholesome types of consciousness belong neither to the former term (sarāga) nor to the latter term (vītarāga). "With hate (sadosaṃ)" refers to the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion (domanassa). "Without hate (vītadosaṃ)" refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. The remaining ten unwholesome types of consciousness belong neither to the former term nor to the latter term. "With delusion (samohaṃ)" is of two types: consciousness accompanied by doubt (vicikicchā) and consciousness accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca). However, since delusion (moha) arises in all unwholesome states, the remaining unwholesome types of consciousness are also included here. Indeed, in this very dyad (samoha/vītamoha), all twelve unwholesome types of consciousness are fully comprised. "Without delusion (vītamohaṃ)" refers to mundane wholesome and indeterminate consciousness. "Shrunken (saṅkhittaṃ)" refers to a mind overcome by sloth and torpor (thina-middha); this is called a shrunken mind. "Distracted (vikkhittaṃ)" refers to a mind accompanied by restlessness; this is called a scattered mind.

"Great (mahaggataṃ)" refers to the fine-material and immaterial-sphere consciousness. "Not great (amahaggataṃ)" refers to the sensual-sphere consciousness. "Surpassable (sauttaraṃ)" refers to the sensual-sphere consciousness. "Unsurpassable (anuttaraṃ)" refers to the fine-material and immaterial-sphere consciousness. Therein, "surpassable" refers to the fine-material sphere consciousness,
367:
while "unsurpassable (anuttaraṃ)" refers only to the immaterial-sphere consciousness. "Concentrated (samāhitaṃ)" refers to a mind that possesses either absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) or access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). "Unconcentrated (asamāhitaṃ)" refers to a mind devoid of both types of concentration. "Freed (vimuttaṃ)" refers to a mind freed by way of temporary deliverance (tadaṅga-vimutti) and deliverance by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimutti). "Unfreed (avimuttaṃ)" refers to a mind devoid of both types of deliverance. As for deliverance by eradication (samuccheda), by tranquilization (paṭippassaddhi), and by escape (nissaraṇa), there is no occasion for them in this context.

Thus, by discerning the mind with lust and so forth in the manner of "internally (ajjhattaṃ vā)," etc., one dwells contemplating the mind in one's own mind, or in the mind of others, or at times in one's own mind and at times in the mind of others, noting whatever mind occurs at each moment. In the passage "contemplating the nature of arising and vanishing (samudaya-vaya-dhammānupassī)," the arising and vanishing of consciousness (viññāṇa) should be drawn out through the five modes each, such as "with the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of consciousness." From this point onwards, the method is the same as that already stated. In this Contemplation of Mind, it should be understood that the mindfulness which discerns the mind is the Truth of Suffering. By thus connecting the words, the way of exit for the monk who discerns the mind should be understood. The rest of the sequence of words is just the same.

## The Contemplation of Mind is Finished.

## Commentary on the Section on Hindrances in the Contemplation of Phenomena

Having thus taught the Contemplation of Mind in its sixteenfold division, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with "And how, bhikkhus (kathañca, bhikkhave)," to teach the Contemplation of Phenomena (Dhammānupassanā) in its fivefold division. Alternatively, the Blessed One taught the discernment of pure materiality (suddha-rūpa) by way of the Contemplation of the Body, and the discernment of pure mentality (suddha-arūpa) by way of the Contemplation of Feeling and the Contemplation of Mind. Now, to teach the discernment of materiality and mentality mixed together, He spoke the words beginning with "And how, bhikkhus." Or else, He taught only the discernment of the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha) by way of the Contemplation of the Body, only the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) by way of the Contemplation of Feeling, and only the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha) by way of the Contemplation of Mind. Now, to teach the discernment of the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) and the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) as well, He spoke the words beginning with "And how, bhikkhus."

Therein, "present (santaṃ)" refers to a hindrance that is existing by way of frequent occurrence. "Absent (asantaṃ)" refers to a hindrance that is not existing, either because it does not occur or because it has been abandoned. "And how (yathā ca)" refers to the cause by which sensual desire (kāmacchanda) arises. "And he knows that (tañca pajānāti)" means he also knows that cause. In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all the terms.

Therein, sensual desire arises through unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) to the beautiful sign (subha-nimitta). Regarding the beautiful sign, a beautiful physical form is called a beautiful sign, and a beautiful object is also called a beautiful sign.
368:
Unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) means attention to what is not the cause, attention on the wrong path, or attention that takes the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the non-self as self, and the foul as beautiful. For one who frequently applies this unwise attention to that object, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is the beautiful sign (subhanimitta); frequently applying unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

By wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) to the foul sign (asubhanimitta), that sensual desire is abandoned. The foul sign refers to both a foul thing and a foul object. Wise attention means attention to the cause, attention on the right path, or attention that takes the impermanent as impermanent, the painful as painful, the non-self as non-self, and the foul as foul. For one who frequently applies this wise attention to that object, sensual desire is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is the foul sign (asubhanimitta); frequently applying wise attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sensual desire, or for the abandoning of arisen sensual desire." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of sensual desire: learning the foul sign, devotion to the meditation on foulness, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, noble friendship, and suitable conversation. Sensual desire is abandoned for one who learns the ten kinds of foul signs, for one who develops them, for one whose sense doors are closed, and for one who is moderate in eating by having the habit of sustaining oneself by drinking water when four or five mouthfuls remain to be eaten. Thus it was said:

"When four or five mouthfuls remain, one should stop eating and drink water; this is enough for the comfortable living of a monk with a resolute mind." (Theragā. 983).

Sensual desire is also abandoned for one who associates with noble friends who delight in the meditation on foulness, like the Elder Tissa who practiced the meditation on foulness, and by suitable conversation related to the ten kinds of foulness while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it was said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of sensual desire." It is understood that sensual desire abandoned by these six things will not arise again in the future through the Path of Arahantship.
369:
Ill will (byāpāda) arises due to unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra) to the sign of irritation (paṭighanimitta). In this context, irritation itself is the sign of irritation, and the object of irritation is also the sign of irritation. Unwise attention has the same characteristic in all instances. For one who frequently applies this unwise attention to that sign, ill will arises. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is the sign of irritation; frequently applying unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen ill will, or for the growth, increase, and expansion of arisen ill will." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

By wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) to the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti), that ill will is abandoned. In this context, when "loving-kindness" (mettā) is mentioned, it includes both absorption (appanā) and access concentration (upacāra). When "liberation of mind" (cetovimutti) is mentioned, it refers only to absorption. Wise attention has the characteristic already mentioned. For one who frequently applies this attention to that object of loving-kindness, ill will is abandoned. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, there is the liberation of mind through loving-kindness; frequently applying wise attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen ill will, or for the abandonment of arisen ill will." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.232).

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of ill will: learning the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the meditation on loving-kindness, reflection on the ownership of kamma (kammassakatā), frequent consideration, noble friendship, and suitable conversation. Ill will is abandoned for one who learns loving-kindness through any of the ways of pervading the directions, whether specified (odissaka) or unspecified (anodissaka), and for one who develops loving-kindness by way of specified or unspecified pervasion.

"What can you do by being angry with this person? Will you be able to destroy his virtue and so on? Have you not come here by your own kamma and will you not depart by your own kamma? Being angry with another is like wanting to strike another after picking up a glowing coal free from flames, a hot iron rod, or excrement. What can this person do by being angry with you? Will he be able to destroy your virtue and so on? This person has also come by his own kamma and will depart by his own kamma; like an unaccepted gift or a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this person's anger will fall back upon his own head."

Thus, ill will is abandoned for one who reflects on the ownership of kamma of oneself and others, for one who stands in consideration after reflecting on the ownership of kamma of both, and for one who associates with noble friends who delight in the meditation on loving-kindness, like the Elder Assagutta. It is also abandoned by suitable conversation related to loving-kindness while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it was said—
370: ## Six things lead to the abandonment of ill will.One understands that for ill will abandoned by these six things, there is no future arising through the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmimagga).Sloth and torpor (thina-middha) arise through unwise attention (ayoni-somanasikāra) to discontent (arati) and so forth. 'Tandī' means laziness of the body. 'Vijambhitā' means bending and stretching the body (yawning). 'Bhattasammada' means drowsiness caused by food and the heat of food. 'Cetaso līnattaṃ' means the sluggish state of the mind. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to these things such as discontent, sloth and torpor arise. Therefore, the Buddha said: "Monks, there are discontent, laziness, yawning, food-drowsiness, and sluggishness of mind; frequently applying unwise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the growth and increase of arisen sloth and torpor."The abandonment of that sloth and torpor occurs through wise attention (yoni-somanasikāra) to the element of initial effort (ārambhadhātu) and so forth. 'Ārambhadhātu' is the first effort exerted. 'Nikkamadhātu' is stronger than that because it has emerged from laziness. 'Parakkamadhātu' is even stronger than nikkamadhātu because it advances to higher and higher stages. For one who frequently applies wise attention to this threefold effort, sloth and torpor are abandoned. Therefore, He said: "Monks, there are the element of initial effort, the element of exertion, and the element of progressive endeavor; frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen sloth and torpor, or for the abandonment of arisen sloth and torpor."Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of sloth and torpor: (1) perceiving the danger in overeating, (2) changing postures, (3) attending to the perception of light, (4) living in the open air, (5) noble friendship, and (6) suitable talk. For a monk who eats in gluttonous ways such as 'āharahatthaka', 'tatravaṭṭaka', 'alaṃsāṭaka', 'kākamāsaka', or 'bhuttavamitaka', and then sits in his night-quarters or day-quarters to practice the Dhamma of a recluse, sloth and torpor come overwhelming him like a great elephant. But for a monk who has the habit of moderation, leaving space for four or five mouthfuls and drinking water, that sloth and torpor do not occur. Thus, for one who sees the danger in overeating, sloth and torpor are abandoned. For one who changes to another posture from the one in which sloth and torpor descended, and for one who attends to the light of the moon, lamps, or torches at night, or the light of the sun during the day...
371: For one living in the open air, and for one associating with noble friends (kalyāṇamitta) who have abandoned sloth and torpor, such as the Elder Mahākassapa, sloth and torpor are abandoned. It is also abandoned by suitable talk (sappāyakathā) based on the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of sloth and torpor." One understands that for sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things, there is no future arising through the Path of Arahantship (Arahattamagga).Restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) arise through unwise attention (ayoni-somanasikāra) to the unsettled state of the mind (cetaso avūpasama). 'Avūpasama' means the state of being unsettled; in essence, it is restlessness and remorse itself. For one who frequently applies unwise attention to that unsettled state, restlessness and remorse arise.
