Therefore, He said: "Monks, there is the unsettled state of the mind; frequently applying unwise attention to it is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, or for the growth and increase of arisen restlessness and remorse."The abandonment of that restlessness and remorse occurs through wise attention (yoni-somanasikāra) to the tranquillity of mind (cetaso vūpasama) known as concentration (samādhi). Therefore, He said: "Monks, there is the tranquillity of mind; frequently applying wise attention to it is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen restlessness and remorse, or for the abandonment of arisen restlessness and remorse."Furthermore, six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse: (1) great learning, (2) being inquisitive, (3) proficiency in the Vinaya, (4) associating with elders, (5) noble friendship, and (6) suitable talk. Through great learning, for one who learns one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas according to the text (Pāḷi) and the meaning, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. For one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and not allowable, for one who is proficient in the Vinaya through mastery of its regulations, for one who approaches senior elders, and for one who associates with noble friends who are experts in the Vinaya like the Elder Upāli, restlessness and remorse are abandoned. It is also abandoned by suitable talk concerning what is allowable and not allowable while standing, sitting, etc. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandonment of restlessness and remorse." One understands that for restlessness and remorse abandoned by these six things, restlessness is abandoned by the Path of Arahantship, and remorse by the Path of Non-returning (Anāgāmimagga).Doubt (vicikicchā) arises through unwise attention to things that are bases for doubt. Things that are bases for doubt are those that repeatedly cause doubt...
372:
Because it is the cause, it is indeed doubt (vicikicchā). In that (basis for doubt), doubt arises in one who frequently applies unwise attention (ayoniso manasikāra). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, there are things that are the basis for doubt; frequently applying unwise attention therein is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen doubt, or for the growth and expansion of arisen doubt."

However, the abandoning of that (doubt) occurs through wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) toward wholesome and other states. Therefore, He said: "Bhikkhus, there are wholesome and unwholesome states, blameable and blameless states, states to be cultivated and not to be cultivated, low and exalted states, and states that are counterparts of dark and bright. Frequently applying wise attention therein is the nutriment for the non-arising of unarisen doubt, or for the abandoning of arisen doubt."

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of doubt: great learning, inquiry, mastery of the Vinaya, abundance of resolution (faith), good friendship, and suitable talk. Through great learning, doubt is abandoned in one who learns even one... or five Nikāyas both in terms of the Pāli text and the meaning. It is also abandoned in one who is frequent in inquiry concerning the Three Jewels, in one who has achieved mastery in the Vinaya, in one who has an abundance of resolution—known as firm faith—in the Three Jewels, and in one who associates with good friends such as the Elder Vakkali, who was foremost among those released by faith (saddhādhimutta). Doubt is also abandoned by suitable talk concerning the qualities of the Three Jewels during postures such as standing and sitting. Therefore, it is said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt." One understands that for the doubt abandoned by these six things, there will be no further arising in the future by means of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga).

"Thus, internally..." means that by thus grasping the five hindrances, one dwells contemplating mental objects (dhammānupassī) either in one's own states, or in the states of another, or at times in one's own and at times in another's states. As for the arising and passing away in this (section on hindrances), they should be extracted as already stated in the section on the five hindrances by way of unwise attention and wise attention toward the sign of beauty (subhanimitta), the sign of foulness (asubhanimitta), and so on. From this point onward, the method is exactly as previously stated. Here, simply...
373:
The mindfulness that grasps the hindrances is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca). In this way, by connecting it, the way of exit for the bhikkhu who grasps the hindrances should be understood. The rest is exactly as stated before.

## The Section on the Hindrances is finished.

## Explanation of the Section on the Aggregates

Having thus analyzed the contemplation of mental objects by way of the five hindrances, the Blessed One now said, "Again, bhikkhus..." and so forth, to analyze it by way of the five aggregates of clinging. In that passage, "in the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha)" means the aggregates of clinging are the aggregates that are the objects of clinging; the meaning is the groups of phenomena or heaps of phenomena that are the conditions for clinging. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation of the aggregates, however, is stated in the Visuddhimagga.

"Thus is form (rūpa)" means one understands form according to its nature, thinking: "This is form, this much is form, there is no form beyond this." The same method applies to feeling (vedanā) and the others. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation of form and the others is stated in the section on the aggregates in the Visuddhimagga itself.

"Thus is the arising of form" means the arising of form in five ways by way of the arising of ignorance (avijjā) and so forth. "Thus is the passing away of form" means the passing away of form in five ways by way of the cessation of ignorance and so forth. The same method applies to feeling and the others. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation is stated in the discussion on the knowledge of arising and passing away (udayabbayañāṇa) in the Visuddhimagga.

"Thus, internally..." means that by thus grasping the five aggregates of clinging, one dwells contemplating mental objects either in one's own states, or in the states of another, or at times in one's own and at times in another's states. As for the arising and passing away in this section, they should be extracted by way of the fifty characteristics stated regarding the five aggregates, such as "with the arising of ignorance, form arises." From this point onward, the method is exactly as previously stated. Specifically, in this section on the aggregates, the mindfulness that grasps the aggregates is the Truth of Suffering. In this way, by connecting it, the way of exit for the bhikkhu who grasps the aggregates should be understood. The rest is exactly as stated before.

## The Section on the Aggregates is finished.
374:
## Commentary on the Section on the Sense Bases
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena (dhammānupassanā) by way of the five aggregates, the teacher now says "Puna caparaṃ" and so forth, in order to analyze it by way of the sense bases (āyatana). In that text, "in the six internal and external sense bases" means in the six internal sense bases: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and in the six external sense bases: visible form, sound, smell, taste, tangible object, and mental object.

"He knows the eye" means he knows the eye-sensitivity (cakkhupasāda) by way of its true nature, function, and characteristic. "He knows visible forms" means he knows the external visible forms produced by the four causes by way of their true nature, function, and characteristic. "He knows the fetter that arises dependent on both" means that dependent on both the eye and visible forms, the ten types of fetters arise, namely: the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāga-saṃyojana), aversion (paṭigha), conceit (māna), wrong view (diṭṭhi), doubt (vicikicchā), adherence to rites and rituals (sīlabbataparāmāsa), lust for existence (bhavarāga), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), and ignorance (avijjā). He knows these fetters by way of their true nature, function, and characteristic.

How do these fetters arise? Firstly, the fetter of sensual lust arises in one who enjoys and delights in a desirable object that has come into range at the eye-door by way of the gratification of sensuality. The fetter of aversion arises in one who is angry at an undesirable object. The fetter of conceit arises in one who thinks, "Apart from me, who else is able to perceive this object clearly?" The fetter of wrong view arises in one who wrongly grasps, "This visible object is permanent and stable." The fetter of doubt arises in one who is uncertain, thinking, "Is this visible object a being, or does it belong to a being?" The fetter of lust for existence arises in one who longs for existence, thinking, "May we easily obtain this object in a prosperous life." The fetter of adherence to rites and rituals arises in one who wrongly undertakes practices, thinking, "In the future, it is possible to obtain such things by undertaking these rites and rituals." The fetter of envy arises in one who is jealous, thinking, "Oh, may others not obtain that visible object!" The fetter of stinginess arises in one who is reluctant to give the visible object they have obtained to others. The fetter of ignorance arises by way of the lack of knowledge that co-arises with all these fetters.

"He knows how the unarisen fetter arises" means he knows the cause by which those ten types of fetters, which have not yet arisen through active manifestation, come to arise. "He knows how the arisen fetter is abandoned" means he knows the cause by which those ten types of fetters, which have arisen either because they have not been abandoned or through active manifestation, come to be abandoned. "He knows the abandoned fetter" means those ten types of fetters that have been abandoned by way of abandonment of specific factors (tadaṅgapahāna) or abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhanapahāna)...
375:
...he knows the cause by which the fetter will not arise again in the future. By what cause does that fetter not arise again in the future? Firstly, the five types of fetters consisting of wrong view, doubt, adherence to rites and rituals, envy, and stinginess do not arise again in the future through the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpattimagga). The two gross fetters of sensual lust and aversion do not arise again through the Path of Once-returning (sakadāgāmimagga), and the subtle forms of these two through the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga). The three fetters of conceit, lust for existence, and ignorance do not arise again in the future through the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga). The same method applies to the ear and sounds, and so forth. Furthermore, this discussion on the sense bases should be understood in detail according to the method stated in the Exposition of the Sense Bases (Āyatananiddesa) in the Visuddhimagga.

"Thus internally" means he dwells contemplating phenomena by grasping the internal sense bases in his own phenomena, or by grasping the external sense bases in the phenomena of others, or at times in his own and at times in the phenomena of others. Regarding the arising and vanishing here, they should be extracted according to the method stated: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of the eye," in the case of the visible sense base within the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha); in the case of the mind base (manāyatana) among the mental bases within the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha); and in the case of the mental-object base (dhammāyatana) within the remaining aggregates. Supramundane phenomena (lokuttaradhamma) are not to be taken. From this point onwards, the method is as already stated. Indeed, it should be understood that the mindfulness that grasps the sense bases here is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca); this is the way of exit for the bhikkhu who grasps the sense bases by such a connection. The rest is exactly as previously described.

## The Section on the Sense Bases is Finished.

## Commentary on the Section on the Enlightenment Factors
Having thus analyzed the contemplation of phenomena by way of the six internal and external sense bases, the teacher now says "Puna caparaṃ" and so forth, in order to analyze it by way of the enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga). In that text, "in the enlightenment factors" (bojjhaṅgesu) means in the factors of a being who awakens [to the four truths]. "Present" (santaṃ) means existing by way of attainment. "Mindfulness as a factor of enlightenment" (satisambojjhaṅga) means the enlightenment factor known as mindfulness. Here, "Sambodhi" (Enlightenment) refers to the practitioner (yogāvacara) from the time they begin insight (vipassanā) onwards, because they awaken to the truths. Alternatively, "Sambodhi" is that collection of seven phenomena, beginning with mindfulness, by which that person awakens, rising from the sleep of defilements, or penetrates the truths. Because it is a factor of that enlightenment, or a factor for that enlightenment, it is called an "enlightenment factor" (bojjhaṅga). Therefore, it is said, "the enlightenment factor known as mindfulness." The definition of the terms for the remaining enlightenment factors should also be understood in this same way.
376:
"Non-existent" (asantaṃ) means non-existent by way of non-attainment. Regarding the mindfulness enlightenment factor, starting with "for the arising of the unarisen mindfulness enlightenment factor"—it is stated: "Monks, there are things that are the basis for the mindfulness enlightenment factor; frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen mindfulness enlightenment factor, or for the growth, increase, and fulfillment by development of the arisen mindfulness enlightenment factor." In this context, mindfulness itself is the thing that is the basis for the mindfulness enlightenment factor. Wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) has the characteristics already mentioned. For one who frequently applies wise attention to those bases, the mindfulness enlightenment factor arises.

Furthermore, four things lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons with muddled mindfulness, associating with persons of established mindfulness, and inclination towards that mindfulness enlightenment factor. The mindfulness enlightenment factor arises through mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven instances such as moving forward, etc.; through avoiding persons with muddled mindfulness who are like a crow that has dropped its food; through associating with persons of established mindfulness like the Elder Tissadatta and the Elder Abhaya; and through having a mind inclined towards establishing mindfulness in postures such as standing and sitting. It is understood that the mindfulness enlightenment factor, having arisen through these four causes, reaches the fulfillment of development through the path of Arahantship.

Regarding the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor (dhamma-vicaya-sambojjhaṅga): "Monks, there are wholesome and unwholesome states... states with and without faults; frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, or for the growth, increase, and fulfillment by development of the arisen investigation-of-states enlightenment factor." Thus is the manner of its arising stated.

Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor: inquiring, cleansing the objects, balancing the faculties, avoiding unwise persons, associating with wise persons, reflecting on the range of deep knowledge, and inclination towards that investigation-of-states enlightenment factor. In this context, "inquiring" (paripucchakatā) means frequent questioning concerning the meaning of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), faculties (indriya), powers (bala), enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga), path factors (magganga), jhāna factors, serenity (samatha), and insight (vipassanā). "Cleansing the objects" (vatthu-visadakiriyā) means making internal and external objects clean. When one's hair, nails, and body hair are long, or when the body is smeared with sweat and dirt and is unpurified, then the internal object is unclean and unbright. When the robes are worn out...
377:
...and soiled with a foul odor, or when the lodging is dirty, then the external object is unclean and unbright. Therefore, the internal object should be made bright by cutting hair, etc., by lightening the body through purgation and emesis, and by anointing and bathing. The external object should be made bright by sewing, washing, dyeing, and smearing the floor with red clay, etc. When these internal and external objects are unclean, the knowledge (ñāṇa) in the arising consciousness and mental factors is also unbright and unpurified, like the light of a lamp flame produced from an unpurified lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. However, when the internal and external objects are bright, the knowledge in the arising consciousness and mental factors is also bright, like the light of a lamp flame produced from a purified lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. Therefore, it is said: "Cleansing the objects leads to the arising of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor."

"Balancing the faculties" (indriya-samatta-paṭipādanā) means making the faculties such as faith, etc., equal. For if one's faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is too strong and the other faculties are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform the function of exertion, the faculty of mindfulness cannot perform the function of establishing, the faculty of concentration cannot perform the function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom cannot perform the function of seeing. Therefore, that faculty of faith should be weakened either by reflecting on the nature of things or by not attending to it in the way that made it strong. The story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration here. If the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) is too strong, then the faculty of faith cannot perform the function of decision, nor can the other faculties perform their respective functions. Therefore, that energy should be weakened by developing tranquility (passaddhi), etc. In this case, the story of the Elder Soṇa should be shown. Thus, it should be understood that if any one faculty is too strong, the others become incapable of their functions.

Particularly, in this context, the equality of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy, is praised. For one with strong faith but weak wisdom is one who has blind faith and gains confidence in improper objects. One with strong wisdom but weak faith tends towards the side of cunning; like a disease caused by medicine, such a person is hard to cure. Thinking that "merit occurs merely by the arising of a thought," such a person overreaches and, failing to perform acts of giving (dāna), etc., may be reborn in hell. When both are equal, one gains confidence only in proper objects. As for one with strong concentration but weak energy, because concentration tends towards sloth, sloth overcomes him. For one with strong energy but weak concentration, because energy tends towards restlessness, restlessness overcomes him. However, when concentration is joined with energy, it cannot fall into sloth; when energy is joined with concentration, it cannot fall into restlessness...
378: (Concentration and wisdom) cannot fall away. Therefore, these two should be balanced. Only when the two are balanced does absorption (appanā) occur. Furthermore, for one practicing concentration, even strong faith is suitable. One who has such faith and conviction will reach absorption. Between concentration and wisdom, for one practicing concentration, one-pointedness (ekaggatā) needs to be strong. Only then can that person reach absorption. For one practicing insight (vipassanā), wisdom needs to be strong. Only then can that person reach the penetration of the three characteristics. Even when the two are balanced, absorption indeed occurs. Mindfulness, however, needs to be strong in all places. Mindfulness protects the mind from falling into restlessness through the power of faith, energy, and wisdom, which are associated with restlessness; and from falling into sloth due to concentration, which is associated with sloth. Therefore, that mindfulness is desired in all places, like salt in all dishes, or like a multi-purpose minister in all royal affairs. Thus, the Blessed One said: 'Mindfulness is said to be useful in all places.' Why? Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge, and mindfulness is manifested as protection. Without mindfulness, there is no uplifting or restraining of the mind. Avoiding persons of poor wisdom (duppañña-puggala-parivajjanā) means avoiding from afar foolish persons who lack the wisdom to penetrate the divisions of the aggregates and so on. Cultivating persons of wisdom (paññavanta-puggala-sevanā) means cultivating persons endowed with wisdom that can grasp the characteristics of balanced wisdom and the wisdom of rise and fall. Reflecting on the conduct of profound knowledge (gambhīra-ñāṇa-cariya-paccavekkhaṇā) means reflecting on the distinctions of profound wisdom occurring in the profound aggregates and so on. Being committed to that (tadadhimuttatā) means having a mind that is inclined, sloped, and directed towards that state to arouse the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas while standing, sitting, etc. One knows that the enlightenment factor of investigation of dhammas thus arisen reaches the fulfillment of development through the path of arahantship. Regarding the enlightenment factor of energy (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga): 'Monks, there are the element of initiative (ārambha-dhātu), the element of launching (nikkama-dhātu), and the element of persistence (parakkama-dhātu). Frequently applying wise attention to them leads to the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of energy, or to the increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of the arisen enlightenment factor of energy.' Thus it arises. Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of energy: reflecting on the fear of the states of deprivation, seeing the benefits of energy, reflecting on the path to be traveled, honoring the almsfood, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of the birth, reflecting on the greatness of fellow practitioners, avoiding lazy persons, cultivating energetic persons, and being committed to that energy.
379:
Among those (four woeful states), in the hells, from the time of being tortured with the fivefold binding onwards, even when experiencing great suffering; in the animal realm, when being caught by nets, traps, and so forth; when being driven by goads and spikes while pulling carts and so forth; in the realm of hungry ghosts (petas), even for many thousands of years or for an entire interval between Buddhas (buddhantara), when being afflicted by hunger and thirst; and among the Kālakañjika Asuras, when experiencing the suffering of wind and heat with a body sixty or eighty cubits high consisting only of skin and bone—at such times, it is not possible to arouse the energy enlightenment factor. 'O monk, only this time is the time for you to exert energy.' Thus, for one who reflects on the fear of the woeful states, the energy enlightenment factor arises.

A lazy person cannot attain the nine supramundane states (nava-lokuttara-dhamma); only one with exerted energy can attain them. 'This is the benefit of energy.' Thus, for one who sees the benefits, it arises. 'I must travel the path traveled by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Great Disciples, and that path cannot be traveled by a lazy person.' Thus, for one who reflects on the path to be traveled, it arises. 'These people who serve you with alms-food and so forth are not your relatives, nor are they your servants or employees. They do not give you excellent robes and so forth thinking they will live depending on you. Rather, they give expecting the great fruit of their own good deeds. Even the Teacher did not allow these requisites thinking, "This person will live happily with a strong body by using these requisites." Rather, he allowed them thinking, "This person will use these requisites, practice the recluse's duties (samaṇa-dhamma), and be liberated from the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha)." Now, if you live lazily, you do not honor that alms-food. Only for one with exerted energy is there the honoring of alms-food.' Thus, for one who reflects on honoring the alms-food, the energy enlightenment factor arises, as it did for Elder Ayyamitta.

The Elder, it is said, lived in Kassaka Cave. In his alms-resort village, a great female lay follower looked after the Elder, treating him like a son. One day, as she was about to go to the forest, she said to her daughter: 'Dear, in such a place there is old rice, in such a place ghee, in such a place milk, and in such a place molasses. When your brother, Elder Ayyamitta, arrives, cook the rice and give it to him together with the milk, ghee, and molasses. You should eat too. As for me, I have already eaten yesterday's leftover rice with sour gruel.' The daughter asked, 'Mother, what will you eat for lunch?' She replied, 'Put in some vegetable leaves and cook a sour rice-scum porridge with rice-bran, dear.'
381:
Knowing that “Today, the task of monkhood of my son has reached its pinnacle,” she said, “Mother, your brother delights in the Buddha’s Dispensation; he is not dissatisfied.”

Indeed, this inheritance of the Teacher, called the sevenfold Noble Wealth (ariya-dhana), is very great; it cannot be obtained by a lazy person. Just as parents might cast out a son who behaves wrongly, saying, “This is not our son,” and that son does not receive the inheritance upon their death, in the same way, a lazy person cannot obtain this inheritance of Noble Wealth; only one who has aroused energy (vīriya) can obtain it. Thus, energy arises in one who reflects on the greatness of the inheritance.

Your Teacher (the Buddha) is very great. When your Teacher took conception in his mother’s womb, when he went forth into the forest, when he attained Buddhahood, when he preached the Dhammacakka, when he performed the Twin Miracle (yamaka-pāṭihāriya), when he descended from the celestial realm, when he relinquished the life-principle (āyu-saṅkhāra-vossajjana), and when he attained Parinibbāna, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled. Is it proper for you to remain lazy after having gone forth in the Dispensation of such a Teacher? Thus, energy arises in one who reflects on the greatness of the Teacher.

By birth also, you are not of a low caste now; you are born in the Okkāka royal dynasty, descended from the unmixed lineage of Mahāsammata. You are the grandson of King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and the younger brother of Rāhula Bhadda. Being a Son of the Conqueror (Jinaputta) like yourself, it is not proper to live lazily. Thus, energy arises in one who reflects on the greatness of birth.

Sāriputta, Mahāmoggallāna, and the eighty great disciples realized the supramundane Dhamma only through energy. Do you follow the path of these fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī), or do you not? Thus, energy arises in one who reflects on the greatness of fellow practitioners.

Energy also arises in one who avoids lazy persons who are like pythons (ajagara) lying down after filling their bellies, whose physical and mental energy is slack; in one who associates with persons who have aroused energy and have a mind directed towards Nibbāna; and in one who has a mind inclined, leaning, and slanting towards the production of energy in postures such as standing and sitting. It is known that this energy, once arisen, reaches the fulfillment of development (bhāvanā) through the Path of Arahatship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of joy (pīti-sambojjhaṅga): “Monks, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy; frequently applying wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of joy, and for the increase, expansion, and fulfillment of development of the arisen enlightenment factor of joy.” Thus is its arising.
382:
Among those (bases for the enlightenment factor of joy), joy itself is called the basis for the enlightenment factor of joy. The attention that produces that joy is called wise attention (yoniso manasikāra).

Furthermore, eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of joy: recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati), recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of virtue (sīlānussati), recollection of generosity (cāgānussati), recollection of devas (devatānussati), recollection of peace (upasamānussati), avoiding coarse persons, associating with refined persons, reflecting on inspiring discourses (suttas), and inclination towards that [joy]. For one who repeatedly recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of joy arises, pervading the entire body up to access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). It also arises for one who recollects the qualities of the Dhamma and the Sangha; for one who reflects on the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhi-sīla) kept unbroken for a long time; for laypeople who reflect on the ten precepts or five precepts; for one who reflects on generosity, thinking, “We have given such excellent food to fellow practitioners during times of famine and danger”; for laypeople who reflect on the gifts given to virtuous ones at such times; for one who reflects on the existence within oneself of such qualities by which devas reached the state of devas; for one who reflects on the peace of mind, thinking, “The defilements removed by the attainments (samāpatti) have not arisen for sixty or seventy years”; for one who avoids coarse persons who are like dust on a donkey’s back because they lack the moisture of faith in the Buddha and others, as shown by their disrespectful behavior when seeing a stupa, a Bodhi tree, or an elder monk; for one who associates with refined persons who have a gentle mind and abundant faith in the Buddha and others; for one who reflects on inspiring discourses that explain the qualities of the Triple Gem; and for one who has a mind inclined, leaning, and slanting towards the production of joy in postures such as standing and sitting. It is known that this enlightenment factor of joy, once arisen, reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahatship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga): “Monks, there is tranquility of the body (kāya-passaddhi) and tranquility of the mind (citta-passaddhi); frequently applying wise attention to them is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of tranquility, and for the increase, expansion, and fulfillment of development of the arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility.” Thus is its arising.

Furthermore, seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility: using fine food, using comfortable weather, using a comfortable posture, balanced application of effort, avoiding persons with restless bodies, associating with persons with tranquil bodies, and inclination towards that [tranquility]. For one who eats fine, oily, and suitable food; for one who uses suitable weather and postures among cold and hot weather and postures such as standing...
383:
For one who associates thus, tranquility (passaddhi) also arises. However, this statement is not intended for a person of the Great Man type (mahāpurisa-jātika) who can endure all climates and postures. For one who has suitability (sabhāga) and unsuitability (visabhāga), tranquility arises only when they avoid unsuitable climates and postures and associate with suitable ones. Reflection on one's own kamma and the kamma of others (kammassakatā-paccavekkhaṇā) is called 'middle effort' (majjhatta-payoga). Through this middle effort, tranquility arises. It also arises for one who avoids a person of rough body and speech who habitually harms others with clods, sticks, etc.; for one who associates with a person of tranquil body who is restrained in hands and feet; and for one whose mind is inclined, sloped, and prone toward producing tranquility in postures such as standing and sitting. One understands that this arisen enlightenment factor of tranquility reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahantship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of concentration (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga), it is said: "Monks, there is the sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta) and the sign of non-distraction (abyagga-nimitta). Frequent wise attention therein is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of concentration, or for the growth, increase, expansion, and fulfillment of development of the arisen enlightenment factor of concentration." In this context, serenity itself is the sign of serenity; it is called the sign of non-distraction in the sense of non-wavering.

Furthermore, eleven factors lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of concentration: making the basis clean (vatthu-visadakiriyatā), balancing the faculties (indriya-samatta-paṭipādanatā), skill in the sign (nimitta-kusalatā), uplifting the mind at the proper time (samaye cittassa paggaṇhanatā), restraining the mind at the proper time (samaye cittassa niggaṇhanatā), gladdening the mind at the proper time (samaye sampahaṃsanatā), looking on with equanimity at the proper time (samaye ajjhupekkhanatā), avoiding unconcentrated persons (asamāhita-puggala-parivajjanatā), associating with concentrated persons (samāhita-puggala-sevanatā), reflecting on the jhānas and liberations (jhāna-vimokkha-paccavekkhaṇatā), and being resolute on that concentration (tadadhimuttatā). Among these, making the basis clean and balancing the faculties should be understood in the manner already stated.

Skill in the sign (nimitta-kusalatā) means skill in learning (noting) the sign of the kasiṇa. Uplifting the mind at the proper time means uplifting the mind by arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation of states (dhamma-vicaya), energy (vīriya), and joy (pīti) when the mind is sluggish due to overly lax energy, etc. Restraining the mind at the proper time means restraining the mind by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility (passaddhi), concentration (samādhi), and equanimity (upekkhā) when the mind is restless due to excessive energy, etc. Gladdening the mind at the proper time means that when the mind is listless due to weak application of wisdom or not attaining the bliss of peace, one gladdens it by reflecting on the eight grounds for urgency (saṃvega-vatthu)...
384:
...and stirs (the mind). The eight grounds for urgency (saṃvega-vatthu) are: the four of birth (jāti), aging (jarā), sickness (byādhi), and death (maraṇa); the suffering of the woeful planes as the fifth; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the past; the suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present. One also generates confidence by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem; this is called "gladdening the mind at the proper time."

Looking on with equanimity at the proper time (samaye ajjhupekkhanatā) means that when the mind, having attained right practice, is neither sluggish nor restless nor listless, but proceeds evenly on the object and has entered the path of serenity, one does not exert effort in uplifting, restraining, or gladdening it. It is like a charioteer with horses that are running evenly. This is called "looking on with equanimity at the proper time." Avoiding unconcentrated persons means avoiding from afar those persons whose minds are distracted and who have not attained access (upacāra) or absorption (appanā) concentration. Associating with concentrated persons means associating with, frequenting, and attending upon those whose minds are concentrated through access or absorption concentration. Being resolute on that concentration means having a mind that is inclined, sloped, and prone only toward the production of concentration in postures such as standing and sitting. For one practicing thus, this enlightenment factor of concentration arises. One understands that this arisen enlightenment factor of concentration reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahantship.

Regarding the enlightenment factor of equanimity (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga), it is said: "Monks, there are things that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Frequent wise attention therein is the nutriment for the arising of the unarisen enlightenment factor of equanimity, or for the growth, increase, expansion, and fulfillment of development of the arisen enlightenment factor of equanimity." In this context, equanimity itself is the basis for the enlightenment factor of equanimity.

Furthermore, five factors lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of equanimity: neutrality towards beings (satta-majjhattatā), neutrality towards formations (saṅkhāra-majjhattatā), avoiding persons who are possessive of beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra-kelāyana-puggala-parivajjanatā), associating with persons who are neutral towards beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra-majjhatta-puggala-sevanatā), and being resolute on that equanimity (tadadhimuttatā). Among these, one brings about neutrality towards beings in two ways: by reflecting on ownership of kamma (kammassakatā), "You have come by your own kamma and will go by your own kamma; this person too has come by their own kamma and will go by your own kamma; whom are you being possessive of?"; and by reflecting on the absence of a being (nissatta-paccavekkhaṇā), "In the ultimate sense, there is no being at all; such being the case, whom are you being possessive of?". One brings about neutrality towards formations also in two ways: "This robe will gradually reach discoloration and wear, become a foot-wiping rag, and be fit to be discarded with the tip of a stick; if it..."
385:
One should attend [to the requisites] by reflecting on the state of being ownerless: “There should be an owner; he would not let it perish like this,” and by reflecting on the temporary nature: “This thing is not lasting, it is only temporary.” As with the robe, so should it be applied to the bowl and other requisites.

Avoiding persons who cherish beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra-kelāyana-puggala) means: in this Dispensation, whether a layperson or a monk, one who is attached to and cherishes their own sons, daughters, etc., or their own pupils (antevāsika), fellow-disciples (saddhivihārika), etc., as “mine.” They themselves perform tasks for them such as cutting hair, sewing, washing and dyeing robes, and baking bowls. If they do not see them even for a moment, they look here and there like a frightened deer in the forest, asking, “Where is such-and-such a novice? Where is such-and-such a young monk?” Even when requested by another to “send such-and-such a person for a moment” for hair-cutting or other tasks, they refuse, saying, “We ourselves have not yet had him do our own work; if you take him, you will make him tired.” Such a person is called one who cherishes beings (satta-kelāyana).

One who cherishes robes, bowls, cups, walking sticks, etc., as “mine,” and does not allow another even to touch them with their hand, is called one who cherishes formations (saṅkhāra-kelāyana). When asked for a temporary loan, they say, “We ourselves cherish this so much we do not use it; how could we give it to you?” One who is neutral and indifferent towards both these types of things is called a person neutral towards beings and formations (satta-saṅkhāra-majjhatta-puggala). Thus, this Equanimity Enlightenment Factor (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga) arises for one who avoids from afar such persons who cherish beings and formations, for one who associates with persons who are neutral towards beings and formations, and for one whose mind is inclined, leaned, and sloped towards the arising of that equanimity enlightenment factor during standing, sitting, etc. One knows that this arisen equanimity enlightenment factor reaches the fulfillment of development through the Path of Arahantship.

“Thus, internally...” and so forth: one dwells contemplating mental objects in mental objects, having grasped one’s own seven enlightenment factors, or those of another, or at times one’s own and at times another’s enlightenment factors. Here, the arising and passing away should be understood by way of the occurrence and cessation of the enlightenment factors. From this point onwards, the method is as previously stated. Specifically, it should be understood that here, the mindfulness that grasps the enlightenment factors is the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); thus should the way of exit for the monk who grasps the enlightenment factors be understood. The rest of the sequence of words is the same.

## Conclusion of the Section on the Enlightenment Factors (Bojjhaṅgapabba).
387: Broken teeth are called khaṇḍita. The state of those with broken teeth is called khaṇḍicca. Hair and body hair that have gradually become white are called palita. One in whom grey hair has arisen is called palita, and the state of such a person is called pālitya. Due to the impact of the wind of old age, the flesh and blood dry up, resulting in wrinkles on the skin; this is called valittaca, and the state of such a person is called valittacatā. By these words, through the showing of transformation in the teeth, hair, body hair, and skin, evident old age (pākaṭa-jarā) has been shown. Indeed, just as the path taken by water, wind, or fire becomes evident through the breaking or burning of grass, trees, etc., and that path is not the water, wind, or fire itself, so too the path taken by old age becomes evident through the brokenness of teeth, etc. It can be seen even by opening the eyes. However, the brokenness of teeth, etc., is not old age itself. Old age is not a phenomenon cognizable by the eye. But because the life of one who has reached old age declines, old age is called "the decline of life" by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), attributing the effect to the cause. The faculties such as the eye, which in youth were very clear and capable of easily grasping even subtle objects, become mature, disturbed, and unclear upon reaching old age, unable to grasp even gross objects. Therefore, old age is also called "the maturation of the faculties" by way of metonymy. In the explanation of death (maraṇa), "that which" (yaṃ) is a neuter usage referring to death. The construction here is: that death which is called "decease" (cuti), which is called "falling away" (cavanatā). Therein, decease is a description of the nature. Falling away is a description of the mode or state. The aggregates of one who has reached death break up, disappear, and go to invisibility; therefore, that death is called "breaking up" (bheda) and "disappearance" (antaradhāna). "Death as the King of Death" (maccu-maraṇa) refers to death by the end of life, not "momentary death" (khaṇika-maraṇa). "Making an end of time" (kālakiriyā) is the act performed at the time of death. All of this is conventional talk (sammuti-kathā). However, "the breaking up of the aggregates" is ultimate talk (paramattha-kathā). In realms of one constituent (ekavokāra-bhava), etc., it is only the breaking up of one, four, or five aggregates, not of a person. But when that breaking up of aggregates occurs, there is the mere conventional expression, "The person has died." The laying down of the carcass means the laying down of the physical body (attabhāva). For the physical body of one who has reached death falls like a useless log. Therefore, that state is called "the laying down of the carcass." The cutting off of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) is, in every aspect and in the ultimate sense, what is called death (maraṇa).
388:
This (cessation of the life-faculty) is also called conventional death (sammuti-maraṇa). Worldly people, based on the cessation of the life-faculty, say, "Tissa is dead, Phussa is dead."

'Vyasanena' means by any kind of ruin, such as the ruin of relatives and so on. 'Dukkhadhammena' means by a cause of suffering, such as killing, imprisonment, and so on. 'Phuṭṭhassa' means for one who is affected or overwhelmed. 'Soka' (sorrow) is the nature of sorrowing that arises in one who is overwhelmed by any cause, such as the ruin of relatives or killing and imprisonment. 'Socitattaṃ' is the state of sorrowing. Because this sorrow arises by drying up and parching the internal [being], it is called 'internal sorrow' and 'internal intense sorrowing.'

'Ādeva' is the act of wailing by repeatedly referring [to the lost] as "my daughter, my son," and so on; it is wailing by means of this [sorrow]. 'Parideva' (lamentation) is wailing by proclaiming various virtues; it is wailing by means of this [sorrow]. The next two terms (paridevitattaṃ, etc.) are terms indicating the state of that very lamentation.

'Kāyikaṃ' means having the sensitive body-matter (kāyapasāda) as its physical basis. It is called 'dukkha' (pain) because of its disagreeable meaning. 'Asātaṃ' means unpleasant (disagreeable). 'Kāyasamphassajaṃ dukkhaṃ' is the pain born of bodily contact. 'Asātaṃ vedayitaṃ' is the unpleasant feeling.

'Cetasikaṃ' means associated with the mind. The remaining words are to be understood in the same manner as explained under the term 'dukkha'.

'Āyāsa' is the mental exhaustion of a mind that has reached a state of despondency and dejection. Intense 'āyāsa' is called 'upāyāsa' (despair). The next two terms are terms showing the state of itself.

'Jātidhammānaṃ' means of those who have the nature of being born. 'Icchā uppajjati' means craving (taṇhā) arises. "O, would that..." is a wish. This non-coming (cessation) of birth cannot be attained by mere wish without the development of the Path. In the word 'idampi', the particle 'pi' is used in consideration of the remaining states mentioned above. 'Yampicchaṃ' means not obtaining a thing that cannot be obtained through a certain state, even though one desires it; the desiring of that unobtainable thing is suffering. This method applies in all cases.
389:
In the exposition of the aggregates (khandha-niddesa), it is called 'rūpupādānakkhandha' (the material aggregate as an object of clinging) because it is both matter (rūpa) and an aggregate as an object of clinging (upādānakkhandha). In this way, it should be understood in all cases.

## Exposition of the Truth of the Origin (Samudaya-sacca-niddesa)

'Yāyaṃ taṇhā' means this very craving. 'Ponobbhavikā' is called 'punobbhava' because it creates a new existence again; it is called 'ponobbhavikā' because it has the nature of creating that new existence again. It is called 'nandīrāgasahagatā' because it arises together with delight (nandī) and lust (rāga). In terms of meaning, it means it has become one with delight and lust. 'Tatratatrābhinandinī' means greatly delighting in this or that state of existence (attabhāva). Or it means greatly delighting in this or that object among the objects such as visible forms; it means delighting in visible forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. 'Seyyathidaṃ' is an indeclinable. It has the meaning of "what is that [craving]?" Craving for sensual pleasures is 'kāma-taṇhā'; this is the name for lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure. Craving for existence is 'bhava-taṇhā'; this is a designation for the lust for fine-material and immaterial existence associated with the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) which arises by way of wishing for existence, and for the attachment to meditative absorption (jhāna). Craving for non-existence (vibhava) is 'vibhava-taṇhā'; this is a designation for the lust associated with the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi).

Now, to show the basis of that craving in detail, [the Buddha] said 'sā kho panesā', and so on. Therein, 'uppajjati' means it arises. 'Nivisati' means it establishes itself by way of occurring repeatedly. 'Yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ' means that which in the world is of a dear nature and of an agreeable nature. In the phrases 'cakkhu loke' (the eye in the world) and so on, beings who are obsessed with the notion of "mine" regarding the eye and so on in the world, while established in prosperity, regard their own eye—the clear fivefold sensitivity (pasāda) according to the grasping of the sign in mirrors and so on—as if it were a jeweled lion-window opened in a golden mansion. They regard the ear as if it were a silver tube or a gold thread. They regard the nose, which is called "prominent nose" (tuṅganāsā), as if it were a rounded rod of orpiment. They regard the tongue as if it were a layer of red blanket, soft, smooth, and having an agreeable sound. They regard the body as if it were a young sal tree or a golden archway. They regard the mind as noble and unlike the minds of others. They regard visible forms as if they were the color of golden kaṇikāra flowers; sounds as if they were the warbling of the intoxicated Karavika bird or the cuckoo, or the sound of a jeweled flute softly blown. They regard the objects of smell and so on, born of the four causes, which they have obtained, thinking, "Who else has such things as these?" To those who regard them thus, those eyes and so on become of a dear nature and of an agreeable nature. Then, the craving that has not yet arisen in them for those objects...
390:
Craving arises; and craving that has arisen tends to cling and persist by way of repeated occurrence. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "The eye in the world is pleasant and agreeable; here this craving, when arising, arises," and so forth. In that text, "uppajjamānā" means that when it arises, it arises in this object (such as the eye). This method is the same in all instances.

## Explanation of the Description of the Truth of Cessation

All terms such as "fading away and cessation without remainder" (asesa-virāga-nirodha) are merely synonyms for Nibbāna. Because craving is completely faded away and ceases depending on Nibbāna, that Nibbāna is called "the fading away and cessation of that very craving without remainder." And because craving is given up, relinquished, released, and no longer clung to depending on Nibbāna, Nibbāna is called "giving up (cāga), relinquishment (paṭinissagga), release (mutti), and non-attachment (anālaya)." Indeed, Nibbāna is only one, but its names are many by way of being the opposite of the names of all conditioned things (saṅkhata). They are as follows: complete fading away, complete cessation, giving up, relinquishment, release, non-attachment, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion, the destruction of craving, non-arising, non-occurrence, the signless, the desireless, the non-exertion, the non-rebirth, the non-reappearance, the destinationless, the unborn, the undecaying, the unailing, the deathless, the sorrowless, the lamentationless, the despairless, and the undefiled.

Now, to show that craving no longer exists in those very objects where its arising was previously shown—because it has been cut off by the Path and has reached non-occurrence depending on Nibbāna—the Blessed One said, "sā kho panesā," and so forth. In that text, for example: a man, seeing a bitter gourd creeper (titta-alābu-valli) growing in a field, searches for the root starting from the tip and cuts it; that creeper gradually withers and reaches a state where even its designation no longer exists. Then it is said that the bitter gourd in that field has ceased and been abandoned. In the same way, craving exists in objects such as the eye, like the bitter gourd in the field. When that craving is cut off at the root by the Noble Path, it reaches non-occurrence depending on Nibbāna. When it has thus reached non-occurrence, craving is no longer perceived in those objects such as the eye, just like the bitter gourd in the field.

Furthermore, as an analogy: if thieves are brought from the forest and executed at the south gate of the city, it is then said that the thieves in the forest are dead or have been killed. In the same way, craving exists in objects such as the eye, like the thieves in the forest. Because that craving has ceased depending on Nibbāna, like the thieves at the south gate, it is said to have ceased in Nibbāna. When it has thus ceased, craving is no longer perceived in those objects such as the eye, like the thieves in the forest; therefore, the cessation of craving in those very objects...
391:
Desiring to show (the places where craving ceases), the Blessed One said: "The eye in the world is pleasant and agreeable; here this craving, when being abandoned, is abandoned; here, when ceasing, it ceases," and so forth.

## Explanation of the Description of the Truth of the Path

The word "ayameva" (this very) is a restriction for the purpose of excluding any other path. "Ariyo" (Noble) is so called because it is far from the defilements (kilesa) that are to be killed by each respective path, and because it makes one a Noble One (ariya). By the words "knowledge of suffering" (dukkhe ñāṇaṃ) and so forth, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of the Four Truths is shown. Among those Four Truths, the first two truths are the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa), and the last two truths are the escape from the round (vivaṭṭa). Among those truths, for a monk, there is persistent application of the meditation subject in the round; there is no persistent application in the escape from the round. For a practitioner performs the work of meditation by learning the first two truths from a teacher—both in brief as "the five aggregates are suffering, craving is the origin" and in detail by the method of "what are the five aggregates? they are the aggregate of form," and so forth—and by reciting them repeatedly with the voice. But regarding the other two truths, he performs the work of meditation through hearing, thus: "the truth of cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; the truth of the path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing."

One who thus strives penetrates the Four Truths only by a single penetration (ekapaṭivedha); he realizes them by a single realization (ekābhisamaya). He penetrates the truth of suffering by penetration of full understanding (pariññā-paṭivedha); the truth of origin by penetration of abandoning (pahāna-paṭivedha); the truth of cessation by penetration of realization (sacchikiriyā-paṭivedha); and the truth of the path by penetration of development (bhāvanā-paṭivedha). He realizes the truth of suffering by the realization of full understanding... and the truth of the path by the realization of development. Thus, for him, in the preceding stage, there is learning, questioning, hearing, memorizing, reflecting, and penetrating regarding the [first] two truths; but regarding the [latter] two truths, there is only penetration through hearing. In the subsequent stage, there is penetration by way of function (kicca) regarding three truths; but regarding the truth of cessation, there is penetration by way of object (ārammaṇa). Reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā), however, occurs for the Noble One who has reached the truths. Since this person is a beginner (ādikammika), that reviewing is not mentioned here.

For this monk, while previously grasping (the meditation subject), there were no such things as advertence (ābhoga), coordination (samannāhāra), attention (manasikāra), or reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) in the sense of "I fully understand suffering, I abandon the origin, I realize cessation, I develop the path"; these occur from the time of grasping onwards. In the subsequent stage, however, suffering is indeed fully understood... the path is indeed developed. Among those truths, two truths are deep because they are hard to see, and two are hard to see because they are deep. For the truth of suffering is manifest due to its occurrence; it even reaches the state of being spoken of as "Oh, what suffering!" when struck by a stump or a thorn, etc. The truth of origin is also manifest due to its occurrence by way of the desire to eat, the desire to consume, and so forth. But in terms of the penetration of their characteristics, both are deep. Thus, they are deep because they are hard to see. The exertion to see the remaining two truths is like trying to grasp the peak of existence...
392:
It is like extending a hand, or like extending a foot to touch the Avīci hell, or like making the tip of a hair, split into a hundred parts, touch another hair-tip. Thus, these Truths are difficult to see because of their depth. Because they are difficult to see, they are deep; and because they are deep, they are difficult to see. With reference to the arising of preliminary knowledge (pubbabhāga-ñāṇa) through learning and so forth regarding the Four Noble Truths, it is said: "This is the knowledge of suffering," and so on. However, at the moment of penetration (paṭivedha), that knowledge is only one.

Right Intention (Sammā-saṅkappa) and others are various and distinct in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions of abstaining from sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty. But at the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa), a single wholesome intention arises, fulfilling the path factor by way of achieving the non-arising of unwholesome intentions through the cutting off of their basis in these three instances. This is called Right Intention.

Abstinence from false speech and so forth are also various and distinct in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions of abstaining from false speech and so forth. But at the moment of the Path, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the path factor by way of achieving the non-arising of unwholesome immoral volition through the cutting off of its basis in these four instances. This is called Right Speech (Sammā-vācā).

Abstinence from taking life and so forth are also various and distinct in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions of abstaining from taking life and so forth. But at the moment of the Path, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the path factor by way of achieving the non-arising of unwholesome immoral volition through non-action and the cutting off of its basis in these three instances. This is called Right Action (Sammā-kammanta).

"Wrong livelihood" (micchā-ājīva) refers to bodily and verbal misconduct performed for the sake of food, snacks, and so forth. "Having abandoned" (pahāya) means having avoided. "By Right Livelihood" (sammā-ājīvena) means by a livelihood praised by the Buddha. "Leads one's life" (jīvitaṃ kappeti) means one carries on the continuity of life. Right livelihood is also various and distinct in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of perceptions of abstaining from scheming (kuhana) and so forth. But at the moment of the Path, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the path factor by way of achieving the non-arising of unwholesome immoral volition of wrong livelihood through the cutting off of its basis in these seven instances. This is called Right Livelihood (Sammā-ājīva).

"Of unrisen" (anuppannānaṃ) refers to those states that have not yet arisen in oneself in a particular life or towards such an object. Seeing them arising in others, one thinks, "Oh, may such evil unwholesome states not arise in me!" Thus, of those evil unwholesome states that have not yet arisen...
394:
The seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) become six (in the fourth jhāna). This method applies from emerging from the fourth jhāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana). In the formless realm (arūpa), jhāna arises by way of the fourfold and fivefold methods; that jhāna is said to be only supramundane (lokuttara) and not mundane (lokiya). How is this so? Here also, for one who has emerged from the first jhāna and so forth, attained the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), developed the formless attainments, and is reborn in that formless realm, the three higher paths arise in that realm for that meditator. Thus, it is only the basic jhāna (pādakajjhāna) that is determined. 

Some elders, however, say, 'The aggregates which are the objects of insight (vipassanā) determine it.' Some say, 'The inclination of the individual determines it.' Some say, 'Insight leading to emergence (vuṭṭhānagāminī-vipassanā) determines it.' The decision on their doctrines should be understood according to the method stated in the section on insight leading to emergence in the Visuddhimagga. 

'Monks, this is called Right Concentration (sammā-samādhi)'—this statement refers to Right Concentration which is mundane in the preliminary stage and supramundane in the later stage. 

'Thus, internally' means having thus grasped the Four Noble Truths of oneself, or of another, or at times of oneself and at times of another, one dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena repeatedly. Here, the arising and vanishing (samudaya and vaya) should be understood by way of the occurrence and cessation of the Four Noble Truths as they correspond. From this point onwards, the method is exactly as previously stated. Indeed, here, the mindfulness that grasps the Four Noble Truths as 'this is the truth of suffering' and so forth should be understood as the door of exit (to Nibbāna) for the monk who grasps the truths; the rest is just the same as what has been said. 

## The Section on the Four Truths is Finished. 

By this much, there are twenty-one meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna): the section on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna), the section on the four postures, the section on the fourfold clear comprehension, the thirty-two parts of the body, the definition of the four elements, the nine cemetery contemplations, the contemplation of feeling, the contemplation of mind, the grasping of the hindrances, the grasping of the aggregates, the grasping of the sense bases, the grasping of the factors of enlightenment, and the grasping of the truths. Among these meditation subjects, mindfulness of breathing, the thirty-two parts of the body, and the nine cemetery contemplations are the eleven subjects of absorption (appanā-kammaṭṭhāna). However, the Elder Mahāsīva, a reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, said, 'The nine cemetery contemplations are stated by way of the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā).' Therefore, according to his view, there are only two subjects of absorption, and the remaining are subjects of access concentration (upacāra-kammaṭṭhāna).
395:
Does clinging (abhinivesa) arise (in all these meditation subjects)? It does not. It is said that clinging does not arise in the postures, clear comprehension, hindrances, and factors of enlightenment, but it arises in the remaining ones. However, the Elder Mahāsīva said, 'Clinging arises even in these. For this person grasps them thus: "Do I have the four postures or not? Do I have the fourfold clear comprehension or not? Do I have the five hindrances or not? Do I have the seven factors of enlightenment or not?" Therefore, clinging arises in all subjects.' 

'Whoever, monks' means anyone—whether a monk, a nun, a layman (upāsaka), or a laywoman (upāsikā). 'Should develop thus' means should develop according to the sequence of meditation stated from the beginning. 'To be expected (pāṭikaṅkhā)' means that which should be expected, desired, or is inevitable. 'Final knowledge (aññā)' means the fruit of Arahatship. 'If there is a residue of clinging (upādisese)' means if the remainder of grasping (upādānasessa) is not yet exhausted. 'State of non-returning (anāgāmitā)' means the state of an Anāgāmī. 

Having thus shown the liberating nature of the Dispensation by way of seven years, the Buddha, wishing to show an even shorter period, said, 'Let alone seven years, monks,' and so forth. All this is said by way of a person to be guided (veneyya) of middle wisdom; but concerning one of sharp wisdom, it is said, 'Instructed in the morning, he will attain distinction in the evening; instructed in the evening, he will attain distinction in the morning.' 

Thus, the Blessed One, having shown, 'Monks, my Dispensation is thus liberating,' and concluding the teaching which was delivered with the fruit of Arahatship as its pinnacle in twenty-one places, said, 'Monks, this path is the only way... etc... thus, what was said, was said in reference to this.' The rest has a clear meaning. At the conclusion of the teaching, thirty thousand monks were established in Arahatship. 

## The Commentary on the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta is Finished.
396:
## 10. Commentary on the Pāyāsi Rājañña Sutta

"Thus have I heard" refers to the Pāyāsi Rājañña Sutta. In this sutta, this is the explanation of terms not previously mentioned—"Āyasmā" is a term of endearment. "Kumārakassapa" is the name of that Elder. Because he ordained while still a youth, when the Blessed One said, "Call Kassapa; give this fruit or food to Kassapa," and was asked, "To which Kassapa should it be given?", he replied, "Give it to Kumārakassapa." Having received the name in this way, he was called "Kumārakassapa" even when he grew up. Furthermore, because he was the foster son of the King, he was known as Kumārakassapa.

This is the account clarifying his past practice: The Elder was the son of a wealthy merchant during the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara. One day, seeing the Blessed One appoint one of his disciples, who was an eloquent speaker (citrakathī), to the foremost position (etadagga), he gave alms to the Blessed One for seven days and made a wish: "Venerable Sir, may I also become an eloquent disciple like this Elder under a future Buddha." Having performed meritorious deeds, he ordained during the Teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa but was unable to attain any special distinction. At that time, when the Teaching of the Blessed One Kassapa was declining after his Parinibbāna, five monks built a ladder, climbed a mountain, and practiced the ascetic life. The senior Elder attained Arahantship on the third day; the next Elder became a Non-returner on the fourth day; the remaining three monks, unable to attain any special distinction, were reborn in the celestial realm.

Among those who enjoyed prosperity in the celestial and human realms for the duration of one Buddha-interval (buddhantara), one was reborn in a royal family in Takkasilā and became a king named Pukkusāti. Having ordained dedicated to the Blessed One and while traveling toward Rājagaha, he heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One in a potter's shed and attained the fruit of Non-returning. One was reborn in a family at a seaport. While traveling by ship, the ship was wrecked; he wore bark clothes and, having gained gain and honor, thought, "I am an Arahant." When a deity who wished for his welfare urged him, "You are not an Arahant; go, approach the Teacher and ask him a question," he did so and attained the fruit of Arahantship.

One was conceived in the womb of a young woman in Rājagaha. That woman first asked her parents for permission to ordain, but not receiving it, she went to her husband's house and [became] pregnant...
397:
That woman, unaware that she was pregnant, pleased her husband and, with his permission, was ordained among the bhikkhunīs. Seeing signs of her pregnancy, the bhikkhunīs questioned Devadatta, who said, "She is not a nun." When they questioned the Blessed One, the Blessed One assigned the Elder Upāli to settle the matter. The Elder summoned the lay devotees living in Sāvatthī and the female lay devotee Visākhā; upon investigating, he said, "The pregnancy was conceived previously (while still a layperson); her status as a nun is blameless." The Blessed One gave his approval (Sādhu) to the Elder, saying, "The legal issue has been well-decided."

That bhikkhunī gave birth to a son who resembled a golden image. King Pasenadi of Kosala took the young boy and had him raised. He named the boy "Kassapa," and later, having adorned him, brought him to the Blessed One and had him ordained. Thus, because he was the king's foster son, the Elder came to be known as "Kumārakassapa." One day, while the Elder was practicing the Dhamma of a recluse in the Andhavana forest, a deity who desired his welfare taught him some questions and said, "Ask these questions to the Blessed One." The Elder asked the questions, and at the conclusion of the answers, he attained the fruit of Arahantship. The Blessed One also placed that Elder in the foremost position among the monks who are eloquent speakers (citrakathika).

'Setabyā' is the name of that city. 'To the north of Setabyā' means in the northern direction from the city of Setabyā. 'Rājañña' refers to a king who has not yet been consecrated. 'Diṭṭhigata' is simply a view (wrong view). Just as when one says 'consisting of excrement' or 'consisting of urine,' there is nothing other than excrement, etc., so too, the view itself is called 'diṭṭhigata'. 'Neither is it thus' means, by pointing to various reasons, it is said that it does not exist for such and such a reason. 'Previously... makes known' means until it is made known in detail (before I have prescribed it).

## Candimasūriyūpamavaṇṇanā

In the words, "Friend Kassapa, these moons and suns," the reason should be understood as follows. When questioned by the Elder, King Pāyāsi thought thus: "This recluse has first brought up the moon and sun as a simile; he must be like the moon and sun in wisdom, and cannot be overcome by others. If I say, 'The moon and sun are in this world,' he will entangle me with questions such as, 'What do those moon and sun depend on? What is their size? How high are they?' and so on. I will not be able to unravel those entangling questions. I will just tell this recluse that they are in the next world." Therefore, he spoke in this way.
398:
When Venerable Kumārakassapa asked using the simile of the moon and sun, King Pāyāsi thought: “This recluse has first asked using the simile of the moon and sun; he must be someone who cannot be suppressed by wisdom, just like the moon and sun. If I say that the moon and sun are in this world, he will entangle me with questions such as what they depend on, how large they are, and how high they are. I will not be able to solve those problems. Therefore, I will only tell this recluse that the moon and sun are in the next world (paraloka).” Thinking thus, he spoke in that manner.

Not long before this conversation between Venerable Kumārakassapa and King Pāyāsi, the Blessed One had preached the Sudhābhojanīya Jātaka. In that Jātaka, it is mentioned: “In the moon mansion, there is Canda, the son of the gods; in the sun mansion, there is Suriya, the son of the gods.” Since the Jātakas or Suttas preached by the Blessed One were spread throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa, King Pāyāsi thought that he could no longer say, “There are no sons of the gods living in these mansions,” and thus he said, “Those moons and suns are only gods; they are not humans.”

“Rājañña, is there another method (pariyāya)?” means asking if there is a reason for the existence of the view. “Ābādhikā” means being possessed of an affliction known as disagreeable sensation. “Dukkhitā” means having reached suffering. “Bāḷhagilānā” means being excessively ill. “Saddhāyikā” means “I trust you; may you be ones whose words are trustworthy to me.” “Paccayikā” means “I rely on you; may you be ones who are reliable to me.”

## Commentary on the Simile of the Robber and Others

“Uddisitvā” means showing and entrusting oneself and one's stored property to those relatives. “Vippalapantassa” means lamenting in various ways such as “My son, my daughter, my wealth.” “Nirayapālesu” refers to the beings who perform the torture in hell. Those who say, “Only kamma performs the torture; there are no hell-wardens,” contradict the Devadūta Sutta which states, “Monks, the hell-wardens [torture] him...” Just as there are executioners in the royal courts of the human world, there are hell-wardens in hell.

“Veḷupesikāhi” means with bamboo splints or bamboo strips. “Sunimmajjatha” means to cleanse or remove thoroughly so that it becomes well-purified.

“Asuci” means being unpleasant. “Asuci-saṅkhāto” means being known as a mass of impurity (excrement). “Duggaṇdho” means smelling like a rotting carcass. “Jeguccho” means being associated with loathsomeness. “Paṭikūlo” means bringing about resentment just by the sight of it. “Ubbādhatī” means that even the smell of humans such as a Cakkavatti king—who bathes twice a day, changes clothes three times, and is adorned with noble ornaments—oppresses the deities who are a hundred yojanas away, just as if a rotting carcass were hung around their necks.
399:
Again, he speaks by way of those who undertake and practice the five precepts such as abstaining from taking life.

416. Regarding the words "Tāvatiṃsānaṃ": He says, "Let those (such as the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas) born in distant realms not come yet; why do these Tāvatiṃsa devas not come?"

418. "Jaccandhūpamo maññe paṭibhāsī" means it appeared like one born blind. "Araññavanapatthāni": They are called *arañña* (forests) because they possess the factors of a forest dwelling, and *vanapattha* (jungle thickets) because of being large forest groves. "Pantāni" means distant places.

419. "Kalyāṇadhamme" refers to those who have a good nature through that very virtue. "Dukkhapaṭikūle" refers to those who do not desire suffering. "Seyyo bhavissati" means that there will be the happiness of a good destination in the next world.

420. "Upavijaññā" means one whose time for giving birth is near, who is heavily pregnant, and will give birth soon. "Opabhoggā bhavissati" means she will be an attendant at the feet. "Anayavyasana" means reaching great misery. "Aya" means happiness; "na aya" is "anaya" (suffering). Because that suffering destroys happiness in every way, it is called "vyasana." Thus, because *anaya* itself is *vyasana*, it is called "anayavyasana" (reaching great misery). "Ayoniso" means by improper means. "Apakkaṃ na paripācenti" means they do not prematurely cut off a life that is not yet mature or exhausted. "Paripākaṃ āgamenti" means they wait for the time of life's maturity. The General of the Dhamma also said:

"I do not delight in death,
I do not delight in life;
I await the time (of passing away),
As a laborer awaits his wages."

421. "Ubbindhitvā" means removing or destroying the coating of fine clay.

422. "Rāmaṇeyyakaṃ" means the state of being delightful. "Velāsikā" refers to playful and frolicsome women. "Komārikā" refers to young girls. "Tuyhaṃ jīvaṃ" is asking whether one sees the "life" (soul) leaving or entering at the time of dreaming. Here, the process of the mind is taken as "jīva" (life/soul). This is because King Pāyāsi perceived that mind as the soul.

423. "Jiyāya" means wrapping the neck with a bowstring. "Patthinnataro" means very stiff and hard. What is shown by this? You say that while alive, a being has five aggregates. But at the time of death, only the form aggregate (*rūpakkhandha*) remains; the three mental aggregates do not arise, and the consciousness aggregate (*viññāṇakkhandha*) departs. Although the remaining form aggregate should be lighter, it becomes heavier. Therefore, it is intended to show that there is no one who goes anywhere.

424. "Nibbutaṃ" means having the heat or power extinguished.

425. "Anupahacca" means without destroying. "Āmato hoti" means half-dead, or in the process of dying. "Odhunātha" means turn it to this side. "Sandhunātha" means turn it to that side. "Niddhunātha" means turn it back and forth. "Tañcāyatanaṃ na paဋisaṃvedeti" means being unable to make that form clear with that eye. This method should be understood in all sections. The rest...
400:
You say that while alive, a being has five aggregates. But at the time of death, only the form aggregate remains; the three mental aggregates do not arise, and the consciousness aggregate departs. Although the remaining form aggregate should be very light, it is actually very heavy. Therefore, it shows the meaning that there is no one who goes anywhere.

"Nibbutaṃ" means having the heat of the fire extinguished.

"Anupahacca" means without destroying. "Āmato hoti" means being half-dead and in the process of dying. "Odhunātha" means turn it to this side. "Sandhunātha" means turn it to that side. "Niddhunātha" means turn it back and forth. "Does not experience that base (āyatana)" means being unable to make that form clear with that eye. This method is the same in all places.

"Saṅkhadhama" means a conch-blower. "Upalāpetvā" means by blowing.

"Aggika" means one who tends the fire. "Āpādeyyaṃ" means I would produce, or I would bring to life. "Poseyyaṃ" means I would nourish with food and so on. "Vaḍဎeyyaṃ" means I would cause to grow. "Araṇīsahitaṃ" means the set of fire-sticks (drill and block).

"Tirorājāno pi" means kings in other countries and provinces also know. "Abyatto" means an unclear or unskilled person. "Kopena pi" means even with the anger that arises toward those who will speak to me thus, I will wander holding onto this wrong view. "Makkhena pi" means also with *makkha* (contempt), which has the characteristic of erasing the proper reasons spoken by you. "Palāsena pi" means also with *palāsa* (domineering), which has the characteristic of competing for superiority with you.

"Haritakapaṇṇaṃ" means any green leaf; it means there is not even a blade of green grass. "Sannaddhakalāpaṃ" means one who has a bound quiver of arrows. "Āsittodakāni vaဋumāni" means roads and ravines overflowing with water. "Yoggāni" means oxen.

"Bahunikkhantaro" means having gone out much, or having gone out for a long time. "Yathābatena bhaṇᎎena" means with the goods such as grass, wood, and water that you have loaded, just as they were brought, just as they were loaded, just as they were taken.

"Appasārāni" means things of little value. "Paṇiyāni" means merchandise or goods.
401:
## Explanation of the Simile of the Dung-carrier, etc.

"Mama ca sūkarabhattaṃ" means this dried dung which is food for me and for the pigs. "Uggharantaṃ" refers to overflowing upwards (leaking upwards). "Paggharantaṃ" refers to leaking downwards. In the phrase "Tumhe khetta bhaṇe", it should be analyzed as "Tumhe kho ettha bhaṇe", or this is simply the reading. "Tathā hi pana me sūkarabhattaṃ" means for that very reason, this dung is food for me and for the pigs.

434. "Āgatāgataṃ kaliṃ gilati" means he swallows the losing die whenever it comes. "Pajjohissāmi" means I will make an offering, I will give a sacrificial offering (bali). "Akkhehi dibbissāma" means we will play with dice. "Littaṃ paramena tejasā" means smeared with poison of supreme power.
