436. "Gāmapaṭṭaṃ" refers to an old village site abandoned by people. There is also a reading "Gāmapada", and the meaning is the same. "Sāṇabhāraṃ" means a load of hemp. "Susannaddho" means well-bound. "Tvaṃ pajānāhi" means you should know. It means "If you wish to take it, take it."

"Khomaṃ" refers to linen cloth from the Khoma country. "Ayaṃ" refers to iron. "Lohaṃ" refers to copper. "Sajjhaṃ" refers to silver. "Suvaṇṇaṃ" refers to a gold coin (suvaṇṇamāsaka). "Abhinandisu" means they rejoiced and were delighted.

437. "Attamano" means having one's own mind [satisfied], thus having a delighted mind. "Abhiraddho" means extremely devoted. "Pañhāpaṭibhānāni" refers to problems (questions) that occur to the intellect. "Paccanīkaṃ kattabbaṃ" means he thought it should be done as an opposition; he stood holding a contrary view.

438. "Saṅghātaṃ āpajjanti" means they meet with destruction or death. "Na mahapphalo" means not of great fruit in terms of the resulting effect (vipāka). "Na mahānisaṃso" means not of great benefit in terms of spiritual quality (guṇa). "Na mahājutiko" means not of great splendor in terms of the radiance of power. "Na mahāvipphāro" means not of great pervasiveness in terms of the spread of the result. "Bījanaṅgalaṃ" means the seed and the plough. "Dukkhette" means in a bad field, a field without essence. "Dubbhūme" means in an uneven ground area. "Patiṭṭhāpeyya" means if one were to place or plant. "Khaṇḍāni" means those that are severed or broken. "Pūtīni" means those without essence.
402:
"Vātātapahatāni" refers to seeds destroyed by the wind and the sun, whose potency to sprout is exhausted. "Asārādāni" refers to straw that is mere chaff, devoid of the essence of grain. "Asukhasayitāni" refers to seeds that are dried and stored in a granary; such seeds are called 'sukhasayita' (well-stored seeds). These seeds, however, are not like those. "Anuppaveccheyya" means should not enter (should not rain). It means it should not rain well; it should not rain once a fortnight, once every ten days, or once every five days. "Api nu tāni" is a question (by Ven. Kumāra Kassapa): "If there are such defects in the field, seed, and rain, can those seeds reach growth upwards in terms of sprouts, roots, and leaves, prosperity downwards, and abundance all around?" "Evarūpo kho rājañña yañño" means: "Prince Rājañña, such a sacrifice is not of great fruit because it is impure due to the sacrificial items obtained by oppressing others, as well as due to the donor and the recipient."

"Evarūpo kho rājañña yañño" means: "Prince Rājañña, such a sacrifice is of great fruit because of the sacrificial items obtained without oppressing others, the virtuous donor who does not oppress others, and the recipient endowed with qualities such as right view. It should be known that if one obtains a recipient who is exceptionally virtuous, such as one emerging from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), and if the intention (cetanā) is abundant due to being full of faith, it gives results even in the present life."

After hearing this Dhamma talk by Ven. Kumāra Kassapa, Prince Pāyāsi invited the Elder, gave a great alms-giving for seven days, and from then on established alms-giving for the public. Referring to that alms-giving, the words "Atha kho pāyāsi rājañño" etc. are said. In that text, "Kaṇājaka" means broken rice with bran, or raw rice. "Bilaṅgadutiya" is rice with sour gruel as the second [dish]. "Dhorakāni ca vatthāni" refers to coarse clothes. "Guḷavālakāni" means clothes with tangled fringes, or large fringes existing in clusters. "Evaṃ anuddisati" means thus he speaks (directs). "Pādāpi" means even with the foot.

"Asakkaccaṃ" refers to an offering lacking faith, given without respect. "Asahatthā" means not with one's own hand, but giving by ordering others. "Acittīkataṃ" means lacking attention; it was given without establishing a respectful manner or a noble mind. "Apaviddhaṃ" means giving carelessly, as if throwing it away. "Suññaṃ serīsakaṃ" means he reached an empty silver mansion named Serīsaka. It is said there was a large Sirīsa tree (Albizia lebbeck) at the gate of that silver mansion; therefore, that mansion is called "Serīsaka".
403:
The Elder Gavampati, it is said, was formerly the leader of cowherd boys in his human life. Having cleared the base of a large Sirīsa tree and scattered sand, he invited a monk who practiced the dhutanga of alms-gathering to sit at the foot of that tree and offered him the food he had obtained. After passing away from that life, he was reborn in a silver celestial mansion (rajata-vimāna) by the power of that merit. A Sirīsa tree stood at the entrance of the mansion. That tree would bear fruit once every fifty years, and whenever those fifty years passed, that deva would experience spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Later, during the time of our Blessed One, he was reborn among humans and, after hearing the Teacher's Dhamma, attained Arahatship. However, due to his former habit, he frequently went to that same mansion for his daytime rest (divāvihāra), as it was said to have a pleasant climate for him. With reference to this frequenting, it is said: "At that time, the Venerable Gavampati..." and so on.

"He gave the gift respectfully" means that the youth [Uttara] gave the gift respectfully even though the gift-objects belonged to another. "He informed thus" means he informed them in such a way as, "Give the gift respectfully," and so forth. Having heard the Elder's exhortation, many people gave gifts respectfully and were reborn in the celestial realm. However, the attendants of Prince Pāyāsi, although they gave gifts respectfully, were reborn in the vicinity of Prince Pāyāsi himself because of their attachment (nikanti) to him (or to that realm). That mansion was a wandering mansion (disācārika-vimāna) and was located in the Vaṭṭani forest. One day, the deva Pāyāsi appeared to some merchants and told them about the deeds he had performed.
